The Same Night,
Seven Ways
a novel
Compline · 1994 · 2024

One night, one house, and seven witnesses.

Every account is true.

A Note on the Time

There were sixteen people on Compline Ness on the night of Saturday the twenty-second of October, 1994, and by the following Monday there were fifteen. Seven of those who were there have left an account of it. This book is those seven accounts, in the order in which I think they should be read, which is not the order in which they were written and not the order in which I found them.

I should say at the beginning what you are going to notice in any case. The accounts do not agree.

They do not agree about small things, such as what was served after the goose, and they do not agree about large ones, such as whether a man was dead. One witness finds a body at a quarter past one. Another wheels the same man across a stable yard twenty minutes later and complains of the weight and the snoring. A third watches him fall forty feet from a clock tower on the stroke of one. A fourth speaks to him in a scullery passage at twenty past two and is spoken to in return. A fifth shot him. A sixth killed him before midnight with a piece of lead, and then, by his own careful account, went back an hour and did not.

I have had these documents for some time now. I have had them on a table in the room where I am writing this, in six piles, and I have done to them the things that a person of my training does. I have been through them with a pencil and a ruler. I have drawn up the hours of that night on a long sheet of lining paper, across and down, and entered every statement of fact in its square. I have checked the weather against the Meteorological Office’s daily report and the tides against the Admiralty tables for the port of reference, corrected for the place. I have checked the moon. I have stood in the yard with a stopwatch. Where a thing could be measured I have measured it.

I want to tell you the result before you begin, because if you do not know it you will read these pages the way a jury reads, looking for the liar, and you will find one. You will find six, one after another, and you will be wrong each time.

None of them lied. I have checked.

I do not mean that they were fair, or wise, or that they understood what they were looking at. Most of them did not. I mean something narrower and harder than that. I mean that wherever one of these people writes I saw, that person saw it; and wherever one of them writes it was such-and-such o’clock, a clock said so. Every account in this book is true. Every account in this book contradicts the others. I am aware that those two sentences cannot both stand. They stand. It took me thirty years to see how, and I had an advantage that you will not have until the end.

Some things it will help you to know.

Compline House stands on an island that is an island for roughly half of every day. The road to it is called the Wade. It is nine hundred yards long, and the sea covers it twice in twenty-four hours, to a depth that depends on the moon and the wind and that on the night in question was a little over six feet. When the Wade is covered there is no way on or off the Ness for a person on foot, and there has never been a telephone line that survived a gale. So the people in these pages were, for the hours that matter, shut in together. If you are of a certain turn of mind you will already have the name for that kind of story. Hold it loosely. It is only one of seven.

It was the night the clocks went back. I do not know how much attention you ordinarily pay to that. Most people pay none; they wake on the Sunday, feel faintly that they have been given something, and reset the oven. But it means that in the small hours of that night there is an hour that happens twice. The clocks run from one to two, and are put back, and run from one to two again. Any event set down as taking place at half past one that night took place at one of two different moments, an hour apart, and unless the witness says which, you cannot tell. Very few witnesses say which. Very few know there is anything to say.

And at Compline, in particular, there was a difficulty about what time it was to begin with. I will leave the first witness to explain it to you, because it was explained to him, and he did not much like it either.

The family there had a name for the hour that comes twice. They called it the Odd Hour. They had a rule about it, which was older than the trouble and which was made, I think, by someone who loved them and was tired: that what was said in the Odd Hour did not count. It was an hour off the ledger. You could say in it what you could not say in the other eight thousand seven hundred and fifty-nine, and at two o’clock it would be put back with the clocks, and nobody would hold you to it.

I mention the rule because every person in this book was relying on it, and it was not true. It all counted. That is not the solution; it is only the thing I am surest of.

A word on what I have done to the text, which is as little as I could.

Each account is given whole. I have not cut them to make them agree or rearranged them to make them clear. Where an author changed the names, I have changed them back, and I say so. Where an account was spoken rather than written, I have set it down as nearly as I can in the way it was spoken, and I say that too. Before each one I have put a note of where it came from and what state its author was in, since I think you are entitled to know who is talking to you. I have tried to keep my own voice out of those notes. I have not always managed it.

You will find that each of these people tells the night as a different kind of story. I did not arrange that. One of them could only see the world as a place where everybody is on the take and the woman is lying; so that is the night he had, and it is a true night. One could not see a disaster except as an embarrassment; one could not enter a house without it having been waiting for her. One was in love. One had come to settle something. One was very old, and believed that he had built a machine. People do not choose the kind of story they are in nearly as often as the story chooses them, and it turns out to matter a great deal, when you are trying to find out what happened, to know which kind of story each witness thought it was. A man looking for a murder will find the body. A man looking for the pudding will walk straight past it.

There is a seventh account. It comes last, and it is the only one for which I will not offer you a note on the author.

For the six, here is my suggestion. Read each one as if it were the only one. Believe it; they have all earned that. Notice the times, and notice who is holding the clock. And when you find that you can no longer believe the one you are reading without calling the one before it a liar, do not choose. Put a finger on the place and go on.

They fit. I promise you that they fit.

We will begin with the man who found the body, because in his kind of story somebody always does.

PART ONE

Dead Man’s Hour

by Harry Cade

Editor’s Note

Henry Arthur Cade was a detective sergeant in the Metropolitan Police until 1988 and a private enquiry agent, working mostly for solicitors, from then until his knees gave out. He died in a nursing home in Southend-on-Sea in the spring of 2019, and the manager, who had no next of kin to send his effects to, kept a cardboard box of them in her office for longer than the rules required because, she told me, she had liked him. The box held a Ronson lighter, a wristwatch with a cracked glass, some photographs of a girl on a pony, and two hundred and eleven sheets of typescript in a Basildon Bond box, typed on a machine with a damaged e.

The title page says Dead Man’s Hour and under that, a novel, and somebody, I assume Mr Cade, has crossed out a novel in blue ballpoint. From internal evidence he began it in the winter of 1995 and went back to it, on and off, for the rest of his life; the last chapters were typed in the home. He sent it to nobody. There is no carbon.

It is written in the manner of the American paperbacks he liked, of which there were about forty in the room where he died. I do not think the manner is an affectation. I think it is how he had come to see things, after the kind of working life he had, and that by 1994 he could no more have looked at a woman opening a door without wondering what she wanted than he could have looked at a clock without reading it.

He is the only one of the seven who was paid to be there, and the only one who was trained to observe. For both reasons he is the most confident of them. You should know that he had been drinking on the night in question, though less than he implies; that he was struck on the head at about ten past midnight, which he tells you himself; and that every time he gives is from his own wristwatch, which he had declined to surrender at the door and which was therefore, for most of the night, the only timepiece on the island that agreed with the rest of England. I have had the watch examined. It is a Tissot, and it keeps good time still.

He names real people. All of those who could be harmed by it are dead, with one exception, and I have asked her.

1. The Wade

Lionel Fenn kept his office over a building society in Colchester High Street, up a flight of stairs that smelled of floor polish and other people’s wills. He was sixty-seven and looked as if he’d been sixty-seven since the Coronation. He had a wing collar, near enough, and a desk you could have landed a helicopter on, and he sat behind it with his fingers together and looked at me the way a man looks at a plumber he has been told is good.

“You were recommended, Mr Cade,” he said.

“That’s nice. Who by?”

“Mr Rudge, at Rudge and Maitland. He said that you were discreet and that you had been a policeman.”

“He’s half right. I’m still discreet.”

It didn’t get a smile. I hadn’t expected one. It was a Wednesday morning in the third week of October, there was rain on the window behind his head, and I had driven up from Leigh with a hangover and forty pounds in the world to hear about what I assumed would be a divorce. In my line it’s usually a divorce. When it isn’t a divorce it’s a man on the sick with a bad back who’s been seen on a roof. Either way you sit in a car.

Fenn opened a drawer and took out a letter and laid it on the blotter and turned it round with one finger so that I could read it. He didn’t push it across. I had to lean.

It was written with a proper pen on thick paper in a hand like an engraving. No address at the top, only a word, Compline, and a date three weeks gone. It said:

Dear Fenn, Someone is taking my clocks and leaving me my own copies in their place. I made the copies. I should know them. I have counted eleven and there will be more that I have not found, since whoever it is has the sense to take the ones I do not often open. I do not want the police, who will tramp, and I do not want it spoken of in the house. Find me a man who can look at people. I will pay him. I want to know which of them it is before the Hour. Yrs, L. Vane.

Under that, in the same hand but hurried, a line that had been added afterwards: I may not remember having written this. Act on it regardless.

I read it twice. It’s a habit. The second time you read the man instead of the words.

“Who’s L. Vane?”

“Leopold Vane. You won’t know the name unless you are interested in clocks.”

“I own one.”

“Mr Vane owns a hundred and eleven. He restored a good many of them himself and he made, in his working life, exact copies of some dozens of the finest, as studies, the way a painter will copy an Old Master. He is, or he was, quite possibly the best restorer of early English clockwork alive. He is eighty-one years of age.”

“And what’s the last line about?”

Fenn looked at the rain for a while. “His memory is not what it was,” he said. “There are good days. That letter was written on a very good day. I telephoned him the following week to say that I was making enquiries on his behalf, and he asked me what enquiries, and was rather short with me.”

“So I’d be working for a client who doesn’t know he’s hired me.”

“You would be working for me, Mr Cade, on the instruction of a client who foresaw precisely that difficulty and provided for it in writing. I have known Leo Vane for forty years. If he says there are eleven copies standing where eleven clocks should be, I should be astonished to find there were ten.”

“What are eleven clocks worth?”

“These eleven? I have had the schedule out.” He had it out now, typed, with a paper clip. “Something over four hundred thousand pounds. Insured for rather less, the valuation being elderly.”

I didn’t whistle. I’d given that up along with the warrant card. But I looked at the schedule with more respect than I’d given the letter.

“Which of them,” I said. “He says which of them. He’s got a list.”

“He has a family, which comes to the same thing.” Fenn took off his glasses and polished them, and did the family for me while he did it, flat, like a man reading the weather for shipping. “The son, Edmund. Fifty-two. He has managed the estate since his father stopped troubling with it, by which I mean since about 1975. I should not say that he has managed it well. The son’s wife, Celia. The grandson, Christopher, who is at one of the music colleges, and who has I believe a young woman. The daughter, Imogen, who lives in Edinburgh and comes down perhaps twice in a year. There is a cook who comes in from the village and a girl who helps her. And there is a young person, lately engaged, a sort of nurse, who sits up with Mr Vane at night, since he walks about.”

“When was she engaged?”

“The first of October.”

“After the letter.”

“A few days after.” He put the glasses back on. “I engaged her myself, Mr Cade. From an advertisement, with references. I think we may leave Miss Quaile out of it.”

I’ve never left anybody out of it in my life, but I let him have that one.

“Any of them short of money?”

There was a pause that a less careful man wouldn’t have left.

“I act for the family,” Fenn said. “All of the family. You will appreciate that there are matters I am not at liberty to discuss with you, and that what I am asking you to find out I should a good deal prefer not to know.”

“That’s a yes.”

“That is a statement of my position.”

“All right.” I sat back. The chair was the kind they give clients so they won’t stay. “How do I get in? I don’t see myself as a long-lost cousin.”

“On Saturday they give a dinner. They give it every year on that night. It is a family occasion, somewhat peculiar, I shall explain it. There will be a few guests from outside; I shall be one. And as it happens the insurers have been pressing for some time for a fresh valuation of the collection. Pemberton’s. I have told Edmund that their man is coming on Saturday to make a preliminary inspection, that it was the only day he could manage, and that as he must come over on the morning tide and cannot get back before the night one he has been asked to dine and stay. Edmund was not pleased. But he could hardly refuse the insurers.”

“He might ring them.”

“He might. I have a friend at Pemberton’s.”

I looked at him again. Wing collar and all. You never know with solicitors. Some of the best liars I ever met had their names on brass plates.

“I don’t know anything about clocks, Mr Fenn.”

“You are not required to. You are required to look as though you do, for one afternoon, with a notebook. I shall give you the insurers’ photographs. Mr Vane’s copies are extremely good, but he was a craftsman and not a forger, and he made no attempt to deceive. Each original has some mark of the maker’s which the copy lacks. You will find a note of them on the back of each print.” He slid a fat buff envelope across. This one he did push. “Your real business is the people.”

“Tide,” I said. “You said tide.”

So he explained about the tide. Then he explained about the time, and I asked him to explain it again, slower.

“In 1974,” Fenn said, “Mr Vane’s wife was drowned on the causeway. It was on the night of this same dinner; the night, as it happens, that the clocks were put back for the winter. I shan’t go into the circumstances. It was held to be an accident. She had misjudged the hour of the tide. Mr Vane took the view that she had been deceived as to the hour by the changing of the clocks, and he has not permitted a clock in that house to be changed since. Not forward in the spring. Not back in the autumn. Compline keeps Greenwich time the year round.”

“So in the summer they’re an hour out.”

“In the summer, Mr Vane would say, the rest of the country is an hour out. From the end of March to the end of October, when it is one o’clock at Compline it is two o’clock here. You become accustomed. One learns to ask. And on the night the clocks go back, the difference ceases, and the house and the world agree again until the spring. That is what the dinner is for. At one o’clock in the morning by the house, which is two by your watch, Mr Vane opens his front door. To let the world back in, as he puts it.”

“And then everyone goes to bed.”

“Then,” Fenn said, “there is an hour during which, by a custom of the late Mrs Vane’s, the family are permitted to say anything they please to one another without consequences. It is called the Odd Hour. I have sat through nineteen of them. I do not recommend the experience.” He squared the schedule on the blotter. “There is one further thing. You will be asked to give up your watch at the door. All the guests are. It is put into a basin in the hall and returned in the morning. You would be wise not to make difficulties.”

“I never make difficulties.”

“Mr Rudge said that you would say that.”

He offered me a hundred and fifty a day and expenses. I’d have done it for eighty. I asked for two hundred, because it was that kind of desk, and he gave it to me without blinking, and I went down his stairs with a cheque for the first day and the envelope under my arm, thinking it was the softest thing I’d been handed in a year. A dinner. A bed. A rich old man’s family, one of them with sticky fingers, and all I had to do was watch them eat.

I used to be good at knowing when a job was wrong. I’d lost that too.

Saturday came up grey and windy with a sky like a dirty sheet. I had the suit cleaned. I bought a notebook and a jeweller’s loupe from a man in Southend who asked no questions because he never does. I spent the Friday evening with Fenn’s photographs spread on the kitchen table and a bottle of Bell’s to hold them down, learning eleven clocks I had never seen and the names of men three hundred years dead who had made them: Tompion, Knibb, Quare, East. On the back of each print somebody at the insurers had written in pencil where to look. Signature on backplate, lower edge. Punch mark inside the door. Initials scratched under the seatboard. It was like being given the answers to a crossword in a language you don’t speak.

The twelfth photograph was different. It was bigger, and there were six views instead of two, and Fenn had put a slip of paper round it with a figure written on it. I looked at the figure and then I put my glass down and looked at it again.

One million two hundred thousand pounds. For a clock.

It didn’t look like much. A brass thing about two feet high under a glass shade, with more dials on its face than seemed decent: a big one and five small, and a little painted moon. The Thorne Sidereal, the caption said. Isaac Thorne, Colchester, 1771. Mean and sidereal time, equation, lunation, and the tide at Compline Bar. The only known example. And on the back, in the pencil: Maker’s mark a sprig of thorn, scratched. (1) Rear of moon disc. (2) Underside of dial foot, left.

It wasn’t on Leo Vane’s list of the eleven. I noticed that. I also noticed that a man who had lifted four hundred thousand pounds’ worth of clocks a piece at a time, starting with the ones nobody opened, was a man working his way up to something. I’m slow, but I get there.

I drove out early, with the lights on. Fenn had been particular about it. The road to the place was open first thing and then not again till the evening, and Pemberton’s man was to go over on the morning tide and make a day of it. It’s forty miles from Leigh as the map has it and a good deal further than that in every other way. After Maldon the road gets narrow and then it gets lonely. The fields go flat and the hedges give up and the sky comes down to meet you, and there’s nothing standing higher than a pylon between you and Holland. I had the Granada’s heater on and the wipers going. Wind kept taking the car by the shoulder.

Thorney Staithe was a street, a church, a pub called the Plough and Sail, and a smell of mud. I didn’t stop. Past the last house the road turned to concrete and ran out along the top of a sea wall, and from there I could see where I was going, and I pulled over and had a look at it, because I like to know the ways out of a place before I go in.

The tide was down, though it was on its way back. What I was looking at was about half a mile of nothing: grey-brown mud, shining, cut up by creeks, with birds picking over it. Across the nothing ran a road. It came down off the wall on a ramp and went out dead straight on a low bank of stone and shingle, with a line of poles either side like a guard of honour that had been stood there too long, and about halfway over there was a sort of dip, and a little flat bridge, and beside the bridge a thing I couldn’t make out, a black box on legs, like a hide for shooting from.

At the far end of the road the ground rose about as high as a bus. There were trees on it, bent one way. In the trees there was a house, long, a lot of chimneys, and off to one side of it a tower with a clock face. That was the island. That was all of it. I’ve seen bigger car parks.

There was a board at the top of the ramp. White paint, black letters, done by somebody who took trouble.

VANE ESTATE. THE WADE. PRIVATE ROAD. DO NOT CROSS WITHIN THREE HOURS OF HIGH WATER. THE SEA COMES IN FASTER THAN YOU CAN WALK.

Under that was a frame with a glass front and a printed card in it, the week’s tides, a column for each day. I got out to read it. The wind tried to shut the door on my leg. Saturday, it said. High water 12.27 p.m.; road closed from 8.40 a.m. until 4.12 p.m. Then high water 12.52 a.m.; road closed from 9.05 p.m. until 4.35 a.m.

I looked at my watch. It was twenty past nine. By the card that road had been shut for forty minutes. I looked at the road. It was lying there in plain view with nothing on it but a few puddles. Then I saw that there was a line along the bottom of the card, small, in red:

All times are Greenwich Mean Time.

I stood and did the sum. I did it with my lips moving. An hour on, all of it. I had twenty minutes, then, not forty less than none. And tonight it would shut at five past ten by any clock a sane person owned, and not open till gone half past five in the morning. I thought about how many people must have stood where I was standing in July, and read that card with a watch on their wrist, and thought they had an hour more than they did. I thought, somebody ought to put that in bigger letters. Then I remembered who the somebody was and what had happened to his wife.

There was a farm just there on the landward side, down off the wall: a low house, tarred barns, a yard. A man was standing in the yard with a horse. It was a big grey horse and he had one of its feet up between his knees and was doing something to it, and when my door banged he looked round without letting go. He was fifty yards off. I couldn’t tell you his face. Lean, a hat, a canvas coat. He looked at me and at the car, and then at the island, and then back at me, and he took his time over each. I’ve been looked at by experts. That was one. Then he went back to the horse.

I filed him. I file everybody. Mostly it’s a waste of the cabinet.

I got in and took the Granada down the ramp and out onto the Wade.

It’s a queer thing, driving on the bottom of the sea. The road was wet and ribbed and had weed on it. Water stood either side in the low places, and the poles went by, each one with a rag of something green at about the height of my head, and it took me half the distance to work out that the green was a tidemark. The sea had come a good way in while I stood reading. It was in the creeks on both sides now, creeping. At the dip the surface dropped away and the mud came up close, glistening. The little bridge was stone piers with planks across, no rail. The creek under it was only a few yards wide but it was cut deep and the water in it was moving fast, inland, with bits of foam on it. And the box on legs was a box on legs. Tarred timber, a ladder up one post, a door. I knew what it was without anyone telling me. It was where you went if you had read the card wrong.

Somebody should have looked at that ladder. I’m not a carpenter, and I could see daylight through the bottom rungs from a moving car.

The woman who opened the door to me was not the cook.

She was forty-something and she’d decided some time ago that it was nobody’s business how much. Fair hair, the colour that’s called ash on the bottle, cut to the jaw. Slacks, a man’s cashmere jersey with the sleeves pushed up, no jewellery except a wedding ring she turned with her thumb. A good face that had been a beautiful one and knew to the day when the change had happened. She had the sort of grey-green eyes that seem to be thinking about something a little way behind you.

“You’re the clock man,” she said. She had a low voice, dry. A voice that had been taught.

“Cade. From Pemberton’s.”

“Celia Vane. We’re all at sixes and sevens, I’m afraid, there’s a goose. Come in out of that.”

I came in out of that. She shut the door on the wind and the first thing I noticed was the noise.

I’d been ready for clocks. A hundred and eleven of them, Fenn had said. I had thought of it as a number. I had not thought what it would be to stand in a stone hall with a dozen of them round the walls, tall ones, in their cases like men in sentry boxes, every one going. It wasn’t loud. That was the trouble with it. It was a sort of whisper from all sides, never quite together, a crowd muttering in another room. You felt talked about.

“You stop hearing it,” Celia Vane said. “After about a year. Then one of them stops, and you wake up at three in the morning wondering what’s wrong.”

“Which one’s right?”

“Oh, they’re all right. That’s the idea. They’re all right, and it’s the rest of us.” She held out her hand, palm up. “I’m afraid I have to ask for your watch.”

There was a table in the middle of the hall, and on it was a grey metal basin about the size of a washing-up bowl, old, with a rim that had been hammered. There were two watches in it already. One was a lady’s and one was something flat and gold on a crocodile strap that had cost more than my car.

“Mr Fenn mentioned it.”

“It’s my father-in-law’s rule. Compline time or none. You get it back at breakfast.” The hand stayed out. “We call it the Font. You can make the obvious joke if you like, everybody does.”

“I don’t wear one,” I said.

Her eyes came down to my left wrist. I had the cuff shot, but I’d worn that watch for eleven years and there’s a mark. She looked at the mark. She looked at it for about as long as it takes to strike a match. Then she looked at my face, and something happened at the corner of her mouth that I wouldn’t call a smile but that lived in the same street.

“How sensible,” she said. “Neither does the goose.”

She dropped her hand and turned and walked ahead of me across the hall, and that was the first conversation I had with Celia Vane. She’d caught me in a lie inside a minute and a half and put it in her pocket for later. I had a Tissot down my left sock, pressing on the ankle bone, and I could feel it ticking against me all the way across that floor, as if it wanted to be found.

I’d like to tell you I wasn’t watching her walk. I told the truth to a disciplinary board once, and look where that got me, but I’ll tell it here. I was watching her walk.

She took me down some stone steps at the back of the hall to what she called the Shop.

It had been a chapel once, or the cellar of one. The ceiling was arches, low, whitewashed, and under them ran forty feet of bench, with lathes on it small enough to put in your pocket and a rack of files in order of size, hundreds of them, and trays of wheels laid out on green baize like a jeweller’s window. It was the cleanest room I had ever seen that wasn’t in a hospital. There were more clocks down here, but most of them were in pieces. And at the far end, under the one good window, an old man sat on a stool with a brass plate in his left hand and a thing like a dentist’s pick in his right, and didn’t look up.

“Leo,” she said. “The man from the insurance.”

“Put him down somewhere.”

“He isn’t a parcel, darling.”

“Then he may sit.” He still hadn’t looked up. “Not on the bench.”

Celia Vane gave me a glance that said all yours, and went back up the steps. I heard her shoes on the stone and then I didn’t. I found a chair with a seat made of string and I sat on it, as told, and I watched Leopold Vane work.

He was a long man folded small. White hair, a lot of it, standing up off a high forehead. A big bony nose with a pair of spectacles on it and a second lens, a watchmaker’s glass, screwed into his right eye and hung on a black cord. An old cardigan with leather at the elbows. I’ve seen a good many men of eighty-one, mostly in the kind of trouble where somebody has taken their savings, and they all had the hands: the spots, the shake, the skin like tissue. He had the spots and the skin. He hadn’t the shake. The pick in his fingers moved about a sixteenth of an inch at a time and stopped dead exactly where he put it.

It went on for four or five minutes. That’s a long time to sit on string. Then he set the plate down on a square of chamois, let the glass drop out of his eye onto his chest, and turned round on the stool and looked at me. His eyes were pale blue and very clear and they went over me the way they’d gone over the brass.

“Pemberton’s sent a boy last time,” he said. “With a camera. He touched a dial with his thumb.”

“I’ll keep my hands in my pockets.”

“You’re not from Pemberton’s.”

I didn’t say anything. In that position you don’t. You let them tell you what they know.

“You have no glass,” Leo Vane said. “A man who came to look at clocks would have a glass in his top pocket and the mark of it round his eye. You have a policeman’s shoes. Fenn sent you. I wrote to Fenn.” He stopped. Something moved behind the blue, like a fish under ice. “Did I write to Fenn?”

“You did, sir. Three weeks ago.”

“What did I say?”

“That someone in this house is taking your clocks and leaving you your own copies.”

“Yes,” he said. “Yes. That is so. Eleven.” He nodded slowly. He was pleased, and I saw what it was that pleased him. Not that I’d come. That his own letter had arrived, like a message a man leaves himself on the hall table. “I counted them in the summer. I wrote them down, and I hid the paper, and I’ve not the least idea where. It’s a great nuisance, Mr—”

“Cade.”

“A great nuisance, Mr Cade, to be robbed by somebody who need only wait. He knows I shall forget that I know. I suppose he’s very patient. Or she.”

“Do you know who it is, Mr Vane?”

“If I knew, I shouldn’t want you.”

“Do you have an idea?”

He picked up the brass plate again and turned it to the window. I thought he wasn’t going to answer.

“I made forty-three copies in my life,” he said. “It’s how I learned. You don’t understand how a man thought until you have tried to make the same cut with the same tool and found out why he held it as he did. I never passed one off. I never signed one with another man’s name. A copy is not a lie, Mr Cade. It is a copy, until somebody stands it in the place of the original and says nothing. Then it’s a lie, and it is his, and not mine. I resent that. I resent having my own work used to lie to me. I think that I mind that more than the money. You’ll think that an old man’s vanity.”

“I think it’s a reason. I’ve known people killed for less.”

“Have you?” He was interested. “I suppose you have.” Then: “It must be someone who knows which they are. That’s the difficulty. I kept the copies in the long cupboard, there, and a ledger. It wants knowledge to match the one to the other and carry it up and put it in the case and set it to time so that I walk past it for a year. Anyone can steal a clock. To steal one from me, in my own house, that wants an education.” His mouth went thin. “I gave the education to one person only.”

“Your son.”

“I had him at this bench from the time he was nine years old. He had better hands than mine. He had the best hands I ever saw on a boy.” He put the plate down. “He stopped. When his mother died, he stopped, he never touched a tool again. I’ve never known why. I don’t say it is Edmund. Do you understand me? I say it wants an education. Imogen has eyes, she restores pictures, she’d know a copy from across a room, and she could be taught the rest by a man who had the rest. Edmund’s wife is a clever woman and is not happy. The boy is a musician, and has good fingers, and no money. There’s a girl who sits with me at night; I can’t at present recall her name, but she looks at everything.” He spread the long hands, the first helpless thing I’d seen him do. “You see how it is. I don’t want it to be any of them. So I’m of no use. I should convict the cat.”

I got the notebook out and wrote some of it down, not because I needed it but because it steadies people. He watched the pencil.

“Fenn’s letter said you wanted to know before the Hour,” I said. “Why before?”

“Because of the rule. What’s said in the Hour is not held against the one who says it. If I know, I can ask. In the Hour I can ask him to his face, and he may answer me, and it need go no further; and if he gives them back, it need never have happened.” He looked at me with the clear eyes. “It was my wife’s rule. She understood us. She said that a family is a clock with too many wheels, and that once in a year you must let it down and take the power off, or something will break. She used to say that the hour was given to us, and that it was bad manners not to use a present.”

“She sounds like a sensible woman.”

“She is in the long gallery,” Leo Vane said. “You should go and look at her. In the grey. She’ll be down directly; she’s dressing.” He frowned, and the fish went under the ice again, and when he looked at me next the eyes were still clear but they had nothing behind them that knew me.

“Are you the man about the Dent?” he said. “It isn’t ready. You may tell them it isn’t ready. I’ll not be hurried over a remontoire by a railway company.”

I said I’d tell them. I put the notebook away. At the foot of the steps I looked back, and he had the glass in his eye again and the pick in his hand, and it was as steady as a surveyor’s mark. Whatever had gone out of the rest of him, it hadn’t gone out of the hands. I’ve thought about that since. I’d been given a description that afternoon of the hands that had robbed him, by the man who trained them. I wrote it down in my book and then I spent the night looking at everything else.

I did what I was paid to pretend to do. I went round the house with my photographs.

It took most of the day and I’ll spare you most of it. Somebody sent me up a plate of cold beef at one. There were clocks in every room and some rooms that seemed to be there only to hold them. I’d open a case, feeling like a man going through a stranger’s coat, and find the place the pencil said, and either there’d be a name cut in the brass or a little punched mark or a set of scratched initials, or there wouldn’t. I found five of Leo Vane’s eleven before four o’clock. Five times I looked where a dead man had signed his work and there was nothing but clean metal. The clocks ticked on at me, all the same. They kept perfect time. That was the insult of it. He was right about that.

Nobody bothered me. A big girl of seventeen or so with a tray passed me twice on the back stairs and said “Sorry” both times. From the kitchen came a woman’s voice raised over a clatter of pans, giving orders, and once, when I was on the top landing by a door with bars on the little window beside it, I thought I heard that same woman’s voice much nearer than it should have been, low, saying something sharp, and then nothing. I tried the door. It was locked or stuck. I stood there a moment. An old nursery, by the bars. It was no business of Pemberton’s.

In the long gallery I met the late Mrs Vane.

She was six feet high in a gold frame at the end, where the light came in. Painted in the fifties, when they still did it properly. A woman in her thirties in a grey silk evening dress, standing, one hand on the back of a chair, and looking out of the picture with grey eyes at somebody she was about to say something funny to. Not a beauty. Better than that. I stood in front of her a while. I’ve looked at a lot of photographs of dead women in the course of work, and it’s a rule that you can’t tell from the picture. But I’d have liked to hear what she was about to say.

On the wall under her a clock was going. There was always a clock going.

I left the big one till last.

The library was at the end of the ground floor, a long brown room with a fire in it and books to the ceiling that nobody had opened since the old king died. In the bay of the window stood a mahogany table, and on the table a square glass case with a brass frame, and inside the glass, with the grey light coming through it, the thing in Fenn’s twelfth photograph. One million two hundred thousand pounds. It was smaller than I’d thought. It was going. The big hand moved while I watched, and the five small dials went about their own affairs, and the little painted moon, three-quarters of a face, looked at me sideways out of its slot.

There was a green baize cover folded on the table beside it, like the cloth off a parrot’s cage.

I checked the door. I got the print out, and the loupe. The case had a lock but the key was in it. I’m not proud of how careful I was. I opened the glass an inch at a time and I didn’t breathe on anything, and I found the left foot of the dial, underneath, where the pencil said, and I got down on my knees on Leo Vane’s carpet with the glass in my eye like a real one and looked for a sprig of thorn.

Brass. Clean, yellow, with the fine lines the file had left. Nothing scratched on it at all.

I shifted. I looked again. I got the angle from the photograph, held the print up beside the clock, and matched them, and in the photograph you could see it, a tiny thing like a bird’s footprint. On the clock I couldn’t. The light was bad. It was coming four o’clock on an October afternoon with rain on the window, and I was a retired copper on his knees with a three-pound loupe he’d owned for two days, looking for a scratch the size of a grass seed, on the wrong side of a dial, in the shadow of its own foot. I couldn’t get at the back of the moon without taking things apart, and I’d promised him I’d keep my hands in my pockets.

I told myself it was the angle.

I want that on the record, because I’ve had a long time to think about it since. I told myself it was the angle, and the light, and that the old man had said eleven and this wasn’t one of the eleven, and that a clock worth more than the street I live in would be the last one anyone dared touch, not the twelfth. I shut the glass. I turned the key. I’ve been wrong about bigger things, but not many, and never on my knees.

“Find any woodworm?”

I got up without hurrying. That’s the main thing, not to hurry.

The man in the doorway filled it. Six foot two and wide with it, in a tweed jacket that had been made for him when he was a stone lighter, with thick dark hair going grey in a handsome way and a face that had been good-looking so long that it hadn’t noticed it was starting to blur. He had a tumbler in his hand, half full, the colour of the stuff I drink myself, and it was not his first. A heavy gold ring on the little finger. He came into the room with a hitch in his walk, the left leg, and stood looking at me, and at the loupe in my hand, and at the clock, in that order. He was smiling. I’ve been smiled at like that across an interview table.

“Edmund Vane,” he said. “You’re the insurance. My wife says you don’t wear a watch. I thought that was rather good, for a man who’s come to count the clocks.”

“Harry Cade. I find I’m never short of the time in this house.”

“No. God, no. One isn’t.” He drank. “You’ll have seen the lot, then. What’s the damage?”

“I’ve only looked at the cases, Mr Vane. A proper valuation takes a specialist a week.”

“Then what’s the point of you?”

“I count them. I see they’re here, and where they’re kept, and what the locks are like. Then I go home and write that the locks are no good.”

“The locks are no good,” he agreed. He strolled to the table. He looked down at the Thorne clock through its glass, and for a second there was something in his face that I couldn’t read and that didn’t go with the rest: a kind of flat distaste, the way you’d look at a dog that had bitten somebody you knew. Then he took the baize off the table and dropped it over the case, and the clock was gone. It ticked on underneath.

“Father covers it at night,” he said. “Like a budgerigar. He thinks the light fades the silvering.” He turned round, and he was close, and bigger than me, and he let me notice both. “Fenn fixed this up. Fenn’s an old woman. I’d have told Pemberton’s to send their man on a weekday like anyone else and not come sniffing round on the one night of the year when the family’s got its hair down. But here you are. So I’ll tell you how it goes. You’ll eat your dinner. You’ll drink my father’s claret, which is the only thing in this house that’s what it says on the label. You will not go poking about after dark, because this is an old house, with a lot of stairs in it, and we’ve lost the electricity three times this autumn. And tomorrow morning when the road dries you’ll drive back to wherever you come from and write that the locks are no good.” He smiled again. “I shouldn’t like you to have an accident. Think of the paperwork.”

“I’m obliged for the warning.”

“It wasn’t a warning. It was hospitality.” He finished the tumbler. “Drinks at six in the hall. That’s six by us. Seven to you, if you had a watch.”

He went out. The hitch in the walk was worse going than coming. I stood where I was and listened to him cross the hall, and I thought, there goes a man who’s frightened of something, and it isn’t me.

Then I went to the window, because I’d heard an engine.

You could see the Wade from there, the whole grey length of it. It had been under the sea since ten that morning and it was only now coming up again, a bit at a time, black and wet, as the tide drew off. Most of it was clear. The dip in the middle still had water lying across it that the wind was pushing along. And right in the dip, in the water, a small red sports car was sitting at an angle with its bonnet up. A tall young man in a yellow pullover was walking round and round it. And from the island end a tractor was grinding out along the causeway, with a thin dark boy at the wheel and a girl with next to no hair standing up behind him, hanging on to his shoulders, and laughing so that I could see her teeth from the library.

Under the tractor’s back axle, where it had been slung for the ride, a black dinner jacket was flapping from a hook like something they were going to bury.

I didn’t know then what it was for. I thought it was a funny thing to take to a breakdown. I found out later that they’d been across to the stable that afternoon, the boy and the girl, dressing a pair of wooden figures on the clock tower for the party, the way the family did every year, and that there’d been a jacket over, and I thought no more about it. That’s the way with the things that matter. They go past the window on a tractor and you’re looking at the girl.

I counted on my fingers. The Wade would close at five past ten, real time. From then until half past five the next morning there’d be six feet of North Sea on that road, and whoever had been stripping Leo Vane’s walls for a year would be shut on ninety acres of mud with a hundred clocks, a frightened husband, a wife who’d read me like a bus timetable, an old man who couldn’t trust his own head, and me.

I liked that fine. It’s how I’d have arranged it myself. Nobody slips out for a quiet word with a fence when the fence would have to swim.

It took me until a quarter past one in the morning to see that it cuts both ways. When the door’s shut, it’s shut on you too. And I had it wrong about the swimming.

2. Thirteen at Table

They’d given me a room on the first floor at the back, over the kitchen yard. It had a brass bed, a washstand, a view of a wet wall, and two clocks. I timed them against the Tissot out of my sock. One was fifty-eight minutes slow and the other was an hour and two. I split the difference and called it house time, and I sat on the bed and smoked and thought about what I had.

What I had was five clean pieces of brass, a threat with a smile on it, and an old man who’d as good as given me his son and then begged me not to take him. In the job we used to say that when the family hands you somebody in the first hour, you thank them politely and go on looking. The first one they hand you is the one they can spare.

At ten to seven by me I put the watch back in the sock, shaved for the second time that day, and went down.

The hall had been got ready. Somebody had lit a fire in a grate you could have roasted the tractor in and put candles about, though the electric was on as well, and the long-case clocks stood round the walls in the moving light with their brass faces shining like a jury that had already made up its mind. The basin was on its table in the middle. The Font. There were more watches in it now.

I got myself a whisky from a tray and a place by the wall, and I did what I do. I watched them come in.

Fenn first, with a clergyman. Fenn in a dinner jacket looked the same as Fenn in a suit, only more so. He gave me a nod that would have fooled anyone and said, “Ah, the gentleman from Pemberton’s,” and I said good evening, and that was all we said to each other until one in the morning. He unstrapped a thin gold watch and laid it in the basin like a man putting money in a plate. The clergyman was seventy-odd and soft and pink, with white floss over his ears and the smile of a man who has been deaf for some years and found that it suits him. The Reverend Stiles. He took a hunter out of his waistcoat, looked at it fondly, said, “Well, goodbye for the present,” and dropped it in.

Then a noise on the gravel like a tank regiment, and the front door opening, and a gale, and with the gale a woman of about eighty in a mackintosh over a black velvet frock, with a face like a good horse and a voice you could have used to bring ships in.

“Leo! Where is he? Don’t tell me he’s still in the cellar with his bits. I’ve come across in the Land Rover with one headlamp and no brakes to speak of, and I want a drink before I want anything.” She saw the basin. “Oh, that damn thing.” She dragged a man’s watch off a wrist like a fence post and threw it in from six feet. “There. Rob me. Edmund, you’ve put on weight.”

“Octavia,” said Edmund Vane. He’d changed. In a dinner jacket he looked like what he must have been at thirty, the kind of man other men’s wives remember. He’d also kept on drinking, at a steady pace, like a man walking somewhere he didn’t want to arrive. “You look magnificent. Like a hearse.”

“I look like an old woman who’s buried two husbands and means to dine. Who’s this?”

This was me.

“Mr Cade,” Edmund said. “He’s come to see whether we’re worth burning down.”

“Insurance,” I said.

“How perfectly ghastly for you,” said Dame Octavia Prowse, and looked me over as if she were thinking of buying me for a child to learn on. “Do you hunt?”

“Only people.”

“Ha!” she said, and took the whisky out of my hand, thinking it was hers, and drank it.

The tall young man in the yellow pullover turned up next, minus the pullover, in a dinner jacket that he’d plainly had since school and grown four inches out of at the wrists. He was pink, with a damp fair forelock and a hopeful expression, like a Labrador that has been told it may come in if it’s good. Toby something. A nephew, or the nephew of a nephew. He came down the stairs explaining to nobody in particular about the carburettor of an MG, shook hands with me twice, and then stood in front of the Font going red.

“I say, must I really? Only it’s a bit—”

He rolled up his cuff. He was wearing a Mickey Mouse watch. The hands were Mickey’s arms, in little yellow gloves.

“It was a present,” he said. “From a girl. It’s ironic.”

“What’s ironic about it?” said the boy who’d driven the tractor.

“Well. I mean. One wears it ironically.”

“Does Mickey know?”

That was the grandson. Christopher, called Kit. Twenty-four, thin as a rail, black hair in his eyes, a pianist’s hands, a mouth too old for him. He stood about with a cigarette and watched his father. I noticed that. All evening, whatever else Kit Vane was looking at, he had a line out to where his father was, the way you’d keep an eye on a pan of milk.

And with him the girl off the tractor. Saskia. She had about a quarter of an inch of dark hair all over her head and a ring through one eyebrow and a pair of boots like a navvy’s, and above the boots she had on an evening dress. It was silk, sleeveless, cut plain and well, and it was green. A real green, a dark jewel of a green, emerald you’d call it. It made the stubble on her head look like something done on purpose. She’d have been twenty-two.

I’m telling you about the dress for a reason.

Because ten minutes later Celia Vane came down the stairs, with a hand on the rail and the candlelight working for her, and got to the fourth step from the bottom, and stopped.

She was wearing the same dress.

Not near enough. Not something like. The same: the same silk, the same green, the same cut at the neck, the same length. On her it sat differently, because she was forty-eight and had the shoulders for it and the girl was twenty-two and had the boots. But if you’d hung the two on a rail in a shop you couldn’t have told them apart, and somewhere, I suppose, somebody had.

There was one of those silences. Even the clocks seemed to hold off.

“Oh, bloody hell,” said Saskia, cheerfully. “The Liberty sale?”

“The Liberty sale,” said Celia Vane.

“It was the only one in the shop that didn’t look like upholstery. D’you want me to go and change? I’ve got a thing with a zip.”

I watched Celia Vane decide. It took her a second, and you could see the woman who’d been on a stage. She came down the last four steps smiling.

“Don’t you dare,” she said. “We’ll tell them it’s a uniform. Edmund, look, there are two of me. You’ve always said one wasn’t enough.”

“I’ve never said that in my life,” said Edmund Vane.

People laughed. The clocks started up again. But I’d seen her face on the fourth step, before she got it under control, and it wasn’t the dress she’d minded. A woman like that doesn’t mind another woman in her frock. She’d minded standing next to twenty-two.

So there were two green dresses in that house that night. I knew it at seven o’clock. I stood there with a fresh whisky and watched the pair of them, the fair head and the cropped one, the same green twice in the firelight. Six hours later I saw that green in two places at once, in the dark, with a headache, and I didn’t put it together for the best part of a year. I’m not offering an excuse. I’m telling you what a detective’s worth with a drink in him. You see everything. You could pass an examination on it. Then when it matters you believe your eyes.

The daughter came down last but one. Imogen. Forty-four, by Fenn’s reckoning, and she looked it honestly and didn’t seem to mind. Dark hair pinned up, with a streak of dead white running back from the left temple, the kind people are born with. A plain black dress. She came down the stairs looking at the room the way I’d been looking at it, taking it in piece by piece, and when she got to me she stopped and took me in too, and I knew where I’d seen the eyes before. They were up in the long gallery in a gold frame.

“You’re the valuer,” she said. “My brother says you’ve been on your knees to the Thorne.”

“It seemed the least I could do.”

“What did you make of it?”

“It makes me feel poor.”

“It makes everybody feel something. I used to think it was watching me. All those faces.” She had a quiet voice with Edinburgh laid over the top of Essex. “I clean paintings for a living, Mr Cade. I spend my days telling what’s two hundred years old from what somebody put there last Tuesday. If you’d like a second opinion on anything in this house, you might ask me.” She said it quite lightly, and she looked across the hall at her brother while she said it, and then she moved on and took a glass of sherry and went to stand by herself in front of the fire.

I thought: that’s two of them. The old man, and now the sister. This family’s got a way of telling you things by not telling you.

Then the old man came in, and the room turned round to face him the way iron filings do.

He’d been got into evening clothes. They hung on him, they’d been made for a broader man, the man he’d been. But he came across his hall at eighty-one as straight as he could manage with his white hair brushed and his eyeglass on its cord, and he was the only one in that house, I’ll say this, who looked as if the clothes belonged to the century they were cut in. On his arm, or rather with her hand under his elbow so that you’d hardly see, came a small plain girl in a dark blue frock with a high neck. Sandy hair. No colour in her face at all. That was the nurse, Miss Quaile.

She looked at everything. He’d been right about that. She came into the hall and her eyes went round it once, the clocks, the fire, the faces, me, and I had the feeling she’d counted us and would know if one went missing. Then she looked at Edmund Vane. It was only for a moment. But I used to sit in court and watch the women in the public gallery, and I know how they look at the man in the dock when they’ve decided he didn’t do it.

Leo Vane stopped at the Font and looked down into it.

“Are we all given up?” he said.

“All present and disarmed, Father,” said Edmund.

“Mr Cade doesn’t carry one,” said Celia. She didn’t look at me.

“Doesn’t he? Doesn’t he. A wise man. A wise man knows he hasn’t the time.” He put a long forefinger into the basin and stirred the watches gently, like a child with pebbles. “Poor things. They are all wrong, you know. Every one of these is an hour wrong and has been since the last Sunday of March, and their owners have gone about consulting them and catching trains. An Act of Parliament. A man called Willett, a builder, who wanted more light for his golf. And so the whole country agrees to tell the same lie about where the sun is, and tells it for seven months in the year, and is very much surprised when things go amiss.” He took the finger out. “Not in my house. You’re on Compline time now. It is seven minutes past six. In six hours and fifty-three minutes they’ll come to their senses and agree with us, and we shall open the door to them. Until then you will kindly take the hour from me.”

“Hear, hear,” said the vicar, who hadn’t caught a word.

“Is Margot down?” said Leo Vane.

Nobody answered him. The nurse’s hand moved a little on his arm. His daughter turned round from the fire.

“She’ll be along, Papa,” Imogen said. “Come and sit down.”

I looked at the faces. I’m a professional and it was the thing to do. Edmund was looking into his glass. Celia was turning her ring. The boy was watching his father. The girl with no hair was whispering to the boy, who’s Margot? and being shushed. The solicitor was studying a clock. Dame Octavia Prowse was looking at Leo Vane with her big plain face gone quiet and I saw, as you sometimes do see it all at once in old people, that fifty or sixty years ago she’d wanted that man and hadn’t got him.

And the pink young man, Toby, was patting his pockets one after another with a look of horror, like somebody who’s left the gas on. He’d been doing it on and off since he came down. I filed that too.

We went in at eight, their time. Nine by the watch in my sock, and the wind getting up outside, so that the long curtains in the dining room breathed in and out.

It was a fine room. Panelling, portraits of people who’d owned the place before the Vanes had, a table that had been polished since the Reform Bill. Candles, again, in silver. There were three clocks: a tall one in the corner, a bracket affair on the sideboard, and a gilt thing on the chimneypiece with a nymph on it. I’d done that room in the afternoon. The nymph was right. The other two were copies.

I counted the places because I count things. There were thirteen.

I counted the people. Leo Vane, Edmund, Celia, the daughter, the boy, his girl. The pink nephew. The vicar, the solicitor, the old woman. The nurse. Me. I made it twelve, and I made it twelve a second time.

The thirteenth place was on the old man’s right hand. It was laid like the others, the knives and the forks and the three glasses and a napkin folded like a bishop’s hat. The chair was drawn up. Nobody went near it. They went round it, I noticed, even the ones who hadn’t been before, the way you step round a wet patch on a floor without looking down.

“I shouldn’t, Mr Cade,” Celia Vane said in my ear. She’d come up beside me. Close to, she had scent on, something old-fashioned and dark with a peach in it somewhere. “That one’s taken.”

“Who by?”

“My mother-in-law. She’s dined with us every year since she died. She has a very small appetite and no conversation, and she’s still the only one at the table my father-in-law listens to.” She showed me my own place with a tilt of the fair head. It was the other side, three down, between the vicar and the girl with no hair. “We’re thirteen. I hope you aren’t superstitious. They say the first to get up is the first to die. Octavia always makes a point of going out for a cigarette before the pudding, so she’s due any decade now.”

“What about you? Are you superstitious?”

“I’m an actress,” she said. “I’m superstitious about everything. I just don’t let it stop me.”

She went to the foot of the table. Her husband, I noticed, was not at the head. The old man had the head. Edmund Vane sat halfway down on the far side, opposite me, with his back to the windows and the curtains moving behind him, and the sister on one side of him and the nurse on the other. He filled his own glass before the girl could get round with the bottle.

I’ve eaten worse dinners. I’ve eaten them off my knee in an Escort, watching a door. There was soup. There was the goose, brought in by the big girl, Gail, who was scarlet with the weight of it, and behind her in the doorway for a second I saw the cook, a square woman of sixty with forearms like a docker’s, checking that we’d noticed. The old man carved. He did it standing, with a knife he’d obviously sharpened himself, and it was like watching him at the bench: every slice the same, nothing wasted, not a tremor. The girl Saskia said that she didn’t eat anything with a face. Dame Octavia said she’d never met a goose with one worth mentioning. The pink young man told a story about the car that went on for some time and had a ferry in it. The vicar smiled at everybody. The claret came round and it was what Edmund had said, the only thing in the house that matched its label.

And all through it the place on the old man’s right. They put soup at it. They took the soup away. They gave it goose. Leo Vane turned to it now and then and said a few words too low to hear, and waited, and nodded. Nobody looked. Everybody knew to the inch where it was.

I’ve sat in rooms with a body in them, and I’ve sat in rooms with a man who was going to be a body by morning and didn’t know it. I won’t say I felt anything that night at the table. I’m not the type and I’d had four whiskies and a good deal of the claret. But I’ll say that it was the first dinner I ever ate where the empty chair was doing most of the talking.

The nurse didn’t eat much. She cut things up. She kept half an eye on the old man and the other half, which she thought nobody saw, on the big man next to her, on his glass going up and down. Once, reaching for the salt, his sleeve brushed her wrist, and the colour came up her neck over the high blue collar like a tide over mud.

Opposite me, through the candles, the sister was talking quietly to her brother. I couldn’t hear. But I saw him say something short, and I saw her say something back, and then I saw her say two words that I can lip-read in any language, because they’re a name and I’d heard it once that day. She said Tom Garrow.

Edmund Vane put his glass down.

“Where?” he said. That I heard.

She said something. Thursday. The funeral.

“He’s got no business here.” He wasn’t keeping his voice down now. “That farm’s out at Lady Day. Fenn’s served the notice. He can go back to his bloody cows.”

“Edmund.”

“Twenty years. And he comes back to stand at a graveside in a hat and look across at this house like—” He stopped. He’d noticed the table had gone quiet. He picked the glass up again and smiled round it. “A tenant of ours,” he said, to me, since I was opposite and a stranger. “Old Garrow, at the farm on the other side. You’ll have passed it. Died a fortnight ago. Rather a character. The son’s turned up from Canada to see what he can get.”

“Lean man? Hat? Grey horse?”

The sister’s head came round.

“I saw him this morning,” I said. “By the road. He had a good look at me.”

“I’ll bet he did,” said Edmund Vane.

Imogen Vane didn’t say anything at all. She looked down at her plate. She had a fork in her hand and she kept on holding it. It’s a funny thing, what the blood does. In the nurse it had gone up. In her it went away. That white streak in her hair wasn’t the whitest thing about her for a minute.

I thought: so that’s how it is. And I thought: it’s nothing to do with clocks. I put it down the side of my mind with the nephew patting his pockets and I gave my attention back to the money.

I’d give a good deal to have that minute over. They all would. It turned out that was the theme of the evening.

They cleared the goose. The big girl put down a dish of something with cream, and Dame Octavia Prowse pushed her chair back with a noise like a gate.

“I’m going out for a gasper,” she said. “Somebody’s got to be first up, and I’ve had my money’s worth. Don’t let him start till I’m back.”

“Sit down, Octavia,” said Leo Vane.

He hadn’t raised his voice. But she sat. He was getting to his feet, pushing himself up with his fists on the cloth, and the nurse half rose behind him and then didn’t. He stood at the head of his table with the candles lighting him from underneath, the long face and the white hair, and he picked up his glass.

“We have a custom,” he said, “which the strangers among us will forgive. Before the sweet, we drink to someone.” He turned to the empty place. He inclined his head to it, an inch. “My dear. With your leave.”

Then to the rest of us.

“To absent time.”

They got up. I got up with them. There was the scrape of twelve chairs and they said it, not all together, raggedly, like a response in church. Absent time. Edmund Vane said it into his glass. The daughter didn’t say it; her lips moved. The vicar said “Amen.”

We sat. The old man stayed on his feet.

“It’s the twentieth,” he said. “Twenty years tonight. I thought I should say something about that, and this afternoon I knew what it was to be, and now I don’t. I’ve lost it.” He said it quite simply, the way you’d say you had lost a collar stud. “That happens. You’ll all have noticed that it happens. You’re very kind about it. You say, Never mind, Papa, and Never mind, Leo, and you look at one another. I notice that. I notice a good deal more than you would like.”

“Father,” said Edmund.

“I’m speaking, Edmund.” The glass in his hand didn’t move. “I have found that when I lose a thing, it’s of no use to hunt for it. I must go on with something else, and it comes back by itself. So I shall tell you the something else. It will interest you. It’s about clocks.”

His eyes went round the table. They were very clear. They went from face to face and they didn’t skip anyone; they stopped on the vicar, and on the girl in the boots, and on me. When they got to me there was nothing in them at all to say we’d met.

“One of you has been robbing me,” Leo Vane said.

Nobody moved. That’s what happens. In the films there’s a gasp and somebody drops a fork. In life they go still, the guilty ones and the others just the same, because the innocent are always sure it means them.

“It has been going on for a year, perhaps two. Not money. I shouldn’t notice money. Clocks. One of you has been taking clocks out of this house, good ones, and leaving copies standing in their cases. My copies. I made them with these.” He put down the glass at last and held up his two hands, backs toward us, the long fingers apart. “It was thought, I suppose, that I should never know the difference. Because I am old, and I say Margot when I mean somebody else, and I can’t always find the room I’m looking for. It was thought I would walk past my own work every day and take it for Tompion’s.”

He let that sit.

“I can’t find my spectacles. I can’t tell you the Prime Minister’s name. But I’ll tell you this. I could go round this house blindfold and put my hand on every clock in it and tell you who made it, and in what year, and whether he was left-handed, and whether on that day he was pleased with himself. There are two in this room that I made. That one. And that.” He pointed, without looking, at the long-case in the corner and the bracket clock on the sideboard. He was right both times. “The nymph is Mr Vulliamy’s own, and she is no better than she should be.”

“Leo,” said Fenn, quietly. “Is this quite the—”

“It is exactly the, Lionel. It’s the one night in the year on which it can be said.” He leaned on his fists. “I don’t know which of you it is. I’m telling you that I don’t know. I’ve a man finding out for me, a very capable man. I can’t at this moment remember his name, nor where I’ve put him, but I have every confidence in him, and he’ll have told me before the door is opened. I shall know which of you it is by one o’clock.”

I kept my face where it was. It wasn’t easy. I had the vicar’s elbow in my ribs and a spoonful of cream halfway to my mouth, and across the table Edmund Vane was looking straight at me, not at his father, with a little smile, as if he’d just been dealt the card he was expecting.

“And then,” said Leo Vane, “it’ll be the Hour. And whoever it is may come and tell me why. That’s all. I shan’t want anything else. Not the police. Not the money. I should like the clocks back, if they are to be had, but I daresay they are not. I should like to know why. Whoever you are, you were taught in this house that what is said in that hour is forgiven when it ends. I taught you that. Your mother taught you that. I have never broken it and I shall not begin tonight.” His voice shook, the first time. “I’ve not got so many hours left that I can afford to waste the odd one. You will kindly not waste it either.”

He sat down. He sat down rather suddenly, and the nurse had her hand under his arm before he was in the chair. He looked at the plate in front of him.

“What is this?” he said.

“It’s a syllabub, Mr Vane.”

“Is it? Did I ask for it?” He turned to the empty place on his right. “Margot, did we order a syllabub?”

I’ve said I looked at faces. I looked at them then as hard as I ever have, and I’ll give you what I got, for what it’s worth, and it was worth nothing, and I’ve gone over it a thousand times.

Edmund Vane was smiling at me. I’ve said that.

His wife was looking at him. Not at the old man, not at me. At her husband, down the length of the table, with no expression at all, and her thumb had stopped turning the ring.

Kit Vane was looking at his father too. But the boy’s face had gone tight and white round the nose. He looked the way a kid looks who’s heard his parents fighting through a wall for years and now somebody’s opened the door.

The daughter was looking at the empty chair.

The nurse was looking at her own hands in her lap.

Fenn had his eyes shut. The vicar was eating syllabub. Dame Octavia was watching Leo Vane with her jaw set, like somebody watching a good horse put at a fence it won’t get over. The girl Saskia was looking round the table from one to the next with her mouth a little open, quite frankly enjoying herself, as you would at twenty-two.

And the nephew. Toby. The pink young man had gone the colour of the tablecloth. He had one hand flat against the right-hand pocket of his dinner jacket, pressing, the way you’d hold a wound shut. There was sweat on his lip. If I’d been asked there and then to put my hand on the collar of the guiltiest man in the room, on looks alone, I’d have gone round the table and lifted him out of his chair.

Which shows you. He had the works of a ten-pound carriage clock in that pocket, as it turned out. He’d knocked it off a table in his bedroom at half past five and trodden on it. I got that from him in the yard next morning, when it couldn’t matter less. All night, that boy thought the old man’s speech was about him.

That’s the trouble with looking at people. Fenn had said my business was the people. But people don’t look guilty of what they’ve done. They look guilty of what they’re thinking about.

The women went out. They still did it in that house. The port went round, the wrong way, because the vicar had it. Edmund Vane came and sat in the chair next to mine. He turned it and sat astride it.

“A very capable man,” he said. “I do hope he remembers where he’s put you.”

“I’m from Pemberton’s, Mr Vane.”

“Of course you are. And I’m the Queen of the May.” He was drunk, but it was the big man’s kind, the kind that’s had a lot of practice. It only showed in how carefully he put things down. “Don’t worry. I shan’t spoil it. I think it’s the first thing he’s done on his own account in five years; I’m rather proud of him. What’s old Fenn paying you?”

“Ask old Fenn.”

“I’ll give you the same again to go to bed with a book.” He said it almost kindly. “I mean it. You’ve had your dinner. You’ve found whatever you’ve found. Tell him at one o’clock that it’s me. You’ll be right, as far as it goes, and he’ll have forgotten by Tuesday, and nobody will be any the worse. But stay indoors tonight, Cade. Stay out of the yard and off the wall. You don’t know this place. There’s people who do.”

“That’s twice you’ve warned me.”

“That’s twice I’ve been hospitable.”

“What’s happening tonight that you don’t want me to see?”

He looked at me for a while. Close to, under the drink, he had a tired face. A decent face gone to seed, I’d have said, if I hadn’t known better, and I’ve often thought since that I didn’t know better at all.

“You were a policeman,” he said. “They tell me you can always tell. So tell me something. You go to a house where there’s been a thing done. A long time ago, say. Years. And everybody in that house has got their own idea of who did it. One thinks it was him, and another thinks it was her, and every one of them’s been carrying that about for so long that it’s worn a groove. And they’re all wrong. What do you do?”

“Find the one who knows.”

“And if the one who knows would rather go to the devil than say?”

“Then in my experience,” I said, “he generally does.”

Edmund Vane laughed. It was the only real laugh I heard out of him. He banged me on the shoulder with a hand like a shovel, got up off the chair, and walked out of the room with the hitch in his step. I never spoke to him again. Not a word. The next time I saw him he wasn’t in a position to hear one.

It was Celia Vane who came and got me. I’d gone looking for a place to smoke and found a small room on the garden side, with a desk and a sofa and French windows and a fire that hadn’t been lit long. A woman’s room. There was a clock in it, naturally. The wind had hold of the French windows and was shaking them. I stood with my back to the fire and lit up with the Ronson, and the door opened, and she came in and shut it behind her and leaned on it.

In the one lamp, the green of that dress was nearly black.

“You don’t wear a watch,” she said, “you don’t know a fusee from a fish-knife, and my father-in-law’s capable man is a secret from precisely one person in this house, and that’s my father-in-law. Shall we stop?”

“I didn’t know we’d started.”

“Give me one of those.”

I gave her a cigarette and lit it. She held my wrist while I did it. Her fingers were cold. She looked at the pale band on the skin where the Tissot lived, and then she let go.

“Where is it, as a matter of interest?”

“Down my sock.”

She laughed. She had a good laugh, low and short, and she looked surprised at it, like somebody who’d found a ten-pound note in an old coat. “God. And I thought you’d swallowed it.” She went and sat on the arm of the sofa. “What time is it? Really. Out there.”

I got it out. I felt a fool, with my trouser leg up. “Twelve minutes past eleven.”

“Then the road’s been gone an hour.” She turned her head toward the dark glass. You couldn’t see anything in it but the lamp and the two of us. “It went during the goose. I always know. I’ve been here twenty-six years and I feel it shut, like a door in another part of the house. Do you know what my husband did in the first year we were married? He drove me across in July with eight minutes to spare, with the water coming over the road behind us like something poured out of a jug, and he laughed all the way. I thought he was the most alive man I’d ever met. I was twenty-two. I’d been playing maids in Frinton.”

I waited. With some people you ask. With her kind you let them work round to it, and they tell you more on the way than they mean to.

“He’s the one you want,” she said. “You know that already. Leo as good as drew you a picture.”

“He said it wants an education.”

“Edmund sat at that bench from nine years old. He could cut a wheel before he could shave. He’s taken thirty or so in all, Mr Cade, not eleven. Leo hasn’t found the half of them. He started four years ago with a little French carriage clock nobody’d looked at since the war, and he was sick afterwards. I mean literally. I held his head.”

“Where do they go?”

“A man comes. Or Edmund goes up to town with a suitcase.”

“What man?”

“I’ve never seen him. He telephones, and he says, Tell Mr Vane that Ronnie rang, and he rings off.”

I’d had the cigarette halfway to my mouth. I finished the journey, slowly.

“Ronnie who?”

“Sears. Is that right? It sounds like a shop.”

“It’s right,” I said.

It was right, all right. I looked at the fire for a bit. I hadn’t heard that name spoken aloud by anybody but me since 1988, and I’d mostly spoken it at night, to a ceiling.

I don’t want to make a meal of this. It hasn’t much to do with clocks. But you’ll want to know why I did what I did later, and some of it’s here. Ronnie Sears had a car lot on the Southend Arterial and an amusement arcade and a share in two clubs, and behind those he lent money, to the kind of people who can’t get it from a bank, at the kind of interest they don’t put on a poster. When the people couldn’t pay, things happened to them. In 1987 a thing happened to a man called Georgiou who ran a restaurant in Westcliff, and he was found in his own cold store, and I was on the team that looked into it. We knew it was Sears. We couldn’t get near him. So my guv’nor got a confession out of a nineteen-year-old kitchen porter with a mental age of about eleven, who’d have confessed to the Great Fire of London for a cup of tea and someone to be nice to him. And I was the one in the room. I didn’t write it. I didn’t hit him. I sat there and I witnessed it and I signed. Then, a year after, when it was going to appeal and they asked me, I said what had happened in that room. I’ve never been sure why. I wasn’t being brave. I think I just got tired of the kid’s face.

The porter came out. My guv’nor took his pension early. And I found that nobody in the Metropolitan Police would sit at the same canteen table with me, and that my wife had been hearing things, and one way and another by the end of that year I was a private citizen with a room in Leigh.

Ronnie Sears sent me a bottle of Scotch. With a card. I’ve still got the card.

“You know him,” Celia Vane said. She’d been watching my face.

“I know of him. How much does your husband owe?”

“A hundred and eighty thousand. That’s what he owed in the summer. I don’t know how it works, it seems to grow by itself. It started with the sea wall, and then there was the roof, and then there were some horses that were going to make our fortune, and then it was just to pay the last lot. He doesn’t tell me. I go through his pockets. That’s what twenty-six years comes to, Mr Cade. I go through his pockets while he’s in the bath.” She tapped ash into the grate, exactly, without looking. “A hundred and eighty thousand pounds. You can’t pay that off in carriage clocks.”

“No.”

“No. So what would you do? If you were Edmund. If there were one thing left in the house that’d clear the whole of it in a night, sitting on a table in the library under a cloth.”

“I’d be very tempted,” I said.

“He’s past tempted. It’s tonight.”

The French windows banged. The lamp dipped and came back.

“How do you know?”

“Because Ronnie rang. On Thursday. I took the call. He didn’t say tell Mr Vane Ronnie rang. He said, Tell him the boat’ll be there at the slack.” She said it in a flat voice, another man’s voice; she was good. “I’ve lived on this island since I was twenty-two. I know what the slack is. It’s the top of the tide, when the water stops. It’s the only time you can bring a boat into the Hythe on a night like this without losing it. Tonight that’s a quarter to one.”

“House time.”

“A quarter to two by your sock.”

“And you’re telling me this why? You want him stopped?”

She got up. She came over to the fire. She was a tall woman and in her shoes she could look me in the eye, and she did. That scent again. I found out later what it’s called. I can’t smell it now without my heart doing something a doctor wouldn’t like.

“I want him watched,” she said. “That’s all. I’m not asking you to do anything to him. You heard Leo. He’s told that table there’s a man finding out. Edmund knows it’s you. Kit knows it’s you, and Kit’s twenty-four and thinks his father’s Lord Byron. And at a quarter to one there’ll be a boat at the Hythe with one of this Sears’s people in it, expecting to be handed a million pounds in a box. And between here and the Hythe there’s half a mile of sea wall in the dark, and my husband, who’s been drinking since noon, and who’s got a bad knee, and who—” She stopped. She put the back of her hand against her mouth for a second. It was well done. I’m saying that now. At the time I didn’t think it was done at all. “They don’t need him once they’ve got it, do they?
