People like that. What’s a hundred and eighty thousand to them against the clock? They could take the box and settle the debt both, with one shove. Nobody’d ever know. He’d have gone off the wall drunk. It’s happened here before.”

“Mrs Vane—”

“I’ve been frightened for four years. I’d like to stop. I’d like somebody else to hold it for one night, somebody who knows what those people are. I’ll pay you. Whatever Fenn’s paying, I’ll double it. I’ve got some money of my own that Edmund hasn’t found yet. Stay near him. See that he gets to that boat and hands the bloody thing over and comes back up the wall on his own two feet. That’s all I want. I don’t care about the clock. Let them have the clock.”

“And Mr Vane senior? I’m supposed to tell him at one.”

“Tell him. Tell him it’s Edmund, he knows it’s Edmund. He’ll forgive him in the Hour and forget the lot by breakfast. Only the clock’ll be gone by then, and so will Mr Sears, and I’ll have my husband.” She looked at me. “It isn’t much of a husband. It’s the only one I’ve got.”

Now I’ll tell you what I thought, standing there. I was fifty-one and I’d been a detective for twenty years.

I thought: she’s lying. Not about the debt, or Sears, or the boat; all that had the feel of the real thing, and it checked with what I’d seen in Edmund Vane’s face. But there was something she wanted that she hadn’t said, and the fright was laid over the top of it like a coat of paint. I’d watched her decide on the stairs. I’d seen how quickly she could get a face on. A woman who turns her ring like that isn’t thinking about how to keep her husband.

And I thought: I don’t care. Because of the cold fingers, and the laugh she hadn’t expected, and because nobody had come and stood that close to me and asked me for anything in six years. And because of Ronnie Sears. You’ll have to believe that part. If somebody came to you and said the man who’d cost you everything was sending a boat, and would you like to be standing there when it tied up, I think you’d go and get your coat.

“I’m already working for one client in this house,” I said.

“I know. I shan’t tell him if you don’t.”

“That’s not how it’s supposed to go.”

“Nothing in this house is how it’s supposed to go, Mr Cade. It isn’t even the right time.”

There was a piano going somewhere, down the passage. Somebody had started to play. Slow stuff, rippling, like water going over stones. She turned her head to listen, and I saw the line of her throat above the green.

“That’s Kit,” she said. “It’s the Schubert. He plays it every year. His grandmother liked it.” She threw the end of her cigarette into the fire. “We’d better go in. They’ll be counting heads.”

At the door she stopped.

“What do I call you? I can’t keep saying Mr Cade. It sounds like a draper.”

“Harry.”

“Harry.” She tried it. “Find him for me, Harry. Don’t lose him. Whatever happens, come and tell me first.”

She went out. I stayed and finished my cigarette, and I took the Tissot out of my sock and strapped it on my wrist, under the cuff, where it belonged. I’d had enough of being told the time by other people.

It was twenty past ten. No. I mean it was twenty past eleven. You see how it gets into you.

I went along the passage toward the music with two clients, three whiskies too many, and a feeling at the back of my neck I hadn’t had in years, as if somebody’d opened a file on me. I got to the drawing-room door. I had my hand on it.

And every light in the house went out.

3. Lights Out

The piano stopped in the middle of a bar. Then it went on. I’ve thought since that that told you most of what you needed to know about Kit Vane. The lights die on him, and he stops for the length of a breath, and then he finishes the piece in the dark with nobody able to see his hands.

I stood in the passage with the door handle in my fist and waited for my eyes. There’s dark and there’s dark. In a town it’s never the real thing; there’s always a street lamp somewhere, or a glow in the sky. This was the real thing, a hundred yards of sea on every side and a gale, and it came down on that house like a lid. All I had was the noise. The wind. The piano. And the clocks, which I’d managed to stop hearing for the best part of an hour, coming back up out of the walls, every one of them, to let me know they didn’t run on electricity and never had.

I opened the door.

The drawing room had a fire, and that was all it had. It was a big room and the fire lit the front half of the people in it and left the rest to guess. I picked them out. The old man in a wing chair with a rug over his knees and the nurse on a stool beside him. Dame Octavia asleep, or dead, on a sofa with her mouth open. The vicar next to her, beating time on his knee, and not the time the boy was playing. Fenn standing. The daughter in the window seat, turned away from all of them, with the curtain pulled back in one hand, looking out at nothing. The cropped girl sitting on the floor against the piano’s leg, her green dress pooled round her boots. And the boy at the keyboard, a thin dark shape, with his head down.

No Edmund Vane. No Celia. No pink nephew.

“That’s the third time since Michaelmas,” Fenn said, to nobody. “There’s a transformer at Thorney that comes down if a gull sits on it.”

“It’s of no consequence,” said Leo Vane. “Let him finish.”

So the boy finished. It took another two or three minutes. I don’t know music; my wife used to say I’d got a tin ear to go with the tin heart. But I stood against the wall at the back of that room, and I’ll say that it got to me, that tune. It keeps coming round to the same place and it’s a little sadder every time it gets there. Somebody had liked it. Somebody who’d stood for her picture in grey silk about to say a funny thing. He played it as though she were sitting where the firelight stopped.

When it was over nobody clapped. The old man said, “Thank you, Kit,” and then, in the quiet, quite clearly: “She has gone up. She always goes up after the Schubert, and takes her shoes off, and comes down for the Hour. Imogen, did you see her go?”

The daughter didn’t turn round from the window. “Yes, Papa.”

“Was she tired?”

“A little.”

I got out. I’d come to that house for money and I’d take money for most things. But I wasn’t paid to stand and listen to that.

In the hall they were doing what people do. The big girl, Gail, was going round with a taper lighting more candles, with her tongue between her teeth. The cook had come up from the kitchen in her apron with an oil lamp in each fist and was setting them down, one on the table by the Font and one at the foot of the stairs, and telling the girl she was dripping wax on a floor that had been there since Henry the Eighth. The nephew was halfway up a stepladder for no reason I could see. He had a candle in his hand and he was explaining about fuses.

“It isn’t the fuses, Mr Toby,” the cook said. “It’s the whole Ness. It’s the whole of Thorney, come to that, you’ve only to look out the scullery. Get down off my steps.”

“I only thought, if one had a look at the box—”

“You’ll have a look at the box and I’ll have you on my floor with your neck broke, and a goose carcass to boil. Down.”

He got down. I liked that woman. I never exchanged ten words with her, but I liked her. She’d a face like a loaf and she ran that house the way a sergeant runs a company whose officers are all drunk.

I asked her for a light of my own. She looked me over, shoes last, the same as the old man had, and reached into a cupboard under the stairs and brought out a hurricane lamp, the kind with the wire cage, and lit it, and gave it me.

“You’ll want that if you’re going out,” she said. “And you’ll want a coat. It’s blowing a hooley.”

“What makes you think I’m going out?”

“You’re not the sort that goes to bed,” said the cook, and went back down her stairs. Mrs Pask, she was called. I’ve sometimes thought that if I’d spent the evening in her kitchen I’d have known more by midnight than I found out all night in the rain. But she wasn’t on Fenn’s list, and I’ve told you about lists.

I stood the lamp on the floor and thought about where a man would go.

He hadn’t been in the drawing room for the music. Nor had she. I didn’t know how long either of them had been gone; I’d been in that little room with her until a couple of minutes before the lights went, and I’d given her a start down the passage. So she could be anywhere. Powdering her nose. But him. The boat was for a quarter to two. It wasn’t half past eleven yet. If I had a box to carry half a mile along a sea wall in a gale, with a bad knee and a skinful, and wanted to do it without the family at the windows, I wouldn’t leave it till a quarter past one, with the old man already in the hall for his ceremony and everybody up and about. I’d do it early. I’d do it when I had the chance, and leave the thing somewhere handy, out of the house, and come back in and be seen.

And somebody had just handed him the chance. The lights were out, and everyone he was afraid of was in one room, listening to Schubert.

I picked up the lamp and went down the hall to the library.

The fire in there had burned low. It gave enough to see the bay of the window and the mahogany table and the square shape on the table with the green baize cover over it. Just as he’d left it at four. Just as the old man had it every night, he’d said, like a budgerigar.

I listened to the room. You get so you can. A room with a hundred thousand books in it is a quiet place, they soak it up. I could hear the fire settle, and the rain on the glass, and one clock, a slow one, somewhere over by the door.

One clock.

I went over to the table and put my ear down by the baize. Then I took hold of the corner of the cloth, between finger and thumb, and lifted it.

The glass case was there. The brass frame, the lock with its key. There was nothing in it. There was a square of darker wood on the tabletop where something had stood for years and kept the light off, and four small dents.

I put the cloth back the way it had been. I did it carefully. I don’t know why. I think it was respect for a neat job.

It was no night to be out in, and I’ll skip how I felt about it. I got my raincoat from the room upstairs and went out through a side door by the gunroom, into a yard, and the wind took me and stood me against the wall and went through my pockets. The rain wasn’t falling. It was going past, level, like something thrown. I had the lamp turned down to a bead and held low against my leg.

I hadn’t walked the island. I should have done that first, before the clocks; I’d have done it in the old days. But I’d looked at it from the library window for a while, and from my own, and I’d a fair idea. The house faced east. In front of it there was a sweep of gravel and then a long block of stables and outhouses with an arch in the middle and the clock tower over the arch. Behind the stables the ground fell to a creek. They called that the fleet. North of everything, on the far side of a spinney of bent trees, was the landing place, the Hythe, and you got to it along the top of the sea wall. The spinney was between. If I was carrying a box from the house to the Hythe, the spinney was where I’d break the journey.

I went along the side of the house and stopped at the corner.

There was a light. A long way off it seemed, though it can’t have been above eighty yards: a little yellow light, low to the ground, moving along the front of the stable block with a hitch in it. It went up and came down, up and came down, like a boat on a swell. I’ve tailed a lot of men. You get to know a walk. I didn’t need to see anything but the lamp to know which leg was bad.

He was carrying something in front of him with both arms, and the lamp was hung off his wrist or his little finger, and banged against the load. He went the length of the stable block and round the end of it and was gone.

I gave him a count of twenty. Then I crossed the gravel after him, on the grass edge where it didn’t crunch, with my lamp shut right down and my free hand on my hat.

I’d been in the open ten seconds when the clock in the tower went off over my head. There was a whirr first, and a clank, and then a bell. It was a small bell and a quick one, two notes, ting-tang, and then again, ting-tang. Half past the hour. I looked up. There was a bit of a moon somewhere behind the cloud, enough to make the sky a shade less black than the tower. I saw the clock face, and above the clock face, under a little pitched roof, there were two people standing.

I nearly dropped the lamp. I’m not ashamed of it. You come round a building in the dark at half past eleven on the trail of a man with a million pounds, and you look up and there are two figures forty feet over your head, a man and a woman, as big as life, looking down at you. One of them moved. The man’s arm came down and the bell went tang, and I understood. They were the things the boy and girl had been dressing. Wooden. A man with a hammer who did the quarters. A woman on the other side of the bell, bigger, with her hammer held up by her shoulder, waiting for the hour. Somebody had hung a black jacket on him, and a white shirt-front, and a bow. On her there was a shawl that the wind had got hold of and was streaming out sideways like hair.

I didn’t like them. I’ll say that now and get it over. I had no reason. But I didn’t care for the pair of them, stood up there in the weather in somebody’s cast-off clothes, hitting a bell every fifteen minutes for two hundred years whether there was anyone to hear it or not. The woman especially. She had a painted face, I could just make out, and a long painted gown under the shawl, grey. She looked patient.

The little man finished. The whirring ran down. I went on round the end of the stables with the back of my neck feeling like a dartboard.

Behind the stable block there was a track going down between a wall and the trees. I could see his light again. It had gone in among the trunks, and it wasn’t moving now; it was sitting still, about thirty yards in, and throwing the shadows of branches out across the track. I got in under a holly and waited. I had the rain down my collar and a twig in my ear. I’ve spent some of the best years of my life like that.

He was four or five minutes. I heard iron: a gate, a hinge that wanted oil. Then nothing, and the light got dim, as if it had gone down a hole. Then it came back. The gate again. And he came out of the trees onto the track with the lamp in his hand and his arms empty.

He passed within six feet of me. He was breathing hard and he was talking to himself, low, the way a drunk does who’s concentrating. I caught some of it. He said, “Right. Right. That’s that, then.” He stopped and stood, swaying a bit, looking back up at the black bulk of the house with its few lit windows. He stood there a good half minute in the rain, without a hat, a big man in a dinner jacket with his hair plastered down, and then he said something else. He said it quite distinctly.

He said, “Sorry, Ma.”

Then he went off up the track toward the house, with his limp.

I’ve given that to you as I got it. I didn’t know what to make of it then and I couldn’t make anything of it for a long time. He’d just put his father’s clock in a hole in the ground for a moneylender’s boat. If he’d said sorry, Dad, I’d have understood it. I put it down to the drink. I put a lot of things down to the drink that night, his and mine.

When his light had gone I turned mine up and went into the spinney.

It wasn’t a hole in the ground. It was a hump in it: a mound about as high as my shoulder, grown over with ivy and old elder, and in the side of the mound a brick arch, and in the arch a gate. Iron bars, close together, the kind they have on a vault. It was standing a few inches open. Behind it there was a short passage, brick, with a second door of wood at the end that stood wide. I put my hand on the gate and it swung in like a bank’s. It had a lock on it that was half a lock and half a latch: a tongue with a spring behind it, bevelled, that would ride over the catch when you pulled the gate to and drop home on its own. I worked it with my thumb. You could open it from outside with a key and from inside not at all. I’ve seen the same thing on a cell.

I took note of that. I’d have done better to take more.

I went in. It was cold the moment I got past the wooden door, a cold that had nothing to do with the night; that was October, and this was January. The passage came out on a little brick landing, and my lamp showed me a round room like the inside of an egg, domed over, all brick, sweating. I was standing at the top of it. A flight of steps went down the curve of the wall, steep, without a rail, maybe a dozen of them, to a floor I couldn’t properly see. There was straw down there, and sacking, and something that gave back the light, wet and grey, heaped. Ice. They had an ice house. In 1994. I suppose if you live where the electricity goes off whenever a seagull sits down, you keep your options open.

On the landing, just inside, against the wall, there was a wooden box.

It was a tea chest, more or less, a plywood crate with tin edges, the lid laid on loose and a length of sash cord round it. He hadn’t even nailed it. I set the lamp down and got on my knees for the second time that day. I undid his knot. It was a fisherman’s knot of some kind, done drunk, in the dark, by a man with a bad leg, and it was a perfect knot. I’d been told he had the hands.

I lifted the lid.

He’d packed it in a blanket, a grey army one, and under the blanket in a pillowcase. I folded the stuff back. The lamp shone on brass, and on glass, and on a white dial about as wide as a saucer with a painted moon looking out of a slot.

It was still going. He hadn’t stopped it. I knelt there on the wet bricks with the cold coming up off the ice, and I listened to one million two hundred thousand pounds ticking in a tea chest, and I’ll admit that for the space of one breath a thing went through my head that had no business there. I could have had the Granada. I knew a man in Southend who knew a man. I’m telling you because I said I’d tell it straight. Then I thought about the Wade, six feet under, and about the kind of people who buy that kind of clock, and what they’d do to the kind of man I am. And I thought about the old boy at his bench saying I should like to know why. I put the pillowcase back and the blanket over it, and the lid on, and I tied his knot again as well as I could, which wasn’t as well as he had.

I’m not a religious man. I don’t claim that last thought was the one that did it.

So. I had him. I had Edmund Vane with the clock in his arms, and the place he’d put it, and from his wife the time of the boat and the name of the man who’d sent it. It was twenty to twelve and I’d done what Fenn was paying two hundred a day for. I could walk back to the house and find the solicitor and tell him, and at one o’clock by the hall, with the door open and the family gathered, the old man could ask his son why.

And I’d promised a woman in a green dress, twenty minutes earlier, that I’d come and tell her first.

I stood on the landing and smoked a cigarette over it, with the lamp at my feet. It ought to have been simple. One of them had hired me straight and the other one was lying to me about something and wore scent. I looked down the steps into the well, at the straw and the wet grey heap. I thought, it’s a long way down for a man who’s had a few. And then I thought about what she’d said. One shove. Nobody’d ever know.

I went out and left the gate the way I’d found it. A few inches open. That’s the kind of thing I notice about myself afterwards. I was so careful not to disturb anything.

I didn’t go back by the yard. I wanted to see the Hythe while I had the chance, and the ground between. So I pushed through the spinney to the far side and came out on the sea wall.

It’s an earth bank with a path along the top, and that night there was nothing on the other side of it but noise. I climbed up, and I had to hold my hat on with both hands and lean. The water was right there. In the afternoon it had been a quarter of a mile off across the mud, and now it was slapping at the stonework eight or ten feet below my shoes, black, with the white coming off the tops of it and blowing in my face. You could taste it. The whole of that flat country I’d driven across was gone. It was the North Sea, all the way to the wall I was standing on, and the wall didn’t seem a great deal to be standing on.

I looked for the mainland. There should have been the lights of Thorney, but the cook had said the whole village was out. There was nothing. No, there was one. It was a single yellow light, low down, a mile off perhaps, hard to say.

It was moving.

I watched it. I thought at first it was a boat, and my stomach went tight, because a boat meant Sears’s man and he was two hours early. But it wasn’t a boat’s light. A boat’s light swings and this one bobbed. It came on slowly and steadily in a dead straight line, and it took me a while to understand why the line was so straight, and then I did. It was coming along the Wade. Somebody was on that road, with a lantern, in the dark, with six feet of sea on top of it.

I’m a townsman. I stood on that wall and I couldn’t make it mean anything. A man can’t walk in six feet of water. A car can’t drive in it. And still the light came on, a yard or two above where the road had to be, rising and dipping, patient. Once it stopped for a while, about where I judged the middle was, where the dip and the little bridge and the black box on legs were, and I thought, that’s it, he’s gone. Then it came on again, lower, and slower.

I never saw what carried it. The rain came down like a curtain between us and when it lifted the light had gone, behind the point of the island or out for good, I couldn’t tell.

I’d seen a man that morning by the road with a big grey horse, lean, in a hat, who’d looked at my car and then at the house. I’d heard his name at dinner, and I’d seen what it did to a woman’s face. I remembered all that standing on the wall. But I couldn’t see what it had to do with me. I was there about a clock. Twenty years in the job, and I’d got it into my head that there was only the one story going on in that house that night. I thought I was in it, and everybody else was scenery.

It was five to twelve by the Tissot. I went back along the wall toward the house. I didn’t get as far as the Hythe. I never have seen it by daylight.

I came in by the yard, and I was passing the dining-room windows when I saw them.

Somebody had put a lamp in there, on the sideboard. The curtains hadn’t been pulled across that end, and I stood in the wet about ten feet off, in the dark, and looked into the room like a man at the pictures. The table had been cleared to the wood. On the sideboard, by the lamp, was a tray with decanters and glasses on it, and standing at the tray, with her back to the window, was a fair-haired woman in a green dress.

It was Celia Vane, I knew that, there was no mistaking the hair that time. She had a glass in her left hand, a balloon glass, a big one. With her right she was doing something to it that I couldn’t see, because her shoulder was in the way. Her elbow was up. She put something down on the tray, a small thing, dark, and picked up a decanter and poured, and swirled the glass round, twice, the way you’d warm a brandy. She lifted it and looked through it at the lamp.

Then the door of the room opened and her husband came in.

He’d got a dry jacket on. His hair was still wet. He said something, and she turned round with the glass in her hand and that smile on, and held it out to him. I’ve seen a lot of wives hand a lot of husbands a drink. It was the nicest thing I’d seen either of them do. He took it. He said something else, and laughed, and put his free hand for a moment on the side of her neck, under the hair, and she let him. She tipped her head against it. You’d have said they were fond of one another. I think now that you’d have been right, and that was the hell of it.

He stood the glass down on the sideboard to get a cigarette out. And the nephew came in.

The nephew came in backwards, the way he did everything. He had a candle. He was talking over his shoulder to somebody in the passage, and he backed into the room, and turned round, saw them, and jumped. He started apologising. I could see his mouth going. He made for the tray, and he had another glass in his hand, a balloon like the first, with something in it; and he was trying to pour himself a drink, hold a candle, and explain something to Edmund Vane with gestures, all at once, and he put his glass down to do it. He put it down beside the other one.

Edmund Vane lit his cigarette and laughed at him and clapped him on the back, so that the candle went out. There was a bit of business with matches. The old vicar wandered in at the door, smiling, with his hand out, and the nephew, who was a well-brought-up boy, picked a glass off the sideboard and put it in the old man’s hand. Then Edmund Vane picked up a glass, and drank some, and made a face, and drank some more.

I’m describing what I saw through a window in a gale, at ten feet, at midnight. I saw two balloon glasses go down side by side, and two get picked up again. I couldn’t tell you which was which. I didn’t try. I didn’t know there was any reason to. I was looking at her. She’d stepped back from the tray when the nephew came blundering in, back against the panelling by the corner clock, and she was standing there with her hands behind her, and she was watching the glasses. Just the glasses. Her eyes went from the one to the other and her face was the face she’d had on the fourth stair.

And the small dark thing was gone off the tray. She had it behind her back.

I thought: aspirin. I swear to you I did. Or one of those powders women take. I’d watched a woman put something in a man’s drink and I was standing in a flowerbed with the rain running off my hat, and I thought, she’s given him something for his head.

I’ve been asked how I could have been a detective. That’s fair.

I should have gone in then. If I’d gone in, and found Fenn, and said what I knew, the rest of it would have gone differently. I don’t know that it would have gone better. I’ve stopped being sure that there was a better. But it would have been somebody else’s night, and I’d have been out of it.

I didn’t go in. What I did was this. I had it worked out that Edmund Vane would have to come back out of the house at about half past one, by my watch, to move his box from the ice house to the landing. I wanted to be there before him, somewhere I could see the track and the spinney both and not be seen, and somewhere dry, because I’d had about enough. I wanted a place to sit for an hour and a half with a view. And I’d noticed, coming round the end of the stable block, a door at the foot of the clock tower.

I went back across the gravel. The two up on the tower were only shapes. I didn’t look at them long.

The door was a plank door with a thumb latch and it wasn’t locked. Inside it smelled of leather and horse and mice. I turned the lamp up. It was the room where they’d kept the harness when there were horses to wear it: pegs round the walls, a couple of saddles on trees, going green, a bench, a heap of old rugs, a corn bin. In the far corner there was a wooden stair like a ladder going up through a hole in the ceiling, and from up the hole, very slow and heavy, came a sound like somebody cutting bread with a saw. Tock. And a long wait. Tock. The works of the tower clock, up over my head.

There was a little window on the side toward the trees. It would do. I’d be able to see his lamp when he came.

I remember what I did next quite clearly. I set my own lamp on the corn bin. I took my hat off and shook it. I got out the half-bottle I’d had in my raincoat pocket since Leigh, because it was the first chance I’d had, and I unscrewed the cap. I looked at my watch. It was ten past twelve.

I heard the floor behind me, one board, and I started to turn round.

I’ve been hit before. I was hit with a bottle in Stratford in 1971 and a length of scaffold pole in the Balls Pond Road. I know how it’s done by people who do it for a living, and this wasn’t that. It was all wrong. It was too hard, and too high, and it was swung flat instead of chopped, with the whole body behind it. That’s how a kid does it who’s never hit anybody and is so frightened that he shuts his eyes. I got an arm halfway up. I saw the lamp, and the wire cage on it, and the whisky going out of the neck of the bottle in a long brown rope and turning over in the air. I thought, that’s a waste.

The stair in the corner tilted up and stood on its end. Something like a door slammed, a long way inside my head.

Then I was lying with my face on a horse rug that smelled of ammonia, and I couldn’t get my eyes to open, and somebody was saying, a long way above me, in a high cracked whisper, a young voice, scared half out of its wits:

“You tell him. You tell Sears he’ll get his money. You leave my father alone.”

Feet went away from me across boards. A door banged. Up in the tower the clock cut another slice.

I thought, I’ll get up in a minute. I thought I’d just lie there till it stopped going round.

That was at ten past twelve. I know it, because the glass on my watch got cracked right across when I went down, and I looked at it just before, and the hands were the first thing I saw when I could see anything again. I’ve had to do sums about that night ever since. Everybody who was there has. That one’s mine. Thirty-five minutes.

4. A Quarter Past One

I came up out of it the way you come up out of a tube station, a step at a time, with the noise getting louder.

First there was the smell of the rug. Then there was the clock overhead, cutting its bread. Then there was my own head, which felt as if somebody had opened it with a tin-opener and left the lid up. I lay and looked at a thing in front of my face without knowing what it was. It was round, with a crack across it, and two little sticks on it, one long and one short. I worked at it. It was my watch, on my wrist, about three inches from my nose. The long stick was on the nine and the short one was just short of the one.

A quarter to one.

I said it aloud. It came out like a man talking through a blanket. I’d been there thirty-five minutes on a floor, and nobody had come to see if I was dead.

I got onto my hands and knees and was sick on the boards. Then I got hold of the corn bin and stood up by stages. The lamp had gone over when I did. It was lying on its side with the glass smashed and the paraffin run out of it into the dust, and why the whole place hadn’t gone up with me in it, I don’t know. Somebody up there was saving me for something. There was a faint grey square in the wall that was the window, and by that I found my hat. I found the half-bottle, too, by treading on it. There was an inch left in the corner and I drank it, and it stayed down, more or less.

Beside the door I put my hand on what he’d hit me with. He’d dropped it as he ran. It was a cricket bat. A good one, old, with the rubber gone from the handle and the face brown with years of linseed oil. I held it in the grey light and felt along the edge and there was something sticky there that was me.

A cricket bat. In my time I’ve been threatened with a sawn-off, a bayonet, and an Alsatian. Twenty years I’d got through, and I’d been laid out in a harness room by a music student, with a thing they give to schoolboys. You leave my father alone. He’d thought I was from Sears. He’d watched his grandfather stand up at that table and say there was a man in the house finding things out, and he had looked round for the hard face among the guests and found it, and gone and got his bat. I couldn’t even be angry with him. I’d have liked a son who’d do that for me. I’d have liked one who knew where I lived.

I felt the back of my head. There was a lump there like half a tennis ball, split, and my collar was stuck to my neck. I could stand. I could see, more or less, though things had a second edge on them, a ghost about a quarter of an inch to the left. I’ve had concussion before and I knew the drill. You don’t drive. You don’t sign anything. You don’t trust what you think for the next twelve hours.

I’d like you to remember I said that.

I opened the door. The wind had gone round. It wasn’t in my face any more as I looked across at the house; it was coming from behind the stables now, colder, and the rain had thinned to a kind of flying wet. There was more light. The cloud had torn in places and what there was of a moon was getting through the holes, on and off, so that the gravel went from black to grey to black again while you looked.

I stood in the doorway holding on to the frame. I was trying to think what I’d been doing. The spinney. The box. A quarter to two, the boat. I had an hour yet. I’d have given the two hundred a day for a chair.

That was when I saw the dress.

Somebody was coming along the front of the stable block from the direction of the house. Quick, light steps on the gravel. No lamp. I pulled back into the door. The moon came through for about three seconds, and I saw a woman, bare-armed, hugging herself against the cold, half running. And I saw the colour. Even by that light you couldn’t miss it. Green.

She went by ten yards from me and didn’t see me, and went in under the arch in the middle of the block. I heard a door scrape somewhere in there, and a voice call something, low, a name, and the door shut.

I thought: Celia. I thought it without thinking, the way you put a name to a tune. She’d come out to the stables, without a coat, in the middle of the night. To meet somebody. To look for her husband. To look for me.

I was going to go after her. I let go of the door frame to do it, and my eyes went past the arch and across the gravel to the house. I wanted to see how many windows were lit.

There weren’t many. The hall. A glow upstairs somewhere. And at the near end on the ground floor, the garden end, where the little room was with the desk and the sofa, there were French windows, and they had a lamp behind them. In front of the lamp, at the glass, looking out, stood a woman in a green dress.

She had her arms up, her hands flat on the panes on either side of her head, as if she were holding the windows shut against the wind. She was eighty yards away. The lamp was behind her. But I saw the dress, and I saw the colour of it where the light came through the skirt.

I looked at the arch. I looked at the window.

I’ve been over this more times than I can tell you. I put my watch up to my face in the moonlight because it was all I could think of to do. I thought, well, at least I’ll know when I went mad. It said five to one. And I am telling you, on anything you want to name, that at five to one that night I saw the green dress go in under the stable arch, and I saw it in the morning-room window, and that the two things were not a minute apart. I’d been drinking, but by then I was sober. I’d been sick, and I’d been out cold on a floor for half an hour, and that takes it out of a man better than coffee. I knew what I saw. Work that out. I couldn’t.

I told you at the beginning there were two green dresses in the house. I’d stood in the hall with a whisky at seven o’clock and watched the pair of them. I knew it as well as I knew my own name. And it didn’t come into my head. Not then, and not that week. That’s what a knock on the skull does. You don’t lose what you know. You lose the string that ties one thing to another. I stood there and thought, she’s in two places. Then I thought, no, she went through the arch and round by the back and in at a garden door. She’d have had to do eighty yards in ten seconds, through a wall. And then I thought the thing that stuck, and it stayed with me the rest of the night and for a long time after.

I thought: I can’t trust anything that woman shows me.

So you see, I was right, in a way.

I leaned on the wall of the tower, out of the wind, and tried to get a cigarette going. It took three tries. My hands weren’t taking orders. The quarter-jack went off above me while I was at it, one o’clock less a quarter by nobody’s time but his, and I didn’t look up.

I’ll tell you how long I stood there, because it matters. I smoked about half the cigarette. Call it five minutes. The window in the house went dark; somebody had moved the lamp, or blown it out. I never saw the dress come out of the stable arch again. But at what I afterwards made to be five past one, or a minute either side, I heard someone running.

It wasn’t on the gravel. It was behind me and to the left, down the track that went between the stable wall and the trees. It came fast, and it was somebody in the wrong shoes for it, slipping. I put my head round the corner of the tower.

She came up out of the dark of that track like something thrown. Both hands had hold of her skirt, up above her knees, and her head was down. The moon was out. I saw the fair hair blown across her face, I saw her face under it, and I saw the dress, which was green, but I wasn’t going by the dress any more, I’d finished with dresses. It was Celia Vane. She passed so near me that I got the scent, even in that wind. Her mouth was open and she was making a noise as she ran, not crying. It was more like the noise a child makes when it’s winded.

She had something in her right hand, held against the bunched-up skirt. It was a small dark bottle.

She didn’t see me. She ran straight across the gravel, lurching, and round the garden end of the house, and was gone.

I looked down the track, where she’d come from. The trees at the bottom were moving about against the sky. There wasn’t any light in among them. No lamp.

I dropped the cigarette. I knew then, the way you know when the telephone goes at four in the morning. I didn’t know what yet, but I knew what kind.

It’s sixty or seventy yards from the foot of the tower to that mound in the spinney. I don’t know how long it took me. I had to stop twice and hold on to things. I’d no lamp of my own any longer, only the moon, on and off, and the Ronson in my raincoat pocket, and I went in under the trees with my arm up in front of my face and the wet branches hitting it.

The mound was a shape. The arch in it was a darker one. I put out my hand for the iron gate that I’d left standing a few inches open an hour and a half before.

It was shut.

I pushed it. It gave about a quarter of an inch and stopped dead, with a little clink, the way a gate stops when the tongue of a spring lock has dropped into its keep. I shook it. It was a good gate. Whoever had built that ice house had meant the ice to stay his.

“Vane,” I said. Then louder. “Vane!”

Nothing. The wind was going over in the tops of the trees. Under that, from in front of me, from inside the mound, was a small steady sound that I couldn’t place for a second, and then I did. It was water, dripping, a long way down.

The wooden door at the inner end of the passage was still wide open, as I’d left it. I could just see the paler oblong of it, six or seven feet in from the bars, and beyond that nothing, black. I got out the Ronson. I had to turn my back to the wind and hunch over it to get a flame, and then I turned round with my hand cupped and put my arm through the bars as far as the shoulder and held the lighter out in front of me, and looked along my arm.

You don’t get much from a lighter. A yellow leaf about an inch high, jumping. It showed me the brick of the passage and the edge of the landing. It showed me there was no crate where I’d left the crate. And past the landing, where the floor fell away, it got down just far enough into the dark of that round room to touch the bottom of the steps. Twelve feet off, perhaps. Fourteen.

There was a man lying there.

He was on his back on the straw, with his legs up the last three steps, higher than his head, the way no man lies who’s got any say in it. He had a white shirt-front on and a black jacket. One arm was thrown out wide, and the hand lay palm up in the wet where the ice had been running, and the fingers were curled a little, and they weren’t moving. There was a ring on the small one. I saw it catch.

His face was toward me, tilted back. It was Edmund Vane. His eyes were open. They weren’t looking at me, or at the light, or at anything. The flame was in them, two little yellow points, and they didn’t blink at it. And the side of his head that was toward the steps, the left side, above the eye, was dark and wet and it had no business to be that shape. It went in where it should have gone out.

I held the flame there until the lighter burned my thumb. I said his name three or four more times. I rattled the gate like a monkey. He didn’t move. His chest didn’t move, not that I could see, under the shirt-front, by that light. Nothing in that place moved but the flame and the water dripping.

I pulled my arm back through the bars and looked at my watch. I didn’t decide to. It’s what’s left when everything else has gone: you note the time. The glass was cracked across but the hands were plain enough in the lighter. And I’ll set it down here just as I’d have set it down in the pocketbook, for the coroner, in the days when I had one.

By my watch it was a quarter past one, and Edmund Vane was lying at the bottom of the ice-house steps with his eyes open and the left side of his head the wrong shape. I have seen what dead looks like. It looks like that.

I’ve been asked, and I’ve asked myself, why I didn’t get in to him.

I couldn’t. That’s the answer, and it’s a true one, as far as it goes. It was an iron gate on a spring lock and I had a penknife. There were two keys to that gate in the world, I learned afterwards. One of them was in the pocket of the man at the bottom of the steps. The other was on a ring on a nail in the cook’s kitchen, and I didn’t know that. If I had known, I’m not sure I could have walked that far and back with my head the way it was. I got down on my knees and tried the lock with the blade and broke the blade. I got my shoulder to the bars and all that did was start my scalp bleeding again. I found a bit of branch and tried to lever the thing off its hinges, and the branch snapped and I went down on my face in the leaf mould. I lay there a minute. I think I might have gone out again for part of it.

But that isn’t all of the answer. There’s another part, and I’ve had it out with myself enough times to say it.

I didn’t try as hard as I would have for a living man. I’d looked along my arm at him for the best part of a minute, and I’d made up my mind. I had been a police officer for twenty years, eleven of them in plain clothes. I’d been to the canal and the railway line and the bedsit with the gas on, and to Georgiou in his cold store with the frost in his eyebrows. You get so you know it from the door. You don’t need to take a pulse. There’s a way they lie. There’s something about the eyes; they go flat, like a fish on a slab. I’d never been wrong. Not once, and some of those I’d have given a month’s pay to be wrong about.

I knew he was dead. So I got up off the ground and started thinking like a copper, and stopped thinking like a man who’s found another man hurt. There’s a difference. One of them runs for a doctor. The other one starts asking who.

And I knew that too. I’d seen her run.

She hadn’t lit the lamp again. I came round the garden end of the house, keeping a hand on the wall, and the French windows were dark, and I thought she’d gone. Then I saw one of them was open a few inches, moving in the wind. I pushed it and went in.

The fire had burned down to red. That was all the light there was, and it was enough. She was sitting on the floor in front of it. Not on the sofa. She was on the hearthrug, with her back against the sofa’s front and her legs out, like a doll somebody had put down. She’d lost a shoe. The green skirt was dark to the knee with wet, and there were dead leaves stuck to it.

On the rug by her hand a small brown bottle stood upright, with a cork in it. It was a medicine bottle, ribbed. It had a label that I couldn’t read from there.

She looked up at me. I don’t know what I looked like. There was blood down the side of my face and mud down my front, and I’d come in from the garden at twenty past one in the morning without knocking. She didn’t scream. She didn’t even seem surprised.

“You’ve been there,” she said.

“I’ve been there.”

“Is he—” She stopped. She wet her lips. “I couldn’t get in. I hadn’t the key. I called him, and he didn’t—I could see his hand. That’s all I could see. I had a candle in a jar and it blew out. I could just see his hand, on the floor, in the water. With his ring on it.”

“He’s dead, Mrs Vane.”

I said it flat. I wanted to watch it land.

I’ve done that a good many times as well, told a woman her husband was dead and watched her. Most of them, you learn nothing from it. They cry, or they don’t. But there’s a kind where you can see it isn’t news. They’ve known for an hour, or a day, and what you see in their face when you say the words is something more like a door closing. Up till then, they could hope they’d got it wrong.

That was her. She shut her eyes. She breathed in very slowly through her nose and let it out, and a shudder went down the whole length of her, and then she was still.

“Yes,” she said.

I went over. I got down, which hurt, and picked up the bottle and held it to the fire. The label was the chemist’s in Maldon. Under the chemist’s name somebody had typed: Mr L. Vane. The Mixture. One 5ml spoonful in water at night. Not to be repeated. And under that was a line in red capitals that said CHLORAL HYDRATE and something about keeping it away from children.

It was a little under half full.

“How much was in it?” I said.

“It was new on Thursday. The nurse keeps it on a tray in the old man’s room, with his spoon. He has one spoonful, and it knocks him out for six hours, and he’s eighty-one and weighs nothing.” She was talking with her eyes still shut. “I thought, Edmund’s twice the size of him. And he’s got a head like teak, for drink, he’s been pickling it for twenty years. One spoonful wouldn’t touch him. I didn’t know how much. I didn’t know. I thought, he’s got to go out like a light. He’s got to be flat on his back on that sofa by half past twelve, and stay there till the tide’s gone, or it’s no use.” She opened her eyes. “I put in half the bottle.”

“In his brandy. In the dining room. At midnight.”

“You saw.”

“I saw you give it him. I thought it was aspirin.”

That nearly made her laugh. It came up, and it turned into something else on the way, and she put her hand flat across her mouth to keep it in.

I sat down on the edge of the sofa. I had to. The room was going round, slowly, like a gramophone record, with her in the middle.

“You’d better tell me,” I said. “Not the one you told me before. The other one.”

She told me. She told it to the fire, mostly, in that trained low voice. She kept turning her ring.

“There were two things in his pocket on Wednesday,” she said. “While he was in the bath. I said I went through his pockets. There was a passport. His. A new one, he’d had the photograph done in Colchester, he looked like a wanted man. And there was an envelope from a travel agent’s with a ticket in it. Harwich to the Hook of Holland, the day boat, tomorrow morning. Sunday. One ticket, Harry. One passenger and no car.”

“He was going with the clock.”

“He was going with the boat. I’d worked it out by Thursday night, after that man rang. They weren’t sending someone to collect a parcel. They were sending someone to collect Edmund. He’d hand it over, and they’d take him off with it at the slack, round to Harwich, I suppose, or wherever these people do things. They’d give him whatever it was worth less what he owed. There’d have been a lot left. You could live a long time in Holland on a million pounds less a hundred and eighty thousand. Or wherever he was going on to. Without me.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I’ve been married to him for twenty-six years, I know what one ticket means. He wasn’t going to tell me. He was going to stand in the hall at one o’clock with his father’s door open and all of us there, and smile, and then go out for a breath of air. And I’d have woken up tomorrow in this house with Leo, and a hundred copies of clocks, and the debts, and Kit. And a note, if I was lucky. He’s quite good at notes.”

The fire shifted. A bit of ash fell through.

“So it wasn’t Sears’s people you were frightened of,” I said.

“Oh, I’m frightened of them. I’m not a fool. But no. That was for you. I had to give you something to make you stay close to him, and I didn’t think you’d do it for a wife who was being left. Men don’t. They think it’s funny.” She looked at me then. “I didn’t want him hurt. That part was true. You can believe that or not. I wanted him stopped. I thought, if he’s asleep, he can’t go. If he misses the tide, they can’t wait for him; a boat can’t lie at the Hythe ten minutes past the slack, not in this. They’d have to go without him and without the clock. And then in the morning he’d wake up, and it would be daylight, and Sunday, and he’d have a head on him, and I could say—”

“What?”

“I don’t know. Something. I hadn’t got that far. I’d have had another day. I’ve been getting through it a day at a time for years. You’d be surprised how long you can do that.”

“And I was the insurance. If the dope didn’t take, I’d be on his heels.”

“Yes.”

“You might have told me the truth and asked me to sit on his chest.”

“Would you have?”

I thought about it. “No.”

“No.” She pushed the wet hair back off her face with her wrist. “It didn’t take. Not the way I thought. He drank about half of it and pulled a face and said the brandy was corked. Then Toby got in the way, and the vicar wandered off with a glass, and Edmund was just—he was perfectly all right. He sat with us. He was a bit slow. He was yawning. At half past eleven he got up and said he was going to see to the generator, and he walked out of the room quite straight. I sat there. I thought, I’ll give him five minutes. I couldn’t follow him straight out, Imogen was watching me, she watches everything. And then I couldn’t find a lamp, and I couldn’t find you. I looked for you. Where were you?”

“Lying down.”

“I went all through the downstairs. I stood at that window for I don’t know how long, trying to see a light, trying to get up the nerve to go out. I’m a coward about the dark. I always have been. In the end I took a candle in a jam jar off the kitchen sill and went. I knew where he’d have put it. He’s used the ice house before, he thinks nobody knows.” She stopped, and put her hands together between her knees. “The gate was shut. I held the jar up to the bars. I saw his hand. I said, ‘Edmund, don’t be an idiot, get up.’ I actually said that. And then the candle went out, and I was standing in the dark with him down there, and he didn’t answer. I knew. You do know. It’s not like someone asleep. It’s like a room with nobody in it.”

She’d said what I’d felt, the same as I’d have said it. Maybe that was what did it.

“He’d gone down those steps to fetch his box,” Celia Vane said. “With half a bottle of that stuff in him and a bottle of Scotch, in the dark, on that knee. He’d have got to the top, and it would have come over him all at once, the way it does with Leo. Leo’s legs go. One minute he’s standing and the next he’s just folded up. And there isn’t a rail on those steps. There never has been.” She picked up the brown bottle off the rug and looked at it. “I did that. Nobody pushed him, you needn’t look for anybody. I put half of this in a glass and I handed it to him and I smiled, and he said, ‘Thank you, old girl.’”

She set the bottle down.

“I killed him,” she said. I believed her. I still do.

I’d better say why. I’ve had a long time to pick at it, and I know how it looks to you. A man who’s been made a fool of once doesn’t like to think it was twice.

I believed her because it fitted, and in my trade that’s all belief is. I’d seen her put the stuff in the glass. I’d seen her run from the place with the bottle in her fist and that noise coming out of her. I’d seen him at the bottom of twelve brick steps with his feet higher than his head. And everything in between she’d just given me, without my asking, and it joined up. The single ticket. The lie she’d told me in that room at eleven, and the reason for it. I know when somebody’s making it up as they go. They watch you. She hadn’t once looked to see how I was taking it.

There were things that didn’t fit. I knew that at the time. The gate, for one. He’d gone in to fetch his box, and the gate had been shut and locked behind him, and a man doesn’t shut himself in a hole he means to come out of with his arms full. And the box. The box wasn’t on the landing. I’d held the flame to where it had been and there was only wet brick. I thought he might have had it in his arms when he went, and that it was down there with him in the dark, past where the lighter reached. I’ve said my head was bad. I had those two things, the gate and the box, and I knew they were wrong, and I couldn’t make them stay still long enough to look at. It was like trying to read a number plate from a moving car.

And there’s this. I wanted to believe her. If she’d killed him the way she said, then it was a stupid, pitiful thing done by a frightened woman who had wanted to keep a man, and not what I’d thought when she first came and leaned on that door. I’d pegged her as the other kind. I’d thought she was working me. Now here she was on a hearthrug with one shoe, telling me she’d done it, when all she had to do was keep quiet and let me find him in the morning with the rest of them. The other kind don’t tell you.

She was shivering. She had been all along; I hadn’t noticed. The French window was still open behind me and the room was as cold as the yard.

I got up and shut it. I took my raincoat off, wet as it was, and put it round her. She let me. She took hold of my hand, as I did it, in both of hers, and held on to it.

“What happens now?” she said. “You were a policeman. Tell me what happens.”

“There’s no telephone.”

“No. It went at eight.”

“And nobody gets off this island before half past five.”

“Twenty-five to six.”

“Then at twenty-five to six somebody drives to Thorney and knocks up the constable, and by eight there’s a detective inspector from Chelmsford standing in the hall with wet feet. He has the gate off. He finds your husband. He has a doctor to him, and they take blood. Then he finds out how much is gone from a bottle that was new on Thursday.” I heard myself saying it. It was like listening to a man in the next room. “They’ll call it manslaughter. They might try for more, with the passport and the ticket; a jury doesn’t like a wife who knew she was being left. Either way, you’ll be a long time finding out.”

“Kit,” she said. That was all. Just the boy’s name. Her hands tightened.

“And there’s a boat coming in twenty minutes.”

She’d forgotten the boat. I saw her remember.

“Oh God. They’ll come up to the house. If he doesn’t come, and the box doesn’t, they’ll come looking. Won’t they? They’ve got a million pounds waiting, they won’t just—”

“No,” I said. “They won’t just.”

I thought about Ronnie Sears’s man walking up the sea wall to Compline House, and what he’d do when he found the family gathered in the hall round an old man and an open door. I thought about the boy with his bat. I thought about the old man, at one o’clock, waiting to ask his son why.

Then I told you what I’d do. I mean I told her. I’m not going to dress it up. I’ve done some things I’m not proud of and I did them for worse reasons.

“Listen to me,” I said. “He fell. That’s all. He was drunk, and he’d been drunk all day, twelve people watched him put it away at dinner. He went out to see to the generator and he missed his way in the dark, and went into the ice house, God knows why a drunk does anything, and he fell down the steps. It’s an accident. It’s nearly true. It only wants a couple of things seeing to.”

“The bottle.”

“You’ll wash that glass he drank out of, if it’s still on the sideboard, and you’ll put this back on the nurse’s tray where you got it, and top it up from the tap to where it was. It won’t stand up to a chemist. It doesn’t have to if nobody’s given a reason to look. A man who’s been on Scotch since noon and falls on his head, they don’t go hunting for chloral. They’ve no call to.”

“And the boat?”

“The boat wants a box. If the box goes to the boat, the boat goes away. Sears gets his clock and your husband’s debt dies with him, and nobody comes up to the house. Then in the morning there’s nothing in that ice house for the inspector to wonder about, except a man who slipped. No crate. No story.” I looked at her. “I need to get through that gate. I need to get the box out from under him and along to the Hythe by a quarter to two, and shut the gate again behind me. Is there another key?”

She stared at me.

“On Mrs Pask’s ring,” she said. “In the kitchen. On a nail by the range. It’s the one with a bit of red wool on it.”

“Can you get it without being seen?”

“Yes.”

“Then get it.”

She didn’t move straight away. She was still holding my hand. She said, “Why are you doing this?”

There were a lot of answers to that. I gave her the one I could stand to hear myself say.

“Because I know who’s sending that boat. And I sat in a room once and watched some people fit up a kid for a thing he hadn’t meant, and I said nothing, and it cost me a year of my life to put right. I’m not going to stand in a hall and watch them do it to a woman.”

It was a good answer. Some of it was true, too. She got up on her knees on the rug, and my raincoat slid off her shoulders, and she put her cold hand on the side of my face, the side without the blood on it, and looked at me in the firelight for a long moment as if she were trying to see what I was. Then she kissed me.

I’d like to say it was a calculated thing and that I knew it. I’d like to say it was a real one and that I knew that. What I knew was that she tasted of brandy and salt, and that it was the first time in six years. And I knew that her husband was lying a hundred and fifty yards away with his eyes open. So did she. We both of us knew it, the whole time, and neither of us stopped.

Some clock in the corner of the room struck one, a thin little silver sound. Half past twelve, it said. It was wrong, like everything else in that house. It was half past one.

“The key,” I said. “Red wool. I’ll be outside this window.”

She went. She left the bottle on the rug, and I picked it up and put it in my pocket to give back to her, and forgot it. I found it there in my raincoat three days later, in Leigh, when I was looking for a match.

5. Slack Water

I waited for her on the terrace outside that window, on the garden side, with my back to the house wall. The wind had dropped. I noticed it then for the first time. It hadn’t gone, but the weight had gone out of it, and in the gaps you could hear the sea, which you couldn’t before. It was a long steady hiss from every side, like a tap left running in an empty house. The moon was out more than it was in.

I had my watch up to my face about every half minute. I’d got a job with a time on it and that was holding me together. There’s nothing like it. You can have your head split and your judgment gone and a kiss on your mouth from a woman who’s just told you she’s killed her husband, and if you’ve got to be somewhere by a quarter to two you’ll put one foot in front of the other.

She came at twenty to. She’d found a coat, a man’s waxed jacket off a peg, far too big, and a pair of gumboots, and she had a torch, a rubber one, with her hand over the glass so that the light came through red between her fingers.

“It’s not there,” she said.

“What isn’t?”

“The key. The ring. The whole ring’s gone off the nail.” She was out of breath. “And Mrs Pask’s not in the kitchen. There’s nobody in the kitchen at all. There’s a goose carcass in a pan and the back door’s standing open.”

I thought about that. I couldn’t get anywhere with it.

“Where is everybody?”

“In the hall, getting ready. Leo’s down. That girl’s got him in his chair by the door with a rug. Fenn. Octavia. I saw Imogen on the stairs—” She caught herself. “No. I don’t know what I saw on the stairs. I’m seeing things. Somebody in grey.”

“Did you put the bottle back?”

“You’ve got the bottle.”

So I had. I didn’t remember putting it in my pocket. I said I’d give it her after. I never did. That’s one more loose end I can lay at my own door.

“We’ll have to break it,” I said. “The gate. Is there a crowbar in this place? An axe?”

“In the gunroom,” she said. “By the side door. There’s a cupboard of tools.”

There was. I went in with her torch. I found a thing at the back about four feet long, iron, with a flat end, which I suppose they’d used for opening packing cases. I brought it out. And we went round by the back of the house and along under the sea wall to the spinney, the way I’d come home at midnight, the two of us, at seventeen minutes to two in the morning, to break in on a dead man. We never went near the stable yard.

I went in front. She kept the torch on the ground at my feet. The trees dripped. I had the bar over my shoulder like a rifle, and I was working out where to put the point of it, in between the gate and the brick, low, where the hinge was.

I never used it.

The torch came up off the ground and onto the mound, and the arch, and stopped. I heard her breath go in.

At a quarter to two the gate was open and the steps were empty.

I’m going to go through this bit slowly. I did it slowly at the time, and it’s the part I’d have been cross-examined on, if anyone had ever asked.

The gate was standing wide. It had been pushed right back against the brick of the passage, the way you’d open it if you wanted to bring something through. It wasn’t forced. I put the torch on the lock. The tongue was drawn back in, and there was a key in the keyhole, on the outside, with a ring hanging from it and half a dozen other keys on the ring. One of them had a twist of red wool round it. That was the one in the lock.

I didn’t touch it. I gave Celia Vane the iron bar to hold, and took the torch, and went in.

The crate wasn’t on the landing. I’d known that. I went to the edge and shone the light down the steps.

I can see it now. I’d only had the lighter before, and that had shown me a man and not much else. Now I had a proper beam. The steps went down round the curve of the wall, twelve of them, brick, worn hollow in the middle, with green on them. At the bottom there was the straw. There was a pile of sacking, and beyond that the ice, a long grey heap of it under more straw, with the wet running out from under and lying in a sheet across the floor. A meat hook hung from the middle of the dome on a chain. That was all there was. It was a round brick room with ice in it.

There wasn’t any man.

I went down. I went down with one hand on the wall, sideways, like a crab, because the steps were slimy and I’d seen what they could do. I stood where he’d been. The straw was pressed flat in the shape of a body. It was as plain as a bed that’s been slept in, the shoulders and the hollow for the head. Where the head had been, the straw was dark, and stuck together, and when I put my fingers on it they came away red. It was on the edge of the bottom step, too, a smear the size of my palm, with some hairs in it. Dark hairs going grey.

So I hadn’t dreamed him. That was my first thought, and I was glad of it. After the business with the dress I’d begun to wonder.

I shone the torch round. I looked behind the sacking. I looked over the ice, in case, God knows why, in case he’d got up and climbed onto it. I went the whole way round that floor, which took about fifteen seconds. He wasn’t there, and the crate wasn’t there.

There were other things. I’ll list them.

On the third step from the bottom, set down neatly out of the wet, was the stub of a candle in a saucer. It was a kitchen saucer, white, with a blue line round it. The wick was still soft.

In the wet straw by the ice was a spoon. It was a big one, silver, the kind you serve with. I picked it up. It had a crest on the handle.

There was a mark on the straw and across the wet floor, from where he’d lain to the foot of the steps. Something heavy had been pulled along. There were two furrows side by side, about the width apart of a man’s heels.

And there were footmarks on the steps themselves, in the green slime, going up. They’d been made by more than one person. One was a big smooth shoe with a leather sole, a man’s evening shoe. The other was a flat broad print with a pattern on it, something like a carpet slipper or a galosh.

“Harry.” Her voice came down from the top, very small. “Harry, where is he?”

“He’s not here.”

“What do you mean, he’s not there?”

“I mean somebody’s had him away.”

I heard the iron bar go down on the bricks. Then she was on the steps. She came down them faster than I had, in those gumboots, holding the wall. She stood at the bottom beside me and looked at the flattened place in the straw, and at my fingers, which I hadn’t wiped.

Then she said, “He’s alive.”

She turned on me. Her whole face had opened up. “He got up. He’s alive. Harry, he got up and walked out of here, he’s only—he hit his head, and he was out, and it wore off, or the cold brought him round. He’s gone up to the house.” She had hold of my lapels. “He’s alive!”

I’ve thought a lot about that minute.

It would be easy now to say she was right and I was a fool. I can only tell you what I was looking at. I was looking at two furrows in wet straw. A man who gets up and walks leaves footprints. He doesn’t leave heel-marks, side by side, in a line, like a plough. Those are what you get when a man is taken under the arms from behind and dragged, with his legs trailing. I’ve seen them on a carpet in Bethnal Green and across a car park in Ilford. And he hadn’t unlocked that gate himself, from the inside, with a key that turned only from the outside, and then left the cook’s ring hanging in it. And there’d been two people on those steps besides, one in slippers.

“Look at the floor,” I said. “Mrs Vane. Look at it.”

She looked. I showed her with the torch. I watched her read it. She was a quick woman.

“Somebody carried him,” she said slowly.

“Dragged him to the steps, and then carried him up. Two of them. And took the box.”

“But then he might—he might still have been—if they came and found him, and he was breathing, they’d have got him out, they’d have—”

“Who would? Who’s they?” I wasn’t gentle. I hadn’t the time. “If somebody in that house had found Edmund Vane at the bottom of these steps with his head broken and breath in him, what would they do? They’d shout the place down. They’d have every lamp on the island out here, and the old man’s nurse, and blankets. You’ve just come from the house. Was anyone shouting? You said they were in the hall getting ready for the party. You don’t quietly lift an injured man out of a hole and go back in for a drink.” I gave her a second with that. “People who move a body at night without telling anybody, and take a box worth a million with it, aren’t doing first aid.”

Her hands came off my coat.

“I saw him,” I said. “I had a light on his face for a minute by the clock. I’m sorry. I’ve seen a lot of them. He wasn’t breathing and his eyes were fixed. He’s been dead since before one, and somebody else knows it besides you and me. And they’ve had the best part of half an hour’s start.”

She stood there. The hope went out of her. I’ve done that to people before. It never gets any nicer to watch.

“Who?” she said.

“I don’t know. Whose is this?”

I held up the spoon. She took it and turned it to the torch.

“It’s ours. It’s one of the Vane spoons, there’s a dozen of them, they live in the pantry.” She frowned at it. “It’s what Mrs Pask uses for—” Then she shook her head. “I don’t understand. I don’t understand any of it.”

Nor did I. I’d got a candle in a kitchen saucer, and the cook’s keys, and a serving spoon, and a slipper print. If I’d had my head, I’d have stood still for five minutes and let those four things talk to one another. Every one of them said kitchen. Every one of them said somebody had come down here from the house on an errand, with a spoon in his hand, for God’s sake, and found a man on the floor. But I’d settled what kind of night it was hours ago. Somebody was coming for a clock, and a man had died of it. So I saw a clean-up. I saw two people who’d come and got rid of what they couldn’t afford to have found. I looked at a pudding spoon and I thought of Ronnie Sears.

It was eleven minutes to two.

“The boat,” I said. “It’ll be at the Hythe now. If they’re Sears’s, the ones who did this, that’s where they’ve taken him. And the box. It’s the only way off.”

“Then let them go. Harry. Let them take him, if he’s—let them have all of it. You said yourself, if the box goes to the boat—”

“And they put your husband over the side halfway to Harwich with a length of chain on him, and he’s never found, and you spend seven years waiting to be a widow, with every copper in Essex wondering where he went and why. Or they don’t bother with the chain. And he comes ashore at Clacton with half a bottle of chloral in him.” I started up the steps. “I want to see who they are. That’s all. I want to see a face.”

“You can’t even walk straight.”

“I walk better than he does.”

It was a rotten thing to say. She took it like a slap. I stopped halfway up and looked back down at her, standing in that brick well in a dead man’s jacket with the torchlight coming up under her chin.

“Go back to the house,” I said. “Go in by the garden and get that dress dry, and be in the hall when the old man opens his door. Stand where everybody can see you. Whatever happens tonight, you were with twelve people at one o’clock by the house. Do you hear me? You never came out here. You don’t know anything about any of it.”

“And you?”

“I’ll come and tell you first,” I said. “Like I promised.”

I left her the torch.

Outside the arch, in the mud, where the torch hadn’t been, I nearly went over something. I got the Ronson out and looked. It was a rut. It was a single line cut into the soft ground, a couple of inches deep and as wide as my hand, going away from the ice house and up the track toward the stable yard. Beside it on either side were the same two sets of feet, the evening shoes and the flat slippers.

One wheel. I thought about that for the time it took the flame to burn down. I didn’t know of any vehicle with one wheel.

I know now. So do you, probably. You’re sitting in a chair with a light on, and you haven’t been hit.

I let it go. It went up toward the yard and I was going the other way, along the wall, to the water.

That walk to the Hythe was about six hundred yards and I’d put it among the worst of my life. The sea wall’s a bank fifteen feet high with a path on top a yard wide, and nothing to hold. I’d walked along it at midnight with a gale trying to pick me off and thought that was bad. Now the gale had dropped and it was worse, because I could see. The moon was out, and on my left hand there was the whole of the tide, right up, brimming, as high as it would go. It was not a foot below the top of the stonework in places, and dead flat, and it wasn’t moving. I’ve never seen anything like it. Water’s always doing something. That water was just standing there, miles of it, as if it had come as far as it was going and was thinking what to do next.

That’s the slack. I hadn’t known what the word meant till I saw it. For a few minutes at the top of a big tide the sea stops. It holds its breath. Then it turns round and goes.

And ahead of me, where the wall bent, there was a light.

It was a small white one, low down, steady. As I got nearer I could see what it was fixed to. There was a wooden staging that ran out from the wall on piles, a jetty, maybe thirty feet of it, and it should have stood well clear. That night the sea was up between the planks. Lying against the end of it was a boat. I’d expected something flash, something with chrome. It was an open launch, twenty-odd feet, heavy, the kind they use for oysters, with a stump of a mast and an engine in a box. The light was a lantern on the mast. The engine was turning over, slow, with a noise like a man clearing his throat.

There was one man in her. He was standing in the stern with a line in his hand, holding her in against a post. He wore a long oilskin and a woollen hat.

I’d thought I might find three or four of them there. I’d thought I might find a box being lowered down, and a long shape in a blanket. I had nothing in my hands. I’d left the iron bar in the ice house.

There was one man and an empty boat. I stood on the wall above the jetty and tried to take it in.

He’d seen me. A torch came on in his fist and came up the bank and found my face.

“You’re late,” he said. “I’d have give you two more minutes.” It was a slow thick voice, local, with the vowels all sat on. The torch went down me and up. “Where’s the box?”

I walked down onto the jetty. The planks were under an inch of water and it came in over my shoes. I kept walking till I was close enough to see him. He was sixty, or near it. He had a wide flat face that the weather had been at, with white bristle on it and little pale eyes. His hands on the rope were like a pair of gloves stuffed with gravel. He’d handled a lot of boats in a lot of weather, and I didn’t think he’d have known Southend if you’d pushed him off the pier.

“You’re not Vane,” he said.

“No.”

“He said a big feller with a gammy leg. He said he’d have a box, heavy, and I was to help him down with it, and take the two of them round to Parkeston by five. Where is he?”

“Who’s he? Who told you all that?”

“I don’t know as that’s yours to ask.”

“A man called Sears?”

The pale eyes didn’t flicker. “I was give a telephone number,” he said. “I rung it Thursday, the way I was told. A feller said what I’ve said. And he give me two hundred pound in the Plough car park yesterday dinnertime in an envelope, and two hundred more to come. I never see who it was from. I don’t arst. I been running a boat off this coast for forty-four year, and you live longer not arsting.” He spat over the side, neatly, into the still water. “I was told a quarter to one. It’s gone that. I’ll not lay here after the ebb starts making. She’ll be running through that gut like a train in a quarter of an hour, and I’m not having my boat stove on this old staging for four hundred pound, nor yet for four thousand. Is he coming or isn’t he?”

“He isn’t coming.”

“Then where’s the box?”

“You haven’t got it?”

He stared at me.

“Nobody’s been down here? In the last half hour? Two men, maybe. Carrying something.”

“There’s been nobody down here,” the boatman said, “since I come in round the point. Only you. And a heron.” He shifted the rope to his other hand. “What d’you mean, have I got it? I come for it. If I’d got it, I’d not be stood here talking to you.”

I believed him. He had no reason to lie, for one thing. For another, I could see the whole of his boat. There was a coil of rope in her and a fuel can and a thermos flask.

So it wasn’t Sears. It hadn’t gone to the boat. Somebody had taken a dead man and a million-pound clock out of that ice house between a quarter past one and a quarter to two, and they hadn’t brought either of them here. There was nowhere else on that island to take them. There were ninety acres of it, and the sea all round, standing still.

“What’s your name?” I said.

“What’s yours?”

“Cade.”

That did something. He turned the name over. I watched it going round behind his eyes.

“Cade,” he said. “There was a Cade the feller spoke of. In the car park. He said, if you see a London copper name of Cade hanging about over there, you’re to tell him Ronnie says he owes him a drink.” He looked me up and down again, by the torch, as if I’d changed. “He said you was the one grassed up your own guv’nor.”

Nobody knew I was at Compline. Fenn knew, and a man at Pemberton’s. That was Wednesday I’d been hired. By Friday dinnertime a man was handing out envelopes in a pub car park at Thorney Staithe and mentioning my name.

I’d like to say I worked out then and there who had told Ronnie Sears. I didn’t, not then. I only felt the ground go, a bit, under my wet shoes, the way it does when you learn you’ve been in somebody else’s plans for longer than you’ve been in your own.

“You tell Ronnie,” I said, and I didn’t get any further, because the boatman had stopped listening.

He’d put his head up, like a dog. He was looking past me, over my shoulder, back along the wall toward the house.

“What’s that, then?” he said.

I turned round.

From the Hythe you could see the stable block end-on, black against the sky, across the dark hump of the spinney, three or four hundred yards off. The tower stood up out of it. I could make out the pale round of the clock face, and above that the little roof where those two stood.

There was a light up there.

It was right at the top, in among them. A yellow light, a lantern, moving about. I could see it going from one side to the other behind the uprights. It swung. Somebody was up on that tower, at the level of the bell, with a lamp in his hand, and he was swinging it in a slow arc, side to side, out toward the sea. Toward us.

“That’s him,” said the boatman. “That’s the signal. He was to show a light if it was off. Three swings and cover it. That’s a hell of a place to show it from. What’s he want to go up there for?”

“That’s not him.”

“Who is it, then?”

I didn’t know. I stood there with the water over my shoes and looked at that light going to and fro on top of the tower. I knew Edmund Vane had been dead for an hour. I’d seen him. Somebody else knew his signal. Somebody was standing up there with the wooden man and the wooden woman, in the place where the lamp was to be shown, showing it. I’ve said I’m not the type to feel things. I felt that. It went right down my back.

The clock began to strike.

You heard the works first, even at that distance, across the water. There was a grinding, and a run of the little bell, the quarters, ting-tang ting-tang ting-tang ting-tang. I thought of the wooden man in his dinner jacket, banging away. Then there was a gap. Then the big bell struck once.

One o’clock, by the house. It was two by me. I looked at my watch to be sure, and it was two exactly, the long hand straight up over the crack in the glass. I thought, the old man’s opening his door.

The bell hadn’t died away when the shots came.

There were two of them. They weren’t together. The first one was flat and heavy, a slam, and you felt it in your chest as much as heard it. After it, quick, before the echo was back off the house, came the second. I know a twelve-bore when I hear one. You don’t forget it. I’d stood behind a van in Walthamstow once while a man emptied one at us through a letter box.

Up on the tower the lantern jumped. It went up, and sideways, and then it dropped. It fell straight down the front of the tower, turning over, a little yellow spark. It went out before it hit anything.

And something else came down after it.
