They left me in a stable yard, in the rain, with the car. Kit said somebody would come. He and the girl went off across the gravel toward a tall tower with a clock on it, hand in hand, arguing about the fiver.

I looked about me. It was a long, low, handsome old place, the stables, built round three sides of the yard, and in the middle of the cobbles stood a block of stone with steps cut in it, about the height of a kitchen table, for getting onto horses from. I took careful note of that block. I did not know why at the time. I think some part of one does know. I sat down on it and emptied my shoes.

“That’s not a car,” said a voice. “That’s a roller-skate.”

I leapt up. There was a Land Rover in the yard, which had not been there a moment before, and getting out of it backwards, rather as one gets out of a bath, was the largest old lady I had ever seen. She wore a mackintosh that had seen service and a hat with a salmon fly in it. She had a face like a kind horse.

“Octavia Prowse,” she said. “You’ll be Dorothea’s grandson. You’ve got her legs. She was a great gawk of a gel too; we came out the same year. Why are you wet?”

I told her.

“Nobody reads the bottom of the card,” said Dame Octavia Prowse. “You were lucky. You made your mistake on the right side of it. I’ve said to Leo for twenty years, put it at the top, in red, a foot high. He says a man who can’t read a notice to the end deserves what he gets. And then he did lose one that way, and you’d think that would have settled it. But no. More stubborn than ever.” She looked at the Midget with real interest. “Does it go?”

“Not at present.”

“I had a hunter like that. Shot him.” She seized my hand and wrung it. “Well, come along in. You’re to have the Blue Room, Celia tells me, which is the one with the damp. Have you come to ask him for money?”

I went the colour of the car.

“Thought so. They all do, the ones who turn up. The ones who don’t want money stay at home, very sensibly, and send a card.” She set off toward the house at a rolling stride, and I trotted beside her. “I’ll give you a tip. Don’t ask him tonight till the door’s been opened. Before one o’clock he’s as tight as a tick; he’ll look at you through that glass of his and tell you what your watch cost. After one, it’s the Odd Hour, and he’d give you the roof if you put it to him nicely. That’s the rule. Nothing counts. I’ve seen him forgive a man in that hour for running off with—well. Never mind what with. But you’ll want to get it in writing, and cash it Monday.”

“That’s awfully good of you.”

“It isn’t good of me at all. I like to see somebody get something out of this family. God knows I never did.”

She stumped up the steps and in at the door, and I followed, and so entered my uncle’s house, and heard the clocks.

I am not going to describe the clocks. Abler pens than mine have had a go. I will say only that there were a great many of them, in the hall alone, and that they were all ticking, and that none of them was ticking at quite the same moment as any other. It was like being inside a typing pool. I stood on the mat and dripped. After a moment I found that I was breathing in time with the nearest one, and trying to stop.

“You get used to it,” said Dame Octavia. “Or you go mad. I’ve never been sure which Leo did.”

The Blue Room was at the top of the main stairs and along a passage. I found it by myself, the household being occupied, as far as I could judge from the smell, with a very large bird.

It was on my way there that the thing happened which, if this were a different kind of book, would have a chapter to itself with a quotation at the top.

I had got to the turn of the stair. I was carrying my suitcase in one hand and my shoes in the other, and I was thinking about a bath. Someone was coming down. I stood aside. And round the corner of the landing, carrying a small tray, came a girl.

I want to be accurate about this. She was not, by the standard of the magazines, a beauty. I have had it pointed out to me. She was small, to begin with; she’d have come up to about my tie-pin. She had sandy sort of hair, pulled back. She was very pale, with those almost colourless eyebrows that go with it. She wore a dark blue frock, absolutely plain, and flat shoes, and no paint of any kind. On the tray she had a brown medicine bottle with a cork in it, a spoon, and a glass of water.

She stopped, because I was in the way. She looked up at me.

She had eyes the colour of the sea off Cornwall on a doubtful day. It was a very thorough look. It started at my wet hair, went down the yellow pullover to my socks, where it paused, and came back up to my face. It took in the shoes in my hand and the crab, which I found afterwards was sitting on my shoulder. I can’t say what her opinion was. But I had the distinct sensation of being entered in a book.

“You’re dripping on the Jacobean,” she said.

It was a low, clear voice, with the north in it. Yorkshire, I learned. From the coast.

I looked down. I was standing on a strip of carpet about four hundred years old, and there was a pool.

“I’m most awfully sorry. I came by sea. I mean, I didn’t mean to. The car—”

“There’s a towel in the Blue Room. And there’s something on your shoulder.”

“Is there?”

“It’s alive,” she said. She said it quite gravely, as one might point out that a man’s shoelace was undone. Then she went on down past me with her tray. At the bottom she turned along the hall toward the back of the house without looking round. I stood on the turn of the stair with a crab on me and my mouth open, and I was a changed man.

I have been in love, by a conservative estimate, eleven times. I have married two of them, and am engaged to a third. I say this so that the reader may weigh my words. I had never before, and I have never since, been looked at by a woman in a way that made me want so badly to be a better kind of thing. I didn’t want to be more amusing, or richer. I wanted to be the sort of man who was not, at that moment, holding his shoes.

I put the crab out of the landing window. It was all I could think of to do for her.

The Blue Room was blue. It was also, as advertised, damp. There was a bed with posts, a washstand, a towel, and a small round table by the bed. On the table stood a little brass clock with a handle on top, about the size of a tin of cocoa, ticking away to itself in a fussy sort of manner.

I have gone over what happened next many times. Counsel for the defence would say that the table was unstable, that the light was poor, that the accused was a tall man in a low room in a state of emotional disturbance, trying to take off a wet pullover over his head. All this is true. The fact remains that my elbow came round, inside the pullover, like the boom of a yacht, and I heard something go.

When I got my head out the table was empty.

I looked under the bed. It was a high bed with a valance. The clock had rolled, or bounced, a surprising distance. I could see it right at the back, against the wall, on its side, still ticking. It looked hurt.

I went in after it. It was a tight fit, and dusty, and I had to go in on my stomach. I had just got my fingers to it when I sneezed, and banged my head on a slat. In backing out I put my knee on something that was not the floor.

I shall not forget the noise. I have described it elsewhere as like stepping on a budgerigar, and people have thought that I was straining for effect. I was not. There was a crunch, and then a sort of soft tearing sound, and then a single clear ping, and something small and bright shot out from under the valance, crossed the room at about the height of the skirting board, and went behind the washstand.

The ticking had stopped.

I sat on the floor of the Blue Room with what remained in my two hands. I am not mechanical. But it did not take a mechanic to see that this was no longer a clock in any useful sense. The front had come away from the back. There was glass, and a number of little wheels, some of which were still going round, slower and slower. Out of the middle of it a spring had got loose and was uncurling across my knee like a fern in one of those nature films.

I had been in my uncle’s house for nineteen minutes. I had come to ask him for five thousand pounds. And I had broken one of his clocks. He was, I had been given to understand, perhaps the greatest living authority on English clockwork, and a man who cared about nothing else on earth.

How good a clock was it? That was the question. I held the bits to the window. It had a name on the dial, in very small letters, which I could not read without my glasses, and my glasses were in the car, under the sea. It might be a nothing. A bedroom clock, for guests, bought by the dozen. Equally it might be the only surviving work of some Huguenot genius, a thing mentioned in books. In that house, how was one to know? They’d all looked ruinous to me.

I will be honest about what I did. I’ve had nine years to think of a better thing I might have done, and I have thought of several. I gathered up the remains: the case, the dial, the wheels, the fern. I fetched the bit from behind the washstand. And I put the whole lot in the right-hand pocket of my dinner jacket, which was hanging on the door.

I reasoned thus. If I left the pieces in the room, they would be found by whoever turned down the bed, and the hue and cry would go up before I had so much as shaken my uncle’s hand. If I put them in my suitcase, I was a thief. But a dinner jacket pocket was neutral ground. I should have the thing about me. And at a suitable moment, I should take my uncle aside and produce it, with a manly word. I’m afraid, sir, I’ve had a bit of an accident with your Tompion. He would respect that. Some time after one o’clock, I thought, when nothing counted.

I had a bath, in rusty water. I dressed. The dinner jacket, which I’d had since I was seventeen, had a tendency to ride up at the wrists. With a third of a clock in the pocket it also hung down on one side and clanked a little when I walked.

At five minutes to six by the house, a number I was already learning to say, I went down the stairs to meet my relations. I had a crunching pocket and Cornish eyes on the brain, and the idea that the evening could hardly get worse.

There was a basin on the hall table. A tall fair woman in a green dress was standing beside it, with her hand out, and she was looking at my wrist.

2. In Which We Are Thirteen

The basin was called the Font. It was explained to me by the fair woman in the green dress, who was my cousin Edmund’s wife, Celia, and who had the kind of voice one associates with the better sort of railway announcement. Guests at Compline gave up their watches at the door. It was my great-uncle’s rule. One had them back with the kedgeree.

I said, “Oh, rather,” and began to roll up my cuff, and then I stopped.

I have promised to explain the watch. In the spring of that year I had been attached, briefly, to a girl called Fenella who worked in advertising. Fenella held that I took myself too seriously. I have never been able to see this; I should have said the difficulty was all the other way. But she held it, and for my birthday she gave me a wristwatch with Mickey Mouse on the dial. His arms were the hands. He wore yellow gloves, and at twenty to four he looked as if he were directing aircraft. Fenella said it was ironic. She left me in June for a man who made documentaries, and I went on wearing the watch. It kept excellent time, and I could not at that stage afford another.

There is nothing wrong with a Mickey Mouse watch in Fulham. I wish to make that clear. Things are different when one is about to lay it in a pewter basin of the sixteenth century, on top of a thing by Patek Philippe, with a family looking on.

“I say, must I really? Only it’s a bit—”

“Everybody must,” said Celia Vane. “Even the vicar.”

I unstrapped it. I held it over the Font, and it was at that moment that my cousin Kit came down the stairs, in a dinner jacket, with the girl Saskia. He looked into my hand.

“Good God,” he said.

“It was a present. From a girl. It’s ironic.”

“What’s ironic about it?”

“Well. I mean. One wears it ironically.”

“Does Mickey know?” said Kit.

I let it go. It lay there among the gold ones with one glove pointing at six and the other at twelve, in the attitude of a man surrendering. I found that I rather missed it.

I now met my family. I shall introduce them in the order in which they frightened me.

My cousin Edmund frightened me first. He was fifty-two, about my height and twice my width, and good-looking in the way that cabinet ministers used to be. He had a tumbler in his hand which he seemed to have been issued with at birth. He looked at me for some time and said, “Dorothea’s lot. You’ll have come for money,” and when I began to explain about the Thracian valley he said, “Don’t. I can’t bear it. I’ll tell you what, I’ll toss you for who asks him first,” and laughed, and gave me a whisky the size of a vase. I never knew, with Edmund, whether I was being teased or warned. I can say that he gave me the drink, and that in my experience the men who really mean you harm don’t.

My cousin Imogen frightened me second. She was quiet, in black, with a white streak in her dark hair like a badger’s, and she had a way of looking at one as if deciding which century one had been painted in. She restored pictures. She asked me what I did, and I said wine, and she said, “And is it going well?” in a perfectly kind voice. I heard myself say, “Not awfully,” which I had not said to anybody, including my mother.

There was a solicitor called Fenn. He looked like a solicitor. There was a vicar called Stiles, a dear old boy with cotton wool in his ears, real cotton wool, who shook my hand and said, “And how is your father keeping?” My father had been dead eleven years. I said, “Much the same,” and he was delighted.

And there was the man Cade.

I have mentioned him. He was presented as a Mr Cade, from the insurance company, who had come to count the clocks. Well. I am not a noticing person. But I had been turned down by enough insurance companies to know one of their men when I saw him, and I knew I was not seeing one now. He was fifty or so, thick in the shoulder, in a blue suit that had been good in another decade. He had the kind of face that is called lived-in, but it looked more as if someone had lived in it and gone, leaving a few things behind. He stood against the wall with a glass. He did not talk to anybody. He just looked, at each of us in turn, slowly and without any expression. When it came round to me I had a strong impulse to tell him where I had been on the night of the fourteenth.

“Who is that?” I asked Dame Octavia.

“The insurance.”

“He doesn’t look like insurance.”

“No,” she said. “He looks like a bailiff. I asked him if he hunted and he said, only people. I thought that was rather good.” She took his whisky away from him a moment later, by mistake, and he let her. I thought that was rather good too.

Then there was an incident on the stairs which I shall touch on only lightly, because a gentleman would not touch on it at all. Celia Vane had gone up to finish dressing, or to see about something. She came down again. And she and the girl Saskia were found to be wearing the same frock.

I mean the very same. Green, silk, expensive, with no sleeves. On my cousin’s wife it looked like something from the cover of a magazine. Saskia wore it with army boots and a ring through her eyebrow, and on her it looked like a costume for an opera about the Amazons. They stood and regarded one another. The hall went absolutely silent. I have known that silence in the mess of a good regiment when somebody has passed the port the wrong way.

“Oh, bloody hell,” said Saskia. “The Liberty sale?”

“The Liberty sale,” said Celia.

I thought there would be blood. But my cousin’s wife was a remarkable woman. She came down the last few stairs, smiling, and said they would call it a uniform, and that Edmund had always said one of her wasn’t enough.

“I’ve never said that in my life,” said Edmund.

Everyone laughed. I laughed. I record, though, that for the rest of the night I was never perfectly sure, at a distance or from behind, which of them I was looking at. This led to one or two awkwardnesses. At about half past eleven I followed a green dress along a dark passage for some way, speaking to it as “Mrs Vane,” and it turned out to be the other one. She said, “Do I look forty?” and I had to pretend to have been choking.

At seven minutes past six by every clock in the hall, my great-uncle came in.

I had expected, I think, something bent and mumbling in a bath chair. My mother had said “nearly dead.” He was eighty-one and he came across that floor like a drawn sword. He was very tall, taller than me, with white hair that stood straight up, and he had a glass screwed into one eye on a black cord, which he let drop as he approached, and caught, and put back, without seeming to know he did it. He stopped at the Font and stirred the watches with one finger. Mine came to the top. He picked it out and held it up to the candles.

There was a pause in which I aged.

“This is an honest watch,” said my Uncle Leo.

Nobody said anything.

“It’s the only honest watch in this basin. Look at it. A plain lever movement, pin-pallet, such as you might have bought for a shilling in 1910. No jewels to speak of. And the maker has put a mouse on the dial, so that no one shall take it for more than it is. I respect that. I wish Monsieur Patek had had the same candour.” He laid it down again, carefully, on top of the others. “Whose is it?”

I put up my hand. I couldn’t speak.

“You are Dorothea’s grandson. You have her wrists. She could never keep a bracelet on.” He looked me over through the glass, and it was the second time in an hour that I had been examined by an expert. “You’ve come to ask me for something. No, don’t tell me now. I shan’t remember. Tell me at one.”

I looked at Dame Octavia. She closed one eye.

And then I saw who had come in with him. She was half a step behind, with her hand just under his elbow, so lightly that you would not have noticed unless you were looking. I was looking. It was the girl from the stairs. She was in the same blue dress, and her hair was the same, and there was no tray. She glanced round the hall once. She found me, and I thought she checked my shoulder, to see whether the crab was still there.

“Who’s that?” I said to Dame Octavia. I said it as casually as I could.

“The nurse. Miss Something. Quaile. She sits up with him. He wanders at night, poor old boy; they found him on the sea wall in September in his pyjamas, winding his watch.” She gave me a sideways look out of her horse’s eye. “You’ve gone pink.”

“It’s the fire.”

“It’s a very plain gel.”

“Is she?” I said. “I hadn’t noticed.”

“Ha!” said Dame Octavia Prowse.

My uncle had turned from the Font. He looked about him, at all of us, and a little frown came between his eyebrows, as if he had mislaid someone.

“Is Margot down?” he said.

Now I didn’t know. Nobody had told me. I thought Margot must be another cousin, and I was about to say brightly that I didn’t think I’d met her yet. Then I noticed that no one in the hall was moving at all. Edmund was looking into his tumbler, and Celia was turning a ring round on her finger. It was my cousin Imogen who answered, from over by the fire, quite gently. She said, “She’ll be along, Papa.”

“Who’s Margot?” I whispered.

“His wife,” said Dame Octavia, without moving her lips. “Marguerite. She’s been dead twenty years. Drowned on that road you came in by, on this night. Don’t sit in her chair.”

“Her chair?”

“You’ll see.”

I saw. We went in to dinner at eight, and I counted the places, as one does, to see who one had got.

I had my cousin Imogen on my left and my cousin’s wife on my right, she being at the foot of the table. Opposite me were Kit, the girl Saskia, and the man Cade. Beyond Imogen, going up my side, were Edmund, and then, three places from me, close enough to see and too far to pass her the salt, the nurse. And beyond her again, on my uncle’s right hand, in the place of honour, there was nobody.

It was fully laid. There were three glasses and a napkin done up like a mitre. The chair was pulled out a few inches, as for someone who has just risen to powder her nose. And when the soup came, the big girl who was waiting, Gail, a jolly red-faced child who breathed through her mouth, put a plate of it down at that place as a matter of course and went on round. Presently she came and took it away again, full. I watched her do it. She did not so much as glance at anyone.

I am not superstitious. I walk under ladders, though I do not, as has been seen, walk up them. But I counted the table over, including that chair, and I got thirteen.

“We’re thirteen,” I said, to my cousin’s wife. I thought she might not have noticed.

“We always are,” said Celia. “Have some bread.”

I should say something about the dinner, since Mrs Pask, who cooked it, deserves to be remembered for more than what happened later with the pudding. It was a goose. It was brought in by Gail on a dish the size of a coffee table, and my great-uncle rose and carved it himself. I have seen sommeliers at the Savoy open a bottle. I have seen a man in Jerez pour sherry into a glass from behind his own head. I have never seen anyone do a thing with his hands so well as that old man carved a goose. He never looked up, and every slice fell the same thickness as the last. When he had finished there was nothing left on the carcass that a cat could have got at.

“He could do that blindfold,” said Imogen quietly, beside me. “He used to, for us, at Christmas. With a table napkin tied round his head. Edmund could too.”

“Could he?” I looked up the table at my large cousin, who was refilling his own glass.

“Edmund had the best hands of any of us. Kit has them from him. You should have seen him at fourteen, with a graver.” She said it, I thought, as one speaks of somebody who has moved abroad.

There was a hitch over Saskia, who announced that she didn’t eat anything with a face. Dame Octavia said that she had been hunting for sixty years and had never yet met a goose with a face worth mentioning, and my Uncle Leo, quite unexpectedly, laid down the carving knife and said that he thought it a perfectly reasonable principle, and that the child was to have whatever she liked. What the child got, in the end, was the vegetables. They had been roasted in the goose’s fat. She ate them with every sign of pleasure and I saw no reason to bring it up.

The claret came round. I may not know clocks, but I knew what that was. It was a Léoville-Las-Cases of the 1961 vintage, and I had only ever met it before in catalogues. I said so, to Edmund, across my cousin Imogen. I may have said it with tears in my eyes.

“Have you?” said Edmund. “Good. Then somebody at this table can tell the real thing when he sees it.” He raised his glass to me and drank it off as though it were barley water. It was a dreadful thing to watch.

I told a story, I recall, about the Midget and a car ferry at Dartmouth, which went quite well, though it has a longish middle. The vicar told me again that he was glad my father was keeping better. Opposite me the man Cade ate steadily and looked at people. And up the table the nurse cut her goose into small pieces and did not eat them. She kept one eye on my great-uncle and, I could not help observing, a part of the other on my cousin Edmund, on her left, who never once spoke to her. His sleeve touched her wrist when he reached for the salt. I saw her colour.

I wasn’t jealous. One can’t be, in the first three hours. But I filled my own glass at that point, and didn’t taste it.

And all the time there was my pocket.

I had forgotten to allow for sitting down. When a man sits, in a dinner jacket, the pocket comes forward onto the thigh, and its contents settle. Mine settled with a noise like a bag of nails. Imogen looked round. I coughed. A little later I leaned forward for the bread sauce and something sharp, a wheel I suppose, came through the lining and got me in the leg, and I said “Ah!” in the middle of one of the vicar’s remarks. He took it for agreement.

It was the spring that worried me most. I could feel it against my hip, moving. From time to time it gave a faint, melancholy twang, like a harp in a distant room. I kept my right hand pressed flat over the pocket to hold it down, and ate my goose with a fork in my left, like an American.

“Have you hurt yourself?” Celia asked.

“No, no. An old wound.”

“In the hip?”

“Rugby,” I said. I have never played rugby in my life.

I had by now arrived at a plan. It was not a good plan, but it was more of one than I usually have. I should wait until one o’clock, as advised. Then I should make a clean breast of it to the old gentleman, produce the remains, offer to pay for the damage out of my future profits, and move straight on to the subject of the Thracian valley while his mood held. In the meantime nobody need know. Nobody did know. I had only to get through dinner without clanking.

It was at this point that Dame Octavia pushed back her chair and announced that she was going out for a gasper, and my uncle told her to sit down.

He got to his feet. He stood at the head of the table with the candles under his chin and picked up his glass. He turned to the empty chair beside him and bowed to it, very slightly, and said something that I didn’t catch. Then he looked at the rest of us.

“To absent time,” he said.

We stood and drank it. I’ve no idea what it meant. I have asked several of those who were there, and they’ve none either. I said it with great feeling, because of the claret.

We sat. He didn’t. He said that it was the twentieth year. He said that he had known that afternoon what he wished to say about it and had now forgotten, and he said it without any fuss, like a man reporting the loss of an umbrella. I thought that rather fine. And then he said that he would tell us something else instead, and that it was about clocks.

I pressed my hand on my pocket. The spring went twang.

“One of you,” said my Uncle Leo, “has been robbing me.”

Now I have often read, in the sort of book my Aunt Hilary likes, of a man’s blood running cold. I had supposed it a figure of speech. It is not. It starts at the back of the neck and it goes down inside the collar.

He said it had been going on for some time. He said clocks, good ones, had been taken out of their places. And he said that it was thought he would not notice, because he was old, and couldn’t find his spectacles. I will never forget his next words. He said he could go round that house blindfold and put his hand on any clock in it and say who made it and when.

He knew. That was all I could think. He knew to the inch what had stood on the table in the Blue Room, and it had been a good one. And he had been up there. Or somebody had. They had found the bare table, and a few splinters of glass, perhaps, on the floor under the bed. The alarm had gone round the house while I was in the bath.

I didn’t follow the details of what he said. There was something about copies. I took that to be a technical term. I suppose I heard about one word in three. One is not at one’s best as a listener when one is sitting on the evidence.

“I don’t know which of you it is,” he said.

I breathed.

“I’ve a man finding out for me. A very capable man. He will have told me before the door is opened. I shall know which of you it is by one o’clock.”

I looked across the table. I couldn’t help it. And the man Cade, with a spoonful of syllabub halfway to his mouth and no expression on his face of any kind, was looking straight at my right-hand pocket.

I knew it then. He wasn’t from the insurance. He’d been engaged. He was the very capable man, and he’d been through my room. He must have stood in the doorway of the Blue Room with those tired eyes and reconstructed the entire thing from a dent in the carpet. He probably knew which knee.

My Uncle Leo was still speaking. He was saying something very decent, I gathered afterwards, about how the guilty party might come and tell him why, in the Hour, and nothing more would be said. I have had it repeated to me. At the time I heard a roaring noise, and through it my own voice, in my head, rehearsing. It was an accident, sir. I was taking off a pullover.

I will confess that I started to get up.

I had my left hand on the table and my weight coming forward. I had got as far as “I say—” in a sort of croak. My idea was to get it over with there and then, in front of them all, and take what was coming. It was the only time in my life I have ever been about to do the brave thing at the right time.

A hand came down on my knee, under the cloth, and gripped it.

It was my cousin’s wife. Celia. She wasn’t looking at me. She was looking up the table, at her husband, with a face like a closed door. But her hand had me by the kneecap, with surprising strength, and she said, very low, hardly moving her mouth:

“Whatever it is, Toby. Not now.”

I sat down. The spring twanged.

My uncle sat down too, rather abruptly, and the nurse had him by the arm. He looked at his plate and asked what was on it, and whether he had ordered it. Then he turned to the empty chair and asked Margot whether they had ordered a syllabub. The dinner went on. I’ve been at some sticky ones, but that was the stickiest quarter of an hour I have known.

I did not find out for years what that hand on my knee had been about. I supposed at the time that she had guessed, and was being kind. I now think my cousin’s wife had no more idea than the vicar what I had in my pocket. She had seen a foolish young man about to stand up and make a scene, at a moment when she had every reason to want the table quiet. She had troubles of her own that night that made mine look like a parking ticket. But it was a kindness all the same, and I haven’t forgotten it. I think of her whenever a spring goes in a sofa.

The ladies withdrew. I had not known that ladies still did. Saskia said, “Are we being sent out?” and was led away by Dame Octavia, who told her it was the only part of the evening when one could get a decent drink and take one’s shoes off.

The port came. It came to the vicar first, through some error, and he, bless him, passed it to his right. I watched it travel the wrong way round that table with the feeling one has watching a child wander onto a railway line. The solicitor shut his eyes. My Uncle Leo watched it come and said nothing whatever, but he took it up when it reached him and set it going the proper way again, with one finger, as he might have corrected a pendulum.

Edmund got up and went round and sat next to the man Cade. He turned the chair about and sat astride it, like a subaltern. I couldn’t hear what they said. I didn’t need to. Edmund was smiling and the detective wasn’t, and from time to time each of them glanced, I was nearly sure, down the table at me.

They were discussing my case. That was plain. My cousin Edmund was no doubt pleading for me. He’s young. He’s Dorothea’s grandson. It was probably only a small one. And the man Cade would be shaking his head, the way they do. At one point Edmund laughed out loud and hit the other man on the shoulder. Then he got up and limped out.

I took that to be a good sign. I thought Edmund had got me off.

I resolved to thank him. More than that, it came to me that Edmund was the man to advise me. He was a Vane. He had grown up with the old gentleman and would know how these things were best put. He had, by his sister’s account, once been handy with clocks himself. For all I knew he could mend it. I had a vision of my cousin Edmund in his shirtsleeves, with a little screwdriver, putting the fern back.

I therefore decided to find Edmund and tell him everything. I should like the reader to mark that decision. All that followed came out of it: the brandy, the vicar, the ice house, and the wheelbarrow.

But first I had a better idea. I have learned to dread those.

It came to me as I crossed the hall. Everybody had gone through to the drawing room, where my cousin Kit was going to play the piano; I could hear him beginning, something watery. The hall was empty. There were the candles and the fire, and the Font on its table. And round the walls stood about a dozen grandfather clocks.

A dozen clocks, I thought. And every one of them was full of wheels.

I ask the reader to follow my reasoning, for it has a certain beauty. I had in my pocket the works of a clock. The difficulty was that they were in my pocket. But suppose they were to be found in a place where one might expect the works of a clock to be? Suppose I were simply to open the door of one of those tall cases and tip the whole lot in at the bottom? Who would look there? And if, years hence, some man came to clean it and found a few extra wheels and a fern lying in the dust, what would he conclude? That they had dropped off. Clocks must shed things. Everything does.

There would then be no evidence. There would be an empty table in the Blue Room, and a mystery, and the very capable man could reconstruct until he was blue.

I chose my clock with care. Most of them were fancy, with gilt and flowers and little windows. But on the left of the fireplace stood a plain, sober one, tall and narrow, in dark wood, with a long glass door down the front. I thought it had a discreet look. It was the kind of clock that would keep a secret.

I went over to it on tiptoe. I looked both ways. I opened the long door. Inside there was a brass pendulum going to and fro, very slowly, with a bob on it like a soup plate. Beside that, hanging on a cord, about level with my waistcoat, was a weight. It was a plain grey cylinder. I should say it was about the size of a large tin of beans.

I mention the weight because I touched it. I had to move it aside to see the bottom of the case, and I was surprised by it. It was a great deal heavier than it looked. It swung back and knocked on the wood, and I steadied it. I can state, therefore, that at about twenty past ten that night, by the dial above it, the weight of that clock was hanging in its case where it belonged, and that it was clean and dry, and cold to the hand. I was asked about that a long time afterwards, by somebody who had a reason for asking. I had never thought it worth mentioning.

I got my hand into my pocket. I got hold of a good fistful, the dial and some wheels. I had it out, and was bending to drop it into the bottom of the case.

And all the lights went out.

I don’t know whether the reader has ever stood in the dark, in a strange house, with his arm inside a grandfather clock and a handful of broken evidence, while somewhere a piano stops in the middle of a note. It concentrates the mind. My first thought was that it was a trap, and that the detective had arranged it. I pictured them rushing in with torches. I snatched my hand back, and barked my knuckles, and the pendulum caught my cuff. The fern got out and went up my sleeve.

Nobody rushed in. The piano started again. It was only the candles I had lost sight of for a moment; my eyes came back, and there was the hall, in the firelight, exactly as before. But I could hear footsteps on the kitchen stairs, and a voice, a woman’s, saying that it was that dratted transformer.

I shut the long door. I put the fistful back in my pocket. When Mrs Pask came through the baize door with an oil lamp in each hand, I was standing in the middle of the hall, whistling.

“Was that you at my regulator, Mr Toby?” she said.

“Me? No. Rather not. I was just—it’s the fuses, I expect. I’ll have a look at the box, shall I? I’m rather good with fuses.”

I am not good with fuses. I have never looked at a fuse box in my life. But there was a pair of steps standing against the wall, and I had got up them, and was holding a candle to the ceiling in a knowledgeable way, when the man Cade came out of the drawing-room passage and stood watching me.

Mrs Pask told me to get down. She said it wasn’t the fuses, it was the whole Ness, and that she would not have me on her floor with my neck broken and a goose carcass to boil. I got down. The detective asked her for a lantern, and she gave him one. He put his hat on and went out of the side door into the storm, without a word to anyone.

I thought that an odd thing for an insurance man to do. Then I remembered that he was not an insurance man. I supposed he had gone out to search the Midget.

3. In Which I Kill the Vicar

A country house without electricity is a very sociable place. Everyone carries a candle, and so one can see nothing of a person but the face, lit from underneath like a pumpkin’s, and one is forever meeting these faces round corners.

I met a good many in the next half hour. I was looking for Edmund.

He was not in the drawing room. My great-uncle was, in a wing chair, with the nurse on a stool beside him, and I stood in the doorway for a moment for the pleasure of looking at the top of her head. Dame Octavia was asleep. Kit had finished at the piano and was sitting with his hands hanging between his knees, staring at the carpet. He looked up and saw me. “If you’re after my father,” he said, “so’s everyone.” Then he got up and walked straight past me and out, as if he had made up his mind about something.

Edmund was not in the library. There was nobody in the library but a clock under a green cloth.

He was not in the billiard room, or in a sort of gunroom that smelt of oil, or in the downstairs cloakroom, where I knocked. I went along a passage toward the back of the house. Ahead of me, going the same way with a candle, was a green silk dress. It turned a corner and I hurried after it.

“Mrs Vane! I say, Mrs Vane! I’m so sorry to bother you, but have you seen—”

The dress turned round. It had army boots under it.

“Do I look forty?” said Saskia.

I had a fit of coughing. It was all I could think of.

“It’s all right,” she said, when I had finished. “Everyone’s doing it. The vicar called me ‘dear lady’ and asked after the roof. Have you seen Kit?”

“He went out of the drawing room. A minute ago.”

“Which way?”

“I didn’t notice. He looked a bit—”

“He’s been a bit ever since the speech. He’s gone all white and won’t say. He keeps looking at that insurance bloke like he wants to hit him.” She chewed her thumbnail. “I don’t get this family. Is it always like this? Nobody says anything. There’s that chair. Then the old man stands up and says somebody’s been nicking the clocks, and they all just pass the port. In my family, if my nan said that at Christmas, there’d be a fight in the car park.”

I said I thought it was a question of how one had been brought up.

“Yeah, well. I’m going to find him. If you see him, tell him I’m in the stables. He goes up that tower when he’s upset. He did when he was little.” She set off, boots ringing on the flags, and then turned. “Who are you looking for?”

“Edmund.”

“He went out,” said Saskia. “The big side door, about ten minutes ago, when the lights went. He was carrying a box. I held the door for him. He said, ‘Thank you, Celia,’ and I didn’t like to say.”

So he had gone to see to something. The generator, I supposed, if there was one. I felt that I could hardly pursue a man into a gale to tell him about a bedside clock. I went back to the drawing room and had a brandy.

I had two, in fact. I’m not proud of it, but I had had a trying day, and the brandy at Compline was on a tray by the piano with the glasses beside it, and nobody was counting. They were large glasses, the balloon kind that one can get one’s whole face into. I mention their size and shape because they come into what follows.

At a little before eleven by the drawing-room clocks, of which there were four, I took my second brandy and a candle and went to have another look for my cousin. I had heard the side door bang.

There was a light in the dining room. I could hear his voice, and a laugh. I was by now in the mood in which one feels that a thing must be got over, and I didn’t knock. I was talking over my shoulder as I went in, to the vicar, who was pottering along the passage behind me and had asked me something about my father.

I therefore entered the room backwards. I do this more often than I should like.

When I turned round, my cousin Edmund was standing by the sideboard with his wife. He had his hand on the side of her neck, and she had her cheek leaned against it. They looked, in the light of the one lamp, like a couple in an advertisement for something expensive. I leapt about a foot.

“Oh! I say! Sorry! I didn’t—I’ll come back.”

“Don’t be an ass,” said Edmund. He took his hand away, without hurry. His hair was wet. “Come in. Have a drink. Have you got a drink? You’ve got a drink. Have another.”

“I really only wanted a word. If it’s not a bad moment. It’s rather private.”

“It’s a perfectly good moment. Celia doesn’t count. She’s heard all my words.” He was feeling in his pocket for cigarettes. He had put a glass down on the sideboard to do it, a balloon glass, with brandy in it.

I went over. I’m bound to say I went in a muddle. I had the candle in my left hand and the brandy in my right. I wanted both my hands, because one can’t confess properly without them. So I put my glass down too. I put it on the sideboard, by the tray, next to his.

I have been asked about this, many times, by one person in particular. I wish I could be more helpful. I put my glass down beside another glass. They were the same kind of glass, with about the same amount in them, and it was dark. That is all I know.

“It’s about the clock,” I said.

Edmund had a cigarette in his mouth and a match halfway to it. He stopped.

“What clock?”

“The one Uncle Leo was—at dinner. What he said. That one of us had been—” I swallowed. “It was me.”

There was a short silence. My cousin’s wife had moved away. She was standing against the wall by a tall clock in the corner, with her hands behind her, quite still. She looked like somebody waiting for a bus that she doesn’t expect to come.

Edmund lit his cigarette. He blew out the smoke. Then he began to laugh.

It started somewhere near his knees and worked up. He had to hold on to the sideboard. “You,” he said. “You. Oh, my God. Dorothea’s grandson. Out of a clear sky.” He wiped his eyes with the back of his wrist. “How many?”

“How many what?”

“How many have you had?”

“Only the one,” I said, bewildered. “Honestly. Just the one.”

“Just the one. He says it like a curate with an egg.” He clapped me on the back, and my candle went out. “My dear boy. I can’t tell you what a relief this is. I’ve been the black sheep of this family for so long, I’d forgotten there was room for another. What did you get for it?”

“Get for it?”

“Who had it off you? You didn’t go to that crook in Camden Passage?”

“Nobody had it off me. It’s in my pocket.”

That stopped him laughing. He stared at me. I had begun to feel that we were not, as they say, on the same page. I was fumbling for matches, to relight the candle, and at the same time trying to get my other hand into my pocket to produce the exhibit. I would have had it out in another second. And my cousin Edmund, who was a clockmaker’s son and had been at the bench from the age of nine, would have looked at it. He’d have said what the man Cade said to me seven hours later in a stable yard, and I should have gone to bed a happy man. The evening would have been perfectly uneventful. I often think of that.

But the vicar came in.

He came in smiling, with his hand out in front of him like a man walking in his sleep. He’d got no candle. He made straight for the lamp, and me. “Ah,” he said. “Here we all are.”

I was, I hope, properly brought up. An elderly clergyman had entered a room where drinks were going and had not got one. I didn’t think. There were two glasses of brandy on the sideboard at my elbow, mine and my cousin’s, and I picked one up and put it into his hand.

“How very kind,” said the vicar. “I don’t mind if I do. Your father always kept a good cellar.”

“There you are,” said Edmund. He reached past me and took up the other glass. “The Church has spoken. We’ll adjourn. Toby, I want to hear this, I want to hear every word of it. But I’ve got to see a man about a boat.” He drank. He stopped and looked into the glass and made a face. “God. What’s this? It’s corked.”

“Brandy can’t be corked,” I said. I did know that. It’s the one thing I do know.

“This is.” He drank some more, to make sure. “It’s got a taste like a chemist’s. That’s Father’s economy; he’ll have had it since the Coronation.” He drank about half of it altogether, with the expression of a man doing his duty. Then he set it down, hard, on the sideboard. “No. Life’s too short. Find me later. I’ll be about; I’m always about on this night, ask anyone. Half past twelve or so. And Toby.”

“Yes?”

“Whatever you’ve done, I’ll lay you any money you like it isn’t a patch on what I’ve done. So cheer up.”

He kissed his wife on the top of the head as he passed her. She didn’t move. He went out, with his limp, and I heard him go along to the drawing room and say something, and my great-uncle answer.

My cousin’s wife came away from the wall. She took up the lamp. She didn’t look at me, or at the vicar, or at the half-glass on the sideboard. She said, “Good night, Toby,” in a queer flat voice, though it was not much after eleven and nobody was going to bed. Then she went out with the lamp and left us in the dark.

I got my candle going. The vicar and I stood and beamed at one another.

“And how is your dear father?” he said.

“Thriving,” I said. I had found by now that this was the quickest way.

“Splendid. Splendid. I buried him, you know. A lovely service.” He drank off his brandy in three swallows, with relish, like a child with cocoa. I should say here that the glass I had given him was, on the evidence, my own, and contained nothing but brandy. I’ve been over it with a pencil. He finished it, and looked into the bottom of it wistfully, and then his eye fell on the sideboard.

There stood my cousin’s glass, where he had left it, half full.

“Now that,” said the Reverend Aubrey Stiles, “would be a sin.”

“I’m sorry?”

“Waste. Waste, my boy. I was at theological college during rationing, and it marks a man.” He set down his empty one and took up the other. “If Edmund doesn’t care for it.”

“He said it was corked.”

“I can’t hear you, but I’m sure you’re right,” said the vicar, and drank it.

He didn’t make a face. I don’t believe he had tasted anything since about 1970. He finished Edmund’s brandy to the last drop, patted his waistcoat, and took my arm. He suggested that we should go and sit somewhere with a fire and that I should tell him all about myself.

We went to the library. It was the nearest. I put him in a leather armchair on one side of the hearth and took the other, and I told him all about myself. I remember that I gave him the whole of the Thracian valley, with figures. He nodded. He said “Dear me” in the right places. He was an ideal listener, and I had reached the question of bonded storage, and was drawing a small diagram in the air, when I noticed that he had stopped saying “Dear me.”

He had also stopped nodding. His head had gone back against the leather. His mouth was open, and his hands lay palm upward on the arms of the chair.

“Vicar?” I said.

Nothing.

“Mr Stiles? I say.”

I got up. I held the candle to his face. He was a very odd colour. I’m aware that candlelight is not kind, but he was the colour of the candle. His eyes were not quite shut. There was a line of white showing under each lid.

I took him by the shoulder and shook him, gently and then not. His head rolled. One arm slid off the chair and hung. I have seen my share of men asleep after dinner, in the trade. They snore. They mutter. If you shake them, they say “What? Quite,” and tell you they were resting their eyes. The vicar did none of these things. He just sat there with his mouth open and looked like a man in a waxworks.

I listened for breathing. I heard the fire, and the clock under its cloth in the window. Then I remembered that the clock under the cloth hadn’t been ticking the last time I was in that room. It was some other clock, by the door. This is not relevant, but in such a moment the mind goes everywhere but where it’s wanted.

And there came into that mind three things, one after another, like coaches of a train.

It’s got a taste like a chemist’s.

I gave him the glass.

One wants to be sure which glass.

I am not going to pretend that I thought it through. I thought, with great speed and no logic at all, the following. Somebody had put something in the brandy. It had been meant for Edmund. Edmund had enemies; the house was full of the atmosphere of it; there was a detective on the premises. Edmund had detected the taste and stopped. The vicar, who could taste nothing, had not. And the vicar had got it from my hand. I had picked a glass off the sideboard and given it to him with a smile. Then I’d stood by while he drank the second one too, and said nothing at all, because I am a wine merchant and I know that brandy can’t be corked.

I had killed the vicar. In my uncle’s library, on the same evening that I had broken his clock.

I should like to put on record my first words on realising this. They were: “Oh, I say.”

There was one person in that house who would know what to do with a dead clergyman. I knew that without having to think. I left the candle with him, for company. I ran.

In the hall I all but knocked down my cousin Imogen. She was making for the stairs with a candle, quickly, and seemed hardly to see me. She had a key in her hand, an old one, and she went up without a word and turned along the gallery. I had no time for her. I was looking for someone else.

I got her on the next flight. That’s twice, on stairs. She had come out of the drawing room and was going up, quickly, with a candlestick, on her own. She had left my great-uncle, which I gathered afterwards she was not supposed to do. She had her head a little on one side, like a person listening to something on the floor above. I came up the flight behind her three steps at a time.

“Miss Quaile! Miss Quaile! Thank God. You’re a nurse.”

She turned and looked down at me. On a staircase she was the taller, which I think suited us both.

“I think I’ve killed the vicar,” I said.

I will always honour her for the next four seconds. She did not say “What?” She did not say “Don’t be absurd.” She looked into my face, and whatever she found there, it satisfied her that I was a person to whom such a thing could happen.

“Where?” she said.

“The library.”

“What with?”

“Brandy.”

She came down past me. She did not run; she never ran. But I had to stretch to keep up.

She set her candle on the mantelpiece and went down on one knee by the armchair. I stood and held my hair. She took his wrist between her fingers and thumb and looked at nothing for a quarter of a minute. She laid the back of her hand against his cheek. She put her thumb on his eyelid and pushed it up, and brought the candle close, and watched. She bent and put her face right down to his open mouth, and I thought for one dreadful moment that she was going to give him the kiss of life, and felt a pang of envy. I’m ashamed of that now. But she was only smelling.

She sat back on her heel.

“He’s asleep,” she said.

“Asleep? He can’t be. Look at him. I shook him. I shook him like a cocktail.”

“He’s very deeply asleep. His pulse is slow and quite steady and he’s breathing, eight or nine to the minute. Look at his waistcoat.” I looked. The fourth button was going up and down, about as often as the tide. “He’ll not wake till morning. You could fire a gun by his ear.” She was frowning, a small straight line between the pale eyebrows. “What has he had to drink?”

“Soup. Claret. Port. I mean, we all did. And then a brandy. Two brandies.”

“Where are the glasses?”

“He left them. No, wait.” I looked. The old boy had brought the second one with him. It was on the floor by the leg of the chair, on its side. I picked it up and gave it to her.

She put her nose into it.

I was watching her face, for the simple reason that there was nothing else in the room I wished to look at. I saw it change. It didn’t change much. She was not a person whose face did. But all the colour that she had, which was none to speak of, went out of it, and her eyes went wide and then narrow. She smelled the glass again. Then she touched the tip of one finger to the dregs in the bottom and put it to her tongue.

“Where did this come from?” she said. She said it very quietly.

“The dining room. Off the sideboard.”

“Who poured it?”

“I don’t know. It was just there. It was Edmund’s. He’d had about half and said it was corked, and left it, and the vicar didn’t like to see it go to waste.”

“Mr Edmund Vane’s glass.”

“Yes.”

“He drank from this? Himself? You saw him?”

“About half. He made a face.” I didn’t care for the way she was looking at the glass. “Why? What is it? Is it poison? I knew it was. I said brandy can’t be corked.”

“It’s not poison,” Miss Quaile said. She said it slowly, as if she were still deciding. “It’s a sleeping draught. Something I give. One spoonful in a tumbler of water, at night, for an old gentleman who won’t stay in his bed.” She looked up at me. She had on her face a look that I couldn’t read at all then. I can read it now, and I wish I could not. “It’s kept on a tray. In a room with the door shut. There’s no way on earth that it should be in a brandy glass on a dining-room sideboard.”

“Then how—”

“I don’t know.”

She stood up. She was still holding the glass. She looked at the vicar, and at the door, and at the ceiling, where there was nothing to see. I thought she was listening again.

“How long ago did Mr Vane drink it?”

“Twenty minutes. Half an hour.”

“And where is he now?”

“He went to see a man about a boat.”

“On his feet?”

“Well, yes. He limps a bit.”

“He’s a big man,” she said, to herself. “And he’s had a great deal of drink, for years, which makes a difference to the liver.” She put the glass down on the mantelpiece, beside her candle. I noticed that her hand was not quite steady. “Mr Pargeter. Listen to me, please. The vicar will come to no harm. He’s had perhaps half a dose, in spirits, on a full stomach, and at his age he’ll sleep twelve hours and wake with a headache. But he mustn’t be left sitting up like that with his head back. He could choke. He must be laid down, on his side, somewhere flat, with something under his head, and somebody should look at him every half hour. Can you do that?”

“Yes. Yes, of course. On his side.”

“The left.”

“The left. Where are you going?”

“I have to look at a tray,” said Miss Quaile.

She took her candle. At the door she turned. She was a small pale girl in a dark dress, in a doorway, with a hundred thousand books behind her going up into the dark. I could have looked at her for a week.

“You didn’t kill him,” she said. “You fetched me. That was right. Most people stand and wring their hands.” Then she was gone. I heard her on the stairs, going up, and this time I think she was very nearly running.

I stood on my uncle’s hearthrug. I had been told I was right, by her, about something. I looked at the vicar with real affection. I would not have changed places with the Aga Khan.

The reader who has never tried to move a sleeping clergyman will think that the next part is easy.

He was a small man, and he looked light. I got my arms under his and heaved. It was like trying to lift a sack of wet sand that somebody has taken the trouble to butter. He came up about six inches, and his head fell forward on my shirt front, and his teeth came out. They were on a plate. They dropped into my breast pocket, on top of the handkerchief, and smiled at me.

I let him down again. I went for help. The hall was empty, but through the baize door I could hear voices, and I went down the kitchen stairs. I found the girl Gail sitting on the bottom step, with her shoes off, eating a goose leg.

“Gail,” I said. “Would you be very kind and help me carry the vicar?”

She looked at me over the leg.

“Where to?” she said.

It was the same sort of question the nurse had asked. I have noticed this about the women of Essex. They don’t waste time on the why.

“Somewhere flat. He’s asleep. Miss Quaile says he’s to be put on his left side with something under his head.”

“Is he drunk?”

“He’s been drugged.”

“Oh,” said Gail. She put the goose leg down on the stair and wiped her hands on her apron. “I thought it’d be something. My auntie says there’s always something, on the night. Last year Mr Edmund was in the vicar’s car, asleep, with the engine going. Year before, Dame Octavia shot the weathercock.”

We carried him between us. I took the top half and Gail the legs. She was a strong girl, used to geese. She said he was heavier than last year’s bird and not so well trussed. I led, going backwards, which as I’ve said is my natural gait, and we got him out of the library, with only one pause, when his foot caught the door.

“Where’ll we put him?” Gail panted. “Upstairs?”

“I’m not carrying him upstairs.”

“There’s the settle. In the hall. It’s long enough if you bend him.”

So we laid the Reverend Aubrey Stiles on an oak settle in the hall of Compline House, on his left side, facing the fire. Gail fetched a cushion from the drawing room and put it under his head. I restored his teeth. I didn’t know how to put them in, so I set them on the arm of the settle by his hand, where he would find them. He looked very peaceful. He looked like a figure on a tomb.

“He’s nice, the vicar,” said Gail, standing back. “He christened me. He thought I was a boy.”

It was about ten to twelve. The hall was all firelight and ticking. As we stood there I happened to look across at the tall dark clock on the left of the fireplace, the discreet one, which I’d had my arm in an hour and a half before.

It had stopped. The pendulum was hanging straight down behind the glass.

I thought nothing of it. Clocks do stop. I may even have thought, with a twinge, that I had done it myself, fumbling about in there. I didn’t open the door. If I had, I should have been able to tell you whether the weight was on its line or not, and it seems that somebody would have liked very much to know. But there it is. I looked at a stopped clock at ten to twelve and thought, I hope that’s not another one.

Gail went back to her goose leg. I set out, once more, to look for Edmund. It seemed to me that he ought to be told he’d had a sleeping draught, before he tried to do anything on a boat.

I didn’t find him. I should have had to go out, and it was pouring. I looked into every room on the ground floor again and met nobody at all.

I ended, as one does in a strange house, in the kitchen.

It was the only warm place. The range was going, and Mrs Pask was at the table in her apron, setting out little glass plates. She was counting under her breath. There was a clock on the wall, a big round one such as they have in railway stations. I looked at it, having no Mickey. I give it as I saw it: thirteen minutes past twelve.

“Mr Toby,” said Mrs Pask, not looking up. “You may make yourself useful. Them glasses on the tray want to go up to the serving pantry for one o’clock, for the champagne, and Gail’s got her feet up, and I’ve only the one pair of hands. You’ll find the lift through there. In the larder, at the back. You put the tray in, and haul on the left-hand rope, and it stops itself.”

I was glad to be of use to someone. I took the tray, two dozen glasses on a butler’s salver, and carried it through a stone passage into a pantry. There were shelves, and a ham. At the back there was a square hatch in the wall with a wooden door. I balanced the tray on my hip and opened it.

There was a shaft, and two ropes hanging. There was no lift. The box part, the thing one puts the tray in, was somewhere up above. I could see the bottom of it, a little way up the shaft, in the light of my candle.

I took hold of the left-hand rope and pulled. Nothing happened. I pulled the right-hand rope. Something creaked. The box came down about a foot, and stuck.

And a voice said, “Hello?”

It was a small voice, quite clear and rather polite. It came from inside the shaft, just above my head.

I stood perfectly still.

“Hello?” it said again. “Is somebody there? Please could you pull the other rope? It’s gone crooked. I’ve been in here for ages.”

I want to describe my state of mind exactly. I wasn’t frightened. One is frightened by things that may be so. This was simply not so. I had in the course of that evening drunk two whiskies, a sherry, a great deal of the Léoville, some port, and two brandies. One of the brandies I now had some reason to think had stood next to a narcotic. I had killed a vicar and seen him raised. I was in love. A man in that condition, when the furniture speaks to him, does not ask what it wants.

“I’m very sorry,” I said to the hatch, quite courteously. “I can’t help you. You aren’t there.”

“I am, though,” said the voice.

I shut the door of the hatch. I shut it carefully and put the catch across. I carried the tray of glasses back along the stone passage into the kitchen, and set it down on the table. I didn’t break a single one.

“That was quick,” said Mrs Pask.

“Mrs Pask,” I said. “I wonder if I might ask you something. Does the lift generally speak?”

She had a glass plate in each hand. She put them down.

I shall not forget her face. I had expected one of two things. Either she would laugh, or she would tell me I had had enough. She did neither. She was a square, solid woman of sixty-odd with a face like a cottage loaf, a woman you would have said nothing on earth could startle. And she looked, for one moment, like a person who has been found out.

“What did it say?” said Mrs Pask.

“It said hello. It asked me to pull the other rope. It said it had been in there for ages.”

“Did it now.” She wiped her hands down her apron, slowly, and I could see her getting her face back, the way one gets a tablecloth straight. “You’ve had enough, Mr Toby. That’s what that is. That’s Mr Vane’s claret, and the wind in the shaft. That old lift’s done that since I was a girl. It moans. You leave my lift be, and I’ll see to the glasses myself.”

“It didn’t moan. It was very well-spoken.”

“I’ll see to it,” she said.

She took a candle and went into the stone passage, and I heard the pantry door shut behind her. Then I heard the bolt.

I sat down at the kitchen table. I helped myself to a piece of cold goose. Through the wall I could hear Mrs Pask in the pantry. She was talking, in a sharp fierce whisper, the kind one uses to a dog that has got on the bed. I caught a word or two. “Told you.” “Not a sound, I said.” “Wait till I get you home.”

It struck me as carrying things rather far, to speak to a dumb waiter like that. I assumed she was humouring me. Country people are full of these old customs.

There was a rumbling in the wall, of ropes. Then silence. She came back, rather red, with her cap crooked, and the tray of glasses was gone.

“There,” she said. “All it wanted was a firm hand.” She looked up at the clock on the wall, and then at me, and I saw her come to some decision. I think she wanted me out of that kitchen. “Now then. If you’ve nothing to do but sit there eating my stock, you can run me an errand.”

“Anything,” I said. “I’m at a loose end. I can’t find Edmund.”

“Nobody can ever find Mr Edmund, not on the night. He’ll turn up; he always does.” She took a ring of keys off a nail by the range and began to work one of them round to the front. It had a twist of red wool on it. “It’s the ice.”

“The ice?”

“The pudding, for the Hour. Mrs Vane’s bombe; her that’s gone. I’ve made it every year since 1952, and they have it at one o’clock with the champagne, when the door’s opened, and Mr Vane says the same thing every year. He says, ‘Ah, Mrs Pask, the ice.’ It was in my freezer. And then the electric went. So I had Gail run it out to the ice house, in its box, and bed it down in the ice, where it’ll take no harm. And now it wants fetching, and she’s got her shoes off, and I can’t leave my kitchen.”

It was twenty-five past twelve by the kitchen clock when Mrs Pask sent me for the bombe. I looked at the clock as she said it. I have been asked the time of that more often than I have been asked my own age.

“Where’s the ice house?”

“Out the back door, across the yard, down the track behind the stables. In the trees. You can’t miss it. It’s a hump.” She put the keys into my hand. “That’s the gate. Red wool. It’ll likely be on the latch, but if it’s shut, it’s locked, and you’ll want that. Mind them steps, they’re greasy, and there’s no rail. The box is at the bottom. Wooden. So big.” She showed me with her hands. “Heavy, mind, with the ice round it. Here.”

She gave me a white saucer with a candle stuck on it in its own wax. She thought, and went to a drawer, and gave me a silver spoon as well. It was a big one, with a crest on the handle.

“What’s this for?”

“You lift the lid and you put that in at the edge. Just the edge. If it goes in like butter, it’s gone soft, and you come straight back and tell me, and I’ll serve them the trifle. If it stands up, bring it.” She fixed me with her eye. “Don’t taste it.”

“I shouldn’t dream of it.”

“You’ve the look of one that would.”

I went out of the back door into the wind, with a ring of keys, a candle in a saucer, and a spoon. I felt rather like an acolyte going up to the altar. And so I came to my cousin Edmund after all. I had been looking for him for two hours, and was no longer thinking about him at all.

4. In Which I Fetch the Pudding

The wind had gone down a good deal. It was still raining, in a half-hearted way, and there was a moon coming and going behind the clouds. I crossed the kitchen yard with my hand round the candle and found the track behind the stables without difficulty. Mrs Pask had said one couldn’t miss it, and I’ve noticed that people who say that are right about half the time. It was a grassy lump among some trees, with a brick archway in the side of it, and an iron gate.

The gate was shut. I pushed it and it was locked. I recall feeling pleased about that, because it meant I got to use the key. I am fond of keys. I put the saucer down, found the one with the red wool, and turned it, and the gate swung in. I left the ring hanging in the lock so as not to lose it.

There was a short brick passage, and a wooden door standing open, and then cold. I have been in the cellars at Épernay in February. This was colder. I came out on a little landing at the top of a round chamber, all of brick, like the inside of a beehive, and a flight of steps went down the curve of the wall into the dark. They were very steep and they shone.

Mind them steps, she had said. They’re greasy, and there’s no rail.

I minded them. I went down sideways, with the saucer held out in front of me in one hand and the spoon in the other, feeling for each step with my foot before I trusted it. I counted nine. On the ninth I put the candle down, on the step, to have both hands for the wall. I looked to see how many were left.

There was a pair of shoes on the bottom three.

They were black evening shoes, large, toes up. They had feet in them. The feet were attached to legs, in black trousers, which ran down the last of the steps onto the floor, and at the end of the legs lay the rest of my cousin Edmund. He was on his back in the straw with one arm flung out. His head was lower than his feet, and tipped back, and his face was toward me. His eyes were open.

I’m not ashamed to say I let out a yell. It went round that brick dome three or four times and came back at me. I sat down on the step. The spoon went out of my hand and I heard it ring on the bricks below and slither.

For a period that I cannot measure, I looked at Edmund and he looked at the ceiling. There was a mark on the left side of his forehead, a dark swelling, with blood on it, and blood had run back into his hair.

I thought: this time it’s real. This is the one. They put the stuff in his glass, and he’s dead of it, and I stood there and said brandy can’t be corked.

And then my cousin Edmund snored.

I want to be exact about that snore, for it’s the most important noise in this narrative. It was not loud, or even much of a snore, as I understand the term. It was a long, slow, rasping breath, drawn in through the open mouth, with a sort of click at the top of it, and then a pause so long that I thought it had been the last. Then it was let out again, in a sigh. I counted. Eight seconds, and another. The fourth button of the vicar’s waistcoat had gone up and down at just that rate, in the library, half an hour before.

Miss Quaile’s voice came back to me as clearly as if she had been standing on the step above. He’s very deeply asleep. He’s breathing, eight or nine to the minute. You could fire a gun by his ear.

Of course. I can’t describe the relief. I very nearly laughed. He had drunk half of the same glass. He was a big man, she had said, and it would take longer with him. He had walked about for half an hour, feeling more and more peculiar, no doubt, and had come down here to see about his boat, or whatever it was. And on these steps, which were greasy and had no rail, it had caught up with him all at once, and he had gone from top to bottom on his head.

I got down the last few steps on my seat and bent over him with the candle.

One of his eyes was not open, in fact. It was the left, on the side of the lump, and it had swollen nearly shut. The right was half open, with the eyeball rolled up, so that there was a good deal of white. I have seen a spaniel sleep like that, in front of a fire, and it alarms one in a spaniel too. I spoke his name. I patted his cheek. I took him by the lapels and gave him the cocktail treatment, as I had the vicar. His head went to and fro and he made a sound.

“Mmf,” said Edmund.

“Edmund! Wake up, old man. You’ve had a fall.”

“Ma,” he said, quite distinctly. Then: “Sorry.” Then he snored again.

Well, there it was. He was alive, he was asleep, and he was talking about his mother. I reviewed my instructions. The patient was not to be left on his back with his head tipped; he could choke. He was to be laid on his side. The left.

I got hold of his far shoulder and his hip and rolled him toward me. He was a tremendous weight. He came over all of a piece, like a log, and settled on his left side in the straw with his cheek on his arm. That did bring the bad side of his head underneath. I saw that as soon as I’d done it, and I didn’t care for it. But she had been most particular about the left. I got some of the dry straw and pushed it under his temple for a pillow. He groaned a bit, and then the breathing went on as before.

I sat back on my heels. I was rather pleased with myself. It was the second casualty of the night that I had dealt with on sound medical lines.

Then I remembered the pudding.

The ice was at the back of the chamber, a long heap of it under sacking and straw, sweating, with the wet running out from underneath in a shallow pool. I held the candle up. I had expected the box to be sitting on top, where I supposed Gail would have put it.

It wasn’t on top. It was on the floor, at the edge of the ice, a yard from my cousin’s outflung hand. It lay partly on its side in the wet. It was a wooden box with tin corners, about two feet each way, and tied round with a length of cord. Wooden. So big. Mrs Pask had shown me with her hands, and that was it to the inch.

I tried the weight. It was just as she’d warned me: heavy, as with ice packed round it. And when I set it upright, something inside shifted and gave a faint metallic chime. That would be the mould. They are made of copper.

I worked out afterwards how it had come to be where it was, and I may as well give the reader the benefit. Gail had put it down on the edge of the heap, in a hurry, in the dark. Edmund, coming down the steps on his head, had fetched up against the ice and knocked it off. This seemed to me at the time a complete and satisfying explanation. I still think it a good one, although I have since been told that it was wrong in every particular.

I looked for the spoon. I was supposed to lift the lid and try the edge. But the spoon had gone into the straw somewhere, by the ice, and the lid was corded down with a knot of a kind I had never seen before and could not begin to undo. I am, as I’ve said, no good with knots. I decided that Mrs Pask could do her own testing. A pudding that had been lying against a ton of ice was not likely to have melted.

So now I had a problem in logistics, of the kind they set at staff colleges. I had one unconscious cousin of sixteen stone and one bombe in a box. It was nearly one o’clock. I had twelve steps and no rail. I could carry the box. I could not, on any reckoning, carry Edmund.

And I could not leave him. That was quite clear. It was like a tomb down there; one could see one’s breath. A man asleep on wet straw in his evening clothes, with a drug in him, would be dead of cold by morning.

I left the candle where it was, on the ninth step, to keep him company. I seem to have spent the night leaving candles with people. I went up the steps and out through the gate and back along the track to the kitchen, as fast as I could go.

“He’s what?” said Mrs Pask.

“At the bottom of the steps. Asleep. He’s hit his head. He’s had a sleeping draught, you see, in his brandy, Miss Quaile says so, the same as the vicar. I’ve put him on his left side.”

She didn’t exclaim. She stood with her hands flat on the kitchen table and her head down, like a woman counting to ten. Then she said a thing I didn’t expect.

“Every year,” said Mrs Pask.

“I beg your pardon?”

“Every year, on the night. Since she went. He can’t abide it, Mr Edmund can’t, he never could. He’s gone by eleven, and the Lord knows where he’ll fetch up. I’ve found him in the stable. I’ve found him in the boathouse, in the punt, with a bottle. The year Miss Imogen didn’t come I found him sat on the Wade in the dark with his feet in the water, crying like a child, and I walked him home and put him to bed and never told a soul.” She looked up. “Is he bad?”

“He’s got a lump. Here. It’s bled a bit. But he’s breathing quite steadily, and he spoke to me.”

“What did he say?”

“He said ‘Ma.’ And then ‘Sorry.’”

Her face did something. It was a good, plain, sensible face, and for a moment it looked like a girl’s.

“He would,” she said. Then she straightened her back, and it was gone. “Right. Mr Vane’s not to know. Not tonight. Not after what he stood up and said at that table, with the whole lot of them looking at Mr Edmund sideways. If he sees him carried in dead drunk with his head broke at one in the morning, that’ll be the finish. Nor madam’s not to know neither. She’s enough to bear.”

“He isn’t drunk. I mean, he is, but it’s the draught, somebody put—”

“I don’t care what it is. I don’t want to know what it is. There’s things go on upstairs in this house that I’ve made it my business for forty years not to know, and I’m too old to start.” She was untying her apron. “And we’ll not have that nurse to him. She’d be bound to tell the old gentleman; that’s what she’s paid for. He wants putting somewhere dry, with a rug over him, where he can sleep it off and come in at breakfast on his own feet like he always does. There’s the end loose box. There’s clean straw in it. He’s slept there before.”

“But Mrs Pask, I can’t lift him. He’s enormous. There’s those steps.”

“There’s two of us,” said Mrs Pask. “And there’s the barrow.”

It was a gardener’s wheelbarrow. She had it out of a shed in the kitchen yard before I had got my breath. It was an old wooden one, long and deep, with a pair of handles like the shafts of a cart and a single iron wheel in front. She threw a couple of sacks into it. She had put on a man’s cap, and over her carpet slippers she had pulled a pair of rubber galoshes.

“I’ve moved bigger than him,” she said. “I moved a pig once, on my own, that’d died in the night. Come on.”

I have told many people that the cook and I carried Edmund up the ice-house steps, and they have nodded. I would like the reader to really consider it.

He was six foot two and weighed, on my estimate, sixteen stone, and he was as limp as a wet coat. There were twelve brick steps, each about nine inches deep, covered with a kind of green grease, going up round a curve, with a wall on one side and on the other a drop. There was one candle. There was me, who has never been strong. And there was a woman of sixty-three in galoshes.

We began by dragging him to the foot of the steps. I took him under the arms from behind, and locked my hands on his chest, and walked backwards. His heels ploughed through the straw. Mrs Pask came after with the candle and told me not to bang his head.

Then we tried it with me at the top end and her at the legs. I got up three steps, backwards, hauling. She got his knees over her shoulders somehow, like a fireman, and pushed. On the fourth step my foot went from under me and I sat down. Edmund sat down on me. Mrs Pask, below, received the whole of us in a sort of avalanche and held it. I do not know how. I heard her say, through her teeth, “That pig was nothing to this.”

“I can’t,” I said. “I’m most frightfully sorry. I can’t feel my arms.”

“You can. Shift your backside up one. Now pull. Now the next. Don’t look down.”

We did it a step at a time. I went up on my seat, one step, and dragged him up after me into my lap, and went up another. It was not dignified. Each time his head lolled back against my shirt front, and each time I heard that long rasping breath and the click at the top of it. I have never been so glad of a noise. Around the seventh step he said something else. He said, “Is it over?” in a thick voice, like a child woken in a car.

“Nearly, Mr Edmund,” said Mrs Pask from below. “You go back to sleep.”

And he did.

At the top we rested, with him laid out along the landing. I thought my heart would come out through my collar. Mrs Pask leaned on the wall and got her wind. She had lost her cap.

“Now the barrow,” she said.

We got him into it. I shall not go into that; the principle was the same as with the steps but in reverse. He went in on his back, on the sacks, with his head toward the handles and his legs hanging out over the front, on either side of the wheel. She tucked his arms in.

“I’ll take him,” she said. “I know the ground. You fetch the ice.”

I went down once more for the box. I looked for the spoon, without much hope, and didn’t find it. I blew the candle out and left it in its saucer on the step, since I had no hand to carry it. I got the box up in my arms, like a man with a suitcase and no handle, and climbed, and came out through the gate. I didn’t shut it. Nor did I take Mrs Pask’s keys out of the lock. I had altogether forgotten that they were there. She was very short with me about it afterwards. It is the one thing, in the whole of this, that she ever held against me.

She was waiting on the track, between the shafts.

“Where’ll I put this?” I said. The box was pulling my arms out.

Mrs Pask looked at the box, and at the barrow.

“He’ll not mind,” she said.
