So I put the bombe on Edmund. There was nowhere else. I set it on his stomach, square, and folded his hands on top of it to keep it steady. He looked like one of those crusaders who are carved holding a model of the church they have founded.

I include that detail knowing that it does not show any of us in a dignified light. But I said I would tell this truthfully.

It is about seventy yards from the ice house to the stable yard, slightly uphill, on mud. Mrs Pask wheeled him the whole way. I walked beside, with one hand on the box. Neither of us spoke. The iron wheel cut into the soft ground and she had to lean her whole weight on it, and I could hear her breathing as well as his.

Once I thought I saw somebody. We were coming up to the end of the stable block, where the track turned into the yard. The moon had come out. And at the corner of the wall, low down, about the height of my waist, there was a face.

It was a small face, quite white, with dark hair, and it was looking round the corner at us with enormous interest. It was there for perhaps two seconds. Then it wasn’t.

I said nothing to Mrs Pask. I’d already had one conversation with her that evening about things I had seen. I put it with the lift.

We came round into the yard. It was cobbled. I had sat there on the mounting block that afternoon and emptied my shoes. The tower with the clock on it stood up over us, and I looked up, as one does, and saw the two wooden figures at the top, under their little roof. Kit and the girl had dressed them. The man had on a dinner jacket and a white front. I thought he looked a good deal smarter than I did.

“Which is the end box?” I whispered.

“There. Past the block. I’ll go round it. Mind, there’s a drain.”

I must now describe exactly what happened, because for nine years, in the telling, I have not.

In the telling it goes like this. We wheel my cousin across the yard by moonlight, with a pudding on his chest. I say that he looked like a crusader, and people laugh. And then I say: “And we tucked him up in the straw with a horse blanket, and I never saw a man sleep sounder.” And we go on to the Odd Hour.

There is a piece missing. It is about four seconds long.

The yard was cobbled, as I say, and the cobbles were wet, and they were the old round kind, like the backs of loaves. A wheelbarrow with an iron wheel does not go over those. It goes between them. Mrs Pask knew it. She was taking the barrow in a wide curve round the mounting block, slowly, picking her line.

And I thought she was tired. She was sixty-three and had been on her feet since six that morning, and I was twenty-nine. I had been walking alongside with one hand on a box, like a passenger. I was ashamed. I said, “Here, let me, do let me,” and before she could answer I had stepped in between the shafts beside her and got hold of the right-hand handle.

“Leave go, Mr Toby,” she said. “I’ve got him.”

“No, really, I insist.”

I pushed. I am told that with a wheelbarrow one does not push one handle. The barrow slewed. The wheel came out of the line she had been keeping and dropped into the gap between two cobbles, and stopped dead, and the whole weight came forward against it and then went over sideways. It was like a boat going over. It took perhaps a second. I had the handle and I couldn’t hold it. She had the other and she couldn’t either.

I saved the pudding. That’s the thing I have to live with. The box started to slide, and I let go of the barrow and grabbed for it with both arms, and caught it. I caught it beautifully.

Edmund went out on the other side. He went out head first.

The mounting block was just there. It was a block of stone, the height of a table, with a square edge. He was on his back, and turning, and it was the back of his head that met the corner. I heard it. I have heard a melon dropped on a kitchen floor, and it was that sound exactly.

He lay on the cobbles at the foot of the block. The barrow lay beside him with its wheel going round.

I stood there with the box in my arms. Mrs Pask had both hands over her mouth.

And then Edmund said, “Ow.”

He said it quite loudly, and in an aggrieved tone. He put a hand up to the back of his head, slowly. He said a word beginning with B. Then he opened his eyes, both of them as far as they would go, and looked straight up at me, standing over him against the moon.

“Who’s that?” he said.

“It’s Toby,” I said. My voice had gone up about an octave. “It’s only Toby. Dorothea’s grandson.”

“What are you holding?”

“The pudding.”

He thought about it. “Good,” he said. “Well done.” And he shut his eyes, and turned over on the wet stones onto his side, the left one, of his own accord, and drew his knees up like a boy, and began again to snore.

Mrs Pask had gone down on her knees by him. She had his head in her hands and was feeling over the back of it with her fingers, under the hair. She took them away and held them to the moon. They were dark.

“It’s cut,” she said. “Not deep. Heads bleed. He’s his father’s skull, thick as a church door; I’ve seen him come off a horse at the point-to-point onto a road and get up and ask who’d won.” She was talking to herself as much as to me. She wiped her fingers on a sack. “He spoke. You heard him. He spoke quite sensible, and knew to ask who it was.”

“He said ‘well done.’”

“He did.”

“Mrs Pask, I’m so sorry. I’m so terribly sorry. I only wanted to help.”

She looked up at me. I had expected her to be angry. I’d have preferred it.

“I know you did, my duck,” she said. “You’ve not the build for it, that’s all. Put that box down and take his feet.”

We got him into the end loose box. It was dry in there and smelled of hay. We laid him down in deep straw, on his left side, and she fetched a horse rug from the place next door and spread it over him and tucked it in at the neck. She went back for a second one and rolled it up and put it under his head. Her hands were as gentle about it as if he had been four years old. I held the lamp she had lit, a stable lantern, and I could see her face, and I understood something I hadn’t before. Mrs Pask had been at Compline since 1952. Edmund would have been ten.

He was breathing in the same way, slow, with the click. There was a little blood on the rug where the back of his head rested, and the lump on his forehead had not got any smaller.

“Oughtn’t we to fetch Miss Quaile?” I said. “Really? Just to look at him?”

“And have her tell Mr Vane? No. I’ve said. He’ll do.” She got to her feet, with a hand on the manger. “I’ll come out to him myself, after the ice is served, with a basin and a bit of lint. And again before I go to bed. He’ll have a head on him in the morning that he’ll remember. That’s all it’ll be.”

“You’re sure.”

“I’ve known him forty-two years, Mr Toby. He’s fallen off or out of or into everything on this island. He bounces.” She took the lantern from me. In the doorway she stopped and looked back at the shape under the rug. “You’ve not to go telling this. Not to anyone. Not to that Mr Cade, nor Miss Imogen, nor your mother. He’d never hold his head up. A grown man, wheeled about in a barrow by the cook.”

“I shan’t say a word.”

“See you don’t.”

I kept that promise for nine years. I told the story, as I’ve said. I told the barrow, and the pudding on his chest, because by then everyone concerned was past minding, and it got a laugh. I never told the mounting block. I never told anyone that I had taken the handle.

There was one other thing in the stables that night that I should mention. When she went into the next-door place for the rug, I followed her to the door with the lamp. It was a harness room. There was a wooden stair in the corner going up into the tower, and you could hear the big clock working overhead, very slowly, like someone sawing. And there had been some sort of a rough-house in there. A hurricane lamp was lying on the floor, smashed, in a pool of paraffin. There was a strong smell of whisky. On one of the rugs in the heap, when Mrs Pask lifted it, there was a patch of something dark and still wet, and I saw her look at it, and then look quickly at me, and take the rug underneath instead.

And leaning against the wall just inside the door was a cricket bat.

I thought, Edmund has been here already. I thought he had come here first, earlier in the evening, with a bottle, and knocked a lamp over and cut himself. Then he’d gone wandering off to the ice house and done it properly. I was sure of it. I could see the whole thing. It didn’t occur to me that there might be more than one person bleeding in a stable at Compline on the same night. One hardly expects it.

We went back across the yard. She wheeled the empty barrow. I carried the box. The moon was fully out now, and the gravel was quite bright, and the house stood at the far side of it with the hall windows lit. I looked up at the tower again as we passed under it. The wooden man in his dinner jacket lifted his hammer, and the little bell went, three times over. Ting-tang, ting-tang, ting-tang. It made me jump.

“Quarter to,” said Mrs Pask. “Lord, and I’ve not got the dish out.”

In the kitchen, the clock on the wall said seven minutes to one. I’ve since been told that it was fast, and that Mrs Pask kept it so. I can only say what I saw. She washed her hands at the sink, for a long time, with a brush. I set the box down on the table.

“Not there,” she said. “The slab, in the larder. It wants to be kept cold till the minute. And don’t you go undoing it; you’ll let the warm in. Where’s my spoon?”

I told her about the spoon.

“And my saucer?”

I told her about the saucer.

“And my keys?”

I was silent.

“You’ve left my keys in that gate,” said Mrs Pask. “My kitchen keys, that’s never been off that nail in forty years but in my own hand.” She breathed in. I waited. But she only dried her hands, and looked at the ceiling, as though she had heard something up there. It was a look I’d seen on Miss Quaile on the stairs. They all seemed to be listening for something above them in that house.

“I’ve a thing to see to,” she said. “Upstairs. I’ll not be five minutes. You put that in the larder and you sit down there and you don’t touch nothing. When I come down I’ll turn it out on the dish, and Gail can carry it in. And then I’m going out for my keys, and you’re coming with me to hold the lamp.”

She took a candle and went up the back stairs. I heard her going up, flight after flight. She was going a long way. The treads creaked right up to the top of the house.

I carried the box through to the pantry and put it on the marble slab, next to a ham. I shut the door on it. I gave the hatch of the dumb waiter a civil nod in passing. It didn’t say anything.

Then I sat down at the kitchen table, as told, among thirteen glass plates. I looked at my hands. They were green from the steps, and there was straw on my trousers. On the front of my dress shirt, where his head had rested all the way up, there was a brown stain the size of a saucer.

I thought about my cousin Edmund. He was asleep under a horse rug, and snoring, with a lump on the front of his head that he had given himself, and a cut on the back that I had given him. I thought, well, at any rate he spoke. He said “well done.”

I had no business to feel as cheerful as I did. But I’d been useful. There were two people lying down in comfort who might have been sitting up choking if I had not been by. And I had the pudding.

I should perhaps have wondered why it ticked.

It did, a little. I’d noticed it as I set the box down on the marble: a faint, irregular tick from inside, like a beetle in a wall. It went on for a few seconds and stopped. I assumed it was the ice settling.

5. In Which the Ice Is Served

Mrs Pask did not come down in five minutes. She did not come down in ten. I sat at the kitchen table among the little plates and watched the hands of the big clock go round to one, and past it.

I may say that I’ve sat in some anxious kitchens. I once waited forty minutes in one in Beaune while a grower decided whether to sell to me or set the dog on. But I have never felt time pass as I felt it in that kitchen at Compline. Every clock in the house was getting ready to strike. One could hear them at it, through the floor, gathering themselves, like a congregation about to stand.

At five past one by the wall, the door at the top of the kitchen stairs burst open and Gail came down them at a gallop, with her cap over one ear.

“Where’s Auntie?”

“Upstairs. She said five minutes. That was a quarter of an hour ago.”

“Upstairs? What’s she want upstairs? They’re all in the hall! Mr Vane’s stood at the front door with his hand on the bolt. Mr Fenn’s got the champagne open. Where’s the ice?”

“In the larder. On the slab.”

“Is it turned out?”

“No. She said I wasn’t to touch it.”

“Oh, my Lord,” said Gail. “Oh my Lord. He’ll say it. He says it every year. He opens the door and says his bit, and then he turns round and says, ‘Ah, Mrs Pask, the ice,’ and it’s there. On the table, with the violets on. It’s never not been there. Not since before I was born.” She ran into the stone passage and I heard the larder door. She came back out with her face puckered. “That’s not our box.”

“I beg your pardon?”

“The ice. I carried it out myself, when the lights went. It’s in a wine box, what the port come in. Says Cockburn’s on the side. That one’s got tin on.”

I felt a slight chill. I put it from me.

“It was at the bottom of the steps,” I said. “By the ice. Exactly where she said, and the right size, and heavy. It’s the only box there. I looked.” I hadn’t looked very hard, to be truthful. I had been thinking about my cousin.

Gail stood on one leg and chewed her lip. Above us, in the hall, the first clock began to strike. It had a silvery, hurried sort of voice. A second joined it.

“Well, it’ll be the ice,” she said. “What else’d be in an ice house? Auntie’ll have changed the box on me. She does that. She says I pack like a navvy.” She made up her mind. “There’s no time to turn it out. You take it in.”

“Me?”

“As it is. In the box. He likes to see it come in; he’ll not mind the box. You put it down on the hall table and get the lid off, and I’ll be right behind with the dish and the big spoon, and we’ll turn it out in front of them. It’ll look like it was meant.” She was already loading plates onto a tray. “Go on, Mr Toby! They’ve started!”

They had. There were six or seven going now overhead, all on different notes and none of them together. It was like bell-ringers who have never practised.

I went and got the box.

It was as heavy as ever. I held it against my chest with both arms and went up the kitchen stairs backwards, pushing the baize door open with my shoulders. Gail had thrust a kitchen knife into my top pocket, for the cord. She was behind me with the tray. I could hear the plates chattering.

I thought, as I went up, of what I should say. It seemed an occasion for a few words. A stranger to the family, a young relation, makes his entrance at the solemn moment bearing the traditional dish. I thought of something light. Uncle Leo, I’m afraid I’ve nothing to give you but what you have already. No. Uncle Leo. The ice cometh. I liked that. I was rather taken with it. I was still polishing it as I came through the door into the hall.

I have to describe the hall as I found it, because I only saw it for about four seconds before events moved on, and I’ve had to piece the rest together.

They had lit every candle in the house. The place was like a church at Christmas. All the tall clocks were striking, and their pendulums winked. On the settle by the fire lay the vicar, as I’d left him, on his left side, with his teeth beside him. In a big chair on the other side of the hearth sat Dame Octavia Prowse, wide awake now, with her feet planted and a glass of champagne. Mr Fenn stood at the hall table by the Font, with the bottle.

My cousin’s wife was there. She was standing by herself at the back, under the largest of the clocks, very straight, with her hands clasped in front of her. Her hair was damp. I noticed that, because she was otherwise so perfectly turned out. She looked like a woman who is sitting for her portrait and wishes it were finished.

Kit and the girl Saskia were on the bottom stair. They had plainly only just come in. Saskia had a man’s overcoat on over the green dress, and there was hay on it. Kit had hay in his hair. He was the colour of the candles and he was holding on to the newel post. He looked at me as I came through the baize door. I thought it was the look of a man who has been waiting for something dreadful and sees it come in carrying a box. He had the wrong dreadful thing in mind, as it turned out, but I didn’t know that.

There was no Edmund. I, of course, knew why. There was no Imogen, and no detective.

And at the far end, at the great front door, with his back to us all, stood my Uncle Leo. He’d let the rug fall off his shoulders. He was standing up straight, as tall as a hatstand, with one hand on the iron bolt. Miss Quaile was half a pace behind his left elbow.

The clocks finished. The last of them was a deep, slow old fellow by the stairs, who took his time over his one note and let it die. There was a moment in which the hall was quite silent, apart from the ticking, which I had stopped counting as noise.

“Now,” said my uncle.

He drew the bolt. He took hold of the two leaves of the door, one in each hand, and pulled them open and walked them back against the wall. The night came in. All the candles down that end lay over flat, and some went out. I could see straight through, from where I stood with my box, across a stretch of wet gravel shining in the moon, to the stables, and the tower, and the pale face of the tower clock.

“Come in,” said my Uncle Leo, to the dark. He spoke as one speaks to a guest who has kept the soup waiting. “Come in, then. You’re late. You’ve been late since the last Sunday in March.”

Out across the gravel, the tower clock began to strike. I could hear the little bell first, the ting-tang, four times. I could even see something moving, up at the top, under the roof. There was a light up there, swinging. I thought it must be part of the ceremony.

Then came the big bell. It struck once.

And there were two bangs.

I can only describe them as I heard them. They were very loud, and flat, and close together. Bang. And then, before one had drawn breath, bang. It was as if somebody had slammed the lid of a grand piano, twice, out in the yard. The echo came back off the front of the house.

Miss Quaile cried out. It wasn’t a scream. It was a short, sharp sound, like someone who has put a hand on a hot stove. She had both hands up to her mouth and she was staring out through the open door, at the tower, with her eyes as wide as I ever saw them. My uncle didn’t move at all. He stood in the doorway with his arms a little out from his sides, looking the same way.

“Ah,” I heard him say. He sounded interested. “Yes. I thought there would be something to pay.”

Nobody else had seen whatever it was. We were all behind them, down the hall, in the light. Mr Fenn said, “Thunder.” Dame Octavia said, “Thunder my foot. That’s a twelve-bore, both barrels. Somebody’s after the duck.” Saskia said, “At one in the morning?” and Dame Octavia said that it was the best time, under a moon, with the tide making, and that her first husband had never been home.

That seemed to settle it. It settled it for me. I had come to a stop just inside the baize door, with twenty-odd pounds of pudding in my arms and a speech prepared, and I had lost my moment. I could feel it going. A nicer judgment would have let it go.

“Uncle Leo!” I said.

He turned round. They all turned round.

“Uncle Leo,” I said. “The ice cometh.”

I advanced up the hall. I have made some entrances in my time, mostly backwards, but I think that was my best. I carried the box before me like a man bearing the crown at a coronation. I reached the table. Mr Fenn, with a solicitor’s instinct, moved the Font out of the way. I set the box down.

“Mrs Pask has been detained,” I said. “But she asked me particularly to see that the tradition was observed. I understand it’s her forty-second.” I drew the kitchen knife from my pocket, with a flourish, and cut the cord.

I lifted off the lid.

There was a blanket. It was a grey army blanket, folded. I was a little surprised. I had expected ice, and salt, and straw. But I reasoned that a blanket would keep the cold in very well, and I folded it back, left and right, like the flaps of an envelope.

Under the blanket there was a pillowcase, with something inside it. The something was about two feet tall. It was the right height for a bombe. It was hard, and cold to the touch, and it seemed to have corners.

I began to have doubts. But there is a point in any performance beyond which one cannot stop. Gail was at my elbow with the big dish. I took the pillowcase by its hem and drew it off upward, in one sweep, in the way that waiters lift the cover from a joint.

“Voilà,” I said.

It was a clock.

I don’t know how to convey the quality of the silence. I’ve told this story a good many times, and at this point people laugh, and I let them. But nobody laughed in the hall at Compline. There were eleven people there, if one counts the vicar, and they were all looking at a table. On it, in a nest of grey blanket, with fifty candles shining in its glass, stood a brass clock. It had a big white dial, and a lot of little ones, and a painted moon.

Gail said, “That’s never the ice.”

I looked at it. I looked into the box, in case the bombe was underneath. There was nothing underneath. I looked at my great-uncle. I believe I said, “It was at the bottom of the steps.”

Several things happened in the hall, and I didn’t see all of them. I heard a sharp sound from the stairs. That was Kit; he had sat down, suddenly, on the bottom tread, and put his head on his knees. I saw Mr Fenn take off his spectacles and close his eyes, like a man who has been expecting a bill and is nonetheless shocked by the figure. I saw my cousin’s wife. She hadn’t moved a muscle. She was looking at the clock, but she looked as if she were seeing something else, about a hundred yards behind it.

My Uncle Leo came down the hall.

He came quite slowly. He fitted the glass into his eye as he walked. He stopped at the table and bent from the waist, with his hands clasped behind his back, and looked at the clock. He looked at the face of it and then, moving round, at the side, and the back. He put out one finger and touched something underneath, very gently. He was a full minute about it. I counted the buttons on his waistcoat.

Then he straightened up and let the glass fall.

“Ah,” he said. “The Copy. I wondered where I had put it.”

I waited to be struck dead.

“It has stopped,” he observed. “It will have been laid on its side. One must never lay it on its side; the moon work is suspended from a single cock and will not bear it. I made that cock in the winter of 1964, and I made it too light. I’ve always meant to do it again.” He turned to me, and he smiled. He had a very sweet smile, when it came. “It was thoughtful of you to bring it, my boy. I am much obliged. It should not have been left in the damp. But I believe we were promised an ice.”

“I—yes. Sir. I’m awfully sorry. I think there’s been a mix-up with the boxes.”

“There often is,” said my Uncle Leo.

“Is it a clock or a pudding?” called Dame Octavia from her chair. She was a little deaf and had not left it. “I can’t see from here. If it’s a pudding, I’ll have some.”

“It’s a clock, Octavia.”

“Another one? Good God. Tell the boy to take it away and bring something one can eat.”

I am aware that the reader, who is cleverer than I am, will have understood a good deal about that clock which I didn’t.

I didn’t know what it was. I had never been in the library by daylight. I had heard nothing about a Thorne Sidereal, or that there was such a thing in the house worth a million pounds and more. Nobody had told me that at twenty past ten that night, when the lights failed, it had gone from its case. All I knew was that I had been sent for a pudding and had come back with a clock, and that my great-uncle called it “the Copy” and seemed mildly pleased to see it.

It was years before I heard the rest. I heard it from a man in the trade who had a cousin in the auction business. He told me what a Thorne Sidereal was, and what had become of the real one, and asked me if it was true that I had once served it at a party. I said it was not true. I said I had served the copy. He said that came to the same thing.

So I can’t tell you what Edmund was doing with that box in the ice house. I have my own idea. But I can tell you that I carried it into the hall and unveiled it in front of the whole family, on the stroke of one, with the words, “The ice cometh.” And whatever plans had been laid for that clock that night, by whomever, I don’t think they can have included that.

I’ve sometimes thought it was the most useful thing I ever did, and I did it by accident, as usual. Whether it was useful to the right people, I’ve never been able to work out.

They lifted it out. Mr Fenn and Kit did it between them, at my uncle’s direction, and stood it on the table on its blanket. Kit’s hands were shaking so that the little glass door rattled. He didn’t once look at his mother.

I took the empty box back to the pantry. It seemed the least I could do. I had a feeling that one of us ought to be put away. I pushed it under the marble slab with its lid. I looked for Mrs Pask in the kitchen, but she had not come down. I called up the back stairs and got no answer. And here I must confess something odd. I thought, standing at the bottom of those stairs, that I could hear her, very faintly, a long way up. She was calling something. It sounded like a name, a short one, said over and over, soft and urgent, as one calls a cat that has got out.

I assumed she had a cat.

When I got back to the hall, Gail had rallied. She had fetched up a trifle that had been meant for Sunday. She served it onto the thirteen glass plates. One was set down on the hall table at an empty chair that somebody had brought through from the dining room. Nobody remarked on it. I ate mine. I was extremely hungry.

And then my Uncle Leo made a speech.

It was not like the one at dinner. He’d stood up for that. For this he sat, in a chair somebody had put for him near the open door, with the night at his back and the rug over his knees. His voice was quite different. At dinner he’d sounded like a judge. Now he sounded like a man talking to his family, late, when the guests have gone.

I didn’t take it all in. I was at the back, with a plate. But I heard the heart of it, and I can give it very nearly as he said it, because I’ve never heard anything I liked better.

“I asked a question at dinner,” he said. “I said that one of you had been robbing me, and that I should know which by one o’clock. Well, it is past one. And I find that I no longer want to be told.”

Nobody spoke.

“I’ve been sitting here trying to think what a clock is for. I ought to know. I’ve given my life to them. It is for telling a man how much time he has got. That is all. It has no other use. And I have got a hundred and eleven of them, and not one has ever told me that. They have only told me how much I’d had.”

He looked round at us. His eyes rested on the clock on the table, and went on.

“If any of you has taken anything from this house, I expect you wanted it. I expect you wanted it more than I did. I hadn’t looked at half of them in years. I daresay there was a reason, and I daresay I’m some part of the reason, and I was not a father that a person could come to and ask. I know that. Your mother knew it. She used to say I could hear a watch losing two seconds a week and could not hear my own children.” He was silent for a moment. “So I shall put it on the Hour’s account. Whatever it is. The matter of the clocks is closed, and I don’t wish to hear it spoken of in this house again. Lionel, you will kindly make a note of that. It’s the only instruction I’ve given you in ten years that I am sure I mean.”

“I have noted it, Leo,” said Mr Fenn.

“Good. And there’s another thing. Get your pen. There is something I owe across the water, at Saltcote, that has been owing a long time. I can’t pay it to the man. I let him die without. I’ll pay it to his name. You’ll write it down as I say it, and Octavia shall witness it, and the vicar, if he can be made to hold a pen.”

“The vicar’s asleep, Leo,” said Dame Octavia.

“Then wake him.”

It took Gail and me and a wet napkin. But we got the Reverend Aubrey Stiles upright for long enough to write his name at the bottom of a paper, with his eyes shut and his teeth in the wrong way up. He said, “Bless you, my children,” and went down again. I didn’t know what the paper was. Mr Fenn folded it into a long envelope and put it in his breast pocket.

I should perhaps say that I had been listening to my uncle’s speech with very mixed feelings.

On the one hand, it was plain by now that it wasn’t the clock in the Blue Room he had meant. Something much larger was going on, and I’d blundered through the middle of it with a pudding box. I could see that. On the other hand, he had said “if any of you has taken anything.” He had said “whatever it is.” And I had, in the strictest sense, taken something. I had a third of it in my pocket at that moment. He had forgiven it, sight unseen, in front of a solicitor.

I felt a great weight go off me. This was premature, as most of my feelings are. But I felt it.

After that there was the dance.

I shall tell this part as plainly as I can. I’ve left it out of the after-dinner version altogether. It doesn’t get a laugh, and it isn’t meant to.

My uncle had finished with Mr Fenn. He sat for a little while with his eyes closed, and I thought he had dropped off. Then he opened them and said, “Kit. Wind the gramophone. I should like the Lehár.”

There was a gramophone in the corner, a real one, with a brass horn like a lily. Kit went over to it. He seemed glad of something to do. He turned the handle and found a record in the cupboard underneath and put it on, and lowered the arm. There was a noise like frying. Then came a waltz, with a great many violins, very sweet and very slow to begin, the sort of thing they must have danced to at Compline when the old gentleman was a boy.

“‘Gold and Silver,’” said Dame Octavia, to nobody. “He would. He danced that with me at the Hunt Ball in 1934. He trod on my foot and talked about escapements.”

I was looking at the gramophone. I didn’t see her come.

It was Saskia who saw first. She was sitting halfway up the stairs, in the overcoat. She said, “Kit,” in a sort of gasp. I looked round.

Someone was coming down the stairs.

It was a woman in a grey dress. It was a long dress, of silk, cut very low at the back and plain in front, of the sort one sees in photographs of one’s grandmother when she was presented. It was a soft, clear grey, and it took the candlelight in a way that made it look almost like water. She had dark hair, put up. She came down slowly, with one hand on the rail, looking straight ahead of her.

It was my cousin Imogen. I knew her at once, by the white streak in her hair. She had gone up and changed.

I thought it a little much. I may as well admit it. It was past one in the morning, everybody else was in what they had dined in, and it did seem to me a strange time to go and put on another frock. But it was a very pretty one. And she looked quite different in it. At dinner she had looked like a clever woman in black who mended pictures. She looked now like somebody about to be painted.

Nobody else, I gradually saw, was taking it as I was.

Dame Octavia had got up out of her chair. I had not seen her stand unassisted all evening. She was holding the back of it, and her big plain face had gone all to pieces. “Oh, my dear God,” she said, under her breath. “Oh, Daisy.” Mr Fenn had bowed his head. My cousin’s wife had her hand at her own throat. Kit stood at the gramophone with his arm half out, and I saw his lips move, and I’m almost sure he said “Granny.”

And Miss Quaile, who had been standing by my uncle’s chair, took one step back, and another. Then she sat down on the floor with her back against the wall, as though her legs had been taken away. She was staring at my cousin Imogen as I hope never to be stared at by anyone.

I didn’t understand it. I’d never been up to the long gallery. I had not seen the portrait at the end of it, as everyone else in that hall had, some of them every day for twenty years. I’d no way of knowing what dress it was, or whose.

My Uncle Leo had risen. He stood by his chair, quite still, with the rug at his feet.

“You came back,” he said. “Margot. You came back.”

My cousin Imogen came across the hall to him. I could see her face then. It was perfectly white, and wet, and she was smiling. She put out her hand.

“Yes, Papa,” she said. And then, very low, and I think she’d been getting ready to say it all the way down the stairs: “Yes, Leo. I came back.”

He took her hand. He put his other hand at her waist. And he danced with her.

I have said he was eighty-one. I’ve said he had to be helped to his chair. He waltzed with that woman in the grey dress the whole length of his hall and back, among the clocks, without a stumble. He held her as if she were made of something that might spill. His eyes were shut. Hers were open, and she was looking over his shoulder, and the tears ran down her face the whole time and she did nothing about them.

He talked to her as they went. I caught a little, when they came round by where I stood. It was a low, quick, urgent murmur, like a man giving directions to somebody who has a train to catch. He said something about the tide. He said, “ten minutes to one,” and “not a minute before,” and “a horse.” He said, “I had it wrong. I had it wrong for you the last time, my dear, and I’ve got it right.” She nodded. She kept nodding.

I’d taken a step forward. I don’t know what I had in mind. I think I felt that somebody ought to dance, besides, to make it look less strange. I thought I might ask Dame Octavia.

A hand like a ham closed on my sleeve.

“Sit down, boy,” said Dame Octavia Prowse. She wasn’t looking at me. She was watching the two of them go round, with her old eyes swimming. “This one isn’t for us.”

So I sat down, on the stairs, a few steps below Saskia. I looked at nothing but my plate. I didn’t understand what I was seeing. But I’ve been in enough churches to know when to keep my head down.

The record ran out. They stopped in the middle of the floor. I heard my uncle say, “There. There, my dear. You see. It’s quite all right. We had the time after all.”

She said something to him that I couldn’t hear. She kissed him, on the forehead, and held his face for a moment between her hands. Then she let him go, and turned, and went away across the hall toward the garden passage. She went quickly, in the grey dress, and she didn’t look back at any of us.

My uncle stood where she had left him. He looked very tired, suddenly, and very old, and entirely happy. Miss Quaile had got up off the floor. She went to him. She moved like a person walking in her sleep. She put her hand under his elbow, and he let her lead him toward his chair.

Kit shut the lid of the gramophone.

I thought someone would say something, and I waited, and nobody did. Dame Octavia lowered herself back into her chair and held out her glass for more champagne, without a word, and Mr Fenn filled it. Celia was gone; I had not seen her go. Saskia was crying into the collar of the overcoat. Kit went past me up the stairs and sat down beside her and put his arm round her.

It was, I suppose, about twenty-five past one.

I looked across the hall at the nurse. She had settled the old man. She was standing by his chair with her hands hanging at her sides. Her face was grey. She had the look of someone who has been ill for a week. She was looking through the open front door, across the gravel, at the tower with the clock on it. I thought she looked as if she were waiting for it to do something else.

I should have left her alone. Any man of sense would have. She had clearly had some kind of shock. I didn’t know what kind. I thought the business with the dress had upset her, as it had upset everybody. I didn’t know that she’d also seen something out of that door at one o’clock that the rest of us had not.

But I had been told by an expert that in this hour nothing counted. One could ask for anything. I had meant to ask my uncle for five thousand pounds, and I found, looking at Miss Quaile, that I had lost all interest in the Thracian valley.

I put down my plate. I pulled my cuffs down, as far as they would go. And I went across to her.

6. In Which I Am Accepted

I have proposed marriage, in the course of a full life, on five occasions. Three were successful, if that is the word, and one of those is still pending. I mention the figure so that the reader will understand that I speak with some authority when I say that the proposal I made in the hall at Compline was, technically, the worst.

I crossed the floor. She was standing by my uncle’s chair. He had his head back and his eyes closed, and his long hands lay on the rug. She was looking out through the front door at the stable tower. When I came up she didn’t turn her head.

“Miss Quaile,” I said.

“Mr Pargeter.”

“I don’t know your Christian name.”

“Hester.”

It suited her. It was a name like a plain white plate. I said it over to myself, and then I found that I had nothing ready to follow it. I had come across the hall on a wave of feeling, and it had set me down at her elbow and gone out again, as waves do.

“The vicar’s still asleep,” I said. “I’ve been looking at him every half hour. As instructed. He’s on his left side.”

“Thank you.”

“And he’s breathing. I counted. Eight to the minute.”

“That’s right.”

She still hadn’t looked at me. I followed her eyes. There was nothing out there but the gravel in the moonlight and the tower, with its clock face, and something or other up at the top under a little roof. I could make out one of the wooden figures. It seemed to have its arm in the air.

“What are you looking at?” I asked.

“Nothing,” Hester Quaile said. “There’s nothing there now.”

I should have noticed the now. I didn’t. I am no good at small words. I was working myself up, and it’s a process, with me, like getting the Midget started on a cold morning. It involves a good deal of choke and several false tries.

“There’s something I ought to tell you,” I said. “I promised I wouldn’t. But I think you ought to know, being a nurse, and it’s been on my mind. It’s about Edmund.”

That got her attention. She turned right round. I’ve mentioned her eyes. They fixed on me as though I had spoken in a foreign language that she happened to understand.

“What about Mr Edmund?”

“He’s all right. I want to say that first. He’s perfectly all right; he’s asleep. But he’s had rather a bang on the head. Two, actually. He had the same stuff as the vicar, you see, out of that glass, and it must have come over him all at once, and he fell down some steps.”

“What steps?”

“In the ice house. I found him at the bottom. I’d been sent for the pudding.” I was speaking very low, and fast, with one eye on my sleeping uncle. “I did exactly what you said. I turned him on his left side. And then Mrs Pask and I got him up, and we’ve put him in the stable. In the end loose box, in the straw, with a rug over him and another under his head. She says nobody’s to know, and particularly not you, because you’d be bound to tell Uncle Leo, and after what Uncle Leo said at dinner it would be the last straw. She says it happens every year. She’s going out to him with a basin.”

Her lips had parted. She put a hand on the back of the chair.

“When?” she said.

“When what?”

“When did you find him? When did you put him in the stable? What time?”

“Well, I was sent at twenty-five past twelve. I know that, because I looked. We’d got him tucked up by a quarter to one, or just after. The clock on the tower struck the quarter as we were coming away.” I thought she might want the clinical details. “He spoke to me. Twice. He was quite sensible. He asked what I was holding, and I said the pudding, and he said, ‘Well done.’”

“A quarter to one.”

“About then.”

“In the stable. Under the tower.”

“Next door to it. Yes.”

“Asleep. You left him asleep.”

“Snoring like a grampus.”

She looked back at the open door. It was the most extraordinary look. I have thought about it for nine years. I know now what was going through her head, more or less, because I have read what she wrote about that night; she let me see it, a long time afterwards. I shan’t steal her thunder. I’ll say only that she had seen something at one o’clock, through that door, on that tower. I’d just told her where my cousin had been lying fifteen minutes before it. She was putting the two together, and what she made of them was not what I’d have made.

“Then he woke,” she said, almost to herself. “He woke, and he went up.”

“I don’t think so. He’d had enough to sink a ship. You said yourself the vicar would be out for twelve hours.”

“Yes,” she said. “I did say that.”

She was shivering. I’ve said she wasn’t a person who showed things. But I was standing very close, and I could see it. It was a fine, steady tremor, like a tuning fork. I wanted to put my jacket round her. I remembered what was in the pocket, and thought it would clank.

So I proposed instead. It was the only other thing I could think of to offer.

“Miss Quaile. Hester. May I call you Hester? I want to ask you something. I know this isn’t the time. I’ve been told that in this house it never is. But I’ve also been told that for the next half hour it doesn’t count, whatever one says, so if you think it frightful cheek you can simply forget it at two o’clock, and I’ll never mention it again.”

She said nothing. I took that as leave to go on.

“I’ve known you for eight hours and twenty minutes. I’ve been counting. In that time I’ve broken a clock, and drowned a car, and I thought I’d killed a clergyman. Then I dropped a—well. Never mind what I dropped. The point is that you were there every time it mattered, and you didn’t laugh, and you told me what to do. Nobody’s ever done that. People generally tell me what I ought to have done, afterwards.” I was going rather fast. I had my hands going too; I could feel them. “I’m not anybody. I’ve got three hundred and twelve pounds and a share in some Bulgarian wine I haven’t bought yet. I’m not clever. But I’d look after you. I mean it. Whatever’s happened tonight, the glass, and the tray, and Edmund, and whatever it is you saw out there that’s upset you so. I’d look after all of it. You wouldn’t have to say a word to anyone. You wouldn’t have to explain. I’d simply be there.”

I stopped. I’d run out of road.

I started again. “What I’m trying to say. The thing I came over to ask. I expect you know what it is. People always do, with me. I’m told it’s written all over my face in large print.” I swallowed. “Will you?”

She looked up at me.

It was a long look and I couldn’t read it. I had expected surprise, or pity, or possibly a kind word and a pat on the arm. There was nothing like that in it. It was a grave, measuring look, the look she’d given the vicar’s pulse. I had the impression that she was not thinking about me at all, but about a much larger thing that I happened to be standing in front of.

“You’re asking me to say nothing,” she said slowly.

“I’m asking you to let me—yes. If you like. That’s part of it.”

“About any of it.”

“Not a word. Unless you want to. I’d never press you.”

“And you’d say nothing yourself. About the glass. About where it came from.”

“Good Lord, no. Why should I? It was nobody’s fault. These things happen.”

She shut her eyes for a second. When she opened them she had made up her mind. I saw it happen.

She nodded, once.

“Yes,” said Hester Quaile.

She said yes.

I’ve set it down as it happened. Those were the words I used and those were hers. I asked, “Will you?” and she said, “Yes.”

I am aware that the reader may by now have a suspicion. The reader has had the advantage of seeing that conversation written down, in cold print, with both sides of it. I had only my own side. I knew what I was asking. It didn’t cross my mind that she might have heard a different question. I asked a girl to marry me and she nodded and said yes, and I went up like a rocket.

I think I said, “Oh, I say.” I know that I seized her hand. It was very cold. She let me have it for a moment, in an absent way, and then she drew it back. She didn’t do it unkindly. Her attention had gone elsewhere.

“He’s awake,” she said.

My uncle had opened his eyes. He was looking at me.

“You’re Dorothea’s grandson,” said my Uncle Leo. “You were to ask me something at one. I’ve a note of it.” He hadn’t, of course. But he tapped his forehead. “It’s past one. Ask.”

Now here was a thing. I had come to Compline to borrow five thousand pounds. For the last several hours I had thought of nothing but clocks, vicars, and a pair of Cornish eyes. I’d honestly forgotten the Thracian valley. But I was now an engaged man, with responsibilities. And Dame Octavia had told me to get it in writing.

“Well, sir,” I said. “It’s rather a cheek. The fact is, I’m in the wine trade.”

“Are you good at it?”

“No, sir.”

“Why do you do it?”

I had never been asked. “I like the people,” I said. “And I like the stuff. I like the fact that somebody spent a whole year making it and you can tell what sort of year he had.”

“That is a reason,” said my uncle. “It’s very nearly mine. Go on.”

So I told him about the Bulgarian and the four hundred cases. I told him the price. I told him I had three hundred and twelve pounds and needed five thousand by the end of the month.

“Is it a good wine?” he asked.

I have been proud of very few things in my life, but I’m proud of what I said next. I’d had a great deal to drink and I had just been accepted, and I suppose I was past lying.

“No, sir,” I said. “It’s a cheap wine. It’s a perfectly honest cheap red that tastes of plums and doesn’t give you a headache. People will be able to buy it for two pounds ninety-nine who can’t afford anything else, and they won’t be cheated. That’s all I can say for it.”

My uncle looked at me through his glass.

“It’s the same as your watch,” he said. “Lionel!”

Mr Fenn came. He had the look of a man who has been called to a bedside too often.

“My cheque book. The left-hand drawer of the morning-room desk. And a pen that writes.”

“Leo, I really must advise—”

“You’ve been advising me for forty years, Lionel, and I’ve taken it for thirty-nine. It is the Odd Hour. Fetch the book.”

He fetched it. My uncle wrote the cheque on his knee, on top of the rug. He wrote it in a hand like copperplate, without a tremor. Pay T. Pargeter Esq. Five thousand pounds. He signed it, and he blotted it on his own cuff, which already had a mark or two on it. I noticed that. I remember thinking he had been at the claret himself. I thought nothing more about those marks for years.

Where the date should go, he hesitated. He looked up at the nearest clock. Then he wrote the time. He put 1.31 a.m. and nothing else.

“There,” he said, and held it out. “For plums. Cash it on Monday morning before I forget that I wrote it.”

“Sir, I don’t know how to—”

“Don’t. I can’t bear to be thanked. It makes me feel that I’ve been stingy up to now, which I have.” He was struggling up out of his chair. Hester went to help him and he put her aside, quite gently. “No, my dear. I’m very well. I’ve never been better. I have had an hour I didn’t expect.” He stood, swaying a little, and looked round his hall as if he were counting it. “I must just see to something. There’s a clock stopped.”

I had the cheque in my hand. I had one more thing to do, and I felt that there’d never be a better moment. I felt in my pocket and got hold of a wheel.

“Uncle Leo. There’s something else. I ought to have told you at once. It’s about a clock. A small one. In the Blue Room. I’m afraid I—”

He held up a hand. It was a long white hand, with the palm toward me, and it stopped me like a policeman’s.

“No,” he said.

“But sir—”

“I said that the matter of the clocks was closed. I said that I didn’t wish to hear it spoken of in this house again. You were present. I meant you along with the rest.” He looked down at me quite sternly from his great height. “Whatever you have done to a clock, young man, I forgave it half an hour ago. I’ll not have it dug up to be forgiven twice. It is untidy.”

He walked away. He went across to the fireplace, to the tall dark clock on the left of it, the discreet one, and opened the long door and stood looking into the case. I saw the man Cade come in from the back of the hall and go over to him. Cade was soaked to the thighs and had dried blood down one side of his face. He looked like a man who has been in a fight with a canal.

I didn’t hear what they said to each other. I turned to Hester.

She had gone a few steps after my uncle and stopped. She was watching the two of them at the clock.

“I only wanted to tell him,” I said. “It’s been on my conscience all night. You don’t think it was one of the good ones?”

“What?”

“The clock. In the Blue Room. I trod on it.”

“I don’t know anything about clocks,” Hester said. It was the last thing she said to me that night. I’d only turned my back for a minute, to fold the cheque and put it in my note-case. When I looked again, my uncle had gone out of the front door and she was standing at the tall clock with her hand on its glass. She shut the case, and went upstairs.

I told Dame Octavia. I had to tell someone.

She was in her chair by the fire with her shoes off and her feet on the fender. They were large feet, in grey wool stockings. She heard me out.

“The nurse,” she said.

“Miss Quaile. Hester.”

“You met her this afternoon.”

“On the stairs. At twenty past five.”

“And she’s accepted you.”

“Just now. By the door.”

“In so many words?”

“In one word. But it was the right one.”

Dame Octavia looked at me for some time. She had small, shrewd, pouchy eyes, like an elephant’s.

“Your grandmother took three years to accept a man,” she said. “And then it was the wrong one. So perhaps there’s something in doing it quickly. I refused Leo Vane, did you know that? In 1935. I’ve never told anybody. He asked me at a meet, on a horse, and I thought he was asking because his mother had told him to, and I said no to teach him a lesson. I thought he’d ask again. He went off to Switzerland to learn about watches, and when he came back he’d got Marguerite.” She drank some champagne. “She was the right one. I’ll say that. I never could dislike her, and God knows I tried. She had more life in her than the rest of this house put together. She used to stand in the middle of that floor on this night and make them all say what they thought of each other. It was like lancing a boil. They hated it, and they were better for a year.”

“Was that her dress? The grey one?”

“That was her dress. That was the one she’s painted in. I don’t know what Imogen was thinking of. Or I do, and it was a brave thing, and I couldn’t have done it.” She was quiet. “He thought it was her. Did you see his face? He’s waited twenty years for somebody to come down those stairs, and tonight she came. And he got to tell her whatever it was. I’ve no idea what he said. I hope it was the right thing.”

“He told her the time of the tide,” I said. “I heard him.”

“Did he.” Her big face worked. “Yes. He would. That’s about as near as Leo ever got.”

She held out her glass. I filled it.

“Did you get your money?”

I showed her the cheque. She held it at arm’s length.

“He’s not dated it.”

“He’s put the time.”

“So he has. Half past one in the morning. Well, that’s Leo all over; it’s the only thing he’s ever been sure of.” She gave it back. “Cash it Monday. First thing. Be on the doorstep when they open. Fenn’ll stop it if he can; he’s got that look.”

“He wouldn’t. Would he?”

“He’s a solicitor. It’s what they’re for.” She patted my hand. “Never mind. You’ve got the gel. That’s more than I came away with.”

The tower clock struck two.

I heard it through the open door. It was the big bell only, twice, quite slow. I remember thinking that there was something missing. All night there had been that little ting-tang before the hour, like a man clearing his throat before he speaks. This time there was nothing. Just the two strokes, out of the dark, and then the dark again.

All the clocks in the hall took it up. They struck two, one after another, the silvery one and the cracked one and the deep slow one by the stairs.

“That’s that,” said Dame Octavia. “It’s over. Nothing we’ve said counts. You may consider yourself unengaged, if you like.”

“I don’t like.”

“No. I didn’t suppose you would.” She shut her eyes. “Go away, boy. I’m eighty next month and I’ve been up since six.”

The hall had emptied. Mr Fenn had gone off to the library with his envelope. Gail came and took the plates. Kit and Saskia had vanished. The vicar slept. My uncle had not come back; I supposed that he was seeing to his clock, wherever it was, and that Hester had gone after him. I shut one leaf of the front door, because of the draught, and left the other.

The clock was still on the hall table, on its blanket. The Copy. Nobody had come to take it away. Its little moon looked at me out of the corner of its eye. I thought it had the air of a guest who has stayed after the others have left and doesn’t know how to go.

I found that I was ravenous. I’d had a plate of trifle since dinner, and I had carried two men and a clock. I thought of the goose.

So at a quarter past two I went down the kitchen stairs. I know the time, because I looked up at the wall clock from the bottom step, from habit, and it said twenty-three minutes past. I’ve since had that corrected.

The lamp was burning on the table, and somebody was sitting on the table next to it, with his feet on a chair.

It was Edmund.

I stood still. I think my mouth was open.

He had a plate beside him with the remains of the goose on it, and he was pulling the meat off a thigh bone with his fingers and eating it. He had a tumbler of something. He had taken his tie off and opened his collar. He was soaking wet. His hair was plastered down, and his trousers were dark to the knee.

He was a sight. The lump on the left side of his forehead had come up to the size of a hen’s egg and gone purple, and the eye below it was half shut. There was dried blood in his hair at the back. And there was more, which I hadn’t seen before and couldn’t account for. The left side of his neck and his left ear were speckled with it, in little dots, like a man who has cut himself shaving a dozen times. His collar on that side was red. He kept hitching his left shoulder, as if his braces were too tight.

But he was sitting up, on a table, eating. He looked round when he heard me on the stairs. And he grinned.

“Hallo,” he said. “It’s the pudding.”

“Edmund! Good Lord. You’re awake.”

“So they tell me. I’m not altogether convinced.” He waved the bone at me. “Come in. Sit down. Have some goose. Was it you who put me in a wheelbarrow?”

I sat down on the chair nearest the stairs. My legs had gone.

“It was Mrs Pask, mostly. I helped.”

“I thought I’d dreamed it. I dreamed I was being wheeled to my own funeral. I was holding a church on my stomach. It was heavy, and somebody kept telling me to go back to sleep.” He drank. “I’ve had some bad nights on this island, but I don’t think I’ve ever before been buried by the cook.”

“You’d fallen down the ice-house steps.”

“Had I? Is that what I did?” He put his hand up, gingerly, to the lump. He looked for a moment as if he were listening for something that he couldn’t quite hear. “No. I didn’t fall. But let’s say I did. It’s as good as anything.”

“You’d had a sleeping draught. In your brandy. The vicar had the other half; he’s still out. Miss Quaile says—”

“I know what I’d had. I knew when I tasted it. I’ve lived in the same house as that bottle for three years.” He laughed, shortly. “Poor old girl. She must have been desperate. I’d no idea she cared that much.”

I didn’t follow that. I let it go by.

“Edmund, your neck’s bleeding.”

“Is it still? It stings like the devil.” He hitched the shoulder. “Some damned fool letting off at duck. I was up the tower, with a lamp. I suppose I looked like a goose. I got the edge of the pattern. If I’d been standing a foot to the left you’d be picking shot out of me with a fork.” He shook his head. “Don’t mention that upstairs. Father’s had quite enough to forgive for one night.”

“Up the tower? But you were asleep. We left you asleep. You were snoring.”

“I woke up.”

“With that much inside you? The vicar—”

“The vicar’s seventy-four and weighs nine stone, and his idea of a debauch is a second sherry. I’ve been drinking a bottle a day since 1974. It takes more than that to keep me down.” He pulled off another strip of goose. “Mind you, I shouldn’t care to do it again. I got up those stairs on my hands and knees. I had the idea that there was a boat, and that I had to tell it to go away.”

“A boat?”

“Never mind. It’s gone. It went without me, and without what it came for, and I find that I don’t give a damn.” He looked at me with his one good eye and the other. “Do you know, Toby, I haven’t felt like this since I was a boy? I feel as if somebody had taken a hundredweight off my back. I’ve been hit on the head and wheeled about and shot at, and I’m as happy as a king. I suppose it’s concussion.”

I was very much relieved. I had been carrying that mounting block about with me for an hour and a half. I had my mouth open to tell him. I was going to say, Edmund, there’s something I must own up to. The second bang was me. I had got as far as “Edmund, I’m afraid I—”

“I’ve just had a talk with my father,” he said.

He wasn’t looking at me. He was looking at the bone in his hand.

“In the clock room. Up the tower. He came up, by himself, in his pumps. God knows how he managed the ladder. He stood there in the door and looked at me as if I’d risen from the dead. He kept touching me. He put his hand on my face.” He turned the bone over. “It’s the first time I’ve talked to him in twenty years. I mean talked. We’ve said good morning. He thinks he’s travelled in time, or that I’m a ghost, I couldn’t make out which. It doesn’t matter. He was listening. So I told him a thing.”

“What thing?”

“A thing I should have told him in 1974. And my sister. And a man across the water who’s dead now, so that’s one I’ve missed.” He was silent a moment. “I’ve had it in my throat for twenty years, like a fish bone. And tonight I just said it. It took about two minutes. I’d always thought it would take longer.”

“What did he say?”

“He said, ‘Then she didn’t leave me.’ That’s all. He said it about six times, as if he were winding something.” Edmund put the bone down on the plate. “And then he said, ‘You were only a boy.’ I was thirty-two.”

I didn’t understand a word of it. I don’t think he expected me to. He was talking to me the way one talks to a dog, or a stranger on a train.

He wiped his fingers on his trousers and reached for his glass.

“Well,” he said, in his ordinary voice. “That’s me. What about you? You wanted a word, about nine hours ago. You said you’d pinched a clock, and I laughed at you. What was all that?”

Now I should have told him. I see that. I had only to put my hand in my pocket. But I had a bigger piece of news, and it came out first.

“I’m engaged,” I said.

“You’re what?”

“Engaged to be married. To Miss Quaile. I asked her in the Hour and she said yes.”

He stared at me. Then his whole battered face lit up. He looked ten years younger. He put down his glass and held out his hand, and I got up and took it, and he nearly broke my fingers.

“My dear chap. That’s the best thing I’ve heard tonight, and I’ve heard one or two. She’s worth ten of anybody in this house. She’s the only one in three years who’s ever told my father the truth. She told him last week that his wife was dead; she said she wouldn’t lie to him about it, and he could shout as much as he liked. He shouted. Then he thanked her.” He let go of my hand. “She’s had a rotten time of it somewhere. I don’t know where. She doesn’t say. You be good to her.”

“I mean to.”

“And don’t wait. That’s my advice, and it’s the only piece I’ve ever given that was worth having. Don’t wait for the right time. There isn’t one in this house. We don’t keep it.” He laughed. “God, listen to me. I’ll be giving away the bride.”

There was a step in the stone passage that led to the scullery. It was a light, quick step.

Edmund heard it. He turned his head. I saw his face change. He didn’t look frightened. He looked like a man who has been expecting a visitor and hears the gate.

“That’s my sister,” he said quietly. “Run along, Toby.”

“Oughtn’t I to—”

“No. She’s got something to say to me. She’s been saving it up for twenty years. I can tell by her feet.” He picked up the tumbler and finished what was in it. “I’ve said mine tonight. It’s only fair that she should have hers.”

I went up the kitchen stairs. At the top I looked back.

The last I saw of my cousin Edmund that night he was sitting on the kitchen table at a quarter past two, with a plate of cold goose beside him. He had a lump on his head the size of an egg, and he was in the best temper I ever saw him in. He lifted his hand to me. I have seldom seen a man more alive.

I shut the baize door.

7. In Which I Leave, and What I Left Out

I slept in the hall. I had meant to go up to the Blue Room, but there was a second settle on the far side of the fire from the vicar’s, and I sat down on it to take my shoes off and that was the last I knew. I dreamed that I was pushing a clergyman up a flight of steps in a wheelbarrow and that at the top there was a girl with a tray, who said, “On his left side.”

I was woken by somebody shaking my foot. It was still dark.

“Mr Toby. Mr Toby. It’s gone half past five.”

It was Mrs Pask. She had a candle. I sat up, and every clock in the hall told me at once that she was quite right.

I looked at her, and I was shocked. I had left her at ten to one, a strong square woman going up the back stairs with a candle to see to something. She looked now as though she had been ill. Her face had fallen in. Her cap was gone and her grey hair was coming down, and there were cobwebs on her shoulders and on the front of her apron. The hem of her skirt was wet, and there was mud on her galoshes that had not been there before.

“Mrs Pask! Where have you been? I waited. We had to serve the trifle.”

“I know. Gail said.” She didn’t seem to care about the trifle. “I’ve been looking for something.”

“Your keys? I’m most awfully sorry about the keys. I’ll go out now and—”

“They’re on the nail. Somebody’s put them back. I don’t know who, and I’m past asking.” She sat down, heavily, on the end of my settle. I’d never seen her sit. “I’ve been in every room in this house, Mr Toby. Every cupboard. I’ve been in the roof. I’ve been round that sea wall with a lamp, twice, and down to the boathouse, and I’ve looked in places I’ve not set foot in since Miss Imogen was in her cot.”

“For what?”

She opened her mouth to tell me. I’m sure of that. I watched her decide against it.

“Something I’d the minding of,” she said. “That I’d no business to bring. It’ll have gone home. That’s what I keep saying. It’s a sensible little thing, and it’ll have gone home when the water dropped, and I’ll find it sat on my step.” She twisted her hands in her apron. “You never saw nothing? In the night? Nothing that’d no call to be there?”

I thought of the dumb waiter. I thought of a small white face at the corner of the stable wall. I said, “Only the lift.”

“Ah,” said Mrs Pask. “Well. That’s that, then.”

I thought she was talking about a cat. I had heard her calling one. I said, with the idea of comforting her, that cats always came back. She looked at me as if I’d spoken Chinese.

Then she asked the question I had been dreading.

“Did you look in on Mr Edmund? I never got out to him. I’d the basin ready, and then I went up, and I never came down.”

“There was no need,” I said. “He’s up. He was in your kitchen at a quarter past two, sitting on the table, eating your goose. He’d been up the tower. He was as right as rain. He was laughing.”

She shut her eyes. She let out a long breath.

“Thank the Lord for that,” she said. “That’s one, anyhow. I told you he bounced.” She got up, with a hand on my shoulder. She was Mrs Pask again, or nearly. “Now. You’re wanted. It’s the vicar. He’s Communion at eight, at Thorney, and he can’t be woke, and somebody’s to get him there. The road’ll be dry in five minutes. Your motor’s no use; Kit’s had the bonnet up and says the salt’s been in it. So you’re to take the vicar in his own, and leave it at the vicarage, and get the bus.”

“Me? But oughtn’t I to say goodbye? I haven’t seen my uncle. I haven’t seen—” I stopped.

“If it’s that nurse you’re thinking of, she’s sat with Mr Vane in his room with the door locked, and she’ll not open it. I tried. She said through the door that he was asleep and she’d thank me to go away.” Mrs Pask gave me a look in which there was a good deal of knowledge. “You’ll keep. Write to her. She’ll have had a night of it, the same as the rest.”

Gail and I loaded the vicar. I shan’t describe it. The reader knows the method by now. We put him in the passenger seat of his Morris Minor with a rug round him, and his teeth in his pocket, and he said, “Is it Easter?” and went back to sleep.

It was beginning to get light. There was a yellowish streak in the east, behind the stables. I drove round into the yard. I’d never driven a Morris Minor, and one sits very upright in them, like a child in a high chair.

There was a big Ford standing in the yard with its engine running. The man Cade was at the wheel.

I’ve said that I intended to make a clean breast of things to somebody. My uncle had refused to hear me, and Edmund had been interrupted. Hester had other things on her mind. And here, by himself, at six in the morning, was the very capable man in person. I felt that Providence had sent him. I stopped the Morris and got out.

He wound his window down. In the grey light he looked dreadful. There was a dressing of sorts on the back of his head, made out of a handkerchief, and one of his arms hung as if it didn’t belong to him.

“I say, Mr Cade. Might I have a word? Only I gather you’re by way of being a sort of detective. Kit says. And I think I’d better own up to somebody, and I’d rather it was a professional.”

He just looked at me. He had the most tired eyes I’ve ever seen in a human head.

“It was me,” I said.

“What was?”

So I told him. The Blue Room, the pullover, the bed. I told him about the noise like a budgerigar. I took the whole sad handful out of my pocket and held it out to him, on my palm, in the dawn. The fern had got tangled with my cuff link.

“I’ve had it on me all night,” I said. “I kept thinking he was looking at me. Do you suppose it was one of the good ones?”

He looked at it. He didn’t even use a glass.

“It’s a ten-pound carriage clock,” said Mr Cade. “They sell them in Woolworth’s.”

I could have kissed him. He wasn’t a man one would kiss, but I could have. I had gone through fourteen hours of torment. I’d nearly confessed at dinner in front of a solicitor. And it was Woolworth’s.

“Oh, thank God,” I said. “You’ve no idea.”

I put the clock away. I ought then to have gone. But I was in a confessing mood, the way one gets into a swimming mood once one is wet. I had got the small thing off my chest, and there was still the large one.

“There’s another thing, actually,” I said. “Rather worse. I don’t know whether I ought to mention it.”

“Then don’t,” said Mr Cade.

“No. Only I can’t find him to apologise, and we’re off now, and I shouldn’t like him to think I’d just—” I looked at the mounting block. It was ten yards away. It was just a block of stone, with the light coming up on it. There was a dark place on one corner about the size of a penny. “It was the wheel, you see. On the cobbles. They aren’t built for it.”

The vicar had woken up. He leaned across and sounded the horn. A Morris Minor has a horn like a sheep.

“Write him a letter,” said Mr Cade.

I thought that excellent advice. It was a great weight off. One can say things in a letter. I said that I would write to Edmund from town, when he had cooled down. I said cheerio.

I did write. I wrote it on the Sunday night, in Fulham, four pages. I told him about the handle. I posted it on the Monday morning on my way to the bank. It came back to me in December from Mr Fenn’s office, unopened, with a compliments slip.

As I got back into the Morris I looked up at the tower. I don’t know why. One did look at it. And there was something different, which took me a moment to place. There had been two wooden figures at the top. The woman was there, with a wet shawl on her. The man was gone, the one in the dinner jacket, who’d hit the little bell.

I thought the gale had had him. I remember hoping that it wasn’t the good dinner jacket.

I drove off the island at a quarter to six by Mickey, whom I had fished out of the Font on my way through the hall.

The causeway was dry, or what passes for dry on the bottom of the sea. I took it at the pace of a funeral. I had a clergyman aboard, and I’d lost one car on that road already. I kept my eyes on the surface immediately in front of the bonnet. When we came to the dip, and the plank bridge, I looked at nothing in the world but the planks.

So I didn’t look at the hut on legs beside the bridge. I drove past it at eight miles an hour, with my nose on the windscreen, and I didn’t turn my head.

I have been told what I should have seen. Mr Cade came over the same road a quarter of an hour behind me, and he did look. I met him again, years later; it was at a funeral, as it happens, and afterwards in a public house in Leigh-on-Sea. He told me that the door of the hut was open and banging. And he said that the ladder had no bottom to it. From about the height of a man’s chest down to the ground the rungs were gone, snapped off short, and the breaks were white.

He told me as a thing he had noticed and never been able to place. He had no idea that it would mean anything to me. I didn’t tell him. I bought him another whisky and talked about something else.

I had stood at the foot of that ladder at five o’clock on the Saturday afternoon. I’d put my foot on the bottom rung, and it came away in my hand. Then I pushed it back into its socket, with the nail sticking out, because it seemed rude to leave it. I left it looking sound, for anybody who might come along after me and need it.

I don’t know who came along. I don’t know who was climbing that ladder in the night, or why, or what happened when the rung went. Nobody has ever been able to tell me. The road was under six feet of water from ten till half past five. I have asked myself how anyone could have been out there at all.

But I think about that rung. I said I’d come back to it.

The rest is quickly told. For nine years it was all there was.

I got the vicar to his church. There were four old ladies waiting in the porch, and a churchwarden, a Mrs Dace, with a face like a hatchet. She came out to the car. She looked at the Reverend Aubrey Stiles, who was asleep with his mouth open, and she said, “Compline?” I said yes. She said, “It was the weathercock last year,” and went back and pinned a notice on the door. I read it as I walked to the bus stop. No service. The Vicar is indisposed. Somebody had added underneath, in pencil, (Vanes).

On the Monday morning at half past nine I presented myself at my bank in the Fulham Road with a cheque for five thousand pounds. The cashier was a girl of about nineteen. She looked at it for a long time.

“There’s no date,” she said.

“There’s a time.”

“We can’t take a time.”

“It’s a very exact one.”

She fetched the manager. The manager telephoned to a bank in Colchester, and came back, and was sorry. He said that a Mr Fenn had been on the line to them at one minute past nine. The cheque had been stopped.

I walked home. I wasn’t even angry. I had been warned, by an expert. I told the Bulgarian that afternoon that the Thracian valley would have to manage without me, and he took it very well and sold me a watch.

That would be the end of that, in the telling. People like it. It rounds things off. But it isn’t quite the end. About three weeks later I had an envelope from Fenn & Ruddock. There was a cheque in it, drawn on the firm’s client account, for five thousand pounds. It was correctly dated. There was a letter, of two lines. It said that Mr Vane had asked every morning since the twenty-third whether the young man had got his plums, and had become so distressed at being put off that Mr Fenn had felt obliged to reconsider his position.

I bought the wine. It was just as I’d told my uncle. It tasted of plums and it didn’t give you a headache. I sold four hundred cases by Christmas at two pounds ninety-nine, and I ordered a thousand more. It’s the only real money I have ever made, and I made it by telling an old man the truth at half past one in the morning. The firm has been called Pargeter & Plum ever since. People assume there was a Mr Plum.

And Hester.

I wrote to her, as Mrs Pask had advised. I wrote four times. She answered the fourth. She said that she had an afternoon free on the following Thursday and would be in Colchester, and that there was a tea shop near the castle.

I took my grandmother’s ring. I had had it cleaned. I got there twenty minutes early and sat at a table in the window with a pot of tea, and she came in out of the rain in a grey mackintosh. She looked smaller than I remembered, and thinner. She sat down opposite me and took her gloves off and folded them.

I’m not going to give that conversation. It was the kindest thing anybody has ever done to me, and she did it without smiling once. She let me say all of it. She let me get the box out. And then she told me, very carefully, what she had thought I was asking her, by my uncle’s chair, at half past one in the morning.

She had thought that I was asking for her silence. She’d thought I was offering mine. I had told her about Edmund and the stable, and that she mustn’t tell; and I had said that whatever had happened that night, the glass and the tray and all of it, she need never say a word to anyone. And then I had said, “Will you?”

“But you said yes,” I said.

“I’d have said yes to anything that night that let me stop thinking,” said Hester Quaile. “I’m sorry. It was wrong of me. I ought to have listened to what you were asking. I wasn’t in a fit state to hear it.”

I looked at the ring. I’d been engaged for sixteen days. They were among the happiest of my life, and it turned out she had not been present for any of them.

“I suppose there’s no chance,” I said. “If I were to ask again. Now that you know what the question is.”

She didn’t answer at once. She turned her teacup round in the saucer. I shall always be grateful that she thought about it.

“There’s a thing I did,” she said. “That night. After you spoke to me. I’m not going to tell you what it was. I’ve thought about it every day since, and I shall go on thinking about it. I can’t marry anyone while I’m doing that. It wouldn’t be fair. They’d think they had all of me.” She looked up. “And I’m not leaving Mr Vane. He’s only got me now. I’ll stay till he doesn’t need anybody.”

“And after?”

“I don’t know about after.”

She put her gloves on. At the door of the tea shop she turned and held out her hand, and I took it. It was quite warm this time.

“You were kind to the vicar,” she said. “And you fetched me. I haven’t forgotten that. Most people don’t fetch anyone.”

I did not see her again for seven years. I have since married two other people, and am about to try a third. I was fond of all of them, and I think I’d have been a better husband to each if I hadn’t once stood on a staircase with a crab on my shoulder.

That is the Compline business, as I’ve told it at a great many dinners.

I end it in the tea shop. I say, “And so I was engaged for sixteen days to a woman who didn’t know it, on the strength of a cheque that had no date, having served my great-uncle a clock for his pudding. And the only casualty of the whole night was a ten-pound carriage clock from Woolworth’s.” People laugh, and somebody passes the port. I am rather good at it by now. I’ve got the timing of the “voilà.”

I said at the beginning that nobody died. I said I was in a position to know.

I’m going to write down the rest. I’ve never told it. I have decided that a man shouldn’t publish a book called Mostly My Fault and leave out the one thing that was.

On the Tuesday after I came back from Compline, my mother telephoned. She’d had it from a cousin, who’d had it from Imogen. Edmund was dead. He had not been seen since the small hours of Sunday. He had been found on the Monday afternoon, on a sandbank seven miles down the coast, by a man digging for worms.

I said that it was impossible. I said I had seen him at a quarter past two, in the kitchen, eating goose. He had been laughing.

“Well, he’s not laughing now,” said my mother. She is not a sentimental woman. “They say he drowned. They say he must have walked into the sea.”

There was an inquest in December. I wasn’t called. Nobody knew that I had anything to tell. Mrs Pask had sworn me to silence in a loose box, and she kept her own side of it; she told the police that Mr Edmund had been in liquor and that she had last seen him at dinner. I read the report in a cutting that my mother sent me.

I read it standing up, in my hall in Fulham, with my coat on.

The doctor said that Edmund had drowned. There was no doubt of that. But he had found a number of other things, and he went through them in order, and I followed him down the column with my finger. There was a fracture on the left side of the forehead. I knew about that. I had seen it by candlelight at the bottom of twelve steps. There was the drug. I knew about that too. There were some pellets of shot in the neck. He had told me about those himself, on the kitchen table, and laughed.

And then there was a sentence that I can repeat from memory. I’ve had nine years to learn it.

A second injury, a large contusion over the occiput, separate from the first and sustained somewhat later.

I had to look up “occiput.” It is the back of the head.

I’ve told this as a comedy, and so it was. It was a funny night. A man does not carry a pudding into a room and find that it’s a clock every day of his life. I have told it for laughs so many times that there are mornings when I very nearly believe that is all it was. I think of him still sitting on that table with a goose bone, saying, “Hallo, it’s the pudding.”

But I know what a large contusion over the occiput is. I was there. I heard it. It sounded like a melon dropped on a kitchen floor.

He was awake afterwards. I hold on to that. He spoke to me in the yard, and he was sitting up an hour and a half later, eating and talking, in the best spirits I ever saw in him. I’ve asked two doctors, without saying why. I asked them at dinner, as a general question. They both said the same. A man can take a blow like that and walk about for hours.
