The door of the harness room was beside it. I opened it. There was a smell of paraffin and spirits, and a broken lamp on the floor. The ladder-stair went up in the corner into the dark. Overhead I could hear the great clock, slow and heavy.

And I could hear voices.

They came down through the trap from the clock chamber. There were two. One was Mr Vane’s. I knew it at once, thin and exact. I could not hear what he said. The other was lower. It was a man’s voice, deep, and very tired, and it spoke for a long time together without stopping, as a person speaks who is telling something from the beginning.

I put my foot on the stair. I climbed four rungs. I stood with my head just beneath the level of the floor above. I could see nothing; there was no light up there at all.

The low voice had stopped. There was a silence. Then the old man spoke, and I heard him plainly.

“Then she didn’t leave me,” he said. “She was coming back.”

The low voice said something short.

“She was coming back,” said Mr Vane again. “Then she did not leave me.”

He said it a third time, and a fourth. He said it as I have heard patients say a thing over when they have been given good news and dare not stop saying it in case it should cease to be true.

I should have gone up. I was four rungs from the top. I had only to climb, and lift the lamp.

I did not. I am going to try to tell the truth about why. I knew that voice. I had listened for it for three weeks. I had last heard it in the library that afternoon, saying, Good girl. And I had seen a man fall from the top of this tower forty minutes before, backward, with his arms out, into water that went to the sea. I had just stood on the bank and looked.

I thought: he is up there with his father. The old man has gone up to his machine, as he said he would. He has taken his hour back, and gone through it again, and he has found his son.

I thought that if I climbed the last four rungs and held up my lamp, I should see Mr Vane in that chamber, talking, and nobody else.

I had borne a good deal that night. I had found a warm bed with no child in it. I had seen a woman pass me in a gallery who had been twenty years in her grave. I could not have borne that as well.

So I called. I stayed where I was, and I called up through the trap.

“Mr Vane! Mr Vane, it’s Hester Quaile. You must come down. You’ll take your death.”

The voices stopped. I waited. Nothing moved above. I could hear the pendulum.

Then I heard his thin shoes on the boards, and his legs came through the trap, and he climbed down to me, slowly, feeling for each rung. I went down ahead and held the lamp.

He reached the floor. He turned round. I have never seen a human face so happy.

“He is alive,” he said. “I’ve been through it twice. It was all just as I calculated. I went to the ice house the second time and there was nobody there, and I came here, and he was sitting against the frame. I did not strike him. I put my hand on his face. He is quite warm.”

“Who is up there, Mr Vane?”

“Edmund. I’ve told you. He has been telling me about his mother.” He took my arm. He was trembling all over with joy and cold. “She did not leave me. She had gone, and she turned back. Did you know that? He was there. He saw. She turned back on the Wade.”

I looked up at the black square of the trap.

“Mr Edmund,” I said. I said it quite loud. “Mr Edmund, are you there?”

There was no answer. There was no light, and no step. I listened until my ears sang. I could hear the great clock cutting the time into pieces, and that was all.

I have gone over that silence a thousand times. If there was a living man in that chamber, why did he not speak? He had only to say, “Yes, Miss Quaile.” He knew my voice. He had talked with me that afternoon as he had talked with no one for twenty years.

I have told myself that he was hurt, and had no strength. I have told myself that he did not wish to be seen. Mr Pargeter has written that he met him afterward in the kitchen, eating, and laughing. Miss Vane says in her letter that she spoke to him. I have never asked either of them to their face whether they were sure. I am afraid of how they would answer. I think that on that night more than one person in that house saw what they most wanted to see.

I only know that I stood at the foot of the stair and called his name into the dark, and that nothing answered me. I did not climb up to look.

The old man was pulling at my arm. His teeth were chattering. I took him out into the yard.

We had got halfway across the gravel when the clock struck over our heads. I stopped and looked up.

The grey woman brought her arm down. The great bell sounded. She raised her arm, and brought it down again.

It was two o’clock. There had been no quarters. The small bell had not rung. All that night, and every night for two hundred years, there had been four chimes before the hour. She had struck without them. There was nobody now on the left side of the bell to give them.

“The Hour is over,” said Mr Vane. He sighed. “I should have liked it longer. But it was enough. One must not be greedy.”

I come now to the thing that I did.

I did not take him in through the hall. I took him by the gunroom door and up the back stair, which is shorter, and put him to bed. There was no draught to give him. He did not need it. He lay down on his back, with his hands folded, and was asleep before I had drawn the curtains of the bed. He was smiling. I turned the key on him from outside and put it in my pocket.

Then I went down. It was about half past two.

The hall was nearly dark. The candles had burned low and most had gone out. One leaf of the front door had been shut. Dame Octavia was asleep in her chair with her mouth open, and the vicar on his settle. On the other settle, across the hearth, the tall young man lay with his knees drawn up and one shoe off, sleeping like a child. On the table the brass clock stood on its blanket.

Nobody stirred. I could have been the only person awake in that house.

I went to the regulator. I opened the long door.

I had no plan when I came down the stairs. I do not think that I had one when I put my hand on the catch. I looked at the weight, hanging there, with its dark smear and the hairs. I thought of the old man overhead, on his back, smiling. He had looked a hundred years old when I laid him down. He had looked like something that would break if it were lifted wrongly.

I thought of what would come. The sea gives things back. I am from the coast, and I know. In a day, or two, or three, there would be a man found on a beach, with a wound in his head. There would be a policeman in this hall. He would ask what had been done, and with what, and by whom. He would go round the house, and he would open this case. And he would see what I was looking at.

Then they would take the old man. They would not hang him; he was eighty-one and out of his mind. But they would take him out of this house and put him in a place with locked doors. They would ask him, every day, quite kindly, whether he remembered striking his son. And every day he would hear it new.

I had told him the truth for three weeks because he asked me to, and because I thought that a person has a right to it. I still think so. But I had learned something at twenty to one, kneeling on that floor. There are truths that a person has a right not to be told.

I took out my handkerchief. I wet it with my tongue, as my mother used to do for my face. I took the weight in my left hand, and I cleaned it.

It did not come off easily. I had to rub. I did it thoroughly, as I have been taught to do everything, turning the cylinder on its line, working round the rim and into the join where the brass meets the lead. I picked off each hair with my nails. When I had done, I held the lamp to it. It shone. It was a clean brass weight, such as might hang in any clock.

I went to the fire and put the handkerchief on the coals. It was a small linen one, with an H in the corner, that my mother had worked. I watched until there was nothing.

Then I came back and shut the case.

I have thought about that every day since. I told Mr Pargeter so, in the tea shop. I did not tell him what it was.

I had been a nurse, and I had resigned because I failed to watch. I had come to this house to sit awake by an old man and do no harm. And I ended that night by rubbing a man’s blood and hair off a piece of brass with spit, so that nobody should ever know how he had come by his death. It was a man I had loved, in my fashion.

I did it for the father. I say that, and it is true. I have asked myself whether I did it also for myself, so that no one should ask where the nurse had been between half past eleven and ten past twelve, and I cannot swear that I did not.

I went up. I let myself into the Admiral’s room and locked the door on the inside. He had not moved. I sat down in the low chair by the fire. I had the red book in my pocket, and a child’s drawing, folded small.

I had promised to bring the book to the Shop after breakfast. He had said that he would stand beside me.

I sat and waited for it to be morning.

VII. The Hurdle

The windows of the Admiral’s room look east. I drew back one curtain at about five and watched it get light.

There is not much colour in a dawn on that coast. The sky went from black to the grey of a slate, and then a yellow line came along the bottom of it, behind the stables. The tower stood against that. I could see the clock face, and the hands, and the roof over the bell.

She was there, on the right. Her shawl hung straight and wet. On the left there was an iron stump, and the sky.

I looked at the gap for a long time. I thought of what Dame Octavia had said in the hall. The Jack had gone, then. That much was not in doubt. Something of oak in a dinner jacket had been on that tower at midnight and was not there at dawn.

I ought to have been comforted. I told myself to be.

A little before six, by the clocks behind me, two cars went out of the yard. The first was the clergyman’s, driven very slowly. Some minutes afterward a large one followed. I saw the heavy man from the insurers at the wheel. Beside him, in a pale coat, with a scarf over her head, sat Mrs Edmund Vane.

She did not look back at the house. I watched the car go down the track toward the Wade, and I knew that she would not return. I knew it as surely as one knows that a patient has decided not to get well. I said nothing about it to anyone that day. I had begun to count the things that I was saying nothing about, and that was the fifth.

At seven Mr Vane woke. He lay for a while looking at the canopy. Then he turned his head on the pillow and found me.

“Has she gone?” he said.

I did not ask whom he meant.

“I believe so, Mr Vane. I’ve not been down.”

“She will have waited for the horse. I told her twenty minutes to three.” He was quite clear, and very tired, and peaceful. “Did she get across?”

I had lied to him three times in the night. I had cleaned a weight. I found that I could not add to it.

“I don’t know,” I said. “I didn’t see.”

“No. You were with me. You’re a good girl.” He closed his eyes. “She got across. I gave it to her to the minute. A horse can do it at that state of the tide, if he knows the Rill, and the Garrows’ horses always did.” He smiled. “I should like my tea. And then I must go down to the Shop. Edmund is coming to me there after breakfast. He said so, in the tower. He has something more to tell me, and he wants the girl by, he says, to hold his coat.”

I was folding the rug. I went on folding it.

“Did he say that, Mr Vane?”

“He did. He said, ‘I’ve told you the worst of it, Father, and I’ll tell you the rest in the morning, in the Shop, with Miss Quaile there to keep me to it. She’s got a book of Mother’s that you’re to see.’” He opened his eyes. “Have you a book of my wife’s?”

“Yes.”

“Then bring it.”

I had heard a voice in the clock chamber, and had not dared to climb four rungs to see whose it was. I had told myself afterward that the old man had been talking to the dark. And here he lay, in the morning, with his wits about him, repeating to me an arrangement that I had made with his son in the library the afternoon before. No one else alive knew of it.

I shall leave that as it stands. I have not been able to do anything else with it.

I took him down to the Shop at nine. I had the red book in my pocket.

He sat at his bench, under the window. He was happier than I had ever seen him. He took up a small brass plate that he had been engraving and looked at it through his glass, and hummed. It was the waltz.

I stood by the steps, where I could see the door. I had my hands clasped to stop them shaking. I listened for an uneven step on the stone.

It was a quarter past nine by the Shop clocks, of which there were nineteen. It was half past. I heard the hall clocks tell ten, overhead, one after another. The old man worked on. From time to time he looked up at the door, mildly, and then at me, and went back to his plate.

At a quarter to eleven he laid down his graver.

“He is not coming,” he said.

“He may have overslept, Mr Vane.”

“No. He would have come. He gave me his word, and he has never given it before, so that I know he meant it.” He turned on his stool. “Something has prevented him. It doesn’t matter. He told me the chief thing. What was the rest, do you know?”

I came forward. I took out the book.

“He said that if he was not here, I was to give you this anyway. And I was to tell you that Edmund said he was sorry, and that it wasn’t the clock.”

“It was not the clock,” Mr Vane repeated. “No. He told me so. She knew I’d put it back; she had her watch. She went in good time. And she turned round, on the Wade, and came back.” His voice was steady. “He told me why she turned. I shan’t tell you, my dear. It’s his to tell, and he was only a boy. But she was coming back to this house when the water took her. That is what I have. I thought for twenty years that she drowned going away from me.”

He held out his hand. I put the diary into it.

He did not open it. He held it on his palm, and looked at the red cover, and the gilt year. He ran his thumb along the edge of the pages, as he would test the edge of a wheel.

“That’s her hand,” he said. “On the tide tables. I’d know it. Where was this?”

“In the little gilt clock on her desk. The one that doesn’t go. The works had been taken out.”

A slow smile came over his face. It was the first time I had seen him look like the man that the woman in the portrait was laughing at.

“In the one that was allowed to be wrong,” he said. “Oh, Margot. Of course it was. She knew I should never open that case. I had given her my word in 1948.” He was silent for some time. “What is in it?”

“The year 1974, Mr Vane. Up to the day.”

“Does she speak of me?”

“Yes.”

“Kindly?”

I thought of the cathedral, and the cold feet. I thought of I do love him.

“Very kindly,” I said. “And truthfully.”

“And of someone else.”

I did not answer. He nodded.

“Yes. Amos Garrow. I knew it then and I’ve not let myself know it since. He had a way with a horse that I never had with anything living.” He looked at the book. “If I read this I shall hear her say it. I shall hear exactly how she said it; she had a way of putting things. And I shall know what she thought of me in the last year, to the word.”

He closed his hand on it. Then he held it out to me.

“No. I’ll not read it. She hid it from me. If she had wished me to see it she would have left it on my bench. She was not a careless woman.” His hand was quite firm. “She turned back. That is enough for an old man. I’ll not go behind it and ask what she turned back from. Put it where you found it.”

“In the clock?”

“In the clock that’s allowed to be wrong. It may stay there until I am dead, and then you may do as you think right. You’re a truthful girl. But you have learned something about truth in this house, I think, that you did not know when you came.”

I took the book. I could not see him clearly.

“I’ve lied to you, Mr Vane,” I said. “Three times, last night. I said I never would.”

“I daresay you had reason. People do.” He picked up his graver. “My wife lied to me for ten years, it appears, and Edmund for twenty. And I find that I can forgive the pair of them between breakfast and luncheon. It is extraordinary how little it weighs, afterward. I wish I had known it sooner.”

I put the red book back that afternoon, in the gilt drum between the cupids, and shut the little door. It stayed there till the spring.

By noon the house knew that something was wrong.

Miss Vane’s bed had not been slept in. There was a line on a leaf torn from the game book, left under a cartridge on the gunroom bench: Gone across to Saltcote. Don’t wait luncheon. I. Gail brought it to me, since there was no one else to bring it to. Mrs Edmund Vane had gone to the chemist’s at Maldon at six in the morning, on a Sunday, and had not come home. Mr Fenn and the old lady had driven off at eight. The young man and the vicar were gone.

And Mr Edmund was not to be found.

That in itself troubled nobody at first. Mrs Pask told me so, in the kitchen. She was back at her range. She had been to her cottage on the mainland at first light, she said, to see to something, and had come back across on her bicycle. I had expected to find her as I had left her the day before, and I was startled. She looked as though she had not slept for a week, and yet her face was lighter than I had ever seen it, and while she worked she sang under her breath. I had not known that she could.

“He’ll be laid up somewhere,” she said. “He was sat on my table at a quarter past two eating goose; Mr Toby saw him. He’d a head on him. He’ll have gone to ground, like a dog. I’ve known him not come in till the Monday.”

“Mrs Pask. You were in the stable with him. Mr Pargeter told me.”

She gave me a look.

“Mr Pargeter’s a tongue like a bell-clapper. Yes. I was. And I’ll thank you to keep it from the old gentleman.”

“Was he badly hurt?”

“He’d a lump on his brow like an egg. And a cut at the back, that he got in the yard.” She stopped singing. “He spoke to us. He was sensible. I’d not have left him else.” She turned a pan. “You’ve not said nothing upstairs? About where he was found?”

“No.”

“Nor I shan’t. It’s the old man I’m thinking of. He’s had the best night he’s had in twenty years; Gail says he was dancing. I’ll not have it spoiled with tales of Mr Edmund lying drunk in the ice house.”

I said nothing. I thought of what else she did not know about that ice house, and who had been there before her. I held my hand over the place on my dress, though I had changed it.

“Mrs Pask,” I said. “I went up to the nursery last night. The door was open.”

She did not turn round.

“Was it.”

“The bed was warm. There was a plate, and orange peel. There were wet footmarks.”

“You’ll have been dreaming. You were up all night.”

“I have a drawing that I found on the floor. It is in my pocket now.”

She put down her spoon. She stood with her back to me and her two hands on the rail of the range. I saw her shoulders rise and fall.

“Miss Quaile,” she said. “I’ve been in this house forty-two years. I’ve kept more than you’ll ever know, and none of it my own. I’m going to ask you to leave that be. There’s no harm come of it. I swear that on my mother. There’s nobody been hurt by what was in that room, and nobody will be, so long as it’s let alone. You’d oblige me by putting that paper on the fire.”

“Whose was the voice?”

“There wasn’t any voice,” said Mrs Pask.

She took up the spoon again. In a moment she had begun to sing.

I did not put the paper on the fire. I have said that I kept it. But I did not ask her again. She had sworn that there was no harm, and I had believed her about the wind in the flue, and been wrong. I believed her about this. I do not know that I was right.

It was Mr Kit who raised the alarm.

He had gone out at nine to look for his father, with the cropped girl. He was in a queer state. He would not look at anyone, and he started at every sound, and twice that morning I saw him go to the door of the harness room and stand there, staring at the floor, as though he expected to see something lying on it. He had asked Gail three times whether the gentleman from the insurers had been at breakfast. When she told him that Mr Cade had driven off at six with Mrs Vane, he sat down on the stairs and laughed until he cried.

I did not understand it. I have learned since that he had his own reasons for watching that floor.

They searched the stables. They went up the tower. He came down and said that the Jack was gone off his pin, sheared clean through, and that the post behind was full of shot. He said the trap had been open and there was blood on the boards of the clock chamber, a little, and a handkerchief. He held it out. It was a small one, a child’s, with a pattern on it of red maple leaves.

“That’s not Dad’s,” he said. “Whose is that?”

Nobody knew. I looked at it in his hand. I thought of footprints with stars.

They went along the sea wall, north and south. The tide had gone out in the night and come half in again. At about ten the girl, who had run ahead, began to shout from the outfall, where the fleet goes through the wall into the saltings.

I was at the Admiral’s window. I had gone up to fetch the old man’s spectacles. I saw the boy begin to run.

I must tell this exactly as it came to me.

For an hour and a half there was nothing. I could not leave Mr Vane. I got him his luncheon on a tray. I stood at one window and then another. From the gallery, on the west side, one can see along the wall as far as the outfall, and I saw figures there, small and dark, bending. There were four of them. The boy and the girl had fetched two men from the oyster sheds on the point. They had spades.

They were digging something out of the mud.

I watched until I could not watch. I went and sat with the old man and read to him, I do not know what. The clocks told half past eleven. They told the quarter.

At noon I heard the front door, and feet in the hall, a number of them, heavy, and going carefully, as people walk who are carrying something between them. I heard Gail scream.

I went down the stairs. I did not run. I held on to the rail.

They had set it down in the middle of the hall, on the flagstones, where the old man had danced. It was a sheep hurdle, such as they use on the marsh. Something long lay on it, under wet sacking. The four of them were standing round, with mud to their thighs. The cropped girl had her knuckles in her mouth.

From under the edge of the sacking, on my side, an arm hung down. It was in a black sleeve. There was a white cuff at the end of it, soaked and grey, and it trailed on the stone.

I came to the bottom of the stairs. I stopped. I thought: I shall see his face. I must be ready to see it. I have seen the faces of the drowned before, at home; they bring them into the lifeboat house.

Mr Kit stooped. He took hold of the sacking at the head end and turned it back.

They brought him in at noon on a hurdle, and he was made of wood.

It was the Jack. He lay on his back with his painted face to the ceiling. I had only ever seen him from far below. He was smaller than a man and thicker. His features had been cut with a chisel two hundred years ago, by someone who made figureheads, and they were broad and simple: a nose, a ledge of brow, a mouth like a slot. There was mud in the mouth. One arm was raised from the shoulder, stiff, with the fist closed round a peg where the hammer had been. Someone had put a dinner jacket on him and buttoned it, and a starched front, and a black bow.

The front was torn open. The wood beneath was pale and fresh, and splintered, in a patch as wide as two hands, and there were small dark holes in it, a great many, close together.

“He was in the outfall,” the boy said. His voice cracked. “Jammed in the grating. Face down. We saw the jacket. We saw the back of his head and the collar. I thought—Sass thought—” He stopped. He put the back of his muddy hand against his eyes. “For about a minute down there I thought it was Dad.”

The girl began to laugh. It was not a good sound. One of the oystermen patted her on the back, as one would a horse.

I stood and looked down at that wooden face. I had thought that I should feel relief. The old lady had been right, and my eyes had been wrong. A dummy had been shot off a clock by someone after duck, and here it was. The sensible woman had won her case.

It was not what I felt. I had seen a man in evening dress go backward off that tower. I had been told since, by two people, that a living man had been lying in the stable beneath it a quarter of an hour before. I had heard a voice in the clock chamber that I knew. I had stood on the bank of that creek and held a lamp over the water.

And now they had gone down to the place where the creek runs out, and dug, and brought back what the water had kept. It lay on the stone at my feet, and it had never been alive.

I thought: then where is the other?

I looked up. The front door had been left open behind the bearers. Through it, across the gravel, I could see the tower. She stood alone, with her arm lifted. She was looking at the house.

I am going to write down what came into my mind. I have said that I despise this kind of thing. But I have been told to leave nothing out.

I thought: she has changed them. A man went up to her on the stroke of one. He had done her a wrong, a long time ago, on the Wade, and had kept it twenty years, and that day I had set a term to his keeping. He stood beside her at the hour. She brought down her arm. And what the house gave back to us, in the morning, on a hurdle, was the thing that had stood there before him. She had kept the man.

I know what that is. I have known all along. I do not need to be told.

Mr Vane had come to the head of the stairs. He came down them slowly, with his hand on the rail. He stood by the hurdle, and screwed the glass into his eye, and bent.

“Number five shot,” he said. “Both barrels, I should think, at thirty yards. It has gone through the lime and into the heart-oak. He can be mended. I have some seasoned oak in the Shop that was his brother’s.” He straightened. He looked round at our faces. “Why are you all so white? It’s only the Jack. He has been loose on his pin since 1941.”

Nobody answered him.

“Where is Edmund?” he said.

They found Edmund on the Monday afternoon.

A man who was digging for bait came upon him at low water on a bank they call the Ray Sand, seven miles to the south. He was in his shirt and trousers. He had no coat.

A policeman came to the house in the evening. I was in the hall when Mr Fenn, who had driven over, went into the drawing room to tell the old man. He was in there four minutes by the clock at the foot of the stairs. When he came out he was grey.

“He says that it is a mistake,” Mr Fenn said to me. “He says that he saw to it. He says that he went back.” He took off his spectacles. “I have told him twice. I can’t do it a third time. Miss Quaile, I must leave him to you.”

I went in. He was in the wing chair. He looked up.

“Fenn has been talking nonsense,” he said. “He says that Edmund is drowned.”

I knelt down by the chair. I had made a rule on the first of October, and I had broken it on the twenty-second, three times, and done a worse thing than break it. I thought that I would mend it now, if it could be mended.

“It’s true, Mr Vane. They have found him. He was drowned on Saturday night, or Sunday morning. I am very sorry.”

He looked at me for a long moment with his pale eyes.

“No,” he said gently. “You’re mistaken, my dear. I do not blame you; you were not in the tower. I killed him at ten minutes to twelve. That is quite true. And then the hour was given back, and I went through it again, and I did not. I found him alive at ten minutes to two. I touched his face. He talked to me for a quarter of an hour.” He patted my hand. “A man cannot be dead who has been made not to have died. You must see that. It is a matter of simple sequence.”

“He was alive when you saw him. I believe that. He died afterward.”

“Afterward? Of what?”

“He was drowned.”

“But why should he be drowned? He had no reason to go near the water.” He frowned. He was working at it, honestly, as he would have worked at a train of wheels that would not mesh. “Unless there was a second debit. I had not thought of that. There was the Jack. I supposed that the Jack had paid for the hour.” His face cleared a little. “No. No, I’ve done the sum too often. It comes out. You will find that he is somewhere about. He’ll be in to dinner.”

He was not in to dinner. On the Tuesday morning the old man asked me where his son was. I told him. He heard it as though for the first time, and wept, and then, by degrees, remembered that he had put it right, and comforted me.

It went on so all the winter. He asked, perhaps one morning in three. I told him each time that Edmund was dead. He was grieved, and then he corrected me. We were both of us telling the truth as we had it. I have nursed a great many old people who had lost the thread of their lives, and I never had another who held on to two ends so firmly that neither would give.

I came to think, toward the end, that his was the better thread. I had seen a body identified. He had put his hand on a warm face in the dark, after he had struck it, and had been spoken to. I do not know which of those is the stronger evidence.

There was an inquest, in December. I was called, as the person in charge of the drug.

I said that the bottle had been in my keeping. I said that I had left it on a tray in an unlocked room for three and a half hours, and that when I returned it was gone, and that I did not know who had taken it. The coroner asked whether that had been in accordance with my instructions. I said that it had not. He wrote something down. He was not unkind.

I listened to the doctor. He read from a paper. He said that Mr Edmund Vane had died by drowning and had been alive when he entered the water. There was a fracture on the left side of the brow, made some hours before death by a heavy blunt object of small surface. I looked at my hands. There was a later injury to the back of the head. There were shot wounds in the left shoulder and neck. There was chloral in the blood.

The palms of his hands were torn, the doctor said, and the insides of his arms, and there were splinters of tarred wood in them. It was as though he had held on to something for a long time.

I thought of the black box on its legs in the middle of the Wade. I had passed it on the first of October and had known that someone had once sat in it through a night. I did not know why I thought of it then. I do not know now.

The coroner said that he had never known a man come to his death by so many roads. He said that he could not find how the deceased had got into the sea, and that he hoped somebody’s conscience would one day supply what the evidence did not. He looked along the benches.

I looked down. I was not the only one. I have wondered since about the others. I knew what I had to look down for. I had wiped a piece of brass with a handkerchief. I did not know what was on the consciences of the rest, and I have never asked.

I stayed at Compline through the winter. There was no one else. Mrs Edmund Vane did not return. Mr Kit went back to London, with the girl. Miss Vane came on Sundays from the farm across the water, where she was living by then. She had a look on her face that I could not interpret, happiness and something under it that was not.

In January she went up to the Grey Room by herself. When she had gone I walked along the gallery. The door was locked. Through the keyhole I could see the wardrobe, shut. I do not know whether the gown was back on its hanger. I should think that it was.

I did not look at the portrait any more. I passed it every night, with the old man on my arm, and he would stop, and speak to it. I kept my eyes on the floor. I had no fear of what I should see there. It was only a picture now. She had gone out of it at midnight on the twenty-second, and she did not come back. I think that she had done what she had waited for. Or else I had only then begun to see it as it was.

The tower clock struck the hours all that winter, and never the quarters. One grew used to it. The old man had the Jack down in the Shop, on trestles, and worked on him a little each day. He cut away the shattered wood and let in a new piece, and carved it to match, so that one could hardly find the join. He meant to have him back on his pin by the spring. “She’ll be glad of him,” he said. “It is dull work, counting alone.”

In the evenings, from December, he dictated to me. He said that he wished to leave a true relation of the experiment, for the benefit of whoever should come after. I took it down in exercise books, as he spoke it, and I did not alter a word. I learned from it a number of things about the night that I had not known. I learned what he had meant to do, and what he believed that he had done. It is in his own voice and I shall not repeat it.

I will say that when he came to dictate the part about the ice house, he gave it as he had given it to me in the hall, word for word. He remembered the weight. He remembered that he had hung it up again, and that the nurse had helped him.

“There was blood on it,” he said. “I recollect that. I must have wiped it, afterward; I looked at it the next week and it was clean. I have no memory of wiping it. One does these things.”

I wrote it down as he said it. My hand did not shake. It ought to have.

The child I never heard again. I went up to the top landing in November, by daylight. The nursery door was locked, as it had been at four o’clock on that afternoon. I looked through the keyhole. The rocking horse stood in the middle of the floor. The bed had been stripped. There was no plate. I stood there for some time. I put my face to the crack of the door, and I thought that there was still, very faintly, the smell of an orange.

He died in the spring. It was the last Saturday of March.

He had failed all that month. He did not walk any more at night. He lay in the big bed, and I sat by him, and the seven clocks went on. He asked me that afternoon what day it was. When I told him, he smiled.

“Then it is tonight,” he said. “They take it back. At one o’clock by this house the rest of England will put its clocks on to two, and be an hour wrong again until October. I shall be sorry to see them go. We have agreed very well this winter, they and I.”

“Don’t talk, Mr Vane. Rest.”

“I’ve rested for eighty-one years. I was resting while I worked; it is the only rest I ever understood.” His voice was a thread. “I should like the window open. I should like to hear the tower.”

I opened it. It was a still night, and not cold. One could hear the sea, a long way off.

He slept. He woke at midnight, when the house told it, and listened to the hour go through the rooms. He woke again at the half.

“Is Margot come in?” he said.

I had my answer ready. I had had it ready for six months.

“She’s dead, Mr Vane. She was drowned. But she had turned back. She was coming home to you.”

“Yes,” he said. “Yes. That is right. Thank you. I had it, and it went round the corner.” He lay quiet. “And Edmund?”

I took his hand. I did not know what I should say until I had said it.

“You found him in the tower. He was alive. You touched his face.”

“I did. He was warm.” He sighed. “You see, you do believe it. You’ve come round. I knew that you would. You are too truthful to hold out for ever against a fact.”

He did not speak again. At five minutes to one, by the seven clocks, his breathing changed. I knew the change. I held his hand and counted. It was very easy. There was a long breath, and no other.

I looked at the dial of the nearest clock. It was three minutes to one. In three minutes the world would move its hands and leave that house behind for another seven months. He had gone while they still agreed. He had always hated to be made late.

I closed his eyes. I folded his hands. Then I did what he would have wished, since there was no one else in the house who knew the custom.

I stopped the clocks.

I began with the seven in his room. I opened each case and laid my finger against the pendulum until it was still. I went out into the passage, and along the gallery, and down the stairs. I took a lamp. I went into every room. I did not know how to stop some of them; I had to search for the way. There were clocks that I had never noticed, in cupboards, and on the backs of doors. It took me until it was light.

I counted as I went. I had been told not to. There were a hundred and ten.

The last was the regulator in the hall. I opened the long door. The weight hung at the end of its line, bright and clean. I put my hand on the pendulum and held it.

Then I stood in the hall of Compline House and listened.

I had not heard silence since the first of October. I had forgotten what it was. It came down through the house from the top, room by room, as the hours used to. It was like being let out of something. And I thought that I could hear, under it, how large the place was, and how empty, and how the sea lay all round.

The tower clock struck. I had not stopped that one; I had not the strength to wind it down. The great bell sounded once across the yard. One o’clock. By the time the note had died it was two in every other house in England.

She was still counting, out there. I do not know to what.

That is all. I left Compline a week after the funeral. Before I went I took the red book from the gilt clock, since he had said that I might do as I thought right. I have it here. I have not yet decided what is right.

I went home to my mother. I found that I could not sleep at night, or by day either. In June they brought me to this place.

Dr Imrie has read the three books as I finished them. He has asked me a question, and I have promised to answer it in writing, at the end, as honestly as I am able.

He asked what I believe that I saw.

I believe that there was a child in the house. I heard her, or him, and I touched the bed. A woman I respect has told me there was not. I cannot make those agree, and I have stopped trying.

I believe that a man fell from the tower at one o’clock. I have seen what they brought in. I know what a jury would say. I say that someone held the lantern.

I believe that I heard Edmund Vane’s voice in the clock chamber forty minutes after I saw him fall. When I called his name, he did not answer me.

And the gallery. I know whose dress lay on the bed. I know whose hair was in the brush. I have had a letter. I have set all that down, and hidden nothing, and I would say every word of it on oath.

I do not say that there are ghosts. I have never said so. I am a nurse, and I was taught to report what I observe and to leave the diagnosis to those who are qualified.

I say that I saw her.

PART FOUR

The Turn of the Tide

by Imogen Vane, writing as Margaret Wade

Editor’s Note

In the autumn of 1998 a firm that published paperback romances, two a month, with a rose on the spine, brought out a short novel called The Turn of the Tide by Margaret Wade. It sold about as well as the others. It was set at a house called Vespers on an island in the Essex marshes, and it told how a woman named Isobel, after twenty years, crossed the sea at night on a grey horse behind a man named Daniel.

Margaret Wade was Imogen Vane. She told nobody. I learned of it only this year, a few weeks before she died, when she sent me to the bottom drawer of her desk for a parcel. It held the contract, the six author’s copies still in their wrapper, and beneath them the typescript.

The typescript has the real names. She had written it with them, straight through, and changed them afterwards in ink for the printer: Imogen struck out and Isobel written above, Tom made Daniel, Compline made Vespers. I have gone back to what she first wrote. I have also put back her sixth chapter. The publishers cut it. There is a letter from an editor explaining, quite kindly, that a scene between the heroine and her brother in a scullery was felt to be out of key with the list and to cast a shadow on the ending, and asking whether the brother might not simply give his blessing at the door. She agreed. In the printed book he gives his blessing at the door. What follows is what she wrote first.

I should say why I think she wrote it as she did. She was a restorer of paintings and a reticent person, and she could not have set this down as a confession; it was not in her. But she had read romances all her life, secretly, in the bath, and she knew how they went. I think she found that she could tell the truth about that night only inside a form that guaranteed her beforehand that it would end well. It did end well, for her. That was the difficulty. She could not get past having been given so much on a night when someone else was not.

It is told in the third person and it stays close to its heroine. Her times are from the clocks of the house and from what her father told her. She wore no watch; she never did.

One warning. In the fourth chapter a man comes to an orangery, and what he says there you will hear again, in the next part of this book, from himself. The two versions do not match. I have had both of those people at my own table, a great many times. I can tell you only that each of them was sure.

Chapter One

The taxi would not take her across.

“Not in the dark, love,” the driver said. “Not for a tenner, nor yet for twenty. I’ve a wife.”

“The tide’s well out. Look at it. It’s been out for two hours.”

“That’s as may be. I had a mate drove a wedding party over there in ’eighty-six and they found the car in March.” He had already switched off the meter. “There’s a pub. They’ll ring across for you.”

“There’s no telephone at the house that works.”

“Then I should stop the night at the pub,” said the driver, and held out his hand for the fare.

So Imogen Vane came home to Compline as she had left it twenty years before, on foot, with a bag in her hand and the wind in her face.

She stood at the top of the ramp until the tail lights had gone. It was the Friday evening, a little after seven. Behind her were the few lit windows of Thorney Staithe. In front of her was the dark. It had been a clear cold day and the last of it still showed in the west, a band of green light low over the flats, and against that she could see the line of withies going out, each one thinner than the last, and at the end of them the low black shape of the Ness with one lamp burning.

That would be the lamp in the porch. Her father had it lit at dusk every night of the year. He said that a house with a tide in front of it owed the traveller that much.

She had not meant to feel anything. She had sat in the train from Edinburgh for six hours with a book open on her knee, telling herself that she was a woman of forty-four going to visit an old father, as she did twice a year. But she had never before come in October. She had managed that for twenty autumns. There had always been an exhibition to hang, or a panel in the studio that could not be left, or a cold. Celia had stopped asking. And then Fenn had written, in his dry hand. Your father has said that this will be the last time he keeps the night. I think he means it. I think you should be there.

The wind smelled of mud and salt and rotting weed. It was the smell of her whole childhood. She had forgotten that a smell could do that, come straight in under the ribs without asking. She was nine years old, in gumboots, with a shrimping net. Then she was twenty-four, running.

She picked up her bag and went down the ramp.

To her left, as she came off the wall, there were the buildings of the farm. She had told herself that she would not look. She looked. Saltcote lay under the bank as it had always lain, long and low, tarred black, with its barns round it. There was a light in the kitchen window. There was smoke going up straight from the chimney in the cold. And in the yard, tied to the ring by the door, a big grey horse was standing with a rug on.

Her heart did something foolish. She stood still on the shingle with her bag.

It was only a horse. Amos Garrow had always had greys; he had bred them. He would be sitting in that kitchen now with his boots off, an old man of seventy-seven, and he had never spoken to a Vane since the day they buried her mother. He had stood at the back of the church, by himself, with his hat in his hands. When they came out he was gone.

His son had been gone longer. She did not let herself say the name, even now, even here. She had found, over the years, that it was like a bad tooth. One could live with it perfectly well if one kept one’s tongue away.

She walked out onto the Wade.

There was a moon rising behind her, nearly full. By the time she was a quarter of the way over it had cleared the sea wall and laid her shadow down on the stones in front of her, long and thin, with a bag. The mud on either side shone like pewter. Somewhere out on it a curlew called, and another answered, a long way off.

She had walked this road ten thousand times. Her feet knew it. They knew where the surface was sound and where the winter had got under it, and she let them go and did not look down.

She was thinking, as she always did here, of her mother.

It was not grief, exactly, after so long. Grief wore itself smooth. It was more like a room in the mind that one walked through every day and no longer saw. But tonight every piece of it was sharp-edged again. It was the moon that did it. There had been a moon that night too, in ’seventy-four, though later, and smaller. She remembered it standing over the orangery roof.

She had been twenty-four, and she had known everything.

She knew that her mother was leaving. She had known for a fortnight, since she walked into the Grey Room without knocking and found the jewel case open on the bed. She knew for whom. And that had been the part that she could not forgive, though she had cried in her mother’s arms and promised to say nothing. It was not that her mother loved another man. Imogen was not a child; she had seen how it was between her parents, the kindness and the distance. It was which man. It was the farm. Her mother had been crossing this road at night for ten years to the same yard that Imogen herself had been crossing to since May, and neither of them had known it of the other.

She had thought she had found something that was hers alone. A boy with brown arms, who could not put three words together, and who looked at her as though she had hung the moon. She had gone to him through the dusk with her heart in her mouth, the squire’s daughter, feeling wicked and free. And all that time she had only been walking in her mother’s footprints.

With Tom’s father? You?

She had said it like an accusation. She could hear her own voice now, shrill, twenty-four years old. And her mother had laughed, and then stopped laughing, and said, “Oh, my darling. I’m so sorry. I ought to have told you. I hadn’t the face.”

They had made it up. They had made a plan. On the night of the Hour her mother would say what she had to say to Papa, and then go, on foot, at one. Imogen would walk with her as far as the farm. Amos would be waiting at the Wade head with a lantern. And Tom would be there. The four of them would stand in that kitchen. After that, her mother had said, with the old amusement back in her eyes, the Vanes and the Garrows might as well put up the banns in pairs and save the vicar a journey.

It should have happened. It had been so nearly managed.

Imogen stopped walking. She had come to the dip.

The Rill lay in front of her, black, with the moon in it. The planks of the Clapper were silver. And beside the bridge, on its four legs, stood the Perch.

She had not been as near to it as this since she was a girl. On her visits she had always crossed by car, and looked at the far withies. It was smaller than she remembered. A tarred box, a ladder, a little door. Her brother had been going to mend that ladder for as long as she could remember.

They had found her mother a hundred yards from here. On the seaward side. The ebb had left her on the mud, on her back, with her grey eyes open, and her stockinged feet. Imogen had not seen it. She had been told. Dolly Pask had told her, in the kitchen, holding both her hands. She had said, “She looked surprised, Miss Immy. That’s all. She just looked surprised.”

Imogen put her bag down on the planks. She stood with her hand on one of the posts of the Perch. The tar was cold and a little sticky.

“I should have come with you,” she said aloud. “I said I would. I’m sorry.”

Nobody answered. The curlew called again. The water went by under the bridge, very quietly, toward the sea.

Dolly Pask opened the kitchen door to her and said, “Well. So you’ve come,” and then put her arms round her.

It was the only embrace Imogen had had in that house in twenty years. Dolly smelled as she had always smelled, of flour and coal smoke. She was sixty-three now and as broad as a door. She held on for a moment longer than was needed, and then stood back and looked her up and down.

“You’re thin. They don’t feed you up there. You’ve walked it? In them shoes? Sit down. Your father’s in the Shop and Mr Edmund’s out and madam’s lying down with her head. There’s only me and the nurse.”

“The nurse?”

“Miss Quaile. For the old gentleman’s nights. Mr Fenn got her. She’s a queer little thing, white as a candle, but she’s good with him. She tells him the truth.” Dolly said it as one might say of a new dog that it bit. “He asks is your mother come in, and she tells him. Straight out. I thought he’d go for her. He thanked her.”

Imogen sat down at the long table. She had sat there as a child to shell peas. “How is he?”

“He’s eighty-one. Some days he’s sharp as a tack. Some days he calls me Nanny.” She was cutting bread. “He’s been up to something this month. Out to the tower at all hours, with his tools. I asked what he was doing and he said he was getting something back that he’d lent. I don’t ask twice.”

“And Edmund?”

Dolly’s knife paused, for the space of a breath, and went on.

“Mr Edmund’s as he is,” she said. “It’s October.”

It was all she would say. It was all that anyone at Compline ever said. Imogen ate bread and cheese and drank tea out of a blue-striped mug that she had drunk from at seven years old. She looked round the kitchen. Nothing had moved. The same clock on the wall, eight minutes fast. The same nail by the range, with the keys.

“There’s a horse at Saltcote,” she said. She had not meant to say it. “In the yard. A grey.”

“That’ll be Mab. The old man’s mare.”

“I thought he’d given up keeping them. He must be nearly eighty.”

Dolly put the knife down.

She turned round. She wiped her hands on her apron, slowly, looking at Imogen with small brown eyes that had seen her through measles and her first communion.

“You’ve not heard, then,” she said. “No. Who’d tell you? Amos Garrow’s dead, Miss Immy. He went a fortnight Tuesday. It was his chest. They buried him yesterday at St Botolph’s. I was there. There was a good few; he was respected.”

Imogen sat quite still. She had not known the old man, not to speak to. He had been a figure at the edge of things. But he had loved her mother. He had waited at the Wade head with a lantern for a woman who never came, and had gone home alone, and lived twenty years with it.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “I’m very sorry. Was he—was anyone with him?”

“I was. I’ve neighboured that farm thirty year.” Dolly was still looking at her. “And his son come. He got there the day before. They’d sent to him.”

The kitchen clock ticked. It seemed very loud.

“His son,” Imogen said.

“Tom. From Canada. He’s been out on the prairies all this while, with cattle. He come in at the door in a big hat like the pictures, and I didn’t know him. He’s gone grey at the sides. He’s as thin as a rail.” Dolly’s voice was carefully flat. “He sat with his father the last night and held his hand. I don’t know what was said. He carried the coffin, Thursday, at the head end. And he stood at the grave after, on his own, a long time, and looked over here.”

Imogen found that she was holding the blue mug with both hands. It was empty. She set it down, very precisely, in the ring it had left on the table.

“Is he staying?”

“I couldn’t tell you. He don’t say much; he never did. There’s the stock to see to.” Dolly hesitated. “There’s a notice come to the farm. From Mr Fenn. Mr Edmund’s giving them notice to quit, at Lady Day. He’s a buyer for the land, I’ve heard. For caravans. That come the morning of the funeral.”

“Edmund sent a notice to quit on the day they buried Amos Garrow?”

“I don’t say he knew what day it was. Mr Edmund don’t always.” But her mouth was hard. “A hundred and eighty year the Garrows have had that ground. Tom read it in my kitchen, standing up. He read it twice, and folded it small, and put it in his shirt. He never said a word. I’d sooner he’d shouted.”

Imogen got up. She went to the window over the sink and looked out. There was nothing to see. There was the dark yard, and beyond it the black line of the sea wall.

She had spent twenty years keeping her tongue from a tooth. She had done it by living four hundred miles away, in a tall cold flat in the New Town, among other people’s pictures. She had been engaged once, for five months, to a decent man who collected Scottish watercolours. She had given him back his ring one evening without being able to tell him why.

And he was there. Half a mile from where she stood, across the water, in a kitchen with a lit window. He had gone grey at the sides.

“He’s a child with him,” said Dolly behind her.

Imogen turned round.

“A little girl. Nine or ten. Dark, like a gypsy. He was married out there, and the wife died, two year back. Cancer.” Dolly had gone back to her bread. She spoke without looking up. “She’s a sharp little thing. Don’t miss nothing. She sat in my kitchen all Thursday afternoon while they was at the church, drawing, and never spoke, and when I give her her tea she said, ‘Thank you, Mrs Pask,’ as nice as you like, in that voice they have. And then she said, ‘Is that the house where the lady drowned?’ She’d been looking at it out the window.”

“What did you tell her?”

“I said it was. I don’t hold with lying to children.” Dolly set a plate down, rather hard. “I’m minding her tomorrow. He’s to go to Colchester, to see a man about the notice. So if you see a little dark thing about my cottage, that’s who.”

Imogen said that she would remember. She said that she was tired, and would go up. She took her bag.

At the foot of the back stairs she stopped, with her hand on the rail.

“Dolly. Did he ask about us? About any of us?”

“He asked was your father living. I said he was. He asked was Mr Edmund still at the house. I said he was.” Dolly’s back was toward her. “He never asked for you by name, Miss Immy. But he looked at me. When I said that Miss Imogen was in Scotland and never come home this time of year. He looked at me as if I’d took something off him that he’d been carrying.”

She did not go to her own room. She went along the gallery.

There was a lamp burning at the far end, on the table beneath the portrait. It was always left. She walked the length of the sunk floor toward it, past the dark windows, with the clocks going on either hand. Under the frame the old cracked one was ticking. It had gained four seconds a week for as long as she could remember, and her father had never found out why.

She looked up at her mother.

She had been six years old when it was painted. She remembered the man, who had a beard and smelled of turpentine and had let her squeeze white out of a tube. She remembered her mother standing for him in the morning room, hour after hour, in the grey silk, with one hand on a chair. Imogen had sat on the floor and watched the dress come on the canvas, a stroke at a time. She thought now that it was where she had first learned what paint could do. She had been cleaning pictures for twenty years. She had never had her hands on a better piece of silk than that.

“I’m home,” she said. “Papa says it’s the last one. So I’ve come.”

The grey eyes looked down, amused, as they had always looked. Have you, darling? And what do you mean to do, now that you are here?

She did not know. She put her hand in her coat pocket and felt the key.

It had been her mother’s own. It was a long iron key with a loop of ribbon through it, gone the colour of weak tea. Dolly had given it to her on the day of the funeral. You’d best have this. Your father’s is in his waistcoat, and he’ll lose it. She had carried it for twenty years, in one bag after another. She had never once used it.

The door was six feet from where she stood.

She told herself that she was only going to look. She was a grown woman, and it was a room. There was nothing in it but furniture.

The lock turned as though it had been oiled yesterday. She pushed the door and went in, with the lamp from the gallery table in her hand.

The cold met her like a wall. And with it, so faint that she thought for a moment she was imagining it, there was a scent. Lavender. Camphor. And under those, something that stopped her breath. It was the stuff her mother had worn, that came in a square bottle from a shop in Jermyn Street. Imogen had not smelled it since she was twenty-four.

She stood in the doorway and let her eyes go round.

Nothing had been touched. Her father had seen to that. The white counterpane. The triple glass, with the silver brushes in their row. The book by the bed with a marker in it; she went and looked, and it was Persuasion. The clock on the mantel, stopped. And on the floor by the bed, side by side, with their toes to the wall, the grey satin shoes.

She stood over them. She had not been ready for the shoes.

I shall go in my stockings, her mother had said, that last afternoon, laughing, sitting on this bed. The Wade eats shoes. I’ve lost three pairs to it in ten years. I shall leave them just here, where your father will find them, and he’ll know then that I meant it and haven’t simply fallen in a ditch.

She had meant it. She had taken them off and set them down, neatly, as she did everything. Then she had gone down the stairs in her stockinged feet and out of the garden door.

Imogen had been waiting for her in the orangery.

That was the arrangement. They were to meet there at one, among the vines, and go together. Imogen had gone out early. She had not been able to bear the hall, and the clocks, and her father’s face. She had quarrelled with Edmund at tea, about nothing, about a horse, and it had come out of her mouth before she knew. Mother’s going to him tonight. To Amos Garrow. She’s leaving. Ask her yourself if you don’t believe me. She had seen his face go. She would see it until she died. She had run from the room.

So she had sat on an upturned pot in the orangery, in the dark, from eleven o’clock, sick with what she had done. She had heard the house clocks strike. And when her mother came through the garden door at one, in her tweed skirt and her stockings, with a lantern, and called softly, “Immy? Are you there? It’s time,” Imogen had not answered.

She had sat there in the dark behind the vine. She had held her breath.

She could not have said why, then. She was not sure that she could now. She had told Edmund. She had broken her word, and he would be coming, and there would be a scene, and it was her doing. She could not face her mother. She could not face Tom, who would see it in her. She was twenty-four years old and she hid in a greenhouse like a child who has broken a vase.

Her mother had waited. She had called once more. Then she had said, quite gently, to the dark, as though she knew perfectly well who was in it:

“Never mind, my darling. Come over in the morning.”

And she had gone.

Imogen had watched the lantern cross the lawn and go down to the Wade. She had watched it for a long time, getting smaller. It had gone out along the road, steadily, a little yellow star. It had got more than halfway. She was sure of that. It had been well past the Perch.

Then a second light had left the house. It moved fast and unevenly. It was a man with a lantern, running.

She had known who it was. She had sat on that pot with her knuckles in her mouth and watched her brother go after her mother across the sea.

She had seen the two lights come together, far out. She had seen them stand. They stood for a long time, and she grew cold, and the moon moved over the roof. At some point she must have slept. She was twenty-four and had cried herself stupid. When she woke the glass was grey. There were no lights on the Wade. There was water where the Wade had been.

And across the lawn, from the direction of the sea, a man was walking toward the house. He was walking slowly. He was soaked to the neck, his hair flat on his head, his good suit black with wet. He went past the orangery not ten yards from her and did not turn his head.

It was Edmund. It was six o’clock in the morning. He had been out on the Wade with their mother at one, and he had come back, and she had not.

He went in by the garden door. An hour later he came down to breakfast in dry clothes and said that he had slept in the stable. Imogen had heard him say it. She had sat at the table with the toast going cold and said nothing at all. And at nine Dolly’s husband had come up from the saltings at a run.

She had never told anyone. Not her father, who believed from that day that his clock had done it. Not the police, who asked a few questions and went away. She had never told Edmund that she knew. She had looked at him across this house for a week, across the coffin, and he had looked back, and it had lain between them like a blade.

She had refused to see Tom. He had come to the kitchen door three times that week. The third time he had stood in the yard for two hours in the rain, with his cap in his hands, looking up at her window. She had watched him from behind the curtain. She had thought: I told Edmund. I sat in the dark and let her go alone. If I had walked with her, she’d have crossed in twenty minutes, and we should all four be sitting in his father’s kitchen. How can I ever go into that kitchen now?

In November she heard that he had gone abroad.

Imogen knelt down, slowly, on the cold carpet. She touched one of the satin shoes with the tip of her finger. It was stiff, and a little dusty.

“I didn’t come over in the morning,” she said. “I never came at all.”

When she got to her feet her knees ached. She was forty-four; one’s knees did. She took up the lamp.

She would go now. She had looked. She had seen what there was. She would lock the door and go to her own room and sleep, and tomorrow she would put on her black dress and sit at her father’s table and get through it.

The lamp, as she turned, sent her shadow across the wardrobe. It was the big mahogany one with the long glass. She saw herself in it: a thin dark woman in a travelling coat, with a white streak in her hair and a careful face.

She did not decide to open it. Her hand did.

The dresses hung in a row, each in its cotton bag, as Dolly had put them away. Imogen knew what was in every one. The blue that her mother wore to church. The tweeds. The black velvet for funerals. She ran her hand along them, and the bags whispered.

At the end of the rail, by itself, on a padded hanger, there was one that was longer than the rest.

She lifted the cotton. She knew before she saw.

It came out of the bag like water. It was heavier than she expected, and cold, and when the lamplight touched it the whole length of it woke. Grey silk. Not the dull grey of a mouse or a pavement. It was the grey of a pigeon’s breast, with rose in it, and blue. She had spent her life looking at how painters got that colour. She knew that it could not be got. One could only suggest it, with white dragged over a warm ground.

Her mother had worn it every year, for the Hour. It was the Hour dress. She had been painted in it, and she said that she must go on wearing it so that people could tell her from the picture. She had worn it that last night, at dinner. Imogen could see her at the foot of the table, with the candles on her shoulders, saying something that made even Papa smile.

And at half past twelve she had come up here and taken it off. She had hung it on its hanger and put on a tweed skirt and a jersey, to cross the sea to a farm.

She had taken off this dress to go to Amos Garrow. And she had never got there.

Imogen stood holding it. The silk slid over her arm.

It was mad, the thing that had come into her head. She was not a person who did such things. She mended what other people had made. She wore black, and grey flannel, and a watch she never looked at—no, not even a watch. She had not worn a colour since she was twenty-four.

She held the dress against herself and looked in the long glass.

A woman looked back at her with her mother’s eyes. She had forgotten that she had them. One did not see one’s own eyes. The grey silk lay under her chin and gave them back their colour. She saw the white streak at her temple. Her mother had never had that. But the rest—the brow, the set of the head, the mouth that she kept so carefully shut—

And what do you mean to do, darling, now that you are here?

“Nothing,” Imogen said to the glass. “I don’t mean to do anything. He’s got a child. He never asked for me by name.”

She put the dress back in its bag. Her hands were not quite steady. She hung it at the end of the rail and shut the wardrobe door.

She locked the room behind her. She set the lamp back on its table under the portrait and did not look up.

But when she lay in her own narrow bed that night, in the room she had slept in as a girl, she could not get warm. She lay awake and listened to the clocks tell eleven, and midnight, and one. She thought of a light in a kitchen window across the water.

He looked at me as if I’d took something off him that he’d been carrying.

Somewhere toward two, by the house, she got up and went to the window. Her room was on the west side. The moon was high. The Wade was gone. The tide had been over it for hours, and there was only water, white and still under the moon, from the garden wall to the far shore.

On the far shore, under the sea wall, the lamp in the farmhouse was still burning.

He was awake, too.

She stood there in her nightdress with her forehead against the cold glass. She stood until the light across the water went out.

Chapter Two

It had begun with a foal.

That was in the May of 1974. She was home from London, where she had been two years at the Institute learning to take varnish off dead men’s pictures. She was twenty-four, and clever, and bored. She had a small green car and a way of looking at people, and she thought that the Ness was the dullest ninety acres in England.

She had driven across on the evening ebb with the windows down. It was one of those long light evenings that the marsh has in spring, when the whole sky seems to rest on the ground and the larks will not stop. She was halfway over the Wade when she saw the horse.

It was a grey mare, out on the saltings to the north of the road, a couple of hundred yards off, where the Garrows ran their stock. It was lying down. There was a man kneeling beside it.

She would have driven on. A tenant’s mare was nothing to her. But the man got up, and turned, and waved his arm. It was not a greeting. It was the way one waves at a boat.

She stopped the car. She got out and stood on the road in her London shoes.

“Can you hold a lamp?” he shouted.

She had never been spoken to in that way by anyone on the estate. She was Miss Imogen. Men touched their caps to her.

“I beg your pardon?”

“A lamp! Can you hold one? She’s foaling, and it’s coming wrong, and I’ll lose the light. I can’t hold it and get my arm in.”

She looked at the saltings. They were green and wet and seamed with little creeks, and she knew what they would do to her shoes. She took the shoes off. She left them on the bonnet of the car and went down off the road in her stockings, with her skirt held up, across two hundred yards of sea lavender and mud.

It was the first thing she ever did for him. She thought afterwards that it had settled the rest.

He was a year younger than she. She knew him by sight, as one knows the children of the farm; she had seen him at harvest suppers, a silent brown boy at the end of a bench. He had been away at an agricultural college and come back with shoulders. He had his shirt off and his right arm was red to the elbow. He did not look at her. He put a storm lantern into her hands.

“There. Down by her tail. Hold it steady. Don’t mind what you see.”

She held it. She held it for an hour and ten minutes, kneeling in the wet, while the light went out of the sky and the mare groaned. Imogen had never seen anything born. She saw his arm go in to the shoulder. She saw his face, turned away, with the eyes shut, as though he were listening with his fingers. He talked the whole time. He did not talk to her. He talked to the mare, low and steadily, a string of words with no gaps, the way one would talk to a child in a fever. There, my old girl. There. I’ve got him. He’s got his leg back, the fool, I’ve got to turn him. Wait now. Wait for me. That’s it. That’s my beauty.

She had never heard anybody speak with so much tenderness. She had not known that it could be done.

It came all at once, in the end. There was a rush, and something long and dark and shining lay on the grass in a bag of its own, and he tore the bag with his hands. It was a foal. It was black and wet and all legs. It lay with its sides heaving. The mare swung her great head round and breathed on it.

He sat back on his heels. He was shaking. He wiped his face with his forearm and left a streak across it.

“It’s a filly,” he said. He was grinning like a boy. “Look at her. Look at the length of her. She’ll be grey, like her dam; they’re born dark.” Then he looked at Imogen for the first time, properly, in the lantern light. She saw him see who she was. The grin went. “Miss Vane. I never—I’d not have called you down, only I didn’t know the car. I’m sorry. Your stockings.”

She looked down. She was mud to the thighs. There was blood on her skirt, and something worse.

She began to laugh. She laughed until she had to put the lantern down. After a moment, uncertainly, he laughed too.

“What will you call her?” she said.

“I don’t know. Dad names them.”

“Call her something from a poem. She was born in a salt marsh by lamplight. She ought to be out of a poem.”

“I don’t know any poems.”

“I’ll find you one.”

She found it that night, in the library, in a book that nobody had opened since her grandfather. She copied out two lines on a sheet of her mother’s writing paper. In the morning she walked across the Wade, on her own feet, and put it into his hand in the yard at Saltcote, with his father looking on. Queen Mab. He read it slowly, moving his lips. He folded it small and put it inside his shirt.

“Mab,” he said. “That’ll do. That’s a name you could call across a field.”

It was the name of the mare that stood in that yard tonight, under a rug. She was twenty years old.

Imogen lay in her narrow bed on the Saturday morning and watched the ceiling lighten. She had not slept. She had gone through it all in the night, every piece, as one goes through a drawer that has been shut for years.

It had lasted from May to October. Five months. She had been at Compline for all of them. She had told her tutors that there was a picture in the house that wanted treatment. It was true; she had spent the summer in the morning room with the portrait of a Georgian Vane face down on a table, relining it. In the evenings, when the tide served, she had gone out.

They had met in the orangery.

It was her idea. He would not come into the house. He said so flatly, the first time she asked him. I’ll not. Not by the kitchen, and I’d not be let in by the front. It was the only thing she ever heard him say with anger in it. So she showed him the old glasshouse on the south side, with its broken panes and its vine. Nobody went there. Her grandmother had grown oranges in it, in tubs, and there was still a smell, in warm weather, of earth and something sweet. The vine had got through the roof and filled the whole place with green. In August there were grapes, small and sour and black.

He would come across at dusk on the ebb, walking, and round by the sea wall to the garden side. She would be waiting among the leaves. They sat on two upturned pots. They hardly touched, at first. He was shy of her, and of her voice, and her hands. He held his own hands between his knees as though they were something he had brought by mistake.

She talked. She had never talked so much in her life. She told him about London, and the pictures, and what it was to take a brown fog of old varnish off a sky and find that the painter had meant it blue. He listened with his head down. She thought at first that he did not follow. Then one evening he said:

“It’s like the land.”

“How?”

“You take off what’s been put on. Bad drainage. Wrong crop. A man that didn’t know it. And underneath it’s what it always was. You don’t make it. You just clear off and let it be seen.” He went dark red. “I can’t say things. I’d sooner show you.”

So he showed her. He showed her the marsh. She had lived in the middle of it for twenty-four years and never looked. He took her out on the saltings at five in the morning and made her lie on her front to watch a redshank on its nest. He showed her where the samphire grew, and how the creeks filled from the far end first. He stood her on the sea wall at the top of a spring tide and said, Now. Watch. It’ll stop, and it did, the whole sea, as if someone had laid a hand on it.

“It’s the slack,” he said. “It only lasts a few minutes. Dad says it’s the tide thinking better of it.”

He knew to the minute when the Wade would open and when it would close. He did not look at a table. He looked at the sky, and smelled the air, and said, “Half past nine,” and was right.

“How do you do that?”

“I don’t know. It’s like knowing when you’re hungry.”

She fell in love with him as one falls asleep, without marking the moment. She knew only that some time in June she had stopped thinking of him as the Garrow boy. She listened all day for the tide.

He kissed her on the tenth of July. She had the date by heart. There had been a thunderstorm, and the rain was coming through the broken roof in ropes, and they had backed under the thickest part of the vine. A drop ran down her neck. He put up his hand to brush it away, and did not take the hand back.

It was not practised. He had kissed nobody, she thought, or nobody much. He did it as he did everything, slowly and completely. When he stopped, he looked at her with a kind of dread.

“I’ve no right,” he said.

“I gave you the right in May. I held your lamp.”

“You’re Miss Vane.”

“I’m Imogen. Say it.”

He could not, for a week. He called her nothing at all. Then one night, leaving, with his hand on the door frame, he said it, very low, like a man trying a word in a foreign language. Imogen. He made it sound like the name of a place.

At the end of August he gave her the ring.

He had made it himself. He was learning the smith’s work from the man at Thorney, to shoe his father’s horses. It was a horseshoe nail, bent round into a circle, with the head of the nail beaten flat and square for a stone. He had filed it smooth, and it shone like silver.

“It’s only iron,” he said. “It’ll rust if you let it. You’d have to keep it oiled.”

She put it on. It was a little large.

“I can’t offer you anything,” he said. “You know that. I’m a tenant’s son. I’ll have Saltcote after Dad, if your father lets me, and that’s a hundred and forty acres of grazing and a house with the damp in. You’ve been to London. You could have anyone.”

“I don’t want anyone. I want a man who can tell the time by the smell.”

“Your people won’t have it.”

“My mother will.”

She had believed that. It was the thing that made what came afterwards so hard. She had been certain of her mother. She had been saving it up, to tell her. She had pictured the amused grey eyes, and the laugh. Imogen. A Garrow? How perfectly sensible of you.

And then she had walked into the Grey Room in October and found the jewel case on the bed.

She got up. It was seven by the house. She washed in cold water and dressed in a grey jersey and a tweed skirt, and went down the back stairs. The kitchen was empty; Dolly had not yet come over. She made tea and drank it standing.

She would not think about the rest. She had been over it enough. The quarrel with Edmund. The orangery, in the dark, with her mother’s voice. Come over in the morning. The two lights on the Wade, and the grey dawn, and the man walking up the lawn with the sea running off him.

But the mind does not ask leave. It went on by itself.

Tom had come three times that week.

The first time was the Monday, the day after. He had walked over at low water and knocked at the kitchen door. Dolly came up to say so. Imogen was lying on her bed with her face to the wall. She said, “Tell him I can’t.”

The second was the day of the inquest. He had waited an hour on the gravel.

The third was the Saturday. The funeral had been the day before. It rained. He stood in the kitchen yard, bareheaded, with his cap in his two hands, and looked up at her window. He stood there from ten in the morning until past noon. She watched from behind the curtain. He did not move at all. The rain ran down his face and he let it. She had seen him stand like that beside a sick ewe, for a whole night, waiting to see which way it would go.

She had wanted to run down to him. Every part of her had wanted it. She had put on her coat twice.

And each time she had seen her mother’s lantern going away across the lawn. She had heard her own voice at the tea table. She’s going to him tonight. To Amos Garrow. She had done that. She had told, out of spite, because she was jealous of her own mother; and her brother had gone after her; and now her mother lay in St Botolph’s churchyard with the earth still raw.

If she went down to that yard, she would have to tell him. He would look at her, with those steady eyes, and she would have to say, It was me. I told Edmund. And I hid, and let her go alone. And then she would see his face change. She thought that she could bear anything but that.

So she had stayed behind the curtain. At a quarter past twelve he put his cap on, and turned, and walked out of the yard.

He left a letter with Dolly. It was one sheet, in pencil, in a round careful hand like a schoolboy’s.

I don’t know what I done. If it is on account of my father and your mother I never knew of it till after. I would not have kept it from you. I will be at Saltcote till the 14th of November. Then I have took a passage. If you will come I will stay. If you send word I will stay. I will not come to the house again as I think it troubles you. T. G.

She had read it standing at the scullery window. She had it still. It was in Edinburgh, in the lid of her workbox, with an iron ring that she had kept oiled for twenty years.
