He had done it as a boy with his father every year on the day after Michaelmas. It was the way the old man reckoned up. He would go round the whole of it on foot, the hundred and forty acres, with a stick, and look at every gate and every yard of fence and the state of every ditch, and say nothing. At the end he would stand on the sea wall and look back over it. Then he would go in and pay the rent.

The man took the child. She had her notebook, in the pocket of the blue coat, and a pencil on a string.

They went north first, along the foot of the wall. It was a still grey morning with the tide making. The home pastures lay inside the wall, eleven fields of them, small and square, cut out of the marsh by somebody’s grandfather with a spade. The grass was good. It had been grazed right and rested right for a hundred and eighty years and it had a sole on it like a carpet. He bent and pulled a handful and smelled it.

What are you doing, the child said.

Seeing what he’s left.

What has he?

He’s left it better than he found it.

The ditches were clean. That surprised him. The old man had been seventy-seven and alone and the ditches had been dug out that spring, every one, to the clay. The gates hung true. On one of them the bottom rail was new, split oak, and he could see the adze marks.

He stood and looked at that rail. His father had cut it and hung it with a bad chest in the last summer of his life, on ground that he held from year to year, for a landlord who did not know his face.

Why did he fix it if it’s not his, the child said. She was looking at the rail too.

I don’t know.

I wouldn’t.

No. He put his hand on the top bar. I reckon he didn’t think of it that way. I reckon he thought it was the gate’s.

She wrote something in the book.

They went on. Beyond the last pasture the wall turned east and there was a sluice, a brick arch with an oak door that let the land water out at the ebb and shut against the flood. He looked at that. The door was sound. The brickwork wanted pointing. It was the landlord’s to do, by the lease, and it had not been done in his lifetime or his father’s.

Outside the wall were the saltings.

They ran north and east for half a mile, eighty acres of them, flat as a table and cut all over by creeks. It was not land and it was not sea. The big tides covered it and the small ones did not. Nothing grew there but sea lavender and purslane and the coarse grey grass that sheep will eat if they are bred to it. The Garrow sheep were bred to it. They were out there now, three hundred ewes, moving ahead of the water in a long file the way they had been taught by their mothers.

He stood on top of the wall with the child and watched them come.

Who tells them, she said.

Nobody. They know.

How?

The old ones know and the young ones follow. He pointed. See that one in front, with the black on her face. She’ll have been doing that ten year. She can feel it. She’s a good quarter hour ahead of the water and she’ll bring them in over the hard by the sluice and never wet a foot.

What if she got it wrong?

She don’t.

But if she did.

Then they’d drown, he said. The lot. They’d follow her.

The child watched the sheep. She had her head on one side.

That’s a lot to put on one sheep, she said.

They ate their bread on the wall. The tide came up the stones below them. It came slowly and without any noise. He had forgotten that. On the range the weather came at you. You could see a storm for forty miles, walking on its legs of rain. This came from underneath. One minute there was mud and the next there was a skin of water on it, and you had not seen it arrive.

The child had her boots hanging over. She was looking across at the island.

It had come nearer with the flood. That was a trick of it. With the tide out, the Ness looked a long way off, at the end of its road. With the tide in it seemed to float up close, and a man could count the windows.

Why is there a road if it goes under, she said.

There was always a road. The monks made it. They had the island before the Vanes.

What monks?

I don’t know. Old ones. They had a church over there. They’d sing a thing at night, the last thing before bed. That’s where the name’s from.

What name?

Compline.

She tried it over. She wrote it down and showed him and he said he thought that was how it went.

What’s the box?

He looked where she was looking. Halfway across, with the water already round its legs, the Perch stood up black.

That’s for if you get caught, he said. If you’re on the road and the sea comes. You climb up there and wait.

How long?

Till it goes down. Five hours. Six.

In the dark?

If it’s dark.

Has anyone?

He did not answer at once. He was looking at the box. He had passed it ten thousand times and touched the post each time, the way his father did, without ever asking why.

I’ve heard there was a man once, he said. A long while back. A carrier with a cart. He lost the horse and the cart and sat up there all night and they fetched him off in the morning with his hair gone white.

Is that true?

It’s what’s said.

She looked at the box for some time.

The lady didn’t, she said. The one that drowned. She didn’t get in the box.

No.

Why not? It was right there.

I don’t know, the man said. She was past it. She was a good way past it, coming this way. And then she went back.

Back to the box?

Back toward it. She never got in.

The child turned that over. He could see her doing it. She had a way of holding a thing in her head and walking round it, the way a buyer walks round a horse.

That’s a clue, she said.

It’s a what?

A clue. It’s a thing that doesn’t fit. When there’s a thing that doesn’t fit, that’s where you look. She had the notebook open. It’s in my book. The girl in it finds a glove on the wrong side of a fence and that’s how she knows.

Knows what?

Who did it.

He looked at her. She was nine. She had sat for eight months on the edge of a bed in a rented house reading aloud to a woman who was dying, and after that she had not spoken for some weeks. Then one day she had come into the barn with a paper book from the school library, about a girl who solved things. She had been reading that kind ever since. He had thought it a good sign. He had thought, she wants there to be an answer.

Nobody did anything, he said. The sea did it.

Then why did Grandpa want you to ask?

He had not known she heard. She had been in the cottage across the yard, in bed. But there was a window, and it had been a still night, and she missed nothing.

That’s not for you, he said.

OK.

I mean it, Wren.

I said OK. She shut the notebook. She did not put it away. She held it on her knee with her finger in the place.

In the afternoon he went through the buildings.

The barn was dry. There was hay to the tie-beams, good hay, cut early. There was a cake store, and a root house with mangolds clamped in straw. In the stable there were two stalls and a loose box. The mare had the loose box. The other stall had a Fordson tractor in it that he remembered his father buying second-hand in 1961.

He looked at the mare’s feet. She wanted shoeing behind. He found his father’s tools in the forge, a lean-to at the end of the barn with a hearth no bigger than a kitchen fire. The anvil had been his grandfather’s. The hammers hung on their nails in order of weight. He took down the rasp and felt the edge. It had been kept oiled.

He had learned the trade in that lean-to, the summer he was twenty-three, from the smith at Thorney. He had made a ring there out of a horseshoe nail. He remembered beating the head flat. He had spoiled eleven before he got one that would do.

He hung the rasp back.

In the house he went through the old man’s papers. They were in a biscuit tin on the dresser. There were the rent books, every one, back to 1919, in his grandfather’s hand and then his father’s. He turned the pages. Lady Day. Paid. Michaelmas. Paid. There was never a quarter missed. In 1947, the year of the great frost, when they lost half the flock, somebody had written Paid and underlined it twice.

There was the lease. It was a single sheet. It said that the tenant held from year to year at the landlord’s pleasure.

There were his own letters. They were at the bottom of the tin, tied with binder twine. There were twenty of them. Not one had been opened.

He sat at the table with the bundle in his hand. I don’t read them. I can’t see to. The old man had been able to see well enough to hang a gate. He had kept them, all the same. He had put each one in the tin as it came and tied the string again.

Under the letters there was one thing more. It was a tide table, a little yellow book, such as they sold at the chandler’s. It was for the year 1974. He opened it. Someone had gone through it in pencil and put a ring round certain nights. It was a woman’s hand, small and upright. Against the twenty-sixth of October there was a ring, and a word.

Come.

He closed the book. He put it back under the letters and put the lid on the tin.

He sat a while. Then he took out the oilcloth packet from his shirt and unfolded it on the table. There was the blue paper from the solicitor. He read it again. Vacant possession. The twenty-fifth day of March.

He thought about three hundred ewes that knew the tide. They could not be moved. A marsh flock was hefted to its ground; put them on another farm and they would stand at the gate and pine. They would have to be sold, as mutton. The old one with the black face would go up the ramp of a lorry with the rest.

He thought about the gate with the new rail.

A hundred and eighty years. His people had kept that wall and dug those ditches and bred that flock. They had done it well, and gone on doing it, for wages they paid themselves. And at the end of it a man they had never spoken to could write one page and have them off by spring. He would put caravans on it. Dolly had told him. There would be a shop, and a road laid in concrete across the home pasture, and lights.

He had seen men in the west lose ground. He had seen a family that had ranched a creek for three generations sold up in an afternoon by a bank, and the wife standing in the yard holding a clock. He had thought it hard. He had not thought that there was anything to be done. That was how it was; land belonged to whoever had the paper.

He found that it was different when the gate was one his father had hung.

Dad.

The child was in the doorway. She had been with Dolly Pask, learning to make pastry. She had flour on her chin.

There’s a lady on the road, she said.

He went to the window.

It was nearly dark. There was a band of green light left in the west, over the flats, and the first of the moon coming up behind the house. The tide had gone out again and the Wade lay bare.

Someone was walking out along it.

It was a woman. She had come down the ramp from the wall, not thirty yards from his door, while he sat reading, and he had not heard her. She was a good way out already. She was thin and dark-headed and she wore a long coat. She had a bag in her hand. She walked quickly and did not look down at her feet.

He stood with his hand on the sill.

Who is she, the child said.

I don’t know.

Is she going to the house?

There’s nowhere else that road goes.

Is she allowed? It’s nearly night.

She’s two hours yet. More. He was reckoning it without thinking, from the feel of the air. She knows it. Look how she goes. She’s not minding the stones. She’s walked that before.

The woman went on. She got smaller. The moon came clear of the roof behind him and put her shadow down on the road in front of her.

She came to the dip. She came to the bridge, and the box on its legs. And there she stopped.

He saw her put the bag down on the planks. He saw her stand. She was too far off now, and the light too poor, for him to see more than a shape. But he saw the shape put out an arm and lay its hand on the post of the Perch.

She stood like that for a long time.

He did not move. He did not know why he could not. A woman had stopped on a road and touched a post. Every Garrow did it. Half the village did.

She’s sad, the child said.

How d’you know?

You can tell. She’s got her head down. The child had her nose against the glass. Is she the lady’s girl? The one that drowned?

He looked down at her.

What makes you say that?

Mrs Pask said the lady had a girl and a boy. She said the girl went away to Scotland and doesn’t come. But that’s who’d be sad there. She said it reasonably. It’s where her mom was.

The man looked out again. The woman had picked up her bag. She was going on, toward the island, up the far slope of the dip. The moon was full on her back. He could see how she held her head.

He had seen that head held so across a harvest supper, at the far end of a barn. He had seen it bent over a lantern on the saltings, with the hair coming down.

It could not be. Dolly had said it plain. She’s in Scotland. She never comes home this time of year.

He stood at the window until the woman had gone up off the Wade into the trees and there was nothing on the road. He stood after that. The green went out of the sky. The lamp in the porch of the house across the water burned small and yellow, as it had every night of his boyhood.

Dad.

What?

You’re holding the window.

He looked. He had hold of the frame with both hands. He let go.

Go and wash your face, he said. You’ve flour on it.

He did not sleep that night.

He put the child to bed in the small room over the kitchen that had been his. He sat by the range. At ten he made up the lamp and set it on the sill, in the window that looked at the island. He did it without deciding to. His hands knew where it went.

He sat and looked at it.

He thought about his father. He thought about the question that had been put on him. He had turned it over all the week and he had not known what he would do. He had thought that he might write to the man. He had thought he might go to the lawyer and say, I’ll be off your ground by March, and before I go I want five minutes with Mr Edmund Vane. He was not a man who went to another man’s door at night.

He thought about a woman with her hand on a post.

If it was her. If she had come. Then she was in that house now, half a mile off. She was sitting at a table with her brother.

He got up and walked about the kitchen. He was forty-three years old. He had been married nine years to a good woman and had buried her. He had a child asleep overhead. He had thought that the other thing was done with. He had carried a piece of paper inside his shirt for twenty years the way a man carries a scar. He did not expect it to open.

It had opened. It had opened at a window, at the sight of a shape half a mile away that might be anyone.

Toward two he heard the tide come over the road. A little after, he went to the door and looked out. The moon was high and the water lay white to the island.

There was a light over there besides the porch. It was on the upper floor, on the west side. It was a window he knew.

He stood in the doorway in his shirt. The night air was cold on his arms.

It burned for a long time. He thought that somebody stood behind it. He could not see. But he stood and looked at it, and he had the feeling that he had on the range sometimes, at night, riding fence, when he would know without turning that there was a deer at the edge of the trees watching him.

After a while it went out.

He went in. He turned down his own lamp. He did not go up. He sat in his father’s chair until it was light, with his boots on.

In the morning he took the gun down from the corner and looked through the barrels.

He was not going to use it. He told himself so. A man looks at a gun that has been left to him. It was a twelve-bore, a plain one, by a Birmingham maker, with the blueing worn silver at the breech where his father’s hand had carried it for fifty years. The barrels were clean. There was a box of cartridges on the dresser. Number five shot, for duck.

He set it back in the corner.

He would go to the lawyer first. That was the right way. He would put on a clean shirt and drive to the county town and see this man Fenn, and ask him civil who a Garrow was to speak to. If there was a way to do it with his hat in his hand, he would do it that way.

He woke the child at seven. She came down with her notebook.

I’ve to go to Colchester, he said. To see a man about the paper. You’re to stop with Mrs Pask. She’ll be at the cottage with her sister.

Can’t I come?

No.

Can I ride Mab?

Not on your own. Not till I’ve shod her.

Can I go on the road?

He took her by the two shoulders. He had never raised his hand to her and he never would. But he held her so that she looked at him.

You are not to set foot on that road, he said. Not a foot. Not if the Queen of England was to call you from the other end. You don’t know it, and it don’t care who you are. It took a grown woman that had lived beside it thirty year. Do you hear me?

Yes.

Say it.

I’m not to go on the road.

Not for anything.

Not for anything, the child said.

She looked at him steadily while she said it. She was a truthful child. He had never caught her in a lie, and he never did. He let her go.

3. The Town

He took the child across the yard to the cottage at half past seven. It was a raw morning with the light just coming.

Dolly Pask was loading her van. It was a small grey van with the name of a baker painted out on the side, and she had the back doors open and was putting in crates. There were geese in the crates, plucked, four of them, and a sack of something, and a tin trunk. Her niece was helping, a big red girl of seventeen who stopped and stared at his hat.

I’d forgot, Dolly said. It’s the night. I’m over there till morning. They’ve a dinner.

What dinner?

The same as they’ve always had. For the clocks. Thirteen to table and one of them a ghost. She shut her mouth on that. Vi’ll have the child. She’s deaf, mind, but she’s not daft. She raised six.

The old sister was in the doorway. She was eighty-three, small and bent, in a man’s cardigan. She looked at the child and held out her hand and the child went and took it.

You be good, the man said.

I’m always good.

You be good anyhow.

He walked back to the farm. He did not look round. If he had, he would have seen Dolly Pask standing by the open doors of the van with her hands on her hips, looking at the old woman and the child, and then at the tide board on the wall, and then at the child again.

He caught the mare and brought her into the yard. He lit the forge and blew it up. He had the two hind shoes off her and was dressing the near foot with the rasp when he heard the van start. He did not lift his head. It went up the ramp behind him in low gear and along the wall, and down onto the Wade.

He glanced at it then, under his arm. It was going out over the stones with the sea in the creeks on either hand. It had twenty minutes to spare, not more. He could see the crates through the back window, and the sack on top of them, and Dolly’s niece in the passenger seat with her head turned, saying something over her shoulder into the back.

He thought nothing of it. He bent to the hoof.

He went on thinking nothing of it for the rest of his life.

He was fitting the second shoe when the car came.

It came along the wall from the village and stopped at the head of the ramp. It was a big car, a town car, the colour of mud. A man got out of it. He was heavy and grey-faced and wore a raincoat and a hat with the brim turned down. He stood and read the tide board. He read it and looked at his watch, and looked at the road, and read it again.

The man in the yard watched him.

He knew the kind. He had seen them in the stock towns, at the edge of a sale ring, with their thumbs in their belts. It was the way the stranger stood, square, and the way his eyes went over a thing and took its number. He had a policeman’s shoes.

The stranger turned and looked down into the yard. He looked at the horse and the forge and the man. He took his time. The man let him. He had the hoof between his knees and he did not put it down.

Then the stranger looked at the island. He looked at it the way a man looks at a job of work.

He got into his car and drove down onto the Wade.

The man watched him the whole way over. The tide was at the stones. The car went slowly through the dip and across the planks, past the Perch, and up the far side, and out of sight behind the point.

So the Vanes had sent for the law. Or the law had come for the Vanes. He did not know which. Either way there was a policeman going to that house on the day of its dinner, in a plain car, alone, and he had gone over on the last of the ebb so that he could not get back.

He finished the shoe. He ran his thumb round the clenches. He let the foot down and straightened his back and took off his hat and wiped his face.

He looked across at the house.

It was the habit of a fortnight. He had done it every morning since he came. He looked at the long roof and the chimneys and the row of upper windows on the west side.

He could not have said what he was looking for. He was half a mile off. But he stood there with his hat in his hand, and he felt it again, what he had felt at the door in the night. Something was looking back.

He put his hand inside his coat. The oilcloth was there.

He put the mare in the barn.

He drove to the county town in the hired car. It was twenty miles. He had a clean shirt on and his father’s black tie.

The lawyer’s office was up a stair over a building society. A girl at a desk said Mr Fenn did not see people on a Saturday without an appointment. He said he would wait. He stood by the door with his hat in his hands. He stood for forty minutes. People came and went. The girl looked at him now and then, and at last she got up and went through.

The room she showed him into had a desk as big as a hay wagon. There was a man behind it. He was old and dry, with a stiff collar, and he had his fingers together.

Mr Garrow, he said. I am sorry about your father.

You wrote him a letter.

I wrote to his representatives. It reached you, I think, at an unfortunate moment. I was not informed of the date of the funeral. Had I been, I should have held it back a week.

It’d have said the same in a week.

It would. The lawyer did not look away. He had pale tired eyes. I act for the estate, Mr Garrow. I was given an instruction and I carried it out. I do not expect you to think well of me for it.

Who give the instruction?

Mr Edmund Vane.

It’s his land?

It is his father’s land. Mr Leopold Vane is the owner. He is eighty-one. He has not concerned himself with the estate for some years, and Mr Edmund has his authority to manage it.

Then I’ll see the father.

You will not find that possible. He sees no one. He is not always— The lawyer stopped. He is an old man.

Then I’ll see the son.

On what matter?

The man stood in front of the desk. There was a chair. He had not been asked to sit in it and he would not have.

There’s two, he said. There’s the farm. My people have had that ground since 1811. There’s three hundred ewes on it that can’t be moved; they’re hefted. If he wants it for caravans, I’d like him to tell me so himself. I’d like him to stand on it and say it.

And the other?

The other’s not about the farm.

The lawyer was quiet. He took his spectacles off and held them.

It’s about a thing that happened on the Wade, the man said. Twenty year back tonight. My father saw the half of it from our wall. He’s dead. He left me to ask after the other half.

I see, the lawyer said.

He said it very low. He put the spectacles down on the blotter and looked at them. The man waited. Out in the street a bus went by.

Mr Garrow. I knew your father for thirty years. He came up those stairs every Lady Day and every Michaelmas and paid his rent in notes, in this room. He never once sat down. I asked him to, each time. He would say, I’ll not stop, Mr Fenn. In thirty years I do not think that we exchanged a hundred words. But I formed an opinion of him.

He looked up.

I am going to say something to you that I ought not. I have been solicitor to the Vane family since 1954. There are matters in that house which I have made it my business not to know. I was there on the night you speak of. I have been there on the same night every year since. I do not know what your father saw from his wall. I have never asked what anyone saw. I am not a brave man, and I have a wife.

But I will tell you this. If you go to Compline and ask Edmund Vane that question, I think that he will answer it. I think that he has been waiting twenty years for somebody to ask.

Then I’ll go.

Not tonight.

Why not tonight?

Because tonight the family keeps its anniversary. There will be guests. The old man intends to say something; I do not know what. There is a person in the house, sent by me, on a matter that does not concern you. And Edmund will have been drinking since noon. The lawyer put his hands flat on the desk. Go tomorrow, Mr Garrow. Go on Monday. I shall speak to him myself this evening; I dine there. I shall tell him that you have a right to be heard, on both counts. I can do that much. I ought to have done it for your father.

The man turned his hat round in his fingers.

Tomorrow, he said.

Tomorrow. In daylight. By the road.

He nodded. He put his hat on. At the door the lawyer spoke again.

Mr Garrow. He is not a wicked man. I should like you to know that before you see him. I have watched him for twenty years. Whatever he did, he has not had a day’s peace from it.

Nor had my father, the man said.

He went down the stairs.

He meant it. He would wait till the Sunday. He drove home through the flat fields with the tie loosened and the window down and he thought that it was the right way. The lawyer had talked sense. A man did not go to another man’s house on the night of a family dinner with a question like that.

He would go in the morning. He would walk across at the ebb with his hat in his hand.

He stopped at the public house in the village. He had not been in it since he was twenty-three. He wanted bread and cheese and he wanted to hear what was said of the farm.

It was the same room. There was the same long settle under the window and the same fire. The same dart board, he would have sworn. There were eight or nine men in it. They were men he had known as boys, grown thick and grey, and their fathers, grown small. The talk stopped when he came in.

He went to the bar. The landlord was a stranger, a young man.

A half of bitter, he said. And something to eat.

You’ll be Garrow.

I am.

Your father had a slate here. It’s clear. He come in the week before he was took bad and paid it to the penny. He said he’d not go owing.

The man put a note on the bar.

Then I’ll pay for mine, he said.

He took his glass to the end of the settle. He did not drink it. He had not drunk in nine years. His wife had asked it of him when the child was born, and he had found that he did not miss it. He sat with the glass in front of him and ate the bread.

The talk came back by degrees. They talked round him. They talked of the price of lambs and a man who had lost a boat. One of them said across the room, You’ll have had your letter, Tom. He said he had. Another said it was a wicked thing. A third said the Vanes had always been hard landlords and soft-headed with it, and that Mr Edmund would sell his own grandmother for the price of a case of Scotch.

He’s sold near enough everything else, somebody said.

That was a man by the fire. He was sixty or so, broad, in a blue jersey, with a face like a board that had been left out. He had hands on him like a pair of dock fenders. The man on the settle knew him. He was Ostler, from the point, who had the oyster layings. He had been a hard drinker and a good boatman twenty years ago, and he was plainly both still. He had three empty glasses in front of him and a fourth going.

What’s he sold now, Dick, somebody said.

I couldn’t say. I’m not paid to say. Ostler drank. I’m paid to be at the Hythe at the slack with my launch and no lights, that’s all I know. Two hundred pound. In an envelope. Give me in that car park yesterday dinnertime by a feller in a camel coat, out of a Jaguar motor car.

For doing what?

For taking a box off. And a passenger.

What passenger?

A big feller with a gammy leg, I was told. Who’s that sound like to you?

There was a laugh. It was not a kind one.

He’s running, a man said. By God. He’s doing a flit.

I never said so.

Where to?

Parkeston Quay. By five in the morning. There’s a boat goes from there to the Hook of Holland at nine o’clock of a Sunday. I’ll leave you to do the sum.

What’s in the box?

Whatever’s left, I should think, Ostler said. He was pleased with himself. He had the room. Whatever the old man’s got that’s worth the lifting. He’s had the silver, I’ve heard, and the pictures. There’ll be a clock or two.

Tonight, the landlord said. On the night of their dinner.

Top of the tide. Quarter to two. That’s the only time you’d get a boat in there, a night like it’s going to be. There’s wind coming. Ostler tapped his nose. I didn’t ought to have told you. I was told to keep it close. But I’ve took against that family. My father fished off that Hythe forty year and old Vane put a chain on it.

The man on the settle had put down his bread.

He sat still. He looked at the glass of beer. There was a ring of froth going down the inside of it.

Tomorrow, the lawyer had said. In daylight. By the road. I shall speak to him myself this evening.

And at a quarter to two in the morning Edmund Vane would step down off the Hythe into a boat and be carried out of that country. By nine he would be on a ship. By Monday he would be somewhere in Europe with a box of his father’s clocks, where no Garrow could ever find him.

The lawyer did not know it. He had sat behind his desk with his dry honest face and said, go tomorrow. He was going to that dinner tonight to plead for a hearing from a man who would be gone before the port was round.

There would be no tomorrow. The man saw that quite clearly. If the question was to be asked, it would be asked tonight, on the Ness, before the slack. Or it would not be asked at all, and his father had held on for it for nothing.

He got up. He left the beer.

You’ve not touched your drink, Tom, somebody said.

No.

You’re a changed man.

I’ve a child, he said.

He went to the door. Ostler was looking at him from the fire. The oysterman had gone a little red. He had remembered, late, whose son was sitting on the settle, and whose landlord he had been talking about.

Here, he said. You’ll not go saying where you had that.

I never heard it, the man said.

He went out. The wind had begun. It was coming off the land, as yet, light, with rain in it. He stood by the car and smelled it. It would back, by dark. It would go round into the south-west and blow.

He looked at his watch. It was a quarter past two. The Wade would open a little after five, and shut at five past ten.

He had seven hours and three-quarters to think of a way to stand in front of Edmund Vane.

4. The Gun

He cleaned the gun that afternoon at the kitchen table.

It did not want it. His father had kept it as he kept everything. But the man took it down and broke it and drew a rag through the barrels, and oiled the action, and wiped the stock. It was something to do with his hands while he thought.

He thought it out as he would have thought out a piece of work with stock.

Vane would be at the Hythe at a quarter to two. That was sure. A man who has paid two hundred pounds for a boat is where the boat is. The Hythe was on the north shore of the Ness, away from the house, at the end of the sea wall. There was nothing there but the staging and a spinney of thorn. A man could wait in that spinney and not be seen.

To be at the Hythe he must be on the island. To be on the island he must cross before five past ten.

He would not go to the house. He had never been in it and he would not begin on a night when they had company and a policeman. He would cross at nine, on the mare, and put her in the old glasshouse on the south side, where no one went. He knew that place. He would walk round by the wall to the spinney and sit down under a thorn. He would wait there four hours and a half, if he had to.

And when Edmund Vane came along the wall with his box, he would step out.

He turned the gun in his hands. The wood was dark with fifty years of his father’s palm.

He was not going to use it. He had told himself that in the morning and he told himself again. He was a stockman. He had killed sick beasts and he had killed coyotes and once a bear that was at the calves. He had never pointed a gun at a man and did not mean to.

But he knew Vane. He knew what would happen if he stepped out of that spinney with nothing in his hands. Vane would look at him. He was six foot two and had been to a school where they teach it. He would say, Garrow, isn’t it? You’re trespassing. And he would walk on to his boat, and the man would be left standing on the wall with his question in his mouth, as his father had stood for an hour with a lantern.

His father had said it. He always minded a gun. He was gun-shy as a boy.

He would carry it broken, over his arm. He would let Vane see it. That was all. He wanted him stopped for the length of time it takes to answer one thing. Which was it. Was she coming or was she going. And when he had his answer he would stand aside, and Vane could go to Holland or to hell.

He put two cartridges in the pocket of his coat. He looked at them first. Number five. He told himself that an empty gun is a thing a man can see is empty, in a good light, and that he would not have Vane laugh.

He found the canvas case in the cupboard under the stairs and strapped it under the flap of his own saddle. He had brought the saddle with him across the Atlantic in a crate. It was the one thing he owned that he would not have sold. It had a deep seat and a horn, and the men in the village had come to the yard gate to look at it.

When it was done he sat down in his father’s chair. It was four o’clock. He looked at the window, and the lamp on the sill, unlit.

He thought about the woman on the road.

He had not let himself, all day. He had kept it out with the lawyer and the public house and the gun. But it had been there underneath, like water under ice.

If she was in that house.

He would not see her. He was not going to the house. He would be in a spinney at the other end of the island, in the dark, and she would be at a table with candles on it. She would never know that he had been within a quarter mile.

He told himself that that was best.

At dusk he went across to the cottage.

The old sister opened the door a hand’s breadth. She had a shawl on and a candle. She looked up at him with her head on one side like a hen.

I’ve come to see the child, he said.

Eh?

Wren. The child.

She’s abed.

It’s not six.

She were tired. She been drawing all day. She had her tea and went up with her book. The old woman’s eyes were small and bright and they did not quite meet his. Don’t you go waking her, Tom Garrow. She’s a good little thing and she wants her sleep. You’ll have her in the morning.

I’d only look at her.

You’d wake her, with them boots. And then I’ll have her down here till midnight asking what things are for. She began to close the door. Dolly said she’s to stop the night and that’s what she’ll do. You go on home.

He stood on the step. He could have put his hand on the door. She was eighty-three and weighed less than a ewe lamb.

But he had been brought up in that yard, and Vi Pask had boxed his ears there when he was six for chasing her ducks. He took off his hat.

Tell her I came, he said.

I’ll tell her.

The door shut. He heard the bolt.

He stood a moment in the yard looking up. There was a small window under the thatch at the gable end, where the stairs came out. It was dark. He thought of her up there with her notebook under the pillow.

He has been asked since if he felt nothing. Standing in that yard. He felt that he would have liked to see her face before he did what he was going to do. That was all he felt. He put his hat on and went to see to the stock.

It was the stock that undid his plan.

He went round them at eight with a lantern, as his father had every night of his life. The wind had got up. It had gone into the south-west, as he had known it would, and it came across the flats in long hard gusts with rain in them. The tide had turned an hour since. He could hear it, out in the dark, beginning to talk in the creeks.

The ewes should have been in. On a making tide with weather coming they should have been up on the hard ground by the sluice, in a bunch, with their backs to the wind. He stood on the wall and held up the light.

They were not in. He could see them, a long way out on the saltings, a pale smear in the rain. They were standing. They were all facing one way. And they were making a noise, a low steady uneasy sound, that he had not heard since he was a boy and knew at once.

The leader was down.

He went out to them. It was half a mile, over ground that was all holes, and he went at a run with the lantern swinging. He jumped the small creeks and waded the big ones. There was water in them already. He could feel it pulling at his boots.

He found her by the noise the others made. They were stood round a creek on the far side, a deep one, with steep clay banks. She was at the bottom of it.

She was on her back. A sheep that gets on its back in a hollow cannot rise; the weight of the fleece holds it. She had gone to cross, as she had crossed ten thousand times, and the bank had given under her. She lay with her four legs in the air and her black face turned up to him. Her fleece was full of water. The tide was in the creek, a foot of it, and climbing. It was over her ears.

She did not struggle. She had done that and it was past. She looked at him out of one yellow eye.

He put the lantern on the bank. He went down into the creek.

He has told this part more than the rest. The one who listened would ask for it. It took him two hours.

She weighed, wet, as much as a man. The clay would not hold his feet. He got his arms under her and heaved and went down on his face in the water with her on top of him. He got up and tried again. He got her onto her side and then onto her breast, and she could not stand; her legs had no feeling in them. He had to hold her head up out of the tide with one hand and rub her legs with the other, there in the creek, with the water at his waist and the rain coming flat.

He talked to her. He did not know what he said. It was what he said to any beast.

When she could bear weight he tried to drive her up the bank. She could not climb it. He got under her. He put his shoulder to her rump and pushed her up that clay a foot at a time, and slid back, and pushed. He lost count of the times. He tore the nails of one hand.

He got her out. She stood on the top with her head hanging and the water running off her. The others closed round her. They put their noses to her.

And they would not move.

That was the thing. She was the one who knew. They had stood out there on the open saltings for two hours with the sea coming, three hundred of them, rather than leave the place where she was. Now she was up, and they waited for her to lead them home. And she could not. She took three steps and stopped. She was spent.

The water was over the low ground between them and the wall. He could see it in the lantern, a sheet of it, shining, with the grass tops showing through. In half an hour it would be over their backs.

He picked her up. He got her across his shoulders, as a man carries a deer, with her forelegs in one fist and her hind legs in the other. He took the lantern in his teeth by its wire.

He walked. He went straight for the hard by the sluice, through the water, with a hundredweight and a half of wet sheep on his neck. He did not look round. He heard them come. He heard twelve hundred feet go into the tide behind him.

They followed him in. All of them. They came up onto the hard in a long file, at his heels, and stood.

He set her down under the wall, out of the wind. He knelt by her. He was shaking so that he could not unclench his hands. She lay with her legs folded and her eyes shut. He thought she had died. He put his palm on her side, and it rose.

That’s a lot to put on one sheep, the child had said.

He looked at his watch. He had to hold it close to the lantern. The glass was smeared with clay.

It was twenty past eleven.

He stood up. He turned and looked at the Wade.

There was no Wade. There was the sea. It ran from the foot of the ramp to the island, black, with the white coming off the tops of it and blowing. It had been over the road for an hour and a quarter. He could see the nearest of the withies standing out of it, and beyond them nothing.

He had been going to cross at nine.

He stood on the hard with the rain in his face. He had forgotten. For two hours and more he had not once thought of Edmund Vane. He had thought of a sheep. There had not been room in him for anything else. He had been his father’s son. He had done what any Garrow would have done on that ground on that night, and it had cost him the one thing his father had asked.

At a quarter to two there would be a boat at the Hythe. He would be standing here. He would watch its light go out past the point and down the river.

He began to laugh. It was not a good sound, and the wind took it. He had saved the old man’s flock. They would be mutton by March; the paper was in his shirt. He had carried a ewe half a mile on his back so that she could go up the ramp of a lorry on Lady Day with the rest. And for that he had let the man go who was putting them off.

He walked back to the yard. He was so tired that he could not feel his feet.

As he came round the end of the barn, every light in the village went out.

He saw it happen. There had been a string of them along the wall behind him, small and yellow. They went together, like a hand closed. There was the dark, and the wind, and across the water one lamp, in the porch of the house. That one burned oil.

He stood in the yard. He was wet through and plastered with clay. He had lost his hat in the creek.

He thought, I will go in. I’ll light the range. I’ll sit in his chair and tell him that I tried.

The mare whickered.

She was at the door of the loose box. He could see the white of her in the dark. She had her head out over the half door. She was not looking at him. She had her ears pricked, hard forward, and she was looking past him, down the yard, at the ramp, and the sea.

She whickered again. It was low. It was the sound a mare makes to a foal that has gone too far off.

He went to her. He put his hand on her neck. She was trembling. It was not fear. He knew every sign in a horse, and that was not it. She leaned on the door so that the bolt rattled.

What is it, old lady?

She threw up her head. She struck the door with her knee.

He looked where she was looking. There was nothing. There was the black water.

No, he said. Not you. You’re twenty year old.

She stood. She breathed. She looked at the sea.

He had drawn her out of her dam on that marsh, by lamplight, beside that road. She had been foaled within sound of the Rill. She had gone over the Wade a thousand times, at every state of it, with his father on her back, in fog, in snow, when the old man had lain late at the market and cut it fine. She knew where the stones were as she knew where her feet were.

She had been his father’s horse for twenty years. She had stood in this yard every night, looking over that door at a lamp in a window. He wondered what she knew.

It can’t be done, he said to her. There’s five foot on it. There’s seven in the Rill. An hour and a half before, the Wade belongs to God. That’s Dad’s own word.

The mare put her nose against his chest. She pushed.

He stood there in the rain with his forehead on her face.

He has said since that he did not decide it. He says that it was decided in the stable, by a horse. He does not expect to be believed. He only knows that he went into the loose box for the saddle with his mind made up to hang it on its peg, and that he found he was putting it on her.

He cinched it. He strapped the gun in its case under the near flap. He put the two cartridges where he could reach them. He lit his father’s big lantern, the one that had been held up on the wall, and hung it from the horn.

He led her out. She came like a colt.

At the foot of the ramp he stopped her. The sea was at his boots. It came in and drew back. He could hear the Rill, out in the middle, a long way off, like a train on a bridge.

He looked back at the cottage. The window under the thatch was dark.

If I go in this, he said aloud, and don’t come out, she’s nobody.

He has thought about that too. He stood on the edge of that water for perhaps a minute, with one hand on the horn, and he thought of the child asleep under the thatch. He very nearly turned the mare round.

But he thought of what he would have to say to her when she was grown. Your grandfather asked one thing of me. I’d the chance, and I was afraid of getting wet.

He looked at his watch. It was twenty to twelve.

He put his foot in the stirrup. The mare did not wait to be asked. Before he was fairly in the saddle she had walked down off the land into the sea.

5. The Wade

The water was cold enough to stop a man’s heart. It came over his boots at the foot of the ramp and to his knees before the mare had gone her own length.

He let her have her head. He sat down in the saddle and kept his hands low and did nothing. There was nothing he could do. He could not see the road. He could see the lantern, and in its light a few yards of black water going by from left to right, fast, with rain driving into it. Now and then a withy came up out of the dark on one hand or the other, and passed, and was gone.

She was walking. He could feel the stones under her. She put each foot down as if she had counted them.

The wind was on his right cheek and the sea was against his left leg. It leaned on the mare like a man leaning on a gate. She leaned back. Where the road had been built up on its bank the water was at her belly. Where the bank had sunk she went in to the shoulder, and he felt her float for a stride and find it again.

He looked back once. There was nothing there. The farm was gone. The wall was gone. The whole of England had been put out like the lamps of the village.

He looked ahead. He had steered by the porch lamp at Compline as a boy, coming home late from the island side with a message. It should have been dead in front of him, over her ears.

A squall had come across. He could see rain and the lantern and the mare’s white neck.

He took out his watch. He held it to the light. He does not know why he wanted the time. A man in that place does a thing because his hands are used to it.

At midnight the man was in the Wade with the sea to the mare’s shoulder and no house in sight.

He put the watch away. He remembers thinking that it was a strange hour to be anywhere, and that in the house they would be at their port, with the candles lit.

He knew when they came to the Rill by the sound.

It had been a mutter and then a roar, and now it was all round him. The mare stopped. She stopped of her own will, with her forefeet together, and stood. The water was at her chest and it was different water. It did not lean. It tore. He could feel her whole body quivering against it.

He held up the lantern.

In front of them the road ended. He could see where it went down. The surface of the sea dipped there, in a long smooth slope, like the lip of a weir, and beyond the lip it was running north with a hump on it, and streaks of white. It was thirty yards across. He knew what was under it. There were the planks of the Clapper, and under the planks seven feet of tide going through a gut no wider than a barn.

On the other side, somewhere, the road came up again.

He sat her on the edge of it. He does not know how long. The rain had eased. He could see a little further, and to his right, downstream, black against the black, there was something standing in the water on legs.

It was the Perch.

He looked at it. He had looked at it from the wall the day before with the child. The lady didn’t get in the box. Why not? It was right there.

She had been out here. On this road, in the dark, with the tide coming. Not in a gale; it had been a still night, his father said, with a moon. But the same water. She had stood somewhere near where he sat now, a small quick woman of fifty-four in her stockings, with a lantern, and her son had been with her, drunk, on the ground.

And she had been past it. She had been a hundred and fifty yards from his father’s hand.

He thought, sitting there, that he did not want to know. That was the truth. His father had asked which it was, and he had put on his coat and taken the gun and come. But with the Rill going by in front of him he found that he was afraid of the answer. If she had been dragged, then Edmund Vane had killed her. And if she had not, then she had stood in this place and looked at Amos Garrow’s light, and turned her back.

He did not know which he could better carry home.

The mare shifted. She put her head down to the water and blew at it.

No, he said. That’s enough. I’ll not ask it of you. We’ll go back.

He meant it. He had his weight in the off stirrup and the rein against her neck to turn her. It was too much. She was twenty. He would sit on the wall at Saltcote and watch the boat’s light go down the river. He would tell the child, when she was grown, that there were some things a man could not get an answer to.

The mare took the bit.

He felt it go out of his hands. She had it in her teeth; she pulled the rein through his fingers like a rope running out. She gathered herself under him, all at once, the way a young horse does at a fence.

And she went in.

It took them both under.

He had been in rivers. He had swum cattle over the Oldman in the June rise with the snow water coming down brown and trees in it. He had thought he knew what water could do.

This was not like a river. A river goes one way. This went north and down and round, all together. The cold shut on his chest like a door. He had the horn in one hand and a fistful of mane in the other and the sea was in his eyes and his mouth. He felt the mare go from under him. For a moment there was nothing of her but the mane.

He thought, that’s it. That is the finish.

He has said what he thought of, then. He said it once to the woman, and once more, a long time after, to the one who has set this down. He did not think of Vane. He did not think of his father. He thought of a girl of twenty-four kneeling on the saltings with her skirt in the mud, holding a lamp. He thought, I’ll not have seen her.

That was all. It was not a long thought. But it had been waiting twenty years, and it came up through him like a cork.

The lantern had gone out. It was still on the horn; he could feel it bang against his knee. They were in the dark, in the sea, being carried.

Something stood over him.

It was there and gone. Four black legs, crossed with bracing, and above them a box, and a ladder. They went under it, or beside it. It was so close that the mare’s shoulder struck one of the posts. He put out his hand. He did not mean to. His palm met tarred wood, cold and rough, and slid along it, and it was behind them.

He had touched the post. He had done it all his life, going by on the road. He did not know why he did it then, with the water closing over his head. But he remembers the feel of it. He remembers thinking that it was solid, and that everything else in that place was moving.

The mare screamed.

It was not pain. She had got her head up. She was swimming. He felt her come alive between his knees, the big shoulders driving, and he let go of the horn and lay along her neck to give her her back. She was not fighting the set. She was going with it, and across. She knew. She was letting it carry her down, and all the time working over, a yard and a yard, toward where the bottom shelved.

Her off fore struck something. She lurched. She struck again.

She stood.

She stood up out of the sea with the water pouring off her and her legs spread and her head between her knees. He was half off. He hung on her neck. Under her feet there was shingle, hard, ribbed, going up.

She had found the road.

They were forty yards north of it. She had come out on the tail of the bank, where it ran out into the mud, the one place below the Clapper where a horse could land. A length either side and she would have been in the soft. He does not believe that she saw it. He believes that she had it in her feet.

He slid down. The water was at his waist. He stood with his arms round her neck and his face in her mane, and he could not speak.

She turned her head and looked at him. Her nostrils were red. She blew out, long, and shook herself, so that the saddle rattled.

Then she began to walk. She did not wait for him. He had to wade beside her with his hand on the stirrup leather. She went up the slope of the bank and onto the crown of the road, and turned her face to the island, and went on.

The rest was a walk. The water shoaled. The rain had gone over and there was a moon somewhere, behind cloud. He could see the withies again, and after a while the porch lamp, small and steady, where it had always been.

He got up on her when it was to her knees. He had no strength left to walk.

They came up the ramp onto the Ness at twenty past twelve. He looked at his watch on the dry ground. He had been forty minutes in the sea.

There was an orchard. He remembered it. He slid off under the first trees and stood holding the saddle. He was shaking, in long hard spasms. His teeth would not stay shut. He had lost the feeling in his hands.

He sat down with his back to an apple tree and the reins round his wrist. He does not know for how long. He has said that it was the cold, that he could not have stood if the Vanes had come down through the orchard with dogs. When he could feel his fingers he tried to relight the lantern. It took nine matches. He had them in an oilskin pouch, inside his shirt, with the packet. When he looked at his watch by the flame it was twenty to one.

Then he led her through the orchard and along under the garden wall. He knew the way. He had come it a hundred times, twenty years ago, on summer nights, with his heart going like a hammer. He had not thought that his feet would remember. They did. They took him along the brick path, past the water butt, to the wide door at the end of the glasshouse where the gardeners had brought the tubs through.

It was there. It leaned on its hinges. The glass above it was mostly gone.

He put his shoulder to the door and it gave.

He backed the mare in. He was talking to her. He was telling her that it was done. He did not look round until he had her under the roof and had turned to shut out the wind.

There was a candle burning.

It stood on an upturned pot in the far corner. He knew that pot. Beside it there was a woman.

He has never told what he saw, in so many words. He would say, there was a woman there, in a grey dress. Then he would stop. The one who listened learned not to ask.

But once he said more. It was late, and he was old. He said that she was standing with her hands down at her sides, and bare arms, and her hair up, in a long gown the colour of rainwater. The candle was behind her. He could not see her face.

He said that he thought he had drowned.

He had heard of it. Men who had come near it in the big rivers told how it went easy, at the last, and you saw things. He thought that he had gone down in the Rill with the mare, and that this was what there was. It was a glasshouse with a vine in it, and Mrs Vane, who had died on that road twenty years ago trying to come to his father. She had been waiting, and had lit a candle.

He said her name. He said, Mrs Vane.

No, the woman said. Tom. It’s me.

She came forward. The light came round onto her face. There was a streak of white in her hair that had not been there. There were lines at her eyes. She was thin.

It was the girl who had held the lamp.

He does not tell what was said. He has been asked. He says that it was between the two of them and that it was a good while ago.

He says that she told him a thing she had carried for twenty years. It was the reason for a curtain. It was not the reason he had thought. He had gone to the other side of the world on account of the wrong one.

He says that he told her why he had come. He did not dress it. He had a gun on the saddle and she had seen it. She asked what it was for.

Vane, he said.

That is the word he gives. He will say that part. He says, I told her straight, I came for Vane. He says it as a thing that he wants known. He would not have her think afterwards that he had crossed that water for her and brought a gun along by chance.

What he said after that he does not say.

The one who set this down has heard another account of that hour. It was written by the woman, a long while later, in a book. In her account the man says something else as well. He says it at the end, after she has told him her part. She gives the words. They are not words that he would use, telling this. He was asked about it once, with the book open on the table.

He looked at the page for some time.

She’s put it better than I said it, he said. I never had that many words.

But did you say it?

I’d not have crossed that water for Edmund Vane, he said. Not when the mare took the bit. I’d turned her. I’ve told you. I was going home.

Then why do you always say you came for him?

Because I did. I got on her for that. I rode down that ramp for that. A man ought to say what he set out to do. What he found when he got there is another thing.

That was all he would give. He shut the book and went out to look at a ewe.

He will tell this much more.

She would not go with him then. He had asked her. He had said the mare could do it again at twenty to four, with the ebb, and he would have her at Saltcote by four. She said that she must go into the house first. There was a thing she had to say to her father, in front of the rest of them, at one o’clock by their clocks. She had sat in that glasshouse twenty years ago when she should have been in the hall. She would not go to him from behind a curtain a second time.

He understood that. He had come across the sea on much the same errand.

She asked him to leave the gun.

She asked it twice. She said that her brother laughed when he was frightened, and that the man did not know what he would do if he were laughed at. She said that he had a child.

He looked at it. It was on the saddle, where he had set the saddle down, on the edge of a stone trough. The case had fallen open. The candle was on the barrels.

He did not say that he would leave it. He would not say a thing he was not sure of. She saw that he did not.

He said that he would be there at two by her father’s clocks. That was three by his. He said if he was not, she was to get up on the mare and let her go home.

She went in. He watched her to the door. She went along the path in that grey gown with the wet of his coat on her shoulders, and she did not look round.

Then he was by himself. There was the mare, and the candle, and the rain on what was left of the glass.

He looked at his watch. It was a quarter to two.

He had been on the Ness an hour and twenty-five minutes. He had not once thought of the boat.

It came back to him like a blow. A quarter to two. That was the slack. That was the hour Ostler had named, in the public house, with four glasses in front of him. Top of the tide. A box and a passenger. At this minute, at the other end of the island, a launch would be lying against the Hythe with its engine turning. A big man with a hitch in his walk would be coming along the sea wall with a box.

He had come through seven feet of water to stand in front of that man. He had lost his hat and near enough his life. And then he had stood for an hour and a half in a glasshouse, holding a woman’s hands, and forgotten what he came for.

He was not sorry. He would not say that he was. But his father had held on six days in a chair for it.

He went to the trough. He stood over the saddle.

You’d not know what you were until you’d done it. And then you’d have to carry it.

She was right. He knew that she was right. He was a man who had carried a sheep half a mile that night rather than leave it.

He thought, I will go without. I’ll go along the wall with my hands empty and stand in his road and ask.

And he saw how it would be. He saw Vane stop, with the box in his arms, and look at him. He was hatless, and soaked, and smeared with marsh clay to the hair. He was the tenant’s son. Garrow. What the devil are you doing on the Ness? Get out of my way, man. I’ve a boat to catch. And he would shoulder by. He would go down the staging, and the engine would open up. And there would be nothing to do but stand and watch him go, as his father had stood on the ramp.

The man found that he could not do it. He could take the answer, whichever it was. He could not take being walked past.

He drew the gun out of its case. It was wet. He broke it and wiped the chambers with his thumb. He took the two cartridges out of his pocket. They were dry; he had had them in the oilskin with the matches.

He stood with them in his palm.

For her sake he ought to leave them. He could carry it empty. A man forty yards off cannot tell.

He thought of Vane, who had been to a school, looking at a gun held by a Garrow and knowing by something in the way it was held that there was nothing in it. He thought of the laugh.

He put them in. He closed the breech. It made a small sound, like a gate latch.

He was not going to use it. He said that to the mare. She had turned her head and was watching him with one dark eye, and the lantern in it.

I’ll be back, he said. You stand.

He blew out the candle on the pot. He left the lantern burning low for her. He went out of the wide door with the gun under his arm, into the wind, and turned north along the wall.

6. The Tower

The rain had stopped. The wind was dropping. There was a moon coming and going in the cloud, and by it he could see the top of the sea wall running north like a pale road.

He went along it fast. He had the gun in the crook of his arm with the muzzles down. On his left hand the tide lay right up to the stonework. It was full. He had never seen it so high. There was not a foot between the water and his boots, and it had stopped moving. It lay as still as milk in a pan.

That was the slack. He had shown it to a girl once from the other wall. It’s the tide thinking better of it.

He had ten minutes, if Ostler had told the truth. Perhaps less.

The wall bent. He came round the bend and he saw the light.

It was a white light, low, a lantern on a mast. There was the staging, running out on its piles, and at the end of it a launch lying. He could hear her engine. He stopped where the spinney came down to the wall, and got in among the thorns, and looked.

There were two men.

One was in the boat. He was standing in the stern with a line in his hand, in a long oilskin. That was Ostler; he knew the set of him. The other was on the staging. He stood with his feet apart and his back to the wall, bareheaded, in a raincoat, and the water was over his shoes.

The man in the thorns looked for a box. He looked for a hitch in the walk.

There was neither. The one on the staging was short and thick. He stood like a post. And the lantern was on his face, and it was not the face of Edmund Vane. It was the stranger who had read the tide board that morning, the one with the policeman’s shoes.

He did not understand it. He crouched with the gun across his knees and tried to make it come out.

Vane was to be here with a box. Instead there was the law, standing on the Hythe at the top of the tide, talking to the boatman. He could hear their voices. He could not hear words. The policeman said something short. Ostler answered him long.

So they had caught him. Or they were waiting to. Or the box had gone already and Vane with it, and this was what was left.

He had come too late. He had come through the Rill and stood in a glasshouse, and the law had got there first.

He ought to have been glad. A man who is taken by the police can be found again. He can be asked a question through a grille.

He was not glad. He found that he was angrier than he had been all night. It was not the policeman’s to do. That one had come in a town car that morning and read a board. He did not know what was owed. He had not knelt on a brick floor with a dying hand on his wrist.

He stayed where he was. He did not know what to do.

It was the boatman who saw it first. He put his head up, and looked past the man on the staging, back along the island. He said something and pointed.

The man in the thorns turned his head.

Behind him, over the dark of the spinney, the stable tower stood up against the sky. He could see the clock, a pale round, and above it the little pitched roof.

There was a light up there.

It was a lantern. Someone had it in his hand. It was swinging, slowly, from side to side, in a wide arc, like a man waving a train out of a station. It went three times across. It stopped. It went again.

He knew the tower. Every child in the village knew it. There were two wooden people up there who struck the bell. They called them Jack and Jenny. As a boy he had been lifted up on the wall at Saltcote to watch them through his father’s glass.

But there was a man up there now. Wooden people do not swing lamps.

He looked at the Hythe. The policeman had turned round. He was staring up at the tower with his mouth open. Ostler had the line half off the post.

And he understood.

It was a signal. It was to the boat. Vane was not at the Hythe; he was up there, forty feet over the yard, with a lamp, telling his boatman something. Wait. I’m coming. Or, Go; it’s off. He had seen the law on the staging and gone up where he could be seen from the water.

He was not taken. He was not gone. He was two hundred yards away, on top of his own stable, by himself.

The man got up out of the thorns. He went back through the spinney, running.

There was a track. He found it with his feet. It went by a mound with an iron gate standing open in the side of it, and a ring of keys hanging in the lock; he saw them shine and did not stop. It went up between the trees and a wall. The moon was out. He came round the end of the stable block onto cobbles.

He was in the yard.

It was a square of wet stone with buildings on three sides, and a mounting block, and at the far end the arch. The tower went up from beside the arch. He had never stood beneath it. He had not known that it was so high.

The house was behind him across the gravel. He did not look at it. He heard something there, a great door opening, and voices. He did not turn his head.

He was looking up.

The lantern was right over him. It hung out from under the little roof. It lit the bell, a green shape, and the beams. It lit a face.

It was a big face, white, with dark hair wet on the forehead. One side of it was wrong. There was a swelling over the eye, black, as large as a fist, and blood had run down from it and dried. The good eye was open and staring out toward the sea. The mouth hung.

He had not seen that face close in twenty years. He had seen it through a glass, on the Thursday, from a churchyard. He knew it.

Vane, he said.

It did not carry. He filled his chest.

VANE.

The face turned. The lantern came round with it and the light fell down the front of the tower into the yard, and onto him.

He stood in it. He had the gun in his two hands, across his body. He was hatless and caked with clay to the eyes, and the sea was still running out of his coat.

Who’s that?

It was a thick voice. It slurred, like a man talking in his sleep.

Garrow.

Who?

Tom Garrow. From Saltcote. You looked at me Thursday through a glass.

There was a silence. The lantern swayed. Up in the works of the clock something had begun to whirr.

Garrow, the voice said. Good God. It laughed. It was a short broken sound. How did you get over? You can’t have got over. There’s six feet on the road.

I swum it.

You swam the Rill? At the flood? Then you’re a bigger fool than I am. The lantern dipped. He’s swum the Rill, Ma. Did you hear that? Old Amos’s boy. He’s come for his rent.

The man in the yard did not know who was being spoken to. There was nobody up there with him.

I’ve a thing to ask you, he said.

Not now.

It’s from my father. He’s dead. He held on a week to give it to me.

Not now, man. Can’t you see I’m busy? I’ve a boat. I’ve to tell the boat— The voice lost its way. It came back loud and angry and frightened. You’ve no business here. This is the Ness. Get off my land.

It’s your father’s land.

Get off it! You’ve no land. You’ve none. Fenn’s sent the paper. Go home to your bloody sheep.

He laughed again. It went on. It rang down the tower into the yard.

It was the laugh she had told him of. It’s what he does when he’s frightened. He knew that. He had been told an hour ago, by a woman holding his sleeve. He had the knowledge in his head, and it did him no good. He stood in that yard at the foot of forty feet of brick. He had carried a ewe through the tide for that family’s rent. His father was four days in the ground. And he was being laughed at from a height by the man who had put them off.

He felt his hands close on the gun.

Was she coming or was she going, he shouted.

The laughing stopped.

My father stood on our wall with a lamp. He see her light come three parts over. He see yours go after. He stood an hour. And hers turned back. He never knew which it was. He’s laid awake on it twenty year. Did she turn of herself? Or did you turn her?

There was no answer. The lantern had gone still. The face above it looked down at him, with its one eye, and it had changed. It was not laughing. It was open, like a wound.

You tell me, the man said. You’ll tell me now. I’ve come through the sea for it.

The whirring in the tower had grown. There was a clank.

And the small bell began to ring.

It rang over his head, sharp, two notes together, and again. He had heard it across the water all his boyhood, thin, like a bird. He had never stood under it. It was as loud as an anvil.

Something moved beside Vane.

It was on his left, on the near side of the bell. It had been in the dark behind the lantern. Now it came forward to the edge of the roof. It was a man. It was a man in a black coat with a white front. He stood straight up at Vane’s shoulder, close, and the light caught him.

He lifted his arm.

He lifted it from the shoulder, stiff, with a thing in his fist. He swung it up and over, and brought it down, straight out, toward the yard.

The man below saw it come. It had a head on it, dark, and a long handle. It came down and pointed at his chest.

He had thought that Vane was alone.

There were two of them. There had been a second man up there the whole while, in the dark, in evening clothes, saying nothing. He had stood and let Vane talk. And now he had stepped out with a thing in his hand and levelled it.

The arm went up again. It came down.

The big bell struck.

It struck once. The whole yard shook with it. It went through the man’s feet and up into his teeth. In the same moment the lantern swung, and the two shapes up there ran together, the white face and the black coat, so that he could not tell one from the other. There was only something tall, leaning out over him, with its arm stretched down, and metal at the end of the arm.

He did not think. He has said so, and he says it without excuse. He had been twenty years in a country where a man who sees a thing levelled at him from above does not stop to ask what it is.

The gun came up. He did not feel it come. It was at his shoulder, and his cheek was on the wood where his father’s had been.

Vane stood up on the tower with something levelled and the man shot him off it. Both barrels. He watched him go down into the fleet.

He will tell exactly what he saw. He has gone over it enough.

The first barrel took the black coat full in the chest. He saw the white front go. The figure jerked. It did not double; it went rigid, all of a piece, and rocked back.

The second he fired before the first had done kicking. It went a little left, and high.

The lantern flew up. It turned over in the air, and fell, straight down the face of the tower, and struck the cobbles at his feet and went out.

By the last of it he saw the man fall.

He went backward. He went slowly, with his arms out from his sides, like a tree that has been cut through and takes its time. There was a moment when he lay on the air, stiff, with his white front to the sky. Then he had gone over the far side, where the tower stood on the creek.

There was a sound from down there. It was a flat hard slap, like a plank dropped on water.

And then nothing. There was the smoke, hanging. There was the ringing in his ears. Above him, under the little roof, in the moonlight, something tall and grey stood on the other side of the bell with its arm raised.

That was the wooden woman. He looked at her. She was looking over his head, at the house.

There was nobody else up there at all.

He broke the gun. The two cases jumped out and rolled on the stones. He bent and picked them up and put them in his pocket. He does not know why. A man who has shot rabbits all his life picks up his empties.

He went under the arch.

He had to feel his way. It came out at the back of the stables on a strip of grass, and below the grass was the fleet. He knew it. It was a ditch at low water. It was full now, twenty feet across and black, and it had begun to move. The slack was over. The whole length of it was sliding north, smooth, toward the wall and the sea.

He stood on the bank. He looked down at the foot of the tower.

There was nothing there. He looked along the water. The moon came out. Forty yards down, going away, in the middle of the stream, there was something long and dark. It lay low. It turned as it went. He saw a white cuff.

He started along the bank after it. He ran ten yards. There was a brick sluice where the fleet went out under the sea wall, and he saw the thing reach the arch, and check, and go under.

He stopped.

He could hear the water on the other side, falling into the saltings. It was the ebb. It would take whatever went through that arch out over the flats and down the river, to the sea.

He stood with the gun open over his arm.

He had killed Edmund Vane.

He put it to himself in those words, on the bank. He made himself say them. He had come over to ask a question and carry a gun for show. He had loaded it, in a glasshouse, with a woman’s voice still in his ears telling him not to. He had stood in a yard and been laughed at. And when something moved up there that he did not understand, he had let go both barrels at a man.

He had not got his answer. He would never get it now. The one man living who knew what had happened on the Wade was gone down a creek on his face. His father had held on six days for nothing.

And there was the other one. The one in the black coat, who had stepped out with a thing in his hand. Where was he? He had seen only one fall. The tower was empty. He stood and tried to think, and could not make it come. There had been two shapes, and a lantern, and they had run together. He had fired at what was pointed at him. One man had gone over.

He does not know to this day how many were on that tower. He has been told a number of things. He knows what he shot at. He knows whose face was in the lantern. He knows what went through the sluice.

He never asked the question. That is what he says, when he comes to this. He says, I’d come through the sea to ask a man one thing, and I shot him before he could tell me.

He went back into the yard. He stood in the middle of it, on the cobbles, in the moonlight, by the mounting block.

He was waiting to be taken.

He had fired a twelve-bore twice within eighty yards of a house full of people. The front door of that house was open. He could see straight into the hall from where he stood. It was all lit up with candles, like a church. There were figures moving. A woman had cried out; he had heard it between the shots. There was a policeman on the island.

They would come. They would come across that gravel with lamps. He would hand over the gun, stock first, and say what he had done.

He thought of the child. She would wake in the morning under Vi Pask’s thatch, and somebody would have to tell her. He thought of the woman in the grey dress. She was in that hall now. She had asked him twice.

He stood. He kept his eyes on the door.

Nobody came.

He could not understand it. He counted. He counted to five hundred. He saw a tall old man standing in the doorway, with white hair, quite still, looking toward the tower. A small woman stood beside him. Then the old man turned, and went in. The doorway was empty.

He heard a voice in there. It was a young man’s, loud, and cheerful. He caught one word. He thought it was ice.

Somebody laughed.

He stood in the yard for a quarter of an hour by his watch. In that time nobody put a foot outside the house. Nobody called. There was only the light, and the voices going on, mild and easy, like people at their supper.

And then there was music.

It came thin across the gravel. It was a fiddle tune, slow, and sweet as treacle, off a gramophone. He knew the kind. They had played such at the harvest suppers when he was small, for the old people.

It was a waltz.

He stood with his dead man’s blood on his hands, as he thought it, and listened to the Vanes dance.

He has said that it was the strangest quarter hour of his life. He was more afraid in it than he had been in the Rill. In the water he had only been going to drown. Here he had done murder, in the open, with noise. And the house had looked out, and seen, and gone back to its party.

He thought, they know. That was the old man in the door. He saw his son fall. And he turned and went in and called for a tune.

He thought of twenty years of rent, paid to those people, in notes, with a cap in the hand. He had thought them hard. He had not thought them that.

He did not understand then about the house. He was never in it. He did not know that it kept its own hour and its own rules. He knows now that there were eleven people in that hall and that only two of them had been looking out of the door. One was a nurse who thought she had seen a ghost, and the other was an old man who thought he had been paid a debt. He has been told so since, by one who has read what they wrote.

It makes no odds. He stood in the yard, and nobody came. A man who is ready to be taken and is not finds that he has nowhere to put himself.

He looked up, once more, at the tower.

She was there. The wooden woman. She had her arm lifted. The moon was on her painted face. She was looking down the length of the yard, over his head, through the open door, at the hall where they were dancing.

He thought that she had seen it all. He thought, she’s the only one that has.
