It is held to that figure with great strictness by the generating authority, since the cheap electric clocks in people’s kitchens count the cycles and would otherwise go wrong. That is to say, every wire in my walls was carrying, all that evening, a pulse regulated to the false time. I had not considered it. I am not an electrician. But when the lamps went out, I felt something go out of the house with them, a kind of hum that I had not known was there. Everything that was left going under my roof was now driven by a spring or a weight and kept the true hour.

I thought, that is better. That is as it was in Thorne’s day. Now there is nothing in this house to interfere.

The boy finished the piece in the dark. He has his grandmother’s nerve.

§ 31. It was then that I had the third leakage of that day, and the longest.

I heard the music end. I opened my eyes. The room was lit.

It was lit by the old lamps, with the pink shades, that my wife had got rid of in about 1960. There was a different paper on the walls. Edmund was at the piano. He was a boy of thirteen, in a grey flannel suit, with his hair wetted down, and he had just played the Schubert through for the first time without a fault, before company. He was looking across the room at his mother, and not at me.

She was upon the sofa. She had the grey silk on. She was being painted in it that winter. She put down her coffee cup and clapped her hands. She said, ‘Oh, well done! Leo, did you hear him? He never dropped a note.’

I was standing by the fire. I was forty-two. I heard myself answer her. I had forgotten that I ever said it. I said, ‘The left hand was a little hurried in the middle section.’

I saw his face. I had not seen it at the time; I do not see faces. But I was looking at it now, from the place where I had stood, with eighty-one years behind my eyes, and I saw exactly what went out of it.

And I saw her look at me. It was not anger. She looked at me as she did when I had taken the gallery clock down for the fourth time. Then she got up. She said, ‘I’m going up, darlings. I’m going to take my shoes off and read for half an hour, and come down for the Hour.’ She put her hand on the boy’s head as she passed.

She went out of the door. I watched her go. I saw the grey silk go round the edge of it.

Then the lamps were gone. There was firelight, and my grandson sitting at the piano with his hands between his knees, a young man of twenty-four.

I said, ‘Thank you, Kit.’ I said it to him as I ought to have said it to his father, thirty-nine years before.

And I said that she had gone up. I am told that it caused some pain. I said that she always went up after the Schubert, and took her shoes off, and came down for the Hour. I asked Imogen whether she had seen her go.

I had seen her go. I had that moment watched her leave the room. I was not confused as to the year. I knew that it was 1994. But I had been in 1955 an instant before, and the door had not finished closing.

I took it for a sign. I thought, the engine is drawing. It is five hours before the stroke, and already the house is letting me through.

Imogen said that she had seen her. She said that she was a little tired.

§ 32. I slept, I think. I am very old and had been upon my feet since six in the morning.

I do not know for how long. I have no record of that interval and shall not invent one. I was aware of people moving. I was aware that Miss Quaile was by me, and then that she was not.

I was woken by a hand.

It was upon my left shoulder. It rested there. It was a large hand, and warm, and it did not press. It lay for the space of perhaps two beats of the mantel clock, and was lifted.

I knew whose it was without opening my eyes. I should know the weight of that hand anywhere. I had it in mine upon the file, to guide it, every day for six years.

I opened them. He was going from me toward the door. I saw his back.

I have said that I do not read faces. But he turned, at the door, to say something to the room; he said that he was going to look at the generator. And for that moment the firelight was upon his face, and I saw it.

I have seen that face twice before. I saw it when he was eleven, and had taken a watch of mine to pieces without leave and could not put it together, and stood outside the Shop for an hour before he came in to say so. And I saw it upon the morning of the twenty-seventh of October, 1974, at the breakfast table, when he came down in dry clothes and said that he had slept in the stable.

It is the face of a man who is going to do a thing that he is ashamed of.

He went out. I heard his step in the passage. He has had that step since he was fourteen and hurt his knee.

I looked at the clock upon the mantel. It was half past eleven.

I thought: he is not going to wait for the Hour.

And I thought: it is tonight that he means to take the Thorne.

§ 33. I got up out of my chair. No one prevented me. Miss Quaile was gone; I did not know where. My daughter had been in the window and was not there. The solicitor was asleep. Dame Octavia Prowse was asleep, with her mouth open, as she has slept in that chair after dinner since about 1950.

I went into the hall.

I am going to describe exactly what I did there, and why, since it has a bearing upon what followed and I have been asked about it.

The regulator stands to the left of the fire. It is by Benjamin Vulliamy, of the year 1810, a plain month-going movement in a mahogany case, with a dead-beat escapement and a mercury pendulum. It is the master clock of the house within doors. I set all the others by it, and it by the tower.

I opened the case. I stopped the pendulum with my hand. I unhooked the weight.

I had two reasons, and I held them both at once, and I cannot now say which came first.

The one was scientific. I had been considering all that day what would occur at the instant of reversal. If the hour was returned, and I passed through it a second time, then every clock in this house would be asked to register the same sixty minutes twice. I did not know what a fine movement would do under those conditions. A turret clock is a coarse thing and would take no harm. But I did not care to have a Vulliamy regulator, upon which the whole house depends, put through an hour that it had already counted. It seemed to me a prudent thing to take the power off the master clock for the period of the transit, and restore it afterward.

The other was older. One stops the clocks in a house where there has been a death. My mother went round and did it when my father died, with a feather, as her mother had. I did it for my wife. The pendulums are held, and the weights are taken off, and they are not let go again until after the burying.

I stood in my hall with fourteen pounds of lead in my hand, upon its line, and I did not know why I should have thought of that.

I have said that I cannot now tell which reason came first. I must be more honest than that. I think that I knew. I think that when I saw my son’s face at the drawing-room door, some part of me that keeps the count had already reckoned what was to come of that night, and had sent my hand to the clock, as one sends for the undertaker.

But I had not then reckoned what it would be. I supposed, if I supposed anything, that the death was mine. I am eighty-one. I thought that the experiment might very well kill me.

I did not put the weight down. I ought to have set it in the bottom of the case. I had it by the loop of its line, and I had turned from the clock already, toward the gunroom passage and the side door, and it came with me in my hand. I was thinking of my son. I was thinking that he had gone out to the yard, and that it was dark, and that I must find him before he did the thing.

I carried it out of the house as a man carries his umbrella.

It was twenty minutes to twelve. Every clock in the hall but one said so.

IV. The First Passage

§ 34. I come to the part of this relation which I should prefer not to dictate. Miss Quaile has offered to leave it out. I have told her that a paper from which the experimenter omits the observations that he dislikes is of no value to anyone.

I went out by the side door. It was blowing hard from the south-west, with rain. I had no hat nor coat. I did not feel the cold; I record that as a fact, since at my age I ordinarily feel it very much.

There was a lamp ahead of me. It was some sixty yards off, low down, going along the front of the stable range, and it rose and fell with a motion that I knew. I followed it. I had no light of my own and did not want one. I have crossed that yard in the dark to wind the tower upon every night for sixty years.

The lamp went round the end of the stables and down the track to the home copse. It turned in among the trees.

I knew then where he had put it. There is an ice house in that copse, which my great-grandfather built; a brick chamber, sunk in the ground, with a domed roof and twelve steps down. We have kept ice in it within my memory. It is a place that no one visits from November to June. It has an iron gate with a spring lock that fastens of itself.

The gate stood open. There was a light within.

§ 35. I went in. I did not go stealthily. I am told that I must have, since he did not hear me; but it was only that the wind was loud and that I was wearing my evening pumps, which have thin soles.

He was upon the landing at the head of the steps. He had set his lamp upon the floor. He had a box in his arms, a tea chest, and was in the act of lifting it; he had it against his chest and his chin upon the lid. He was swaying. I saw at once that he was more than drunk. His eyes were not right. They were dull, and the lids hung, and when he saw me he was a long moment in understanding who I was.

‘Father,’ he said.

It was said without surprise. He might have been a boy at the bench, looking up.

I said, ‘Edmund. It was you.’

‘Of course it was me.’ His speech was thick. He leaned his shoulder upon the brick to keep upright. ‘Who else in this house could have done it? Who else knows a Knibb from a Quare? You taught nobody else. You hadn’t the patience.’

I looked at the box. The lid had been corded down, but one corner of a blanket showed, and under the blanket a glint of brass.

‘What have you there?’

‘You know what I have. You told the whole table. One of you has been robbing me. Well, here he is, at it.’ He laughed. It was not a pleasant sound. ‘It’s the last one, Father. I give you my word. After this there’s nothing left in the house worth the trouble.’

‘That is the Thorne.’

‘That’s the Thorne.’

‘It is thirty-one pounds, in that box, and you are carrying it down an ice house in the dark, with a bad knee, and you can hardly stand.’

‘I’m not carrying it down. I’m carrying it out. I put it here to wait.’ He shifted his grip. ‘There’s a boat. You needn’t know about the boat. I’ll be gone by two, and you can tell Fenn’s policeman that it was Edmund, and he may put it in his book.’

§ 36. I must set down my own state of mind, as far as I can recover it.

I was not angry. I wish to be exact. I have been asked whether I struck him in anger, and I have considered the question, and the answer is that I do not believe so. I had expected it to be he. I had seen his hand at dinner. I had come out into the rain with one purpose, which was to ask him a question that I had been carrying for the best part of a year.

So I asked it. I said, ‘Why?’

I said it quite quietly. I had thought a great deal about how it should be said.

I think that he had expected something else. I think he had expected me to speak of the police, or to order him back to the house. He looked at me over the top of the box. For a moment his face was that of the boy who had stood outside the Shop with the watch in pieces.

‘Why,’ he said. ‘You want to know why.’

‘I have wanted it since September. I had rather know that than have them back.’

‘Because I owe a man in Southend a hundred and eighty thousand pounds. There. That’s why. Because the sea wall wanted mending in 1988, and there was no money, and I borrowed it. And then I borrowed more to pay that. I’m no good with money, Father. I’m no good with anything. You’ve had twenty years to notice.’

‘You might have come to me.’

‘Come to you?’ He stared. ‘When did anyone ever come to you? You were in the cellar. You’ve been in the cellar since 1948. Mother used to say that if the house burned down you’d come up to ask who had altered the temperature.’

‘I should have given it you. I should have sold whatever was needed.’

‘I know you would. That’s the damnable thing. You’d have looked at me through that glass, and said, “I expect you wanted it,” and written a cheque. And you’d not have asked one question. Not why did the wall want mending. Not why have you been drunk since you were thirty-two. Not what is the matter with my son.’ His voice had risen. ‘Do you know what it is to live for fifty years in a house with a man who can hear a clock losing two seconds a week?’

I did not answer. I was holding the weight by its line. I felt it turn a little, in the draught.

§ 37. I put down what was next said as nearly as I can. It is the centre of the matter.

I said, ‘Edmund, put that box down. You will fall. Come up to the house and we shall talk of it in the Hour. I said so at dinner. I said that whoever it was might come to me and it would not be held against him. I meant you. I knew that it was you.’

‘The Hour.’ He laughed again. ‘God. The Hour. Mother’s parlour game. Do you know what she made it for?’

‘For the family.’

‘For you. She made it for you. So that once in the year there’d be sixty minutes when somebody might be able to get a word through that skull. And in twenty-three years you never asked her anything in it. You danced with her. I used to watch you. You’d waltz her round the hall with your eyes shut, counting, and she’d look over your shoulder at the rest of us, and her face—’ He stopped. He shook his head, as a horse shakes off a fly. ‘Never mind her face.’

‘I’ll ask you now. I am asking you. Why did you take them? Not the money. I have had that. Why mine? Why did you put my copies in their places?’

He looked down at the box in his arms.

I shall always remember how he looked at it. It was with a kind of hatred. I have seen a man look so at a tool that had cut him.

‘Because nobody would know the difference,’ he said. ‘That’s all. That’s the joke. I took your Tompion and stood your own copy in the case, and you wound it for a year. I took the Knibb. I took East. I’d lie awake waiting for you to come down to breakfast and say, “Edmund, somebody has been at the bracket clock.” You never did. You walked past your own work every day and took it for the real thing.’

‘I knew it in September.’

‘After three years! Three years, Father!’ He was shouting now. ‘I thought, he’ll see it. He must see it. He’s the best eye in England. He’ll look at that dial and know it’s his own hand, and he’ll come to me. He’ll have to speak to me then. And you never looked.’

I said, ‘Then you wished to be found.’

He did not answer that. He said the other thing. I have gone over it every night since.

‘It’s a copy, you old fool,’ he said. ‘Don’t you understand yet? They’re all copies. There’s nothing in this house that isn’t a copy of something. You made forty-three of them down there, and then you made me, to hold the file. A copy of you, that was the idea. Only it came out wrong. It would serve, though. Wouldn’t it? You said so. It will serve.’

§ 38. I said, ‘That was unjust of me. I have known it for some time.’

I do not think that he heard. He had gone on. He was no longer speaking to me; he was speaking to the box, or to the dark at the bottom of the steps.

‘You never knew anything. You sat down there with your glass in your eye and you never knew one thing that went on over your head. You never knew about the money. You never knew about Celia. You never knew about her.’

‘About whom?’

‘Ask the girl.’ He jerked his head toward the house. ‘Ask your nurse. The little white one who tells you the truth. She’s got it in her pocket. She found it in the clock. The one clock in the house you were told not to open, and you never did, in twenty years, because you’d given your word. God, you’re a wonder. You’d keep your word to a dead woman and not hear a living one.’

I did not follow him. I asked what Miss Quaile had in her pocket.

‘It’s all there. In Mother’s writing. Where she was going that night, and who to. You’ll like the handwriting; it’s very regular.’ He swayed, and caught himself. ‘She was leaving you, Father. She’d had enough. She was fifty-four and she was walking out of this house to a man with sheep on him, because he used to look up when she came into a yard.’

I said, ‘I know that.’

It stopped him.

‘I have known it since about 1980,’ I said. ‘I did not allow myself to know it. But I am not so great a fool as you think me. A woman doesn’t cross the Wade at two in the morning, in her stockings, to post a letter.’

He stared at me. His mouth was open.

‘It makes no difference,’ I said. ‘She was entitled to go. I ask you to understand that. I should not have stopped her. It is not the going that I cannot forgive myself. It is that she went by my clock. I had put it back that afternoon. She looked at the regulator, and it told her that she had an hour that she had not got. I killed her with a clock, Edmund. That is what I have had to carry. Whoever she was walking to.’

And my son laughed.

It was the worst sound that I have heard in my life. It went round the dome of that chamber. He put his head back against the bricks and laughed until he choked.

‘The clock,’ he said. ‘Oh, my God. The clock. Twenty years. You’ve turned the whole house into a tomb for it. A hundred and eleven of them, all an hour slow, and you going round every week with the key.’ He wiped his mouth upon his shoulder. ‘It was never the clock. Do you hear me? It was never the bloody clock. She knew what time it was. She always knew what time it was. She was the only one of us that did.’

§ 39. I have asked myself what he meant to say next. I believe that he meant to tell me. He had it in his mouth. He told me two hours afterward, in the tower, and it was the same breath going on.

He did not get it said. I prevented him.

I must describe my hand.

I had the regulator weight by the loop of its line. The line is of gut, about eighteen inches of it, with the brass loop at the end, and I had the loop over my right forefinger. The weight hung at the height of my knee. It is a cylinder of lead in a brass jacket. I had carried it across the yard without knowing that I carried it.

When he laughed, I felt it move.

I am going to state this as accurately as I can, since it is the observation on which everything turns, and I have no witness to it but a child, of whom more presently.

I did not decide to strike him. I am certain of that. I have decided a great many things in my life, and I know what the act of deciding is like. One weighs. There was no weighing.

But neither will I say that I did not do it. That would be a coward’s way. It was my arm. He laughed, and said that it was never the clock, and something went through me that I can only compare to the letting-go of a mainspring that has been held wound for twenty years. I had built my life upon that clock. I had stopped the house for it. It was all the reason that I had. He was telling me that I had been mistaken, and he was laughing.

My arm came up. It came from the shoulder. The weight swung out upon its line, in an arc, as a pendulum swings. I have set ten thousand pendulums going with that same motion of the wrist. It took him upon the left side of the brow, above the eye.

It did not make a great noise. It was a small flat sound, like a mallet upon a wedge.

He stopped laughing. He looked at me. I saw surprise in his face, and nothing else. His arms opened. The box went first; it dropped from him, and struck the edge of the landing, and went over. I heard it go down the steps, striking each one.

Then he went. He did not put out his hands. He went backward, quite slowly, and his heel missed the top step, and he fell the length of the stair. There are twelve. I heard every one.

At the bottom there was a sound of something heavy coming to rest in straw. Then there was none.

§ 40. The lamp was still upon the landing. I took it up and held it over the well.

He lay upon his back at the foot of the steps. His legs were upon the lowest three and his head was lower than his feet. One arm was out. His face was toward me. His eyes were open. They did not move when the light came upon them.

There was blood upon his forehead. It was running back into his hair.

I said his name. I said it several times.

I am a man of exact habits. I looked for the signs. I watched his chest, under the shirt front, for as long as it took me to count sixty. I could not see that it rose. I listened. There was water dripping from the ice, into a pool, with a clear sound, at intervals of about two seconds. I heard that. I heard nothing else.

I did not go down. I should say so. I ought to have gone down those steps and put my hand upon him. I could not. They are steep and without a rail, and I am eighty-one, and I had the lamp in one hand and the weight in the other. But that is not the reason. The reason is that I knew what I should find. I had seen my wife. I knew how they look.

I stood upon the landing. I looked at my watch. I do not carry one; I looked at the place upon my wrist where I wore one as a young man. Then I recollected that I had passed the hall clocks as I came out, and I reckoned the minutes from there.

At ten minutes to twelve by every clock in my house I killed my son.

I set that down as an observation. It is entered here in its place, with the time. I do not qualify it.

§ 41. The lamp went out in my hand as I turned. There is a great draught through that passage with the gate open. I set it down upon the landing, dead, and felt my way out by the wall. I have been sorry since that I left him in the dark.

I came out through the passage. At the gate I turned and pulled it to behind me. It shut, and I heard the lock drop. I had no intention in it. One always shuts that gate; I have told the servants so for fifty years; the ice wastes if the air gets to it.

I had the weight in my hand. I held it up, under the trees. There was something upon it that was not rain.

I walked back up the track. I was thinking, quite clearly, of one thing. I was thinking that I must fetch Margot. She would know what was to be done. She had always known, with Edmund. When he was small and had hurt himself he would not let me near him; he would stand and bleed until she came.

I came round the end of the stables into the yard.

There was a child there.

She was standing against the wall of the stable, at the corner, in the rain. She was a small girl, of nine or ten, with dark hair, wet, and a pale face. She had on a coat that was too large for her. She was quite still. She was looking at me, and at what I had in my hand.

I took her for Imogen. Imogen at that age had just such a way of standing at the edge of a thing and watching it, with her head a little on one side. She would come down to the Shop and stand in the door for an hour, and I would forget that she was there.

I said, ‘Go in, Immy. You will catch cold.’

The child did not answer. She looked at me a moment longer. I have not forgotten her eyes. They were very large and they were not afraid of me. They were afraid for somebody.

Then she turned and ran. She ran toward the house, along the grass, and I lost her in the dark.

I have considered that child a good deal. I was not at that moment leaking; of that I am sure; the rain was upon my face and I had the weight in my hand. And yet Imogen is a woman of forty-four. There has been no child in this house since she went to school. I have asked Mrs Pask, who tells me that I was dreaming. I have asked Miss Quaile, who looked at me strangely and said that she did not know.

I record her as an anomaly. I shall return to her under the results.

§ 42. I came in by the side door. I walked the length of the gunroom passage and into the hall.

Someone had laid the vicar upon the settle. I did not ask why.

I went to the regulator. I opened the case. It seemed to me a matter of the first importance that the weight should be hung again upon its line. A regulator must not be left without its weight; the line will take a set. I had the loop in my fingers and I could not find the hook. My hands were shaking. I had never seen them do it. I stood and looked at them as one looks at a tool that has failed.

Miss Quaile came down the stairs with a lamp.

She took the weight from me and hung it. I told her to leave the pendulum stopped. I told her that one stops the clocks.

And I told her what I had done.

I shall not repeat the conversation; she has it in her own account, I believe, and it will be more accurate than mine. I told her the place, and the time, and the number of the steps. She did not believe me at first. Then she looked at my cuff.

She wished to go to him. She said that he might be alive. She was very urgent.

I would not let her. I am ashamed of it. I took hold of her and would not let her go. But I ask the reader to see how it stood with me.

It was ten minutes past twelve. I had killed my son twenty minutes before. And in fifty minutes, by every clock in that hall, the hour was to be returned.

I had built the engine for my wife. I had set it to a night twenty years gone. And I saw, standing there with the girl’s wrists in my hands, that I had been a fool. I had not understood what I was making. I had thought that I should be given back an hour of 1974. But the take-up does not know one year from another. It takes up the hour that is going by. It would give me back this one. The hour between twelve and one, upon the night of the twenty-second of October, 1994, in which I had gone out to the ice house.

I should pass through it again. I should come again to that landing. And I should not lift my arm.

I said this to Miss Quaile. I said that it did not signify. I said that he was dead, and that in fifty minutes he would not be, and that she must on no account leave me, since I should want a witness.

She said that it could not be done. She had said so in the tower. She pulled her hands away. She took up the lamp. She said, ‘I must.’

§ 43. Here there is an interval of which I have no record.

I am told that I fell. Miss Quaile says that I lay upon the floor of the hall for some twenty-five minutes, insensible, with my lips blue, and that she knelt by me and counted my pulse, and could not leave me.

I have no recollection of falling, nor of the floor. I was standing by the regulator, and she had turned from me toward the passage. Then I was in a chair, and the candles had been lit, and she was kneeling beside it asking whether I knew where I was.

I knew where I was. I did not at once know what had happened. It had gone. I looked at my wet shoes and could not account for them. I asked whether I had been out. She said that I had been to the ice house. I asked what for.

She looked at me. She is a truthful person. I saw her prepare to tell me.

And she did not. She said, ‘You didn’t say.’

I knew that it was a lie. I have told her since that I knew. One cannot live with a truthful person for three weeks and fail to mark the first time that she is not. I thought, she is sparing me something. I did not ask what. I was very tired, and I had the Hour before me.

I have considered that interval with care, as bearing upon the experiment.

The physicians would call it a faint. I do not say that they are wrong. I had been out in a gale, at my age, and had had a shock.

But I note the following. It began at about a quarter past twelve. It lasted until twenty minutes to one. During it I was absent from the house, in the sense that nothing reached me. And when I came out of it, I had lost the preceding hour. I did not know that I had been to the ice house. I did not know that I had struck my son. It had been wiped from me as one wipes a slate.

I submit that this is what one would expect.

If an hour is to be gone through a second time, the man who goes through it cannot carry with him the memory of the first. Else it would not be the same hour; he would be a different man in it. The engine had forty-five minutes still to run before the stroke. But a spring begins to draw before it is released. I believe that what Miss Quaile observed upon the floor of the hall was the first motion of the take-up. I was being made ready. The hour that I had lived was being taken off me, so that I might be given it again clean.

I put that forward as a hypothesis only. I am aware that there is a simpler one.

But I ask the reader to hold it in mind against what follows. For at one o’clock I stood at my door with no knowledge that I had killed my son. And at ten minutes to two, I found him alive.

V. The Reversal

§ 44. At five minutes to one I took my place at the door.

I state my condition at that moment, as the experimenter should. I was weak; I had been upon the floor, they said, and my legs were not sure. But my head was as clear as it has been in ten years. I knew the date and the hour. I knew what I had built in the tower and to what I had set it. I knew that my wife had been dead twenty years, since I had been told so that morning.

I did not know that I had been out of the house. I did not know that there was a man lying in the ice house with his head broken. I record that with emphasis. Whatever else may be said of what followed, I went into it with no knowledge of the thing that I afterward found undone.

Miss Quaile stood at my left hand. I had asked it of her. The family were behind us in the hall, with the candles. I did not turn to count them.

I put my hand upon the bolt.

§ 45. The clocks struck one. I listened to each. I have listened to them every hour for sixty years and I know their voices as a shepherd knows his ewes. The Knibb upon the stairs is always first; she runs a little fast in damp weather. The Tompion by the door is last, and takes his time.

They were two short, I noticed. The Knibb did not speak, nor the Tompion. I had forgotten that those were among the eleven. What stood in their cases were of my own making, and my copies have never had the tone.

When they had done, I said, ‘Now.’ I drew the bolt and opened both leaves.

I have described the sensation that I have had at that door upon twenty nights: that something passed, outside, in the dark, going by.

It did not pass.

I am going to describe what I felt as plainly as I can, and I shall not dress it. The night came in, and the wind, and laid the candles over. That was the same. But there was besides a kind of pressure. It came across the gravel from the tower, and it came to the step, and it stopped there. I felt it upon my face and my chest, as one feels the heat of a fire that has been opened. It was not heat. It was not anything that I have a name for. It was large, and it had been travelling, and it had arrived.

I said, ‘Come in, then. You are late. You have been late since the last Sunday in March.’

I spoke to it as to a person. I did not know how else.

And it came in. I felt it go by me into the house, on either side, as a tide comes round a post. I felt the hall fill. Behind me a hundred clocks were ticking, and I had the distinct impression that for the space of two or three beats they hesitated, every one, and then went on.

§ 46. I looked at the tower. I had meant to watch the Jacks; they are coupled to the going train, and I wished to see whether the striking would be affected.

There was a light upon the leads. Someone was up there with a lantern. I was not surprised. It seemed to me only reasonable that at such a moment there should be a light at the top of the engine.

The quarters rang. Then Jenny brought down her arm, and the great bell struck one.

Upon the stroke there were two reports, close together, from the foot of the tower. I took them for the take-up. A fusee that is wound suddenly hard will sometimes crack like a whip. I thought, it has caught. It has taken the load.

The lantern fell. And something fell after it.

It was the figure of a man. He was upon the left of the bell. He went backward off the leads, stiffly, with his arms spread, and was gone behind the roof.

I saw it quite clearly. Miss Quaile saw it also; she cried out.

I did not cry out. I had expected something of the kind. I had not known what form it would take; but I have said already that I do not believe a thing can be had for nothing. An hour was being given to this house which the house had not lent. It stood to reason that something must be taken in exchange. I had wondered all the autumn what it would be.

I said, ‘Ah. Yes. I thought there would be something to pay.’

I took it at the time for the Jack. He stands upon that side, and he has been loose upon his pin for fifty years. I thought, the engine has taken the Jack. It is a fair price. He is two hundred years old and has done his work, and he never kept good time.

I told Miss Quaile to say nothing to the others. I did not think that they would understand the accounts.

I have had to revise that entry since. I shall come to it.

§ 47. I turned from the door. I had the hour. I had felt it come in. It remained to see what it would do.

There now occurred a thing which I did not at the time understand, and which I have since come to regard as the first piece of positive evidence.

A young man came into the hall from the kitchen passage. It was Dorothea’s grandson. He was carrying a wooden box with tin corners. He said something that I did not catch; he seemed to think that it was the ice. He set it upon the table and cut the cord, and took out, from a blanket, a clock.

It was the Copy. I knew it across the room. I went and put my glass upon it. There was no device beneath the dial foot. The moon work had been jarred off its cock, as it will be if the movement is laid upon its side, and it had stopped.

I said, ‘Ah. The Copy. I wondered where I had put it.’

That was the truth. I did wonder. I had set that clock under the glass in the library window, in September, with my own hands. I could not conceive how it came to be in a box, in a blanket, in the arms of a young man who thought that it was a pudding.

I asked him no questions. It did not then seem important. I thanked him, and said that we had been promised an ice.

I ask the reader to mark it now. I return to it in § 61.

§ 48. I sat down in the chair that they had put for me by the door. And I found that I wished to speak.

I had not expected it. I have never been a man who wished to speak. But the hour was in the house; I could feel it standing in the hall, among us, like a guest who has come a long way and is waiting to be told why he was sent for. It was my wife’s hour. She had made it for the purpose of saying what was true. I had wasted twenty-three of them in her lifetime and twenty since.

So I spoke. I am told that I was lucid. Fenn has said that it was the clearest that he has heard me in three years. I do not find that remarkable. I have explained that the hour which I had lived had been taken off me, upon the floor of the hall, and I was the lighter for it.

I said that I had asked a question at dinner and no longer wished to have it answered.

That was so. I had sat at that table and looked at my son’s hand, and I had known. But I found, with the hour standing at my elbow, that I did not care to be told. I had said that I wanted the reason. I saw now that I knew the reason, and had known it for forty years, and that it was I.

I said what a clock is for. I said that it is for telling a man how much time he has got, and that I had a hundred and eleven and they had only ever told me how much I had had. It is the truest thing that I know about my trade. I had not known it until I said it.

I said that if anything had been taken from me it had no doubt been wanted more than I wanted it. I said that I had not been a father to whom a person could come and ask. I said that their mother had told me so.

And I said that the matter of the clocks was closed, and to go upon the Hour’s account. I told Fenn to note it.

I looked for Edmund as I said it. I wished him to hear. I had said it for him.

He was not in the hall. I thought, he has gone out; he will have it from the others. I was not uneasy. I record that also.

§ 49. There was one thing more that I had to do in that hour, and I had been putting it off for thirty years.

I sent Fenn for his pen.

I must here speak of Amos Garrow, who held the farm of Saltcote from me, and from my father before me, and who died a fortnight before the night of which I write.

I knew him all my life. He was four years my junior. We were boys upon the same marsh and never, I suppose, exchanged a thousand words. He came to the estate office upon the quarter days and paid his rent. I would see him across the Wade, with his sheep. He was a silent man, and so am I, and we nodded.

He farmed that ground better than it has ever been farmed. I am not a countryman, but I can see when a thing is kept in order. His gates hung true. He had a way with a horse that I have never had with any living creature.

My wife rode over to Saltcote. She had done so from about the year 1964. She said that it was for the exercise, and to see the mares.

I did not ask. I have said that already and I am tired of saying it. I regulated the gallery clock.

I have told my son, in the ice house, that I knew of it from about 1980. That is when I allowed myself to say it. But I think that I knew before she died. There was a look that she had, coming in from the Wade of a morning, with the salt on her boots. I had seen it upon her face in 1948. I had not seen it since about 1950.

After she was drowned, Garrow did not come to the office. He sent his rent by post, in notes, for a year. Then he came again. He stood in front of Fenn’s desk with his cap in his hand. I was there once. He looked at me. I looked at him. We had each of us lost the same thing, and I was his landlord.

I might have spoken. I had only to say, ‘Garrow, I know where she was going. I do not hold it against you. I am sorry for your loss.’ It would have taken ten seconds. I have had the words ready for him as I had them for her.

I never said them. He died in his chair, a fortnight since, with the lamp in his window. Mrs Pask told me. She said that it had burned there every night for twenty years.

And upon the morning of his funeral my son’s solicitor, who is also mine, sent a notice to quit to that farm. I did not know of it until dinner. I heard Edmund say it across the table. That farm’s out at Lady Day.

I thought of that lamp. I thought: I let that man pay me rent for twenty years, for the ground from which he watched my wife drown. I took his notes. And now my family is turning his son off, upon the day that he was put into the earth beside her.

So I told Fenn to write. I said that there was something that I owed across the water, that had been owing a long time. I said, ‘I can’t pay it to the man. I let him die without. I’ll pay it to his name.’ I gave Saltcote, the house and buildings and the hundred and forty acres, freehold, to Amos Garrow or his heirs, for ever.

Fenn asked for what consideration. I said, ‘For the hour I owe.’

He wrote it. Octavia Prowse witnessed it, and the vicar, when he had been woken.

I do not put that forward as part of the experiment. It was a debt of the ordinary kind. But I should like it understood that it was paid in that hour because I do not think that I could have paid it in any other. I had not the means, in the other eight thousand seven hundred and fifty-nine, of saying such a thing aloud.

§ 50. I closed my eyes. I had done what I could with the hour, as a man. It remained to see what the engine would do with it.

I was listening. I thought that I should hear her upon the stairs. I had the nineteen words ready. Margot, the clock is wrong. I put it back before dinner.

I waited. I heard nothing but the clocks, and my family breathing.

Then I thought, she does not come down until there is music. She never did. She waited for the waltz.

I asked my grandson to wind the gramophone.

It is a Lehár. ‘Gold and Silver.’ I first danced it with my wife at the Hunt Ball of 1947, having been taught the steps the week before by a professional in Colchester, to whom I paid three guineas. She said that I waltzed like a man pacing out a boundary. But she had it played at every Hour afterward, and I learned to do it with my eyes shut. I found that if I did not look, I could feel the beat through her hand.

The record began. I sat with my eyes closed and counted.

At the ninth bar I heard the girl upon the stairs say something, sharply. I heard Octavia get up out of her chair. She said a name. It was the name that only she and one other person ever used.

I opened my eyes.

§ 51. I shall be exact. It is the result of the experiment and I shall not have it said that I recorded it loosely.

She was upon the fourth stair from the bottom. It is where she always paused. She had one hand upon the rail.

She was in the grey silk. I chose that silk. I went with her to the shop in 1955; it was in Bond Street; and I picked it from forty bolts, since it was the colour of Jenny’s gown upon the tower, and she laughed at me. I know the fall of it. I know how it takes a light. I could not be deceived in that stuff any more than in the silvering of a dial.

Her hair was up. Her shoulders were bare. She was looking at me.

I noted her face. I do not read faces, as I have said. But I know my wife’s. It was pale, and it was wet, and she was smiling a little, as she smiled when she had made up her mind to something difficult and meant to go through with it.

I rose. I said, ‘You came back. Margot. You came back.’

She crossed the hall. She held out her hand. She said, ‘Yes, Papa.’

I did not understand that. Then she said, ‘Yes, Leo. I came back.’

It was her voice. It was lower than I recollected, and there was something in it of the north; but twenty years is a long time, and I do not know where she had been.

I took her hand. It was cold. I felt her fingers, and the bones of them, and I knew them. I put my other hand at her back, where the silk is cut low. And I danced with her.

§ 52. I must now deal with an objection, and I shall do so before I go further, since I am aware that it has been in the reader’s mind for some pages.

I have a daughter. Her name is Imogen. She is forty-four years of age. She has her mother’s height and build and colouring, and in particular her mother’s eyes; I have often remarked upon it. She was in the house upon that night. She has a key to her mother’s room.

I am told that it was Imogen who came down the stairs. I am told so by Miss Quaile, by Mrs Pask, by my grandson, and by Imogen herself, who came to me upon the following evening and said that she hoped that she had not done wrong.

I have listened to them. I am a man of science, or have tried to be, and I do not dismiss testimony because it is unwelcome. I set down their account, here, in full: that my daughter, for reasons of her own, put on her mother’s gown upon the twentieth anniversary of her death and came down to me in it; and that I, being old, and expecting my wife, took her for her.

Now I shall set down mine.

I had my hand upon her back. I had her hand in mine. I led her through forty-eight bars of a waltz that I learned in 1947 for one woman and have danced with no one else. I am not a man of feeling. I do not go by impressions. I go by measurement; and there is a kind of measurement that the hands make, which is finer than any gauge. I have told the reader that my son could feel a thousandth of an inch. I taught him.

I know the weight of my wife upon my arm in the turn. I know by how much she anticipated the beat; she was always a shade before it, and I a shade behind, and that was how we went. I know the place at the end of the second strain where she would press my hand, very slightly, to remind me that the reverse was coming, since I never could remember it.

She pressed my hand at the end of the second strain.

My daughter has never danced that waltz with me. She was a child in her nightgown upon the stairs.

I do not say that the two accounts cannot both stand. I have told the reader that a regulator and a sundial may disagree by a quarter of an hour and both be right. It may be that Imogen put on the gown. I think it very likely. She is a good girl, and braver than I knew. But I say that a gown must be put on by somebody before it can be worn, and that an hour must come in at a door before it can be spent; and that when the hour that I had sent for was let out into my hall, along the line that I had laid for it, it found there a woman of the right build, in the right silk, at the foot of the right stair.

I do not think that the engine made my wife. I think that it had only to bring her as far as the nearest thing that would hold her. And I think that my daughter knew, when she said ‘Leo,’ that she was not speaking altogether for herself.

That is my observation. I leave it beside the other.

§ 53. I had the nineteen words. I began upon them. And I found that they were wrong.

I had prepared them for the hall in 1974. It is three, not two. You have a quarter of an hour. But I was not in 1974. I had her in my arms, in the Odd Hour, and the regulator was stopped, and it was this night’s tide that was running outside. If I told her the tide of twenty years ago she would walk out upon the wrong water.

It was fortunate that I had been to the library. I had gone in at three that afternoon, from habit, to read the Thorne. I had forgotten that it was the Copy that stood there; but the Copy is exact, and keeps the same tide. I had the figures.

So I gave them to her. I said that I had had it wrong for her, the last time. I told her what I had done with the hall clocks and that I had never told her. I said it all. It took a good deal more than nineteen words.

And then I gave her the hour. High water at eight minutes to one. No crossing on foot before half past four. A horse at twenty minutes to three, and he must swim at the Rill, with three feet upon it and a set to the north.

I do not know why I said a horse. I had not thought of one. It came with the figures. The Garrows’ horses always could.

She said that she heard me. She said that she would wait for the horse.

I said, ‘Then you will get across. That is all I wanted. I don’t ask you to stay.’

I had not known that I should say that. But it was the thing. I see now that it was what I ought to have said to her in July of 1974, when she stood behind me at the gallery clock for five minutes and I did not turn round. She was waiting to be asked whether she was happy. I did not ask. I should not have known what to do with the answer.

I could not ask it now. It was twenty years too late for a question. But I could tell her that I knew the answer, and that she might go.

She wept. I felt it. She said something to me, low, as we turned beneath the Tompion.

She said, ‘It wasn’t the clock, Leo. It wasn’t your doing. I knew the time. I swear to you, it was never the clock.’

I did not understand her. I thought that she was being kind. She was always kind to me at the last; it was how I knew that she had gone. I told her so.

But I wish the reader to mark those words. It was never the clock. I had heard them once already that night, an hour and a half before, in another voice, upon the landing of the ice house, and had answered them with a piece of lead. I did not then recollect that I had. It had been taken from me. I heard them from her as if for the first time.

I have since had them a third time. I shall say where.

§ 54. The record ended. I said to her that it was quite all right, and that we had had the time after all.

She kissed me. She held my face. I said to her, very low, that she was not to keep him waiting. I knew that there was a man with a lantern. There always had been.

She went from me toward the garden passage. I watched the grey silk go round the edge of the curtain, as I had watched it go round a door some hours before, in another year.

I found my chair.

My wife came back across the hall in her grey silk and I gave her the tide correctly. She did not drown.

I state that as the first result. I have verified it since by enquiry. There was a woman in grey silk upon the Wade that night, upon a horse, at twenty minutes to three. She reached the further shore. My daughter tells me that it was she. I have given my view of that.

No one was drowned upon the Wade in that hour who had been given the tide by me. I had waited twenty years to be able to write that sentence.

§ 55. I sat for some time. I was very tired and entirely content. Dorothea’s grandson came and asked me for five thousand pounds, for wine, and I gave it to him, since he told me the truth about the wine. I dated the cheque with the hour. It seemed to me that it was the only date that signified.

And then, as I sat there, it came back.

I had been told that I had gone to the ice house. I had asked what for. Now I knew.

It returned to me whole, as a dial comes up under the cleaning rag. The lamp upon the landing. The box. His face. It will serve. The weight going out upon its line. The twelve steps.

I looked at my hands. They were quite steady. I looked at my right cuff. There was a stain upon it, brown, that I had taken for port.

I have asked myself why it was given back to me at that moment and not before. I believe that the reason is mechanical. So long as I was in the hour for the second time, and it was still running along the same line as the first, I could not be let to remember the first; I have explained that. But my wife had come down the stairs. She had not gone out by the garden door; she had come to me, and been told the tide. The second passage had parted from the first. It was upon a different line now. And there was no longer any harm in my knowing what had happened upon the other.

I sat with it. I was not afraid. I ask the reader to understand that. I had killed my son, at ten minutes to twelve, and I recollected every particular. But I had also just held my wife, who had been dead twenty years, and sent her safely over the water.

I thought: if she is not drowned, he is not struck.

At one o’clock the hour was returned to me, as I had calculated, and I went through it a second time.

I got up out of my chair. I went across the hall to the regulator and opened the case. The weight hung at the bottom of its line where the girl had put it. I touched it with my fingers.

There was a man standing behind me. He was wet to the thighs, and had been bleeding from the head. He had the hands of a policeman. He asked me a question, and I answered him. I told him that I had killed my son, and that now I had not. I told him that he should write it down. He seemed a capable person and I am sorry that I cannot recall his name.

I told him that the Jack had stopped. I had been listening for the quarter and it had not come.

Then I went out of my front door, alone, to see about Edmund.

VI. The Second Passage

§ 56. I had a candle in a glass, from the hall table. The wind had dropped and the moon was out; I could have done without.

I did not go to the tower. I should have liked to; it was there that the engine was, and I had felt it take the load. But I had resolved, sitting in my chair, upon a method. If I was to claim that an hour had been passed through twice, I must go the second time where I had gone the first, and observe what was different. Otherwise I should have no comparison.

I therefore went as I had gone before. I crossed the yard. I went round the end of the stables and down the track to the home copse.

I shall record the two passages side by side, as a table, since that is how the thing presented itself to me.

Upon the first passage the gate of the ice house stood ajar, and there was a lamp within. Upon the second it stood wide open, pushed back to the wall, and there was no light. There was a ring of keys hanging in the lock. I knew them for Mrs Pask’s.

Upon the first passage there was a man upon the landing with a box in his arms. Upon the second there was no one.

I held my candle over the well.

Upon the first passage I had looked down those steps and seen my son upon his back at the bottom, with his feet higher than his head and his eyes open. I had counted sixty and seen no breath. I had heard the box go down before him.

Upon the second there was straw at the foot of the steps. There was sacking, and the ice. There was no man. There was no box.

I went down. I had not been able to, the first time. I found that now I could. I went down sideways, with my hand upon the wall, twelve steps. I stood where he had lain.

The straw was pressed flat there, in a long shape, and in one place it was dark. I put my candle to it. I shall come to that under the next head. But there was no man in it.

I record one anomaly, for completeness. Upon the third step from the bottom somebody had set down a kitchen saucer with the end of a candle in it. And there was a silver spoon in the straw. I could not account for either. I had put them there in neither passage.

I stood in that place. I am not a man who prays. I said aloud, ‘He is not here.’

For he was not. I had come to the same landing, in the same hour, by the same road; and what I had left there was gone. In the first passage I had struck. In the second I had come out into the hall and been told the tide, and danced, and had not gone to the ice house at all until now; and there was nobody at the bottom of the steps.

I climbed out. It took me a good while.

§ 57. I have said that I do not believe that a thing can be had for nothing, and I should note here an inconvenience in the result, since I do not wish to be thought to have hidden it.

The lamp was still upon the landing. It was the one that had gone out in my hand, upon the first passage, and that I had set down. It was where I had left it, cold.

There was the straw, which kept the print of a body, and was stained.

And there was my cuff. I looked at it by the candle. The stain was there.

Now if the first passage had been wholly undone, there should have been no lamp upon that landing and no blood upon my shirt. I considered this as I went back up the track. I do not find that it is fatal to the hypothesis. It appears that what is returned is the hour, and the acts done in it, and not every particle of matter that was moved. The engine is a timekeeper and not a broom. A man who is given a day over again does not find that the mud has been taken off his boots.

There was the weight itself. I examined it the following week, and it was clean. I must have wiped it, afterward. I have no memory of wiping it. One does these things.

But I record it. An experimenter ought to state what tells against him. There was a residue.

§ 58. I went to the tower.

The door of the harness room was open. There had been a lamp broken there, and spirits spilt. I climbed the ladder. I am told that I ought not to have been able. I went up as I have gone up every night for sixty years, by the count: fourteen rungs, and the trap.

The clock chamber was dark. The moon came in at the louvres, in bars. I could hear the great pendulum, and the train. And I could hear that it was labouring. The beat was uneven; there was a drag upon it.

I held up my candle. The first thing that I saw was the Reconciler.

One of the rods was gone. It had been sheared through, a foot from the cupboard, and hung down. The door of the cupboard was starred all over with small holes, as if someone had thrown a handful of gravel at it with great force. The take-up had been knocked from its clamp and was lying upon the floor in two pieces.

I understood then what the reports had been. The engine had taken the load at the stroke, and it had been more than the work would bear. It had burst.

I did not grieve. A fuse is meant to go. It had done what it was made for; I had the proof of that at the bottom of an empty flight of steps. I thought only that I had made the pinion too fine.

Then something moved against the frame of the clock, low down, and a voice said:

‘Who’s that?’

§ 59. He was sitting upon the floor with his back against the iron frame and his legs out. He had his left hand up at the side of his neck, pressing something to it. He turned his face to the candle.

It was my son.

I shall describe him as I should describe a movement that had been brought to me for repair. There was a swelling upon the left side of his brow, above the eye, the size of a hen’s egg and dark. The eye beneath was half shut. There was dried blood from it down his cheek. His hair was wet. There was more blood, fresh, upon the left of his neck and upon his collar, in a number of small places, and the thing that he held there was a child’s handkerchief with a pattern of red leaves.

He was breathing. His eyes followed the light.

I set the candle upon the floor. I went down upon my knees in front of him. I have not knelt since 1974.

I put my hand upon his face.

It was warm. I felt the bone of the jaw, and the bristle, and under my thumb, at the angle, the beat of the artery. I counted it. It was eighty to the minute, and strong, and perfectly even.

I had stood upon a landing two hours before and counted sixty and seen no breath.

At ten minutes to two I found him in the clock room, alive, and I did not strike him. I submit this as the experimental result.

I have Miss Quaile’s leave to underline that, and she has done so.

§ 60. He said, ‘Father?’

‘Yes.’

‘How in God’s name did you get up that ladder?’

‘I have come up it every night since before you were born.’ I had not taken my hand away. ‘You are alive.’

‘I think so. I’m not altogether sure. I’ve had a peculiar evening.’ He was looking at me strangely. His speech was clear; the thickness had gone out of it. ‘You keep touching my face.’

‘I must be certain. It is the result.’

‘The result of what?’

So I told him. I told him of the hour, and where it is kept, and of the engine. I showed him the cupboard and the rods. I told him that I had built it to give his mother the tide, and that it had done that; she had come down, and I had sent her over upon a horse. And I told him the rest. I said that upon the first passage I had followed him to the ice house and had struck him with the weight of the regulator, and that he had fallen down the steps and was dead; and that at one o’clock the hour had been given back, and I had gone through it again, and had not struck him.

He heard me to the end. He did not laugh. I had been afraid that he would laugh.

He put up his right hand and felt of the swelling upon his brow.

‘You did hit me, Father,’ he said.

‘Upon the first passage.’

‘It still hurts on the second.’

‘There is a residue. I have noted it. There is a stain upon my cuff also.’

He looked at me for a long moment. I saw his face work. I thought that he was going to tell me that I was mad. I had prepared an answer to that.

He did not say it. He let his head go back against the iron. I saw that there was water running from his good eye.

‘All right,’ he said. ‘All right, Father. I was dead, and now I’m not. I’ll not argue. God knows it’s how it feels.’ He took a breath. ‘I woke up in the straw with a horse blanket over me and the cook’s voice going away. I didn’t know where I was. I thought I was eleven. There was a child there. I thought she was Imogen.’

‘A child? With dark hair?’

‘In a coat too big for her. She said she wasn’t a ghost; I’d asked. She gave me this.’ He moved the handkerchief. ‘I don’t know who she is. She’s not one of ours.’

I told him that I had seen her also, in the yard. We looked at one another. Neither of us could account for it.

I record her again as an anomaly. She was observed by two persons, at different times, upon both passages. I have no hypothesis.

§ 61. I return here to the box, as I undertook.

He told me how he had come by it. He said that he had gone into the library when the lights failed, and lifted the clock from under its glass, and crated it, and carried it to the ice house, to wait for a boat. He said that it was to clear what he owed. He said that he had not looked at it. He had thrown the baize over it for three years so as not to have to.

I said, ‘It was the Copy.’

‘What?’

‘It was the Copy that you took. I changed them in September. The Thorne is there.’ I showed him. He could see it from where he sat, through the broken door of the cupboard, upon its shelf, with the moon upon the dial. ‘I wished to learn whether you would know the one from the other. You cut the lunar train of that Copy. You had only to turn it over.’

He stared at the cupboard. Then he began to laugh. He had to hold his neck.

‘I stole your copy,’ he said. ‘Oh, Lord. I’ve been four years robbing you blind, and sick with it, and at the last, for the big one, I walked off with your own work under my arm and never knew. And was going to sell it to a moneylender for a million pounds.’ He wiped his eye with the back of his wrist. ‘You said the best hands you ever trained had forgotten what they were for. Didn’t you? You’ll have said that to somebody.’

I said that I had thought it.

‘You were right. I’ve not looked at a clock in twenty years. Not looked. I couldn’t.’

I then told him what had become of it. I said that the box had been brought into the hall at one o’clock by Dorothea’s grandson, who had taken it for a pudding.

I ask the reader to consider that.

Upon the first passage, at ten minutes to twelve, that box went down the ice-house steps before my son, and lay at the bottom. I heard it. Upon the second passage, at one o’clock, it was carried into my hall, whole, by a young man who had no notion what it was, and set down before me upon the table.

I did not send him for it. No one did. He believed himself to be fetching an ice.

I submit that this is what the hour running back would look like, to those inside it. A thing that had fallen is found standing. A thing that was taken is brought home, and by somebody who cannot say why he does it. He will have a reason. He will say that he was sent for a pudding. Persons inside an hour always have their reasons. But I was at the door and I saw it come in.

My son said, ‘Toby brought it in? In front of everybody?’

‘He said that the ice was coming.’

He laughed again until he was obliged to stop.

§ 62. I come now to what he told me.

I am in a difficulty. Miss Quaile has laid down her pen and asked whether I mean to dictate it. I have considered for some minutes.

I shall not. I give my reasons.

It was said in the Hour. It was the first thing that my son has ever told me in one. My wife made that hour so that her family might say to one another what they could not say at any other time, and she laid it down that it should not be held against them afterward. I never used it while she lived. I shall not break her rule upon the one occasion that I have been the gainer by it.

And it is his. It is not a thing that happened to me. It happened to him, upon the Wade, when he was thirty-two, and he has carried it by himself ever since, in a manner that I should not have thought him capable of. He told me that he had meant to tell his sister, and a man across the water. He said that he would tell them himself, in the morning. I do not think that it would be right for me to put it into a paper before he has done so.

I shall therefore record only so much as bears upon the experiment.

He told me where he was that night, and where his mother was. He told me what lay between them. I knew the place; it is the deepest water upon the road. He told me which of them was upon the wrong side of it, and that it was not she.

And he told me what she did.

I asked him to say it twice. I am not quick at such things. He said it a second time, in the same words, and then he could not speak.

I have it. I shall keep it. I shall say here only what I said to him.

I said, ‘Then she didn’t leave me.’

He said, ‘She’d left you, Father. She was past the Perch. She was nearly at his door.’

‘But she turned back.’

‘Yes.’

‘She was coming back to this house.’

‘She was coming back for—’ He stopped. ‘Yes. Toward the house. She turned round and came back.’

‘Then she did not leave me. She had gone, and she turned.’

I said it several times. I could not seem to get to the end of it. I am told that Miss Quaile heard me from the foot of the ladder.

The reader will think it a small distinction. A woman who sets out to leave her husband, and is drowned upon the road, has left him, whichever way her feet were pointing. I know that. I am not a child.

But I have lived twenty years inside a picture of that night, and in the picture she had her back to me. She was walking away, quickly, as she always walked, toward a light. She did not look round. I have seen it every night; it is the last thing that I see. And my son was telling me that the picture was wrong. At the end, in the last quarter of an hour, she was facing this way. If I had been standing at my front door, as I ought to have been, and had looked out across the Wade, I should have seen her lantern coming toward me.

It was not for my sake. He was clear about that; he would not let me think it. I do not care. I do not ask for what reason a clock is right.

§ 63. He said, ‘It was never the clock, Father. That’s what I was trying to say, down there, before you—before the first time. She knew you’d put them back. She told me so; she laughed about it. She had her watch on. She went an hour and a quarter before the water. She’d have been across with an hour in hand.’

It was the third time that I had been told it that night. I had it from him upon the landing, and struck him. I had it from her in the hall, and thought her kind. Now I had it again.

I said, ‘Then what was it?’

‘It was me.’

He said it without any flourish. I looked at him. He was fifty-two. He had been a beautiful child, and he was a ruin. The best hands that I ever saw upon a boy were lying open upon his knees.

‘It was me,’ he said. ‘I couldn’t let her go. I went out after her. I was drunk. I’d had a bottle of your port in the gunroom. And everything that happened afterward was because of that. She’d be living at Saltcote now, an old woman, with hens. I’ve known it every morning for twenty years. And every morning I’ve come down and heard you winding those damned clocks and telling them it was your fault, and I’ve let you.’

‘Why did you not tell me?’

‘How was I to tell you? You’d have forgiven me. You’d have looked at me through that glass and said that you expected I couldn’t help it.’ His voice broke. ‘I didn’t want to be forgiven. I wanted somebody to hit me. I’ve been waiting twenty years for somebody to hit me, Father. I never thought it’d be you.’

I did not know what to say. I have never known what to say to him.

I put my hand upon his head. It was what his mother did. I had seen her do it that evening, in another year, when he had played the Schubert.

I said, ‘You were only a boy.’

‘I was thirty-two.’

‘You were a boy. You were never let to be anything else. Your mother made too much of you and I made nothing of you at all. Between the two of us, we left you nowhere to stand.’ I found that I could go on. The hour was nearly out, but it had not gone. ‘Edmund. That train that you cut for the Copy. The lunar. In ’seventy-four.’

‘What about it?’

‘It is better than Thorne’s. I have had them both under the glass. His is good. Yours is better. The depthing is finer and the finish of the leaves is as good as anything that I have ever seen out of Switzerland. I ought to have told you so on the day that you brought it down. I knew it then. I said that it would serve.’

He did not answer.

‘It was not that I did not see it. I saw it. I had not the habit of saying such things. I thought that you would know.’ I took my hand from his head. ‘I should like it to go upon the record that I said so. I have said it now. It is twenty years late and you have been dead in between. But I have said it.’

He had put his arm across his eyes. His shoulders were shaking. I sat back upon my heels and waited. One does not hurry a thing that has been wound so long.

§ 64. There was a third person in the chamber.

I set it down, since I have undertaken to record what I observed. I heard it while my son was weeping. There is a closet in that chamber, to the right of the frame, where the weights of the striking train go down; it has a door of slats. From behind those slats there came a small sound. It was like a child sneezing, and trying not to.

I said, ‘What is that?’

My son lifted his head. He looked at the closet. Then he looked at me, and his face was the face of a boy who is hiding a puppy.

‘Rats,’ he said. ‘There’ve always been rats up here.’

I have kept the tower clock for sixty years and there has never been a rat in that chamber; there is nothing for one to eat. But I did not press him. He had told me the truth about a great thing and I thought that he might be let to lie about a small one.

I note it. A sound, as of a child, in the weight closet, at about five minutes to two.

§ 65. I had one thing to give him.

I had carried it in my waistcoat pocket since September, upon a ribbon. It was the key of the Thorne. It is the original; Thorne made it; it is of steel, about three inches long, with a pierced bow in the form of a sprig, and it fits nothing else. The clock is wound with it every eighth day. I have done it myself, upon a Tuesday, since 1960.

I took it out. I put it into his hand.

‘She wants winding upon Tuesday,’ I said. ‘You will do it. You cut her moon. I’ve left her to the Museum in my will, and that must stand. But the winding of her is yours, for as long as you are in this house. You’ll bring her down from here tomorrow and set her back in the library, and look to that cock; I have always meant to. I should like you to put your glass upon her.’

He looked at the key upon his palm.

‘I was going to sell her,’ he said.

‘You were going to sell the Copy. It is a different thing.’

‘Not in my head, it wasn’t.’

‘No. But a man is not hanged for what he does in a passage that has been gone through again.’ I closed his fingers upon it. ‘Put it in your pocket. Not the waistcoat; you will lose it. The coat.’

He put it in the pocket of his dinner jacket. I watched him do it.

He said, ‘I’ll come to you in the morning. In the Shop. After breakfast. There’s more; there’s a thing I’ve not given you. And that little nurse has a book of Mother’s that you ought to see. I’ll have her by, to keep me to it. I don’t trust myself by daylight.’

I said that I should be at the bench at nine.

§ 66. There was a voice from below. It came up the ladder. It was Miss Quaile, calling my name, and telling me that I should take my death.

My son put his finger to his lips.

I did not understand it. I said, quite low, ‘It is only the girl. She would be glad to see you. She thinks a great deal of you.’

‘I know she does.’ He was whispering. ‘That’s why. Look at me, Father. If she comes up that ladder and sees this, she’ll have me in bed with a thermometer in my mouth, and I’ve things to do before morning. I’ve to see Imogen. I’ve to stand on the wall and watch a boat not come.’ He nearly smiled. ‘Go down. Tell her I’m alive, if you like. She’ll not believe you; nobody does believe you, do they? It’s very useful.’

‘I shall not lie to her.’

‘I’m not asking you to. Tell her the truth. It’s the best cover there is, in this house.’

I got to my feet. He helped me, with his good arm. For a moment we stood, the two of us, in that chamber, with the pendulum going between us and the moon upon the wreck of my engine.

I had not stood so near him since he was fourteen.

‘Good night, Father,’ my son said.

‘Good night, Edmund. Mind the fourth rung; it is worn.’

I went down. Miss Quaile was at the foot with a lamp. I told her that he was alive. I told her that I had been through it twice. She looked up at the trap. She called to him.

He did not answer. I thought it a pity. But I had given my word that I should not lie, and I had not; I had only been disbelieved, which is a thing that I am used to.

We crossed the yard. Over our heads the great bell struck two. There were no quarters before it. I looked up. Jenny stood by herself.

The Jack was gone from his pin. So that was correct. I had seen a man fall at one o’clock, upon the left of the bell, and taken it for the price.

I said, ‘The Hour is over. I should have liked it longer. But it was enough.’

§ 67. I now state the results, as they stood at two o’clock in the morning of the twenty-third of October.

First. An hour was received at this house at one o’clock, at the front door, in the presence of witnesses. I felt it enter.

Second. My wife, deceased twenty years, descended the stairs in the hall at about twenty minutes past one and was given by me the correct state of the tide. A woman in her gown subsequently crossed the Wade upon a horse at the time that I had named, and was not drowned.

Third. My son, whom I had struck upon the head at ten minutes to twelve, and observed for sixty seconds without sign of life, was found by me at ten minutes to two, in another place, living. He conversed with me for a quarter of an hour.

Fourth. An object which had fallen upon the first passage was returned to me whole upon the second, by a person who did not know what he carried.

Fifth. I was told three times in one night, by three voices, that it was never the clock.

Sixth. There was a price. A figure was thrown from the tower at the instant of reversal, and the engine was destroyed.

I add the following, which I did not design and cannot classify.

Seventh. In the course of that hour I said four things which I had not been able to say in the preceding eighty-one years. I told my family that I had not been a father to whom a person could come. I paid a debt to a dead man. I gave my wife leave to go. And I told my son that his work was better than mine.

I do not know that the engine was needed for those. It may be that any man could do as much, upon any night, who was willing to open his mouth. I can only report that I was not able to until the hour had been let into the house, and that when it had, I was.

I went to my bed. I am told that I slept without the draught, and smiling.

VII. Results, and the Decay of the Record

§ 68. I have set down the experiment and its result. An honest paper does not end there. It must give what was observed afterward, and in particular whatever tells against the conclusion. I shall do so in the order in which the facts came to me.

Upon the morning of the twenty-third I went down to the Shop at nine. I had an appointment there with my son.

He did not keep it.

I waited until a quarter to eleven. I worked at a small plate. Miss Quaile stood by the steps. At a quarter to eleven I said that he was not coming, and she gave me his message, which she had from him the day before: that he was sorry, and that it was not the clock. She had the book of which he had spoken. It was a diary of my wife’s for the year of her death, which she had hidden in the French clock upon her desk, the one that she would never let me mend.

I did not read it. I should like that noted. I held it in my hand. I knew the hand upon the cover. I had been told three times that it was not the clock, and I had been told that she turned back. I found that I did not require to know anything more. If she had wished me to read what she thought of me in her last year she would have left it upon my bench, and not inside the one case in the house that I was upon my honour not to open.

I told the girl to put it back.

I was not then uneasy as to Edmund. He had said that he had things to do before morning. He has never been punctual.

§ 69. At noon they brought the Jack into the hall upon a hurdle.

He had been found in the outfall of the stable fleet. He had upon him my old dinner jacket, which the children had put on him for the night. He had been shot. I examined the wound. It was a charge of number five, both barrels or near it, at about thirty yards, from below. It had carried away the front of his chest to the heart-oak and sheared him from his pin.

I must here revise an entry.

I recorded, at § 46, that at the instant of reversal there were two reports from the foot of the tower, which I took for the take-up bursting under load; and that a figure was thrown from the leads, which I took for the price of the hour.

It now appeared that the reports were those of a shotgun, and that the figure was the Jack. Some person had been in my stable yard at one o’clock in the morning and had fired at my tower.

I do not know who. I have asked. I am told that it was a man after duck. There are no duck upon my stable roof.

I ask the reader to observe that this does not affect the result. It affects only my account of the mechanism. I had supposed that the engine burst of itself. It seems that it was broken from without; some of the shot had entered the cupboard, and cut the rod, and I have since taken eleven pellets out of the door. But it was broken at the stroke. I have Jenny’s arm for that; she had not finished her blow. Whatever hand fired that gun, it fired it at the single instant in twenty years at which there was something in that chamber to be let go.

I have turned this over. I am inclined to think that an hour, like a tide, will find its own way out. If I had not provided a means of release it would have made one.

I have the Jack upon trestles in the Shop. He can be mended. I had a baulk of the same oak, that was his brother’s.

§ 70. Upon the Sunday evening my daughter Imogen came across from the farm.

She told me that she was to marry young Garrow. I was glad of it. I had given them the ground the night before, and it is as well that someone should have it who knows what to do with sheep.

She brought me a ring.

It was my wife’s wedding ring. I had it made in Hatton Garden in the spring of 1948, by a man called Abrahams, of twenty-two carat gold, which is too soft, and wears. It had worn to a wire. I knew it by the mark inside.

I had believed that she was buried in it. I did not look, at the time. I could not.

Imogen said that Edmund had given it to her, in the scullery passage, after two o’clock that morning. He had told her that their mother took it from her finger, upon the Wade, on the night of her death, and put it into his hand, and said, ‘Give that to your father.’ He had carried it, Imogen said, for twenty years.

That was the thing that he had not given me. He had said so in the tower. There’s a thing I’ve not given you.

I put it on. It goes upon the smallest finger of my left hand. I have it there as I dictate.

I enter it under the results, and I shall say why.

My wife took off that ring upon the Wade, in the Odd Hour of 1974, and sent it to me. It did not arrive. It was kept back, by the messenger, for reasons that I understand, in a waistcoat pocket, for twenty years. And upon the night of the experiment, within one hour of the reversal, it was let go. It came to me by way of a woman who had crossed the same water, in the same gown, at an hour that I had given her.
